qz.why: The dual of the spectral norm is the nuclear norm \({\lVert A\rVert}_*=\sum_i\sigma_i=9.5\), attained at \(B=UV^\top\). \(5\) is the spectral norm itself and \(\sqrt{35.25}\) is the (self-dual) Frobenius norm.

qz.q: Let \(A=\begin{pmatrix}0&2\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\). What are \({\lVert A\rVert}_2=\sigma_{\max}(A)\) and the spectral radius \(\rho(A)\)?
qz.why: Both eigenvalues are \(0\) (\(A\) is nilpotent), but \(A^\top A={\operatorname{diag}}(0,4)\) so \(\sigma_{\max}=2\). For non-symmetric matrices singular values, not eigenvalues, measure size; \(\rho(A)\le{\lVert A\rVert}_2\) can be strict.

cards.name: Sherman–Morrison & Woodbury identities
cards.lay: How the inverse of a matrix changes after a rank-one (or low-rank) update. It gives cheap recursive least squares and is central to analysing how confidence ellipsoids shrink as data arrives.
cards.st: For invertible \(A\) and vectors \(u,v\) with \(1+v^\top A^{-1}u\ne0\): \[ (A+uv^\top)^{-1} = A^{-1} - \frac{A^{-1}uv^\top A^{-1}}{1+v^\top A^{-1}u}. \] Woodbury: \((A+UCV)^{-1} = A^{-1} - A^{-1}U(C^{-1}+VA^{-1}U)^{-1}VA^{-1}\).
ver: Symmetric rank-one update: \((V+xx^\top)^{-1} = V^{-1} - \tfrac{V^{-1}xx^\top V^{-1}}{1+{\lVert x\rVert}_{V^{-1}}^2}\).
Consequence: \({\lVert x\rVert}^2_{(V+xx^\top)^{-1}} = \tfrac{{\lVert x\rVert}^2_{V^{-1}}}{1+{\lVert x\rVert}^2_{V^{-1}}} < 1\).
Push-through identity: \((I+AB)^{-1}A = A(I+BA)^{-1}\).
cards.det: Proof: multiply the right-hand side by \(A+uv^\top\) and simplify. Woodbury is the same computation in block form. Recursive least squares (used inside LinUCB, LSTD with online updates, Kalman filtering) is nothing but Sherman–Morrison applied each round, costing \(O(d^2)\) instead of \(O(d^3)\).
cards.ex: In OFUL/LinUCB, after playing \(x_t\) the design matrix becomes \(V_t = V_{t-1}+x_tx_t^\top\); Sherman–Morrison gives the new inverse in \(O(d^2)\) and shows the uncertainty in direction \(x_t\) shrinks by factor \(1/(1+{\lVert x_t\rVert}^2_{V_{t-1}^{-1}})\).
cards.use: Recursive least squares in linear bandits/LSTD, Gaussian-process posterior updates, Kalman filters for non-stationary tracking, proving the matrix determinant lemma.

qz.q: Let \(V\succ0\) and \({\lVert x\rVert}^2_{V^{-1}}=3\). What is \({\lVert x\rVert}^2_{(V+xx^\top)^{-1}}\)?
qz.why: Sherman–Morrison gives \({\lVert x\rVert}^2_{(V+xx^\top)^{-1}}=\tfrac{{\lVert x\rVert}^2_{V^{-1}}}{1+{\lVert x\rVert}^2_{V^{-1}}}=\tfrac34\): always below 1. \(1/4\) is the shrink factor \(1/(1+3)\) itself, not the new squared width.

qz.q: To remove a data point you need \((V-xx^\top)^{-1}\) with \(V\succ0\). When is the Sherman–Morrison formula (with \(u=-x\), \(v=x\)) valid?
qz.why: The condition is \(1+v^\top V^{-1}u=1-x^\top V^{-1}x\ne0\). When \({\lVert x\rVert}^2_{V^{-1}}=1\) the downdated matrix is singular (e.g. \(V=xx^\top\) in one dimension). Positive definiteness of \(V\) only guarantees validity for additions \(+xx^\top\).

qz.q: In LinUCB, \(V_t=V_{t-1}+x_tx_t^\top\) with \(V_{t-1}\succ0\). For which directions \(y\) is the width \({\lVert y\rVert}_{V_t^{-1}}\) equal to \({\lVert y\rVert}_{V_{t-1}^{-1}}\)?
qz.why: Sherman–Morrison gives \({\lVert y\rVert}^2_{V_t^{-1}}={\lVert y\rVert}^2_{V_{t-1}^{-1}}-\tfrac{(y^\top V_{t-1}^{-1}x_t)^2}{1+{\lVert x_t\rVert}^2_{V_{t-1}^{-1}}}\). Orthogonality must be in the \(V_{t-1}^{-1}\) inner product; Euclidean orthogonality \(y^\top x_t=0\) suffices only when \(V_{t-1}\propto I\).

cards.name: Matrix determinant lemma
cards.lay: The determinant after a rank-one update is the old determinant times a simple scalar factor. Taking logs, the “information gained” by adding \(x\) is \(\log(1+{\lVert x\rVert}^2_{V^{-1}})\), which telescopes over time.
cards.st: For invertible \(A\) and vectors \(u,v\): \[ \det(A+uv^\top) = (1+v^\top A^{-1}u)\det A. \] In particular \(\log\det(V+xx^\top) = \log\det V + \log(1+{\lVert x\rVert}^2_{V^{-1}})\).
ver: Low rank: \(\det(A+UWV^\top) = \det(W^{-1}+V^\top A^{-1}U)\det W\det A\).
Sylvester: \(\det(I_m + AB) = \det(I_n+BA)\).
Determinant–trace bound: \(\det V \le ({\operatorname{tr}} V/d)^d\) (AM–GM on eigenvalues AM–GM inequality).
cards.det: Telescoping the log-det identity over \(t\) gives \(\sum_t\log(1+{\lVert x_t\rVert}^2_{V_{t-1}^{-1}}) = \log\tfrac{\det V_T}{\det V_0}\) — the main step of the elliptical potential lemma Elliptical potential lemma. The right-hand side is \(O(d\log T)\) by the determinant–trace bound.
cards.ex: With \(V_0=\lambda I\), \({\lVert x_t\rVert}\le L\): \(\log\tfrac{\det V_T}{\det V_0} \le d\log\bigl(1+\tfrac{TL^2}{d\lambda}\bigr)\).
cards.use: Elliptical potential lemma; information-gain bounds in GP-UCB; self-normalised confidence radius Self-normalised bound for vector martingales (Abbasi-Yadkori et al.); linear MDP regret.

qz.q: \(V\succ0\) and \({\lVert x\rVert}^2_{V^{-1}}=3\). What is \(\det(V+xx^\top)/\det V\)?
qz.why: Matrix determinant lemma: \(\det(V+xx^\top)=(1+x^\top V^{-1}x)\det V=4\det V\). \(e^3\) would come from confusing \(\log(1+{\lVert x\rVert}^2_{V^{-1}})\) with \({\lVert x\rVert}^2_{V^{-1}}\).

qz.q: \(V_0=\lambda I_d\) with \(d\ge2\), \(V_T=V_0+\sum_{t\le T}x_tx_t^\top\) with \({\lVert x_t\rVert}_2\le L\). Which bound on \(\log\frac{\det V_T}{\det V_0}\) holds for every such sequence?
qz.why: \({\operatorname{tr}} V_T\le d\lambda+TL^2\) and \(\det V_T\le({\operatorname{tr}} V_T/d)^d\) give the first bound. It is attained when the \(x_t\) cycle through \(L\) times an orthonormal basis (\(T\) a multiple of \(d\)), which violates each of the other three.

qz.q: \(\Phi\in{\mathbb{R}}^{n\times d}\) with \(n=1000\), \(d=5\) (e.g. in GP-UCB information gain). Which expression equals \(\det(I_{1000}+\Phi\Phi^\top)\)?
qz.why: Sylvester's identity \(\det(I_m+AB)=\det(I_n+BA)\) moves a \(1000\times1000\) determinant to a \(5\times5\) one. \(1+{\operatorname{tr}}(\Phi^\top\Phi)\) is only correct to first order (exact for rank one).

cards.name: Loewner order facts
cards.lay: \(A\succeq B\) means \(A-B\) is positive semidefinite: “\(A\) is bigger in every direction”. Several familiar scalar facts carry over (inverse reverses order, square root preserves it) but some do not (squaring does not).
cards.st: For symmetric \(A,B\) with \(A\succeq B\succ0\): \[ B^{-1}\succeq A^{-1},\quad A^{1/2}\succeq B^{1/2},\quad {\operatorname{tr}} A\ge{\operatorname{tr}} B,\quad \det A\ge\det B,\quad {\lVert x\rVert}_{A^{-1}}\le{\lVert x\rVert}_{B^{-1}}. \]
ver: Congruence: \(A\succeq B\Rightarrow C^\top AC\succeq C^\top BC\).
Operator monotone functions: \(\log\) and \(t\mapsto t^p\) for \(p\in[0,1]\) preserve order; \(t^2\) does not.
Ratio bound: if \(A\succeq B\succ0\) then \(\sup_x\tfrac{x^\top Ax}{x^\top Bx} \le \tfrac{\det A}{\det B}\) (Abbasi-Yadkori et al., used in rarely-switching bandits).
cards.det: The determinant-ratio bound is what justifies “rarely switching” and batched linear bandits: you only recompute the policy when \(\det V_t\) has doubled, and in between the confidence ellipsoid changes by at most a constant factor. The number of switches is \(O(d\log T)\).
cards.ex: Because \(V_t\succeq V_{t-1}\), uncertainty \({\lVert x\rVert}_{V_t^{-1}}\) is non-increasing in \(t\) for every fixed \(x\) — confidence widths never grow when you add data (with ridge regularisation).
cards.use: Monotonicity of confidence widths, rarely-switching algorithms (low policy-switching cost), batch RL, comparing Fisher information matrices.

qz.q: Let \(A\succeq B\succ0\) be symmetric. Which implication can fail?
qz.why: \(t\mapsto t^2\) is not operator monotone: \(A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}\succeq B=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\) but \(A^2-B^2=\begin{pmatrix}4&3\\3&2\end{pmatrix}\) has negative determinant (adding \({\varepsilon} I\) to both \(A\) and \(B\) keeps \(A\succeq B\), makes \(B\succ0\), and for small \({\varepsilon}\) keeps the determinant negative). Inversion reverses order, and \(t^{1/2}\) and \(\log\) are operator monotone.

qz.q: Rarely-switching linear bandits recompute only when \(\det V_t>2\det V_\tau\), where \(\tau\) is the last switch and \(V_t\succeq V_\tau\succ0\). Between switches (\(\det V_t\le2\det V_\tau\)), which holds for every \(x\)?
qz.why: The ratio bound gives \(x^\top V_tx\le2\,x^\top V_\tau x\), i.e. \(V_t\preceq2V_\tau\); inverting reverses order, \(V_\tau^{-1}\preceq2V_t^{-1}\). The stale width overestimates the current one by at most \(\sqrt2\). Since \(V_t\succeq V_\tau\), the stale width is never smaller, which rules out \({\lVert x\rVert}_{V_\tau^{-1}}\le{\lVert x\rVert}_{V_t^{-1}}\) and the squared bound with \(\frac12\); the \(\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\) bound fails when \(V_t=V_\tau\).

qz.q: Ridge design matrices \(V_t=\lambda I+\sum_{s\le t}x_sx_s^\top\) with all \(x_s\ne0\). Which quantity is non-increasing in \(t\) for every fixed \(x\ne0\)?
qz.why: \(V_t\succeq V_{t-1}\), and inversion reverses the Loewner order, so \({\lVert x\rVert}_{V_t^{-1}}\le{\lVert x\rVert}_{V_{t-1}^{-1}}\): confidence widths never grow. The other three increase with data: \({\operatorname{tr}} V_t\) and \(\log\det V_t\) strictly, and \({\lVert x\rVert}_{V_t}\) weakly.

cards.name: Perron–Frobenius theorem
cards.lay: A non-negative matrix that connects everything (irreducible) has a unique largest positive eigenvalue with a positive eigenvector. For a transition matrix that eigenvalue is 1 and the (left) eigenvector is the stationary distribution.
cards.st: Let \(A\ge0\) entrywise be irreducible. Then the spectral radius \(\rho(A)>0\) is a simple eigenvalue with left and right eigenvectors that are entrywise strictly positive, and every other eigenvalue satisfies \(|\lambda|\le\rho(A)\). If \(A\) is also aperiodic (primitive), \(|\lambda|<\rho(A)\) for all other eigenvalues.
ver: Stochastic matrices: \(\rho(P)=1\), right eigenvector \({\mathbf{1}}\), left eigenvector the stationary distribution \(\mu\) (\(\mu^\top P=\mu^\top\)) Existence & uniqueness of stationary distributions.
Positive matrices (Perron's original theorem): strict positivity gives a spectral gap automatically.
Collatz–Wielandt formula: \(\rho(A) = \max_{x\ge0,x\ne0}\min_{i:x_i>0}\tfrac{(Ax)_i}{x_i}\).
cards.det: The gap between \(1\) and the second-largest eigenvalue modulus governs how fast \(P^t\) converges to \({\mathbf{1}}\mu^\top\) Mixing time & geometric ergodicity. In average-reward RL, unichain/ergodicity assumptions are Perron–Frobenius conditions that make the gain independent of the start state.
cards.ex: For the two-state chain with flip probabilities \(p\) and \(q\), eigenvalues are \(1\) and \(1-p-q\); the stationary distribution is \(\bigl(\tfrac{q}{p+q},\tfrac{p}{p+q}\bigr)\) and \({\lVert P^t(x,\cdot)-\mu\rVert}_{{\mathrm{TV}}}\propto|1-p-q|^t\).
cards.use: Existence/uniqueness of stationary distributions, average-reward MDPs, PageRank-type arguments, mixing-time analyses for policy evaluation from single trajectories.

qz.q: A two-state chain has \(P=\begin{pmatrix}1-p&p\\q&1-q\end{pmatrix}\) with \(p=0.1\), \(q=0.3\). What are its stationary distribution \(\mu\) and second eigenvalue \(\lambda_2\)?
qz.why: Balance \(\mu_1p=\mu_2q\) gives \(\mu=\bigl(\tfrac{q}{p+q},\tfrac{p}{p+q}\bigr)=(0.75,0.25)\): the chain sits more in the state it rarely leaves. \({\operatorname{tr}} P=2-p-q=1+\lambda_2\) gives \(\lambda_2=1-p-q=0.6\), not \(p+q\).

qz.q: Consider \(P=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\) (irreducible but periodic). Which statement is correct?
a: \(\mu=(\tfrac12,\tfrac12)\) is the unique stationary law, but \(P^t\) does not converge
There are two stationary laws, since \(-1\) has modulus \(1\)
There is no stationary law because the chain is periodic
qz.why: Irreducibility alone makes \(\rho=1\) simple with a unique positive left eigenvector. Without aperiodicity another eigenvalue (\(-1\)) also has modulus 1, so \(P^t\) oscillates between \(I\) and \(P\); a simple top eigenvalue is not enough for convergence.

qz.q: Let \(P=I_2\) (each state is absorbing). Which conclusion of Perron–Frobenius for irreducible matrices fails?
a: Simplicity of eigenvalue \(1\): every distribution is stationary
Realness: \(P\) has a complex eigenvalue of modulus \(1\)
qz.why: \(P=I\) is reducible; eigenvalue 1 has multiplicity 2, so the stationary distribution (and, in average-reward RL, the gain) depends on the start state. \(\rho(I)=1\) still, and stationary distributions exist — too many of them, not none.

cards.name: Perturbation of inverses (Banach lemma)
cards.lay: If \(A\) is invertible and \(E\) is small relative to \(A^{-1}\), then \(A+E\) is still invertible and its inverse is close to \(A^{-1}\). Quantifies how sensitive value functions are to model errors.
cards.st: If \({\lVert A^{-1}\rVert}{\lVert E\rVert}<1\) then \(A+E\) is invertible and \[ {\lVert (A+E)^{-1}\rVert}\le\frac{{\lVert A^{-1}\rVert}}{1-{\lVert A^{-1}\rVert}{\lVert E\rVert}},\qquad {\lVert (A+E)^{-1}-A^{-1}\rVert}\le\frac{{\lVert A^{-1}\rVert}^2{\lVert E\rVert}}{1-{\lVert A^{-1}\rVert}{\lVert E\rVert}}. \]
ver: Resolvent identity: \(B^{-1}-A^{-1} = B^{-1}(A-B)A^{-1}\) (exact, no smallness needed).
Condition-number form: \(\tfrac{{\lVert \delta x\rVert}}{{\lVert x\rVert}}\le\kappa(A)\tfrac{{\lVert \delta b\rVert}}{{\lVert b\rVert}}\) for \(Ax=b\).
cards.det: Apply with \(A = I-\gamma P\), \(E = -\gamma(\widehat P - P)\): since \({\lVert (I-\gamma\widehat P)^{-1}\rVert}_\infty\le\tfrac{1}{1-\gamma}\) for any stochastic \(\widehat P\), the resolvent identity directly gives the simulation lemma Simulation lemma (model error \(\to\) value error) without any smallness condition.
cards.ex: \(V_{\widehat P} - V_P = [(I-\gamma\widehat P)^{-1}-(I-\gamma P)^{-1}]r = \gamma(I-\gamma\widehat P)^{-1}(\widehat P-P)(I-\gamma P)^{-1}r\), so \({\lVert V_{\widehat P}-V_P\rVert}_\infty\le\tfrac{\gamma{\lVert \widehat P-P\rVert}_{\infty\to\infty}}{(1-\gamma)^2}\).
cards.use: Sensitivity of values to model error (model-based RL, non-stationary drift), LSTD perturbation analysis, robustness of linear system solutions.

qz.q: Rewards satisfy \({\lVert r\rVert}_\infty\le1\) and the model error \({\lVert \widehat P-P\rVert}_{\infty\to\infty}\) is held fixed. With effective horizon \(H=1/(1-\gamma)\), the bound \({\lVert V_{\widehat P}-V_P\rVert}_\infty\le\frac{\gamma{\lVert \widehat P-P\rVert}_{\infty\to\infty}}{(1-\gamma)^2}\) grows with \(H\) like:
qz.why: One factor \(H\) bounds \({\lVert (I-\gamma\widehat P)^{-1}\rVert}_\infty\), the other bounds \({\lVert (I-\gamma P)^{-1}r\rVert}_\infty={\lVert V_P\rVert}_\infty\). The single-\(H\) answer forgets that the error being propagated is a one-step error multiplied by a value of size \(H\).

qz.q: In some sub-multiplicative norm, \({\lVert A^{-1}\rVert}=2\) and \({\lVert E\rVert}=0.25\). What does the Banach lemma give as a bound on \({\lVert (A+E)^{-1}-A^{-1}\rVert}\)?
qz.why: Here \({\lVert A^{-1}\rVert}{\lVert E\rVert}=0.5<1\), so the bound is \(\tfrac{{\lVert A^{-1}\rVert}^2{\lVert E\rVert}}{1-{\lVert A^{-1}\rVert}{\lVert E\rVert}}=\tfrac{1}{0.5}=2\). \(1\) is the first-order term \({\lVert A^{-1}\rVert}^2{\lVert E\rVert}\) without the \(1/(1-0.5)\) correction; \(4\) is the bound on \({\lVert (A+E)^{-1}\rVert}\) itself.

qz.q: \(Ax=b\) with condition number \(\kappa(A)=100\). The right-hand side is perturbed with \({\lVert \delta b\rVert}/{\lVert b\rVert}=10^{-3}\). What bound holds on \({\lVert \delta x\rVert}/{\lVert x\rVert}\)?
qz.why: \(\tfrac{{\lVert \delta x\rVert}}{{\lVert x\rVert}}\le\kappa(A)\tfrac{{\lVert \delta b\rVert}}{{\lVert b\rVert}}=100\cdot10^{-3}\). Ill-conditioning amplifies relative errors, so dividing by \(\kappa\) (\(10^{-5}\)) has the direction backwards; \(10\) would use \(\kappa^2\).

cards.name: Schur complement & block inversion
cards.lay: For a \(2\times2\) block matrix, the Schur complement is “what is left” after eliminating one block. It tells you when a block matrix is positive definite and gives formulas for conditional Gaussians.
cards.st: For \(M = \begin{pmatrix}A&B\\B^\top&C\end{pmatrix}\) with \(A\succ0\): \(M\succeq0 \iff C - B^\top A^{-1}B\succeq0\), and \[ \det M = \det A\,\det(C-B^\top A^{-1}B). \]
ver: Block inverse: the lower-right block of \(M^{-1}\) equals \((C-B^\top A^{-1}B)^{-1}\).
Gaussian conditioning: if \((X,Y)\) is jointly Gaussian then \({\operatorname{Cov}}(Y\mid X) = \Sigma_{YY}-\Sigma_{YX}\Sigma_{XX}^{-1}\Sigma_{XY}\) — a Schur complement.
Used to prove \(\begin{pmatrix}A & x\\ x^\top & t\end{pmatrix}\succeq0 \iff t\ge x^\top A^{-1}x\) (SDP representation of \({\lVert x\rVert}^2_{A^{-1}}\)).
cards.det: Schur complements show up in EM theory as the missing-information matrix: observed Fisher information \(=\) complete information \(-\) missing information Missing-information principle (Louis) & EM's convergence rate, a Schur-complement-like subtraction.
cards.ex: Kalman filter update: posterior covariance \(= \Sigma - \Sigma H^\top(H\Sigma H^\top + R)^{-1}H\Sigma\), a Schur complement — used in tracking drifting parameters in non-stationary bandits.
cards.use: Gaussian posterior computations (Thompson sampling with linear-Gaussian models), SDP relaxations, missing information in EM, block-structured LSTD.

qz.q: Let \(A={\operatorname{diag}}(1,4)\) and \(x=(1,2)^\top\). What is the smallest \(t\) such that \(\begin{pmatrix}A&x\\x^\top&t\end{pmatrix}\succeq0\)?
qz.why: With \(A\succ0\), the block matrix is PSD iff the Schur complement \(t-x^\top A^{-1}x\ge0\), and \(x^\top A^{-1}x=1+4/4=2\). \(5=x^\top x\) ignores \(A\); \(17=x^\top Ax\) uses \(A\) instead of \(A^{-1}\).

qz.q: \((X,Y)\) is jointly Gaussian with \({\operatorname{Var}}(X)=4\), \({\operatorname{Var}}(Y)=1\), \({\operatorname{Cov}}(X,Y)=1\). What is \({\operatorname{Var}}(Y\mid X=x)\)?
qz.why: Schur complement: \(\Sigma_{YY}-\Sigma_{YX}\Sigma_{XX}^{-1}\Sigma_{XY}=1-1\cdot\tfrac14\cdot1=\tfrac34\), independent of the observed value. \(1/2\) divides by the standard deviation instead of the variance.

qz.q: Let \(M=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}\), viewed in blocks with \(A=2\), \(B=1\), \(C=1\). What is the lower-right entry of \(M^{-1}\)?
qz.why: The lower-right block of \(M^{-1}\) is \((C-B^\top A^{-1}B)^{-1}=(1-\tfrac12)^{-1}=2\) (check: \(\det M=1\), \(M^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\-1&2\end{pmatrix}\)). \(1=C^{-1}\) ignores the coupling, and \(1/2\) is the Schur complement before inversion.

cards.name: Trace inequalities & von Neumann's trace inequality
cards.plain: Trace inequalities & von Neumann's trace inequality
cards.lay: The trace of a product is bounded by pairing singular values: largest with largest. Most often used as \({\operatorname{tr}}(AB)\le{\lVert A\rVert}_2{\operatorname{tr}}(B)\) for positive semidefinite \(B\).
cards.st: (von Neumann) For \(A,B\in{\mathbb{R}}^{n\times n}\) with singular values \(\sigma_1\ge\dots\) and \(\tau_1\ge\dots\): \[ |{\operatorname{tr}}(AB)| \le \sum_i\sigma_i(A)\tau_i(B). \] Consequently \(|{\operatorname{tr}}(AB)|\le{\lVert A\rVert}_2{\lVert B\rVert}_*\) and, for \(B\succeq0\), \({\operatorname{tr}}(AB)\le\lambda_{\max}(A){\operatorname{tr}} B\).
ver: Cauchy–Schwarz for matrices: \(|{\operatorname{tr}}(A^\top B)|\le{\lVert A\rVert}_F{\lVert B\rVert}_F\).
Golden–Thompson: \({\operatorname{tr}} e^{A+B}\le{\operatorname{tr}}(e^Ae^B)\) for symmetric \(A,B\) (used to prove matrix Chernoff bounds Matrix Bernstein / matrix Chernoff (Tropp)).
Lieb's concavity theorem (deep; drives Tropp's matrix concentration).
cards.det: The workhorse corollary: \({\mathbb{E}}[x^\top Ax] = {\operatorname{tr}}(A\,{\mathbb{E}}[xx^\top]) \le \lambda_{\max}(A)\,{\mathbb{E}}{\lVert x\rVert}^2\). Expressions like \({\mathbb{E}}_{\phi\sim d^\pi}{\lVert \phi\rVert}^2_{\Sigma^{-1}} = {\operatorname{tr}}(\Sigma^{-1}\Sigma_\pi)\) (relative coverage) are traces of products.
cards.ex: If the data covariance is \(\Sigma\) and the target-policy covariance is \(\Sigma_\pi\), the offline error is often proportional to \(\sqrt{{\operatorname{tr}}(\Sigma^{-1}\Sigma_\pi)}\le\sqrt{d\,\lambda_{\max}(\Sigma^{-1/2}\Sigma_\pi\Sigma^{-1/2})}\).
cards.use: Coverage coefficients in offline linear RL, expected squared feature norms, matrix concentration proofs.

qz.q: Data covariance \(\Sigma={\operatorname{diag}}(1,0.01)\), target-policy covariance \(\Sigma_\pi={\operatorname{diag}}(0.5,0.5)\). What is the coverage term \({\operatorname{tr}}(\Sigma^{-1}\Sigma_\pi)={\mathbb{E}}_{\phi\sim d^\pi}{\lVert \phi\rVert}^2_{\Sigma^{-1}}\)?
qz.why: \(\Sigma^{-1}\Sigma_\pi={\operatorname{diag}}(0.5,50)\), trace \(50.5\): the poorly covered second direction dominates. \(0.505={\operatorname{tr}}(\Sigma\Sigma_\pi)\) uses \(\Sigma\) instead of \(\Sigma^{-1}\); \(100=\lambda_{\max}(\Sigma^{-1}){\operatorname{tr}}\Sigma_\pi\) is only an upper bound.

qz.q: \(A,B\) are real symmetric \(n\times n\) matrices, and \(B\) is not assumed PSD. Which inequality can fail?
qz.why: The \(\lambda_{\max}\) form needs \(B\succeq0\): \(A=B={\operatorname{diag}}(0,-1)\) gives \({\operatorname{tr}}(AB)=1>0=\lambda_{\max}(A){\operatorname{tr}} B\). The other three are Cauchy–Schwarz, spectral/nuclear duality, and von Neumann's inequality, which hold for all matrices.

qz.q: \(A,B\) are \(2\times2\) PSD with eigenvalues \(\{3,1\}\) and \(\{2,1\}\), and eigenvectors free to choose. What is the largest possible value of \({\operatorname{tr}}(AB)\)?
qz.why: von Neumann: \({\operatorname{tr}}(AB)\le\sum_i\sigma_i(A)\sigma_i(B)=3\cdot2+1\cdot1=7\), attained when the eigenvectors align. \(5\) is the anti-aligned minimum \(3\cdot1+1\cdot2\), and \(12={\operatorname{tr}} A{\operatorname{tr}} B\) is a loose bound that is never attained here.

cards.name: Gershgorin circle theorem
cards.lay: Every eigenvalue of a matrix lies close to some diagonal entry — within a disc whose radius is the sum of the off-diagonal magnitudes in that row. A quick way to prove a matrix is non-singular or stable.
cards.st: Every eigenvalue of \(A\in\mathbb{C}^{n\times n}\) lies in \(\bigcup_i D_i\), where \[ D_i = \Bigl\{z: |z-A_{ii}|\le\sum_{j\ne i}|A_{ij}|\Bigr\}. \]
ver: Column version (apply to \(A^\top\)).
Strict diagonal dominance \(\Rightarrow\) invertibility (Levy–Desplanques).
cards.det: Useful in stochastic approximation: the ODE \(\dot\theta = A\theta + b\) is stable iff \(A\) is Hurwitz. For tabular TD(0), \(A = D(\gamma P - I)\) where \(D\) is the diagonal of the stationary distribution — Gershgorin-type diagonal dominance arguments (together with the \(\mu\)-weighted norm) show its eigenvalues have negative real parts.
cards.ex: Matrix \(I-\gamma P\) with stochastic \(P\): diagonal entries \(1-\gamma P_{ii}\), off-diagonal row sum \(\gamma(1-P_{ii})\); every disc lies in \(\{\mathrm{Re}\,z\ge1-\gamma\}\), so \(I-\gamma P\) is invertible (consistent with Neumann series & the resolvent \((I-\gamma P)^{-1}\)).
cards.use: Stability of linear stochastic approximation (TD, GTD), quick invertibility checks, bounding spectra of iteration matrices.

qz.q: Let \(A=\begin{pmatrix}4&1&0\\1&-3&1\\0&2&5\end{pmatrix}\). Which value does Gershgorin's (row) theorem rule out as an eigenvalue?
qz.why: The row discs are \(\{{\lvert z-4\rvert}\le1\}\), \(\{{\lvert z+3\rvert}\le2\}\), \(\{{\lvert z-5\rvert}\le2\}\). \(0\) lies in none of them (distances \(4,3,5\)), so \(A\) is invertible. \(4.5\), \(-2\) and \(6\) each lie in some disc, so they cannot be ruled out.

qz.q: \(P\) is row-stochastic and \(\gamma\in(0,1)\). Applying Gershgorin's row discs to \(I-\gamma P\), what is the largest \(c\) such that every eigenvalue \(z\) satisfies \(\mathrm{Re}\,z\ge c\) for every such \(P\)?
qz.why: Disc \(i\) has centre \(1-\gamma P_{ii}\) and radius \(\gamma(1-P_{ii})\), so its leftmost point is \(1-\gamma\) for every row. This keeps \(0\) outside the spectrum, consistent with Neumann series & the resolvent \((I-\gamma P)^{-1}\). Indeed \(z=1-\gamma\) is an eigenvalue (eigenvector \({\mathbf{1}}\)), so no larger \(c\) works.

qz.q: Let \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0.1&3\end{pmatrix}\). The first row disc \(\{{\lvert z-1\rvert}\le2\}\) contains \(0\). Is \(A\) invertible?
a: Gershgorin cannot decide it either way
Yes, because all entries are positive
qz.why: Gershgorin also holds for \(A^\top\): the column discs \(\{{\lvert z-1\rvert}\le0.1\}\) and \(\{{\lvert z-3\rvert}\le2\}\) miss \(0\) (indeed \(\det A=2.8\)). A disc containing \(0\) does not mean \(0\) is an eigenvalue, and positive entries do not imply invertibility (consider \({\mathbf{1}}{\mathbf{1}}^\top\)).

cards.name: Banach fixed-point theorem (contraction mapping)
cards.lay: If applying a map always brings any two points closer together by a fixed factor \(\gamma<1\), then repeatedly applying it from anywhere converges — fast — to a unique point that the map leaves unchanged. This is why value iteration works.
cards.st: Let \((X,d)\) be a complete metric space and \(T:X\to X\) satisfy \(d(Tx,Ty)\le\gamma\,d(x,y)\) for some \(\gamma\in[0,1)\). Then \(T\) has a unique fixed point \(x^\star\), and for any \(x_0\), \(x_k=T^kx_0\) satisfies \[ d(x_k,x^\star)\le\gamma^kd(x_0,x^\star)\le\frac{\gamma^k}{1-\gamma}d(x_0,x_1). \]
ver: A posteriori bound: \(d(x_k,x^\star)\le\tfrac{1}{1-\gamma}d(x_k,x_{k+1})\) — gives a computable stopping rule for value iteration.
Eventually contractive maps: if \(T^m\) is a contraction for some \(m\), \(T\) still has a unique fixed point (useful for undiscounted SSPs with proper policies).
Weighted sup-norm contractions: for stochastic shortest path problems, \(T\) is a contraction in \({\lVert V\rVert}_{\infty,w}=\max_s|V(s)|/w(s)\) for a suitable \(w>0\).
Inexact iteration: if \({\lVert x_{k+1}-Tx_k\rVert}\le{\varepsilon}\) then \(\limsup_k d(x_k,x^\star)\le\tfrac{{\varepsilon}}{1-\gamma}\) Geometric series & discounted sums.
Non-expansive maps (\(\gamma=1\)) need not have unique fixed points; see Brouwer/Kakutani Brouwer & Kakutani fixed-point theorems for existence without contraction.
cards.det:
Proof. \(d(x_{k+1},x_k)\le\gamma^kd(x_1,x_0)\), so \((x_k)\) is Cauchy by the geometric series Geometric series & discounted sums; completeness gives a limit, continuity of \(T\) makes it a fixed point; two fixed points \(x,y\) would satisfy \(d(x,y)\le\gamma d(x,y)\), forcing \(x=y\).

In RL the space is \(({\mathbb{R}}^{{\mathcal{S}}},{\lVert \cdot\rVert}_\infty)\) (complete), and the maps are \(T^\pi\), \(T^\star\) Bellman equations & contraction of Bellman operators. Population EM is a contraction near \(\theta^\star\) under the Balakrishnan–Wainwright–Yu conditions Balakrishnan–Wainwright–Yu: population EM contraction, which is how local linear convergence of EM is proved.
cards.ex: Value iteration: \({\lVert V_k-V^\star\rVert}_\infty\le\gamma^k{\lVert V_0-V^\star\rVert}_\infty\le\tfrac{\gamma^k}{1-\gamma}\) for rewards in \([0,1]\), \(V_0=0\). To reach accuracy \({\varepsilon}\) you need \(k\ge\tfrac{\log(1/({\varepsilon}(1-\gamma)))}{1-\gamma}\) iterations.
cards.use: Existence/uniqueness of \(V^\pi\), \(V^\star\), \(Q^\star\); value iteration rates; fitted value iteration error propagation; local convergence of EM and other fixed-point algorithms; existence of solutions to Bellman equations in robust and regularised MDPs.

qz.q: Value iteration \(V_{k+1}=T^\star V_k\) uses a \(\gamma\)-contraction in \({\lVert \cdot\rVert}_\infty\). You stop once \({\lVert V_{k+1}-V_k\rVert}_\infty\le\eta\). Which guarantee on \({\lVert V_k-V^\star\rVert}_\infty\) holds in general?
qz.why: A posteriori bound: \(d(x_k,x^\star)\le d(x_k,x_{k+1})+d(x_{k+1},x^\star)\le\eta+\gamma d(x_k,x^\star)\). It is tight: for \(T(x)=\gamma x\) on \({\mathbb{R}}\), \(|x_k-x_{k+1}|=(1-\gamma)|x_k|\). The bound \(\frac{\gamma\eta}{1-\gamma}\) holds for \(V_{k+1}\), not \(V_k\).

qz.q: Let \(T(x)=x/2\) on \(X=(0,1]\) with the usual distance. \(T\) maps \(X\) into itself and has no fixed point in \(X\). Which hypothesis of Banach's theorem fails?
a: The contraction factor must be below \(\frac12\)
qz.why: \(T\) is a \(\frac12\)-contraction of \((0,1]\) into \((0,\frac12]\), but the iterates converge to \(0\notin X\): the Cauchy sequence has no limit in \(X\). In RL the space \(({\mathbb{R}}^{{\mathcal{S}}},{\lVert \cdot\rVert}_\infty)\) is complete, so this cannot happen.

qz.q: Let \(T(x)=x+1/x\) on \([1,\infty)\) (complete). Then \(|Tx-Ty|<|x-y|\) for all \(x\neq y\), but there is no uniform \(\gamma<1\). What happens?
a: \(T\) has a unique fixed point, by Banach
\(T\) has a fixed point, but iterates miss it
qz.why: \(Tx=x\) would need \(1/x=0\), and the iterates increase to \(\infty\). A strict but non-uniform contraction is not enough on a non-compact space; Banach needs \(d(Tx,Ty)\le\gamma d(x,y)\) with a fixed \(\gamma<1\). Discounting provides exactly that.

cards.name: Non-expansiveness of \(\max\) / \(\sup\)
cards.lay: The maximum of a function changes by at most the largest pointwise change of the function. This tiny fact is what makes the Bellman optimality operator a contraction, despite the nonlinear max.
cards.st: For bounded functions \(f,g\) on any set \({\mathcal{A}}\): \[ \Bigl|\sup_{a}f(a)-\sup_{a}g(a)\Bigr|\le\sup_a|f(a)-g(a)|. \] The same holds with \(\inf\), and for \(\max\) over finite sets.
ver: Soft-max version: \(|\mathrm{LSE}_\eta(x)-\mathrm{LSE}_\eta(y)|\le{\lVert x-y\rVert}_\infty\) Log-sum-exp (soft-max) sandwich.
Min–max: \(|\max_a\min_b f - \max_a\min_b g|\le{\lVert f-g\rVert}_\infty\) (Shapley/Markov games operator is a contraction).
Expectation of max: \(|{\mathbb{E}}\max_a X_a - {\mathbb{E}}\max_a Y_a|\le{\mathbb{E}}\max_a|X_a-Y_a|\).
cards.det:
Proof. For any \(a\), \(f(a)\le g(a)+\sup|f-g|\le\sup g+\sup|f-g|\); take sup over \(a\), then swap roles of \(f\) and \(g\).

Consequence: \(|(T^\star V)(s)-(T^\star U)(s)| = \gamma|\max_a P_{s,a}^\top V - \max_a P_{s,a}^\top U|\le\gamma\max_a|P_{s,a}^\top(V-U)|\le\gamma{\lVert V-U\rVert}_\infty\).
cards.ex: Zero-sum Markov games: the Shapley operator \((TV)(s) = \max_{x}\min_{y}x^\top[r(s)+\gamma\sum_{s'}P(s')V(s')]y\) is a \(\gamma\)-contraction by the min–max version.
cards.use: Contraction of \(T^\star\); Lipschitzness of \(V^\star\) in rewards/transitions (non-stationary drift analyses); stability of greedy policies; Markov games.

qz.q: For bounded \(f,g\) on \({\mathcal{A}}\times\mathcal B\), what is the smallest constant \(c\) such that \(|\max_a\min_bf(a,b)-\max_a\min_bg(a,b)|\le c{\lVert f-g\rVert}_\infty\) always holds?
qz.why: Apply non-expansiveness twice: \(\min_b\) is 1-Lipschitz in sup-norm, and so is \(\max_a\). Taking \(g=f+{\varepsilon}\) shows \(c=1\) is attained. This is why the Shapley operator of zero-sum Markov games is a \(\gamma\)-contraction.

qz.q: The soft Bellman operator is \((TQ)(s,a)=r(s,a)+\gamma{\mathbb{E}}_{s'}\bigl[\frac1\eta\log\sum_{a'}e^{\eta Q(s',a')}\bigr]\), with \(\eta>0\). What is its contraction modulus in \({\lVert \cdot\rVert}_\infty\)?
a: None: it is not a contraction for \(\eta>1\)
qz.why: LSE is 1-Lipschitz in \({\lVert \cdot\rVert}_\infty\) for every \(\eta\) Log-sum-exp (soft-max) sandwich, just like the hard max, and \({\mathbb{E}}_{s'}\) is non-expansive. The temperature affects the bias relative to the hard max (an additive \(\frac{\log|{\mathcal{A}}|}{\eta}\)), not the Lipschitz constant.

qz.q: Let \(f,g\) be functions on a finite set and \(a_f\in{\operatorname*{arg\,max}} f\). Which inequality holds for all such \(f,g\)?
qz.why: \(\max g\ge g(a_f)\) gives the one-sided bound; this is half of the proof of non-expansiveness. Evaluating at \(f\)'s maximiser does not control the other direction: \(f=(1,0)\), \(g=(0,5)\) gives \(|\max f-\max g|=4\) but \(|f(a_f)-g(a_f)|=1\).

cards.name: Mean value theorem
cards.lay: Over any interval, a smooth function's average slope equals its actual slope at some point in between. So bounds on derivatives turn directly into Lipschitz bounds.
cards.st: If \(f:[a,b]\to{\mathbb{R}}\) is continuous and differentiable on \((a,b)\), there is \(c\in(a,b)\) with \(f(b)-f(a)=f'(c)(b-a)\). For \(f:{\mathbb{R}}^d\to{\mathbb{R}}\): \(f(y)-f(x)={\langle \nabla f(z), y-x\rangle}\) for some \(z\) on the segment \([x,y]\).
ver: Lipschitz consequence: \(|f(y)-f(x)|\le\sup_z{\lVert \nabla f(z)\rVert}_*{\lVert y-x\rVert}\).

Vector-valued maps: no exact MVT, but the integral form \(F(y)-F(x)=\int_0^1J_F(x+t(y-x))(y-x)\,{\mathrm{d}} t\) gives \({\lVert F(y)-F(x)\rVert}\le\sup{\lVert J_F\rVert}{\lVert y-x\rVert}\) Taylor's theorem with remainder.
Cauchy's MVT: \((f(b)-f(a))g'(c)=(g(b)-g(a))f'(c)\) (behind L'Hôpital).
cards.det: Typical RL usage: bounding the change in a policy's value as parameters move, by bounding the gradient norm (policy-gradient Lipschitz constants), or showing the EM map is a contraction via \(\sup{\lVert \nabla M(\theta)\rVert}_2<1\) Balakrishnan–Wainwright–Yu: population EM contraction.
cards.ex: For softmax policies, \({\lVert \nabla_\theta V^{\pi_\theta}\rVert}_2\le\tfrac{\sqrt2}{(1-\gamma)^2}\) (rewards in \([0,1]\)), so \(|V^{\pi_\theta}-V^{\pi_{\theta'}}|\le\tfrac{\sqrt2}{(1-\gamma)^2}{\lVert \theta-\theta'\rVert}_2\).
cards.use: Lipschitz bounds for value functions in parameters; contraction proofs via Jacobian bounds; linearisation arguments.

qz.q: \(f:{\mathbb{R}}^d\to{\mathbb{R}}\) (\(d\ge2\)) is differentiable with \({\lVert \nabla f(z)\rVert}_\infty\le L\) for all \(z\). Which bound holds for all \(x,y\)?
qz.why: By the MVT, \(f(y)-f(x)={\langle \nabla f(z), y-x\rangle}\le{\lVert \nabla f(z)\rVert}_*{\lVert y-x\rVert}\): the gradient takes the norm dual to the one on \(y-x\), and the dual of \(\ell_\infty\) is \(\ell_1\). Take \(f(x)=\sum_ix_i\) and \(y-x={\mathbf{1}}\): the change is \(d\), which breaks all three wrong options.

qz.q: Let \(F(t)=(\cos t,\sin t)\) for \(t\in[0,2\pi]\). Is there \(c\in(0,2\pi)\) with \(F(2\pi)-F(0)=2\pi F'(c)\)?
a: Yes: apply the scalar MVT to each component
qz.why: The MVT has no exact form for vector-valued maps: each component has its own intermediate point. What survives is the integral form, \({\lVert F(y)-F(x)\rVert}\le\sup{\lVert J_F\rVert}{\lVert y-x\rVert}\) Taylor's theorem with remainder.

qz.q: An EM map \(M:\Theta\to{\mathbb{R}}^d\) satisfies \({\lVert \nabla M(\theta)\rVert}_{\rm op}\le\kappa<1\) for all \(\theta\in\Theta\). To conclude \({\lVert M(\theta)-M(\theta')\rVert}_2\le\kappa{\lVert \theta-\theta'\rVert}_2\) for all \(\theta,\theta'\in\Theta\), which property of \(\Theta\) does the argument use?
qz.why: The (integral) MVT evaluates the Jacobian along the segment between the two points, so the Jacobian bound must hold there. Compactness is not needed. On a non-convex set the shortest path within \(\Theta\) can be longer than \({\lVert \theta-\theta'\rVert}\).

cards.name: Taylor's theorem with remainder
cards.lay: Near any point, a smooth function is approximately its tangent line (or tangent parabola), and the error is controlled by the next derivative. Every “smooth implies descent” and “local quadratic” argument is Taylor.
cards.st: If \(f\in C^{k+1}\) near \(x\): \[ f(x+h)=\sum_{j=0}^{k}\frac{f^{(j)}(x)}{j!}h^j+R_k,\quad R_k=\frac{f^{(k+1)}(\xi)}{(k+1)!}h^{k+1}=\int_0^1\frac{(1-t)^k}{k!}f^{(k+1)}(x+th)h^{k+1}{\mathrm{d}} t. \] Multivariate second order: \(f(x+h)=f(x)+{\langle \nabla f(x), h\rangle}+\tfrac12h^\top\nabla^2f(\xi)h\).
ver: Integral (first-order) form: \(f(y)=f(x)+\int_0^1{\langle \nabla f(x+t(y-x)), y-x\rangle}{\mathrm{d}} t\).
Gradient-Lipschitz consequence: \(|f(y)-f(x)-{\langle \nabla f(x), y-x\rangle}|\le\tfrac L2{\lVert y-x\rVert}^2\) \(L\)-smoothness & the descent lemma.
Peano remainder: \(R_k=o(h^k)\) as \(h\to0\) (no explicit constant).

Taylor for log-MGF: \(\log{\mathbb{E}} e^{\lambda X}=\lambda{\mathbb{E}} X+\tfrac{\lambda^2}{2}{\operatorname{Var}} X+O(\lambda^3)\) — motivates sub-Gaussian definitions Sub-Gaussian random variables.
cards.det: Taylor expansions underpin: the descent lemma \(L\)-smoothness & the descent lemma; Hoeffding's lemma (second-order expansion of the log-MGF) Hoeffding's lemma; KL local quadratic approximation \({\mathrm{KL}}(p_\theta\|p_{\theta+h})\approx\tfrac12h^\top F(\theta)h\) (Fisher information, natural gradient Natural policy gradient & policy mirror descent convergence); asymptotic normality via the delta method.
cards.ex: Local behaviour of KL for softmax policies: \({\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_\theta\|\pi_{\theta+h})=\tfrac12h^\top F(\theta)h+O({\lVert h\rVert}^3)\), which is why TRPO's KL trust region is approximately a Fisher-norm ball.
cards.use: Descent lemmas, natural-gradient and trust-region analysis, local convergence of EM, MGF bounds, error expansions of discount-sensitive values.

qz.q: \(f\) has an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient and \(x^+=x-\frac1L\nabla f(x)\). Which decrease guarantee holds for every such \(f\), every \(x\) and every \(L>0\)?
qz.why: Taylor with the gradient-Lipschitz remainder: \(f(x^+)\le f(x)-\frac1L{\lVert g\rVert}^2+\frac L2\cdot\frac1{L^2}{\lVert g\rVert}^2\). For \(f=\frac L2x^2\) the step lands exactly at \(0\) and the decrease is exactly \(\frac{g^2}{2L}\), which rules out larger constants (and \(\frac L2\) whenever \(L>1\)).

qz.q: Let \(F(\theta)\) be the Fisher information of a smooth family \(p_\theta\). To second order in \(h\), what is \({\mathrm{KL}}(p_\theta\|p_{\theta+h})\)?
qz.why: KL is \(0\) with zero gradient at \(h=0\), and its Hessian there is the Fisher information, so the Taylor expansion starts at \(\frac12h^\top Fh\). That is why a KL trust region is approximately a Fisher-norm ball (TRPO, natural gradient Natural policy gradient & policy mirror descent convergence). \(F^{-1}\) appears in the natural-gradient direction, not in the divergence.

qz.q: Expand \(\psi(\lambda)=\log{\mathbb{E}} e^{\lambda X}\) around \(\lambda=0\). What is the coefficient of \(\lambda^2\)?
qz.why: \(\psi'(0)={\mathbb{E}} X\) and \(\psi''(0)={\operatorname{Var}} X\) (the cumulants), so \(\psi(\lambda)=\lambda{\mathbb{E}} X+\frac{\lambda^2}{2}{\operatorname{Var}} X+O(\lambda^3)\). The MGF itself has \(\frac12{\mathbb{E}} X^2\); taking the log subtracts \(\frac12({\mathbb{E}} X)^2\). This is why sub-Gaussian parameters behave like variances.

cards.name: Fubini–Tonelli theorem (swapping sums/integrals)
cards.lay: You may swap the order of two integrals (or sums, or an integral and an expectation) when everything is non-negative (Tonelli) or absolutely integrable (Fubini). This licenses writing \({\mathbb{E}}\sum_t=\sum_t{\mathbb{E}}\).
cards.st: Let \(f\) be measurable on \(X\times Y\) with \(\sigma\)-finite measures. If \(f\ge0\) (Tonelli), or \(\int\!\!\int|f|<\infty\) (Fubini), then \[ \int_X\!\int_Yf(x,y)\,{\mathrm{d}}\nu(y){\mathrm{d}}\mu(x)=\int_Y\!\int_Xf(x,y)\,{\mathrm{d}}\mu(x){\mathrm{d}}\nu(y). \]
ver: Series form: \({\mathbb{E}}\sum_{t=0}^\infty\gamma^tr_t=\sum_t\gamma^t{\mathbb{E}} r_t\) when rewards are bounded (dominated by \(\tfrac{R_{\max}}{1-\gamma}\)).
Swapping sums: \(\sum_i\sum_ja_{ij}=\sum_j\sum_ia_{ij}\) if \(\sum_{i,j}|a_{ij}|<\infty\).
Layer-cake / tail formula: \({\mathbb{E}} X=\int_0^\infty\Pr(X>t){\mathrm{d}} t\) for \(X\ge0\) is Tonelli applied to \({\mathbf{1}}\{t<X\}\) Tail-integral (layer-cake) formula.
cards.det: The occupancy-measure identity \(V^\pi(\rho)=\tfrac{1}{1-\gamma}{\mathbb{E}}_{(s,a)\sim d^\pi_\rho}r(s,a)\) Discounted occupancy measures is a Fubini swap: \({\mathbb{E}}\sum_t\gamma^tr(s_t,a_t)=\sum_{s,a}r(s,a)\sum_t\gamma^t\Pr(s_t=s,a_t=a)\).
cards.ex: Counter-example to remember: \(a_{ij}=1\) if \(i=j\), \(-1\) if \(j=i+1\), else \(0\); row sums are \(0\) but column sums are not — swapping fails without absolute summability.
cards.use: Occupancy measures, policy-gradient derivations, tail-integral formulas, expectations of discounted returns, interchanging \({\mathbb{E}}\) and \(\sum\) in regret.

qz.q: For \(i,j\ge1\) let \(a_{ii}=1\), \(a_{i,i+1}=-1\), and \(a_{ij}=0\) otherwise. What are \(\sum_i\sum_ja_{ij}\) (row sums first) and \(\sum_j\sum_ia_{ij}\) (column sums first)?
qz.why: Every row sums to \(1-1=0\). Column \(1\) contains only \(a_{11}=1\), and every later column sums to \(-1+1=0\). The swap fails because \(\sum_{i,j}|a_{ij}|=\infty\), so Fubini does not apply, and neither does Tonelli (mixed signs).

qz.q: Rewards \(r_t\) are non-negative but possibly unbounded, and some \({\mathbb{E}} r_t\) may be \(+\infty\). Is \({\mathbb{E}}\sum_{t\ge0}\gamma^tr_t=\sum_{t\ge0}\gamma^t{\mathbb{E}} r_t\)?
a: Yes, by Tonelli (both sides may be \(+\infty\))
No: the swap needs bounded rewards
qz.why: Tonelli requires only non-negativity and measurability; the equality holds in \([0,\infty]\). Boundedness or absolute integrability (Fubini) is needed only for signed rewards. Independence plays no role.

qz.q: \(X\ge0\) has \(\Pr(X>t)=1\) for \(t<1\) and \(\Pr(X>t)=t^{-2}\) for \(t\ge1\). Using \({\mathbb{E}} X=\int_0^\infty\Pr(X>t)\,{\mathrm{d}} t\), what is \({\mathbb{E}} X\)?
qz.why: \(\int_0^1 1\,{\mathrm{d}} t+\int_1^\infty t^{-2}\,{\mathrm{d}} t=1+1=2\). The layer-cake formula is Tonelli applied to \({\mathbf{1}}\{t<X\}\) Tail-integral (layer-cake) formula. A tail \(t^{-1}\) would give \(+\infty\); \(t^{-2}\) is integrable.

cards.name: Log-derivative (score-function) trick & differentiating under the integral
cards.plain: Log-derivative (score-function) trick & differentiating under the integral
cards.lay: The gradient of an expectation with respect to the distribution's parameters can be written as an expectation of (function \(\times\) gradient of log-density). This turns gradients into things you can estimate from samples, and is the root of REINFORCE and the Fisher identity in EM.
cards.st: If \(p_ heta\) is differentiable in \( heta\) and differentiation under the integral is justified (e.g. by dominated convergence Monotone & dominated convergence theorems): \[ abla_ heta{\mathbb{E}}_{x\sim p_ heta}[f(x)]={\mathbb{E}}_{x\sim p_ heta} igl[f(x) abla_ heta\log p_ heta(x) igr],\qquad {\mathbb{E}}_{p_ heta}[ abla_ heta\log p_ heta]=0. \]
ver: Baselines: \({\mathbb{E}}[(f(x)-b)\nabla\log p_\theta(x)]=\nabla{\mathbb{E}} f\) for any \(b\) not depending on \(x\) (variance reduction).
Trajectories: \(\nabla_\theta\log p_\theta(\tau)=\sum_t\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(a_t|s_t)\) — dynamics cancel (model-free policy gradient Policy gradient theorem).
Leibniz rule: \(\tfrac{{\mathrm{d}}}{{\mathrm{d}}\theta}\int_{a(\theta)}^{b(\theta)}f(x,\theta){\mathrm{d}} x\) including boundary terms.
Reparameterisation alternative: if \(x=g_\theta({\varepsilon})\), \(\nabla{\mathbb{E}} f(x)={\mathbb{E}}[\nabla_\theta f(g_\theta({\varepsilon}))]\) (pathwise gradient).
Fisher identity in EM: \(\nabla_\theta\log p_\theta(x)={\mathbb{E}}_{z\sim p_\theta(\cdot|x)}[\nabla_\theta\log p_\theta(x,z)]\) Fisher's identity (score of the observed likelihood).
cards.det: Derivation. \( abla\int f p_ heta=\int f abla p_ heta=\int fp_ heta abla\log p_ heta\). The zero-mean property follows from \(f\equiv1\). The second moment \({\mathbb{E}}[ abla\log p\, abla\log p^ op]\) is the Fisher information, which defines the natural gradient Natural policy gradient & policy mirror descent convergence.
cards.ex: REINFORCE: \(\nabla J(\theta)={\mathbb{E}}_\tau\bigl[\sum_t\nabla\log\pi_\theta(a_t|s_t)\,G_t\bigr]\) where \(G_t\) is the return from \(t\); subtracting \(V(s_t)\) (a baseline) keeps it unbiased.
cards.use: Policy gradient theorem, REINFORCE and actor-critic estimators, Fisher identity and gradient-EM, score-function gradients in variational inference.

qz.q: In REINFORCE the term \(\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(a_t|s_t)\,(G_t-b)\) appears, where \(G_t\) is the return from \(t\). Which choice of \(b\) keeps the gradient estimate unbiased?
qz.why: \({\mathbb{E}}_{a\sim\pi(\cdot|s)}[b(s)\nabla\log\pi(a|s)]=b(s)\cdot0\) because the score has mean zero; this needs \(b\) not to depend on the action \(a_t\). The other three choices all depend on \(a_t\) (or on what follows it) and introduce bias; \(b=G_t\) makes the estimate identically \(0\).

qz.q: For a trajectory \(\tau\), \(\nabla_\theta\log p_\theta(\tau)=\sum_t\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(a_t|s_t)\), with no transition terms. Why do the dynamics drop out?
a: The reward does not depend on \(\theta\)
qz.why: \(\log p_\theta(\tau)=\log\rho(s_0)+\sum_t[\log\pi_\theta(a_t|s_t)+\log P(s_{t+1}|s_t,a_t)]\), and the \(\theta\)-gradient of the last term is identically zero, not just zero on average. This is what makes the estimator model-free for any stochastic dynamics.

qz.q: For \(x\sim\mathcal N(\theta,1)\), what is the score \(\nabla_\theta\log p_\theta(x)\), and its variance (the Fisher information)?
qz.why: \(\log p_\theta(x)=-\frac12(x-\theta)^2+\text{const}\), so the score is \(x-\theta\). It has mean \(0\), as every score does, and variance \(1\). The sign matters: differentiating in \(\theta\), not in \(x\).

cards.name: Monotone & dominated convergence theorems
cards.lay: When can you pass a limit inside an expectation? If the functions increase (monotone convergence), or if they are all bounded by one integrable function (dominated convergence). These justify infinite-horizon limits and differentiating under the expectation.
cards.st: (MCT) If \(0\le f_n\uparrow f\) pointwise then \(\int f_n\to\int f\). (DCT) If \(f_n\to f\) pointwise and \(|f_n|\le g\) with \(\int g<\infty\), then \(\int f_n\to\int f\).
ver: Fatou's lemma: \(\int\liminf f_n\le\liminf\int f_n\) for \(f_n\ge0\).
Bounded convergence: if \(|f_n|\le C\) on a finite measure space, DCT applies with \(g=C\).
Conditional versions hold for conditional expectations.
Uniform integrability: the sharp condition for \({\mathbb{E}} X_n\to{\mathbb{E}} X\) given \(X_n\to X\) in probability (Vitali).
cards.det: DCT is the technical backbone of differentiating under the integral sign Log-derivative (score-function) trick & differentiating under the integral (needed for the policy gradient theorem with continuous actions) and of optional stopping Optional stopping theorem, where you need \({\mathbb{E}} X_{\tau\wedge n}\to{\mathbb{E}} X_\tau\).
cards.ex: \(V^\pi(s)=\lim_{H\to\infty}{\mathbb{E}}\sum_{t<H}\gamma^tr_t\): partial sums are dominated by \(\tfrac{R_{\max}}{1-\gamma}\), so DCT allows the limit to be moved inside.
cards.use: Infinite-horizon limits, policy gradient regularity, optional stopping, convergence of EM iterates in expectation, average-reward limits.

qz.q: On \([0,1]\) let \(f_n=n\,{\mathbf{1}}_{(0,1/n)}\). Then \(f_n\to0\) pointwise but \(\int f_n=1\) for all \(n\). Which hypothesis of dominated convergence fails?
a: No integrable \(g\) has \(|f_n|\le g\) for all \(n\)
qz.why: Any dominating function must be at least \(\sup_nf_n(x)\approx1/x\), which is not integrable on \([0,1]\). The \(f_n\) are measurable, non-negative and converge pointwise to \(0\); mass escaping into a spike is exactly what domination rules out.

qz.q: Which statement holds for every sequence of non-negative measurable functions \(f_n\)?
qz.why: This is Fatou's lemma: mass can be lost in the limit but not created. The spike \(f_n=n{\mathbf{1}}_{(0,1/n)}\) has \(\int\liminf f_n=0<1=\liminf\int f_n\), which breaks the other three options. The reverse (limsup) version needs an integrable dominating function.

qz.q: \(X_n\to X\) almost surely and \(\sup_n{\mathbb{E}} X_n^2<\infty\). Does \({\mathbb{E}} X_n\to{\mathbb{E}} X\)?
a: Yes: bounded second moments give uniform integrability
No: one needs a pointwise integrable dominating \(g\)
qz.why: \({\mathbb{E}}|X_n|{\mathbf{1}}\{|X_n|>K\}\le{\mathbb{E}} X_n^2/K\) uniformly in \(n\), so the family is UI, and Vitali gives convergence of means. DCT is sufficient but not necessary. A bounded first moment alone is not enough: the spike \(f_n\) has \({\mathbb{E}} f_n=1\) but limit \(0\).

cards.name: Danskin's theorem / envelope theorem
cards.lay: The derivative of an optimal value with respect to a parameter equals the partial derivative of the objective at the optimum — you can ignore how the optimiser moves. Explains gradients of \(\max\) functions and of value functions.
cards.st: Let \(\phi(x)=\max_{z\in Z}f(x,z)\) with \(Z\) compact and \(f(\cdot,z)\) differentiable, \(f\), \( abla_xf\) continuous. Then \(\phi\) is directionally differentiable and its subdifferential is \[ \partial\phi(x)=\mathrm{conv}\{ abla_xf(x,z^\star):z^\star\in{\operatorname*{arg\,max}}_zf(x,z)\}. \] If the maximiser is unique, \( abla\phi(x)= abla_xf(x,z^\star(x))\).
ver: Envelope theorem (economics form): \(\tfrac{{\mathrm{d}}}{{\mathrm{d}}\theta}\max_zf(z,\theta)=\partial_\theta f(z^\star,\theta)\).

Sensitivity of optimal value to rewards: \(\partial V^\star(\rho)/\partial r(s,a)=\tfrac{1}{1-\gamma}d^{\pi^\star}_\rho(s,a)\) when \(\pi^\star\) is unique (via the LP LP formulation of MDPs & its dual).
Min–max games: gradient of \(\min_y f(x,y)\) in \(x\) is \(\nabla_xf(x,y^\star(x))\) — used in GDA analyses for saddle points.
cards.det: In EM, the ELBO \(F(q,\theta)\) is maximised over \(q\) in the E-step; by the envelope theorem \(\nabla_\theta\log p_\theta(x)=\nabla_\theta F(q^\star_\theta,\theta)\) — another view of the Fisher identity Fisher's identity (score of the observed likelihood) and of why EM fixed points are stationary points of the likelihood.
cards.ex: Robust MDP: \(\phi(\theta)=\min_{P\in{\mathcal{P}}}V^{\pi_\theta}_P\); its gradient is the policy gradient evaluated in the worst-case model \(P^\star(\theta)\).
cards.use: Gradients of value functions w.r.t. rewards (inverse RL), robust/adversarial RL, Lagrangian methods in constrained MDPs, EM stationary-point arguments.

qz.q: Let \(\phi(x)=\max_{z\in[-1,1]}xz=|x|\). By Danskin's theorem, what is the subdifferential \(\partial\phi(0)\)?
a: Empty, since \(\phi\) is not differentiable at \(0\)
qz.why: At \(x=0\) every \(z\in[-1,1]\) is a maximiser, and \(\nabla_x(xz)=z\), so \(\partial\phi(0)=\mathrm{conv}\{z\}=[-1,1]\). Danskin returns the convex hull of the active gradients, not just the extreme ones.

qz.q: Let \(d^{\pi}_\rho(s,a)=(1-\gamma)\sum_t\gamma^t\Pr^\pi_\rho(s_t=s,a_t=a)\) be the normalised occupancy, and suppose \(\pi^\star\) is the unique optimal policy. What is \(\partial V^\star(\rho)/\partial r(s,a)\)?
qz.why: \(V^\star=\max_\pi\frac1{1-\gamma}{\langle d^\pi_\rho, r\rangle}\). By the envelope theorem you differentiate at the fixed maximiser \(\pi^\star\) and ignore how \(\pi^\star\) moves with \(r\). Dropping \(\frac1{1-\gamma}\) confuses the normalised occupancy with the unnormalised one.

qz.q: The ELBO satisfies \(F(q,\theta)\le\log p_\theta(x)\), with equality at \(q=p_\theta(\cdot|x)\). Let \(q_0=p_{\theta_0}(\cdot|x)\). What is \(\nabla_\theta\log p_\theta(x)\) at \(\theta_0\)?
a: \(\nabla_\theta F(q_0,\theta)\) plus a non-zero term from \(\partial q_\theta/\partial\theta\)
qz.why: \(\log p_\theta(x)=\max_qF(q,\theta)\), so by the envelope theorem the movement of the optimal \(q\) contributes nothing at first order. The result is the Fisher identity Fisher's identity (score of the observed likelihood). A non-optimal \(q\) leaves a gap whose gradient is not zero in general.

cards.name: Grönwall's inequality (continuous & discrete)
cards.lay: If a quantity grows at most in proportion to itself (plus a forcing term), it is bounded by the corresponding exponential. The discrete version controls accumulated errors in recursive estimates.
cards.st: (Integral form) If \(u(t)\le\alpha+\int_0^t\beta(s)u(s){\mathrm{d}} s\) with \(\beta\ge0\), then \(u(t)\le\alpha\exp\bigl(\int_0^t\beta\bigr)\). (Discrete) If \(u_{n+1}\le(1+b_n)u_n+a_n\) with \(a_n,b_n\ge0\), then \[ u_n\le\Bigl(u_0+\sum_{k<n}a_k\Bigr)\exp\Bigl(\sum_{k<n}b_k\Bigr). \]
ver: Differential form: \(u'\le\beta u\Rightarrow u(t)\le u(0)e^{\int_0^t\beta}\).
Contracting version: \(u_{n+1}\le(1-c_n)u_n+a_n\) with \(c_n\in[0,1]\) gives \(u_n\le u_0\prod_k(1-c_k)+\sum_k a_k\prod_{j>k}(1-c_j)\) — see Recursion lemmas for SA rates (Chung's lemma) for rates.
Bihari–LaSalle: nonlinear generalisation \(u'\le\beta\,w(u)\).
cards.det: Grönwall is central to the ODE method in stochastic approximation ODE method (Borkar–Meyn) & two-timescale SA: it bounds how far an interpolated noisy iterate drifts from the true ODE trajectory over a finite time window. The discrete version also controls error growth in multi-step model rollouts (compounding errors \(\propto(1+L{\varepsilon})^H\)).
cards.ex: Model rollouts: if the learned dynamics \(\hat f\) has one-step error \({\varepsilon}\) and \(f\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz, the \(H\)-step state error satisfies \(e_{h+1}\le Le_h+{\varepsilon}\), so \(e_H\le{\varepsilon}\tfrac{L^H-1}{L-1}\) — exponential compounding unless \(L\le1\).
cards.use: ODE method for SA/TD/Q-learning, compounding errors in model-based RL, stability of continuous-time policy dynamics, tracking drifting targets.

qz.q: In a model rollout the state error obeys \(e_{h+1}=Le_h+{\varepsilon}\) with \(e_0=0\) and \(L=2\) (equality). What is \(e_H\)?
qz.why: Unrolling gives \(e_H={\varepsilon}\sum_{j<H}L^j={\varepsilon}\frac{L^H-1}{L-1}\). With \(L>1\) the errors compound exponentially. The linear rate \(H{\varepsilon}\) is the case \(L=1\), and \(L<1\) gives a bounded error \(\le\frac{{\varepsilon}}{1-L}\).

qz.q: A sequence \(u_n\ge0\) satisfies \(u_{n+1}\le(1+b_n)u_n\) with \(b_n\ge0\) and \(\sum_nb_n<\infty\). Which conclusion holds?
a: \(u_n\) may grow without bound, but at most linearly
No bound follows without a forcing term
qz.why: Discrete Grönwall: \(u_n\le u_0\prod_{k<n}(1+b_k)\le u_0e^{\sum_kb_k}\) Exponential bounds: \(1+x\le e^x\) and friends, a bounded quantity. Nothing forces decay: \(b_n=0\) gives \(u_n=u_0\). With \(b_n=1/n\) the product grows like \(n\), which is why summability matters.

qz.q: A contracting recursion \(u_{n+1}=(1-c)u_n+a\) has \(c=0.1\) and \(a=1\). What is \(\lim_nu_n\)?
qz.why: The fixed point solves \(u=(1-c)u+a\), so \(u=a/c=10\), and \(u_n\to a/c\) geometrically. \(\frac{1}{0.9}=\frac{a}{1-c}\) divides by the contraction factor instead of the gap \(c\), \(1=a\) ignores the accumulation, and \(100=a/c^2\) squares the gap. The same mechanism gives the \({\varepsilon}/(1-\gamma)\) floor in approximate DP Geometric series & discounted sums.

cards.name: Implicit & inverse function theorems
cards.lay: If an equation \(F(x,y)=0\) has a non-degenerate solution, then near it \(y\) is a smooth function of \(x\), and its derivative is computable. Used to differentiate fixed points (e.g. \(\theta^\star\) of EM or of a Bellman equation) with respect to parameters.
cards.st: Let \(F:{\mathbb{R}}^n\times{\mathbb{R}}^m\to{\mathbb{R}}^m\) be \(C^1\) with \(F(x_0,y_0)=0\) and \(\partial_yF(x_0,y_0)\) invertible. Then near \(x_0\) there is a unique \(C^1\) map \(y(x)\) with \(F(x,y(x))=0\) and \[ Dy(x)=-[\partial_yF(x,y(x))]^{-1}\partial_xF(x,y(x)). \]
ver: Inverse function theorem: if \(Df(x_0)\) is invertible, \(f\) is a local \(C^1\) diffeomorphism.

Fixed points: if \(x=G(x,\theta)\) with \({\lVert \partial_xG\rVert}<1\), then \(\tfrac{{\mathrm{d}} x^\star}{{\mathrm{d}}\theta}=(I-\partial_xG)^{-1}\partial_\theta G\) — e.g. \(\tfrac{\partial V^\pi}{\partial\theta}=(I-\gamma P^\pi)^{-1}\tfrac{\partial(r^\pi+\gamma P^\pi V)}{\partial\theta}\).
cards.det: Differentiating the Bellman fixed point in this way is another derivation of the policy gradient theorem Policy gradient theorem. Differentiating the EM fixed point \(\theta^\star=M(\theta^\star)\) shows the EM rate is governed by the Jacobian \(DM(\theta^\star)\), the fraction of missing information Missing-information principle (Louis) & EM's convergence rate.
cards.ex: Bilevel/meta-RL hypergradients: \( frac{{\mathrm{d}}}{{\mathrm{d}}\phi}L( heta^\star(\phi))\) with \( abla_ heta g( heta^\star,\phi)=0\) uses \(D heta^\star=-[ abla^2_ heta g]^{-1} abla^2_{ heta\phi}g\).
cards.use: Differentiating value fixed points, EM convergence rate, bilevel optimisation, sensitivity of equilibria in games.

qz.q: \(x^\star(\theta)\) solves the fixed-point equation \(x=G(x,\theta)\), where \({\lVert \partial_xG\rVert}<1\) near the solution. What is \(\frac{{\mathrm{d}} x^\star}{{\mathrm{d}}\theta}\)?
qz.why: Apply the implicit function theorem to \(F(x,\theta)=x-G(x,\theta)\): \(\partial_xF=I-\partial_xG\) is invertible because \({\lVert \partial_xG\rVert}<1\), and \(Dx^\star=-(\partial_xF)^{-1}\partial_\theta F\). Dropping the \((I-\partial_xG)^{-1}\) factor ignores how the change feeds back through the fixed point.

qz.q: \(V^\pi=r^\pi+\gamma P^\pi V^\pi\). If the reward vector changes to \(r^\pi+\Delta\) (with \(\pi\) fixed), how does \(V^\pi\) change?
qz.why: The fixed point is linear in \(r^\pi\), and the IFT/fixed-point formula gives \(\partial V/\partial r=(I-\gamma P^\pi)^{-1}\). The change is exact, not just first order. \(\Delta/(1-\gamma)\) is correct only when \(\Delta\) is constant across states; in general it is only the sup-norm bound \({\lVert \Delta\rVert}_\infty/(1-\gamma)\).

qz.q: Consider \(F(x,y)=y^2-x\) near \((x_0,y_0)=(0,0)\), where \(\partial_yF(0,0)=0\). What happens?
qz.why: For \(x<0\) there is no solution and for \(x>0\) there are two (\(\pm\sqrt x\)), neither differentiable at \(0\). This is exactly what invertibility of \(\partial_yF\) rules out. For EM it is the analogue of a singular \(I-DM(\theta^\star)\) (no missing-information gap) Missing-information principle (Louis) & EM's convergence rate.

cards.name: Union bound (Boole's inequality)
cards.lay: The chance that at least one of several bad things happens is at most the sum of their individual chances. It is crude but costs only a logarithm when combined with exponential tail bounds — the standard way to make a bound hold for all states, actions and times simultaneously.
cards.st: For any events \(A_1,A_2,\dots\) (finite or countable): \[ \Pr\Bigl(\bigcup_iA_i\Bigr)\le\sum_i\Pr(A_i). \]
ver: Confidence splitting: to make \(N\) events each fail with total probability \(\le\delta\), allocate \(\delta/N\) to each; with Hoeffding this inflates widths by \(\sqrt{\log(N/\delta)}\) instead of \(\sqrt{\log(1/\delta)}\).
Anytime split: allocate \(\delta_t=\tfrac{\delta}{t(t+1)}\) (sums to \(\delta\)) or \(\tfrac{6\delta}{\pi^2t^2}\) to cover all times \(t\ge1\).
Bonferroni inequalities: alternating partial inclusion–exclusion sums give upper/lower bounds.
Expectation form: \({\mathbb{E}}\max_iX_i\le\sum_i{\mathbb{E}} X_i^+\); for tails, \(\Pr(\max_iX_i>t)\le\sum_i\Pr(X_i>t)\) Maximal inequality for sub-Gaussian maxima.
cards.det: Union bounds are where the “\(\log\)” factors of RL come from. In tabular RL one typically unions over all \((s,a)\) pairs, all counts \(n\le T\), and sometimes all value functions in a finite set, giving \(\log(SAT/\delta)\). When the set is infinite (all value functions), one unions over a cover instead Covering & packing numbers (volumetric bound), or uses a chaining/martingale argument to avoid the loss.
cards.ex: For \(K\) arms, Hoeffding + union bound over arms and pulls \(n\le T\): with probability \(\ge1-\delta\), simultaneously for all \(a,n\): \(|\hat\mu_{a,n}-\mu_a|\le\sqrt{\tfrac{\log(2KT/\delta)}{2n}}\).
cards.use: Every high-probability guarantee: uniform confidence sets over states/actions/time, finite-class generalisation, good-event arguments in regret analysis.

qz.q: \(K\) arms, rewards in \([0,1]\), \(\hat\mu_{a,n}\) = mean of the first \(n\) pulls of arm \(a\). For one fixed \((a,n)\) Hoeffding gives \(|\hat\mu_{a,n}-\mu_a|\le\sqrt{\log(2/\delta')/(2n)}\) w.p. \(\ge1-\delta'\). Which width holds w.p. \(\ge1-\delta\) simultaneously for all arms \(a\) and all \(n\le T\)?
qz.why: There are \(KT\) events; giving each failure probability \(\delta'=\delta/(KT)\) makes the total at most \(\delta\), so only the logarithm grows. Multiplying the width by \(\sqrt{KT}\) would be the cost of a much cruder argument, not of the union bound.

qz.q: To make a confidence bound hold at every time \(t\ge1\) with total failure probability at most \(\delta\), you run the time-\(t\) bound at level \(\delta_t\). Which choice of \(\delta_t\) works?
qz.why: The union bound needs \(\sum_t\delta_t\le\delta\), and \(\sum_t\tfrac{1}{t(t+1)}=1\) (telescoping). The harmonic-type choices \(\delta/t\) or \(\delta/(t+1)\) have divergent sums, so they give no guarantee at all.

qz.q: For events \(A_1,\dots,A_N\), when is \(\Pr(\bigcup_iA_i)\le\sum_i\Pr(A_i)\) valid, and when is it tight?
a: Valid for any dependence; equality if the \(A_i\) are disjoint
Valid only for independent \(A_i\); equality if disjoint
Valid for any dependence; equality if the \(A_i\) are independent
Valid only for pairwise independent \(A_i\); never tight
qz.why: The union bound needs no independence at all, which is why it is used everywhere; it loses exactly the overlaps, so it is an equality for disjoint events. For independent events with positive probabilities the overlaps are positive, so the bound is strict.

cards.name: Markov's inequality
cards.lay: A non-negative random variable is rarely much larger than its mean: it exceeds \(k\) times its mean with probability at most \(1/k\). Every other tail bound is Markov applied to a cleverly chosen function.
cards.st: For \(X\ge0\) and \(t>0\): \[ \Pr(X\ge t)\le\frac{{\mathbb{E}} X}{t}. \]
ver: For any non-decreasing \(\phi\ge0\): \(\Pr(X\ge t)\le\tfrac{{\mathbb{E}}\phi(X)}{\phi(t)}\).
Chebyshev: \(\phi(x)=x^2\) applied to \(|X-{\mathbb{E}} X|\) Chebyshev's inequality (and Cantelli); Chernoff: \(\phi(x)=e^{\lambda x}\) Chernoff bound / Cramér–Chernoff method.
Expectation-to-high-probability: if \({\mathbb{E}}[{\mathrm{Reg}}]\le B\) then \(\Pr({\mathrm{Reg}}\ge B/\delta)\le\delta\) (poor \(1/\delta\) dependence).
Reverse Markov: if \(X\le M\) a.s. then \(\Pr(X>t)\ge\tfrac{{\mathbb{E}} X-t}{M-t}\) for \(t<{\mathbb{E}} X\).
cards.det:
Proof. \(t{\mathbf{1}}\{X\ge t\}\le X\); take expectations.

Ville's inequality Ville's inequality & method of mixtures (time-uniform bounds) is the time-uniform analogue for non-negative supermartingales: the probability that the process ever exceeds \(1/\delta\) is at most \(\delta\) times its initial value.
cards.ex: A policy-evaluation estimator with \({\mathbb{E}}|\widehat V-V|\le{\varepsilon}\) satisfies \(|\widehat V-V|\le10{\varepsilon}\) with probability \(\ge0.9\); median-of-means boosts this to \(\log(1/\delta)\) dependence.
cards.use: Converting expectation bounds into probability bounds, deriving Chebyshev/Chernoff, median-of-means arguments, Ville's inequality for anytime-valid confidence sequences.

qz.q: An algorithm has \({\mathbb{E}}[{\mathrm{Reg}}]\le B\) with \({\mathrm{Reg}}\ge0\). Using Markov's inequality only, which threshold \(u\) guarantees \(\Pr({\mathrm{Reg}}\ge u)\le\delta\)?
qz.why: Markov: \(\Pr({\mathrm{Reg}}\ge u)\le B/u\), which equals \(\delta\) at \(u=B/\delta\). A \(\log(1/\delta)\) dependence needs exponential tails (e.g. a martingale argument), which Markov cannot give.

qz.q: Let \(Y=X-{\mathbb{E}} X\) for a random variable \(X\). Why can you not bound \(\Pr(Y\ge t)\) by \({\mathbb{E}} Y/t\) via Markov's inequality?
a: Markov needs \(Y\ge0\); here it would give the absurd bound \(0\)
Markov needs \(Y\) to have finite variance
Markov needs \(Y\) to be bounded almost surely
Markov needs \(Y\) to have a continuous distribution
qz.why: The proof uses \(t{\mathbf{1}}\{Y\ge t\}\le Y\), which requires \(Y\ge0\). Markov needs only non-negativity and a finite mean; variance, boundedness and continuity play no role.

qz.q: \(X\in[0,1]\) almost surely with \({\mathbb{E}} X=\tfrac12\). What is the largest \(p\) such that \(\Pr(X>\tfrac14)\ge p\) for every such \(X\)?
qz.why: Reverse Markov: \(\Pr(X>t)\ge\tfrac{{\mathbb{E}} X-t}{M-t}=\tfrac{1/4}{3/4}=\tfrac13\), and it is attained by \(X=1\) w.p. \(\tfrac13\), \(X=\tfrac14\) w.p. \(\tfrac23\) (mean \(\tfrac12\)). So \(\tfrac12\) is not guaranteed and \(\tfrac14\) is valid but not the largest.

cards.name: Chebyshev's inequality (and Cantelli)
cards.lay: A random variable is unlikely to be many standard deviations from its mean: \(k\) standard deviations happens with probability at most \(1/k^2\). Requires only a finite variance.
cards.st: For \(X\) with mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\), and \(t>0\): \[ \Pr(|X-\mu|\ge t)\le\frac{\sigma^2}{t^2}. \]
ver: Sample mean of \(n\) i.i.d. copies: \(\Pr(|\bar X_n-\mu|\ge t)\le\tfrac{\sigma^2}{nt^2}\) (weak law of large numbers).
Cantelli (one-sided): \(\Pr(X-\mu\ge t)\le\tfrac{\sigma^2}{\sigma^2+t^2}\).
Higher moments: \(\Pr(|X-\mu|\ge t)\le\tfrac{{\mathbb{E}}|X-\mu|^p}{t^p}\).

Median-of-means: split \(n\) samples into \(k\asymp\log(1/\delta)\) groups; the median of group means deviates by \(O(\sigma\sqrt{\log(1/\delta)/n})\) with probability \(1-\delta\) — sub-Gaussian behaviour from only finite variance.
cards.det: Chebyshev is weak in \(\delta\) (\(1/\sqrt\delta\) rather than \(\sqrt{\log(1/\delta)}\)) but needs almost no assumptions. Median-of-means (Chebyshev for each block + a binomial/Hoeffding bound on how many blocks fail) is the standard robust alternative for heavy-tailed rewards, e.g. heavy-tailed bandits.
cards.ex: Importance-sampling off-policy estimates have finite but possibly huge variance \(\sigma^2\le{\mathbb{E}}[w^2]R_{\max}^2\); Chebyshev gives a valid (if loose) confidence interval without boundedness of the weights.
cards.use: Heavy-tailed bandits, robust mean estimation, quick sanity bounds, proving weak laws of large numbers.

qz.q: \(\bar X_n\) is the mean of \(n\) i.i.d. samples with variance \(\sigma^2\) (no other assumption). Which half-width \(t\) makes Chebyshev give \(\Pr(|\bar X_n-\mu|\ge t)\le\delta\)?
qz.why: \(\sigma^2/(nt^2)=\delta\) gives \(t=\sigma/\sqrt{n\delta}\): the right \(1/\sqrt n\) rate but a polynomial \(1/\sqrt\delta\) dependence. The \(\sqrt{\log(1/\delta)}\) form needs sub-Gaussian tails or median-of-means.

qz.q: \(X\) has mean \(\mu\) and standard deviation \(\sigma\). What is the best upper bound on the one-sided probability \(\Pr(X-\mu\ge\sigma)\) that holds for every such \(X\)?
qz.why: Cantelli: \(\Pr(X-\mu\ge t)\le\sigma^2/(\sigma^2+t^2)=\tfrac12\) at \(t=\sigma\), and it is attained by a two-point distribution. Chebyshev's \(\sigma^2/t^2=1\) is vacuous; \(e^{-1/2}\approx0.61\) is valid but looser, and \(1/4\) is violated by that two-point law.

qz.q: Rewards are i.i.d. with finite variance \(\sigma^2\) but possibly heavy tails. Which estimator of the mean deviates by \(O(\sigma\sqrt{\log(1/\delta)/n})\) w.p. \(\ge1-\delta\) for every such distribution?
a: The empirical mean of all \(n\) samples
qz.why: Chebyshev makes each block mean good with probability \(\ge3/4\), and a Hoeffding bound on the number of bad blocks makes the median good with probability \(1-\delta\). The plain empirical mean only gets \(\sigma/\sqrt{n\delta}\) under finite variance; medians target the median, not the mean, of a skewed distribution.

cards.name: Jensen's inequality
cards.lay: For a convex function, the function of the average is at most the average of the function. Moving expectations inside or outside convex/concave functions is one of the most frequent proof steps in all of theory — and the reason the EM lower bound exists.
cards.st: If \(\phi\) is convex and \(X\), \(\phi(X)\) are integrable: \[ \phi({\mathbb{E}} X)\le{\mathbb{E}}\phi(X). \] For concave \(\phi\) the inequality reverses: \({\mathbb{E}}\phi(X)\le\phi({\mathbb{E}} X)\).
ver: Finite form: \(\phi(\sum_iw_ix_i)\le\sum_iw_i\phi(x_i)\) for weights \(w_i\ge0\), \(\sum w_i=1\) (definition of convexity).
Conditional Jensen: \(\phi({\mathbb{E}}[X\mid{\mathcal{F}}])\le{\mathbb{E}}[\phi(X)\mid{\mathcal{F}}]\).

Common instances: \(({\mathbb{E}} X)^2\le{\mathbb{E}} X^2\); \({\mathbb{E}}\sqrt X\le\sqrt{{\mathbb{E}} X}\); \({\mathbb{E}}\log X\le\log{\mathbb{E}} X\); \(e^{{\mathbb{E}} X}\le{\mathbb{E}} e^X\); \(|{\mathbb{E}} X|\le{\mathbb{E}}|X|\); \({\lVert {\mathbb{E}} X\rVert}\le{\mathbb{E}}{\lVert X\rVert}\).
EM/variational: \(\log p(x)=\log{\mathbb{E}}_{q}\bigl[\tfrac{p(x,z)}{q(z)}\bigr]\ge{\mathbb{E}}_q\log\tfrac{p(x,z)}{q(z)}\) — the ELBO ELBO decomposition (free-energy view of EM).
Gap control: \({\mathbb{E}}\phi(X)-\phi({\mathbb{E}} X)\le\tfrac{L}{2}{\operatorname{Var}} X\) for \(L\)-smooth \(\phi\); Jensen gap equals a Bregman divergence in expectation.
cards.det:
Proof. Convex \(\phi\) lies above a supporting line at \(\mu={\mathbb{E}} X\): \(\phi(x)\ge\phi(\mu)+g(x-\mu)\). Take expectations; the linear term vanishes.

Jensen proves: Gibbs' inequality \({\mathrm{KL}}\ge0\) KL divergence & Gibbs' inequality; the EM lower bound ELBO decomposition (free-energy view of EM); AM–GM AM–GM inequality; \({\mathbb{E}}\max\ge\max{\mathbb{E}}\) (optimism bias of maximising over noisy estimates — the reason Q-learning overestimates and double Q-learning exists).
cards.ex: Overestimation in Q-learning: \({\mathbb{E}}[\max_a\widehat Q(s,a)]\ge\max_a{\mathbb{E}}[\widehat Q(s,a)]=\max_aQ(s,a)\) when \(\widehat Q\) is unbiased, because \(\max\) is convex.
cards.use: ELBO/EM derivations, KL non-negativity, maximisation bias, converting second-moment bounds to first-moment bounds, convexity-based regret bounds, \(\sqrt{\cdot}\) of sums of variances.

qz.q: For each action \(a\), \(\widehat Q(s,a)\) is an unbiased estimate of \(Q(s,a)\). Which relation always holds?
a: \(\ge\) holds only if errors are independent across \(a\)
qz.why: \(\max\) is convex, so Jensen gives \({\mathbb{E}}\max_a\widehat Q\ge\max_a{\mathbb{E}}\widehat Q=\max_aQ\) for any dependence between the errors. This is the overestimation bias that double Q-learning is designed to remove.

qz.q: Which inequality is true for every positive, integrable random variable \(X\) (with the relevant moments finite)?
qz.why: \(\log\) is concave, so \({\mathbb{E}}\log X\le\log{\mathbb{E}} X\). The others are reversed: \(\sqrt{\cdot}\) is concave (so \({\mathbb{E}}\sqrt X\le\sqrt{{\mathbb{E}} X}\)), while \(1/x\) and \(x^2\) are convex.

qz.q: In the EM lower bound \(\log p(x)=\log{\mathbb{E}}_{q}\bigl[\tfrac{p(x,z)}{q(z)}\bigr]\ge{\mathbb{E}}_q\log\tfrac{p(x,z)}{q(z)}\), what is the gap between the two sides?
qz.why: Writing \(p(x,z)=p(x)p(z\mid x)\) gives \({\mathbb{E}}_q\log\tfrac{p(x,z)}{q(z)}=\log p(x)-{\mathrm{KL}}(q\|p(\cdot\mid x))\), so Jensen is tight exactly when \(q\) is the posterior (the E-step). The reverse KL is the wrong direction; the prior KL is one term of the ELBO, not the gap ELBO decomposition (free-energy view of EM).

cards.name: Tower property & law of total expectation
cards.plain: Tower property & law of total expectation
cards.lay: Averaging in stages gives the same answer as averaging all at once: first average over what you don't know given partial information, then average over the partial information. This is the probabilistic content of the Bellman equation.
cards.st: For integrable \(X\) and \(\sigma\)-algebras \({\mathcal{F}}_1\subseteq{\mathcal{F}}_2\): \[ {\mathbb{E}}\bigl[{\mathbb{E}}[X\mid{\mathcal{F}}_2]\bigm|{\mathcal{F}}_1\bigr]={\mathbb{E}}[X\mid{\mathcal{F}}_1],\qquad{\mathbb{E}}\bigl[{\mathbb{E}}[X\mid Y]\bigr]={\mathbb{E}} X. \]
ver: Taking out what is known: \({\mathbb{E}}[ZX\mid{\mathcal{F}}]=Z{\mathbb{E}}[X\mid{\mathcal{F}}]\) if \(Z\) is \({\mathcal{F}}\)-measurable.
Bellman: \(V^\pi(s)={\mathbb{E}}[r_0+\gamma{\mathbb{E}}[G_1\mid s_1]\mid s_0=s]={\mathbb{E}}[r_0+\gamma V^\pi(s_1)\mid s_0=s]\) (Markov property + tower).
Law of total probability: \(\Pr(A)=\sum_i\Pr(A\mid B_i)\Pr(B_i)\).
Martingale differences: \({\mathbb{E}}[\xi_t\mid{\mathcal{F}}_{t-1}]=0\Rightarrow{\mathbb{E}}[\sum_tZ_t\xi_t]=0\) for predictable \(Z_t\).
cards.det: Most regret proofs condition on the history \({\mathcal{F}}_{t-1}\), bound a conditional expectation, then use the tower property to remove the conditioning. The difference between a quantity and its conditional expectation is a martingale difference — the starting point for Azuma/Freedman Azuma–Hoeffding inequality (martingales), Freedman's inequality (martingale Bernstein).
cards.ex: Unbiasedness of the TD target given \(s\): \({\mathbb{E}}[r+\gamma V^\pi(s')\mid s]=(T^\pi V^\pi)(s)=V^\pi(s)\), so \(\delta_t=r_t+\gamma V^\pi(s_{t+1})-V^\pi(s_t)\) is a martingale difference sequence.
cards.use: Bellman equations, martingale constructions, regret decompositions, conditioning on good events, Wald's identity, EM's E-step.

qz.q: Actions follow \(\pi\), \(T^\pi V=r^\pi+\gamma P^\pi V\), and \(\delta_t=r_t+\gamma V(s_{t+1})-V(s_t)\) for an arbitrary function \(V\). What is \({\mathbb{E}}[\delta_t\mid s_t]\)?
qz.why: Conditioning on \(s_t\) and averaging over \(a_t,r_t,s_{t+1}\) gives the Bellman backup of \(V\) minus \(V\); it is \(0\) only when \(V=V^\pi\) (then \(\delta_t\) is a martingale difference). Dropping \(r^\pi\) forgets the expected reward.

qz.q: \((\xi_t)\) is a martingale difference sequence for the filtration \(({\mathcal{F}}_t)\), i.e. \({\mathbb{E}}[\xi_t\mid{\mathcal{F}}_{t-1}]=0\), and all products are integrable. For which \(Z_t\) does \({\mathbb{E}}[Z_t\xi_t]=0\) follow?
qz.why: If \(Z_t\) is known at time \(t-1\), \({\mathbb{E}}[Z_t\xi_t]={\mathbb{E}}[Z_t{\mathbb{E}}[\xi_t\mid{\mathcal{F}}_{t-1}]]=0\) (taking out what is known + tower). With \(Z_t=\xi_t\) (bounded and \({\mathcal{F}}_t\)-measurable) one gets \({\mathbb{E}}\xi_t^2>0\).

qz.q: Let \({\mathcal{F}}_1\subseteq{\mathcal{F}}_2\) be \(\sigma\)-algebras and \(X\) integrable. What is \({\mathbb{E}}\bigl[{\mathbb{E}}[X\mid{\mathcal{F}}_1]\bigm|{\mathcal{F}}_2\bigr]\)?
qz.why: \({\mathbb{E}}[X\mid{\mathcal{F}}_1]\) is \({\mathcal{F}}_1\)- hence \({\mathcal{F}}_2\)-measurable, so conditioning on \({\mathcal{F}}_2\) leaves it unchanged; in the other order the tower property also gives \({\mathbb{E}}[X\mid{\mathcal{F}}_1]\). The coarser \(\sigma\)-algebra always wins.

cards.name: Change of measure / importance sampling identity
cards.plain: Change of measure / importance sampling identity
cards.lay: You can compute an average under distribution \(P\) using samples from \(Q\) by reweighting each sample by the likelihood ratio \(P/Q\). It underlies off-policy evaluation, the KL chain rule and most lower-bound proofs.
cards.st: If \(P\ll Q\) (absolute continuity) with Radon–Nikodym derivative \(w={\mathrm{d}} P/{\mathrm{d}} Q\), then for integrable \(f\): \[ {\mathbb{E}}_P[f(X)]={\mathbb{E}}_Q\bigl[w(X)f(X)\bigr]. \]
ver: Trajectory ratio: for policies \(\pi\) (target) and \(\mu\) (behaviour) in the same MDP, \(\tfrac{{\mathrm{d}} P^\pi}{{\mathrm{d}} P^\mu}(\tau)=\prod_t\tfrac{\pi(a_t|s_t)}{\mu(a_t|s_t)}\) — dynamics cancel.

Variance: \({\operatorname{Var}}_Q(wf)={\mathbb{E}}_P[wf^2]-({\mathbb{E}}_Pf)^2\le{\lVert f\rVert}_\infty^2(1+\chi^2(P\|Q))-({\mathbb{E}}_Pf)^2\) \(f\)-divergences: Hellinger, \(\chi^2\) and their relations.
Self-normalised IS: \(\hat\mu=\tfrac{\sum_iw_if(x_i)}{\sum_iw_i}\), biased but lower variance.

Lower-bound (likelihood-ratio) form: \(\Pr_P(A)={\mathbb{E}}_Q[w{\mathbf{1}}_A]\), so if \(w\) is not too small on \(A\), \(A\) is likely under \(P\) too — basis of the Lai–Robbins argument Lai–Robbins asymptotic lower bound.
Marginalised IS: using state-action occupancy ratios \(\tfrac{d^\pi(s,a)}{d^\mu(s,a)}\) instead of trajectory products avoids exponential-in-horizon variance.
cards.det: \({\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)={\mathbb{E}}_P\log w\) and \(\chi^2(P\|Q)={\mathbb{E}}_Qw^2-1\) are both expressed via the likelihood ratio, which is why these divergences control importance-sampling error. Trajectory-level IS weights have variance growing like \((\max\tfrac{\pi}{\mu})^{2H}\) — the curse of horizon in off-policy evaluation.
cards.ex: Off-policy evaluation: \(V^\pi={\mathbb{E}}_{\tau\sim\mu}\bigl[\prod_{t<H}\tfrac{\pi(a_t|s_t)}{\mu(a_t|s_t)}\sum_t r_t\bigr]\); per-decision IS uses only the prefix product up to \(t\) for reward \(r_t\).
cards.use: Off-policy evaluation, EXP3's importance-weighted loss estimates EXP3 & importance-weighted loss estimators, lower-bound constructions, Girsanov-type arguments, PPO/TRPO surrogate objectives.

qz.q: Off-policy evaluation in an MDP with unknown transitions: trajectories come from behaviour policy \(\mu\), target is \(\pi\). What do you need to compute the trajectory weight \(\tfrac{{\mathrm{d}} P^\pi}{{\mathrm{d}} P^\mu}(\tau)\)?
qz.why: Both trajectory laws contain the same transition factors, which cancel, leaving \(\prod_t\pi(a_t|s_t)/\mu(a_t|s_t)\). Occupancy ratios are a different (marginalised) estimator, and a deterministic \(\mu\) breaks absolute continuity for stochastic \(\pi\).

qz.q: At some state \(s\) reachable under \(\pi\), the target policy takes action \(a\) with \(\pi(a|s)>0\) but the behaviour policy has \(\mu(a|s)=0\). What happens to the ordinary trajectory importance-sampling estimate of \(V^\pi\)?
a: It is unbiased but has infinite variance
It is unbiased, since the weights compensate
It is biased, but self-normalising removes the bias
qz.why: \({\mathbb{E}}_\mu[wG]\) only sums over trajectories that \(\mu\) can produce, so the contribution of trajectories using \(a\) at \(s\) is missing: the identity needs \(P^\pi\ll P^\mu\). No reweighting of the observed data can recover that missing mass; self-normalised IS is itself biased.

qz.q: In every state, \(\mu\) is uniform over two actions and \(\pi\) plays them with probabilities \((0.9,0.1)\). What is \({\mathbb{E}}_\mu[W_H^2]\) for the \(H\)-step weight \(W_H=\prod_{t<H}\pi(a_t|s_t)/\mu(a_t|s_t)\)?
qz.why: Per step \({\mathbb{E}}_\mu[\rho^2]=\tfrac12(1.8^2+0.2^2)=1.64=1+\chi^2(\pi\|\mu)\), the same in every state, so the tower property multiplies these: \(1.64^H\). This exponential growth is the curse of horizon in off-policy evaluation.

cards.name: Law of total variance (and the variance of returns)
cards.plain: Law of total variance (and the variance of returns)
cards.lay: Total variance = average within-group variance + variance of the group means. In RL, applied recursively over time, it shows that the sum of per-step conditional variances of \(V\) equals the variance of the return — which is bounded by \(H^2\) rather than \(H^3\). This is the key to horizon-optimal bounds.
cards.st: For square-integrable \(X\) and any random variable \(Y\): \[ {\operatorname{Var}}(X)={\mathbb{E}}\bigl[{\operatorname{Var}}(X\mid Y)\bigr]+{\operatorname{Var}}\bigl({\mathbb{E}}[X\mid Y]\bigr). \]
ver: Finite-horizon RL (Azar et al., 2013/2017): \({\mathbb{E}}\Bigl[\sum_{h=1}^H{\operatorname{Var}}_{P_h(\cdot|s_h,a_h)}(V^\pi_{h+1})\Bigr]={\operatorname{Var}}\Bigl(\sum_hr_h\Bigr)\le H^2\) for rewards in \([0,1]\).

Discounted: \(\bigl\|(I-\gamma P^\pi)^{-1}\sigma_{V^\pi}\bigr\|_\infty\le\sqrt{\tfrac{2}{(1-\gamma)^3}}\) where \(\sigma_V(s)=\sqrt{{\operatorname{Var}}_{P(\cdot|s,\pi(s))}(V)}\) (Azar, Munos, Kappen 2013).

Conditional version: \({\operatorname{Var}}(X\mid{\mathcal{F}}_1)={\mathbb{E}}[{\operatorname{Var}}(X\mid{\mathcal{F}}_2)\mid{\mathcal{F}}_1]+{\operatorname{Var}}({\mathbb{E}}[X\mid{\mathcal{F}}_2]\mid{\mathcal{F}}_1)\).
cards.det: Naively each per-step variance is at most \(H^2\), so the sum over \(H\) steps is \(H^3\), leading to \(\sqrt{H^3}\) factors. The total-variance identity (applied to the return, with \(Y\) the history) shows the sum is in fact only \(H^2\) in expectation. Combined with Bernstein Bernstein's inequality or Freedman Freedman's inequality (martingale Bernstein) bonuses, this gives minimax-optimal \(\sqrt{H^2SAT}\)-type regret (UCBVI-Bernstein, Azar et al. 2017) and the \((1-\gamma)^{-3}\) sample complexity of model-based RL with a generative model.
cards.ex: Two-stage experiment: pick a coin with bias \(B\sim\mathrm{Unif}\{0.2,0.8\}\), flip it. \({\operatorname{Var}}(X)={\mathbb{E}}[B(1-B)]+{\operatorname{Var}}(B)=0.16+0.09=0.25\), consistent with \(X\sim\mathrm{Ber}(0.5)\).
cards.use: Horizon-optimal regret and sample complexity (variance-aware bonuses), Bernstein-based confidence sets, variance of off-policy estimators, Bayesian variance decompositions.

qz.q: Pick \(B\) uniformly from \(\{0.1,0.9\}\), then flip a coin \(X\sim\mathrm{Ber}(B)\). What are \({\mathbb{E}}[{\operatorname{Var}}(X\mid B)]\) and \({\operatorname{Var}}({\mathbb{E}}[X\mid B])\)?
