qz.why: \(\tfrac v{b^2}\cdot\tfrac12(\tfrac{bt}v)^2=\tfrac{t^2}{2v}\): a Gaussian tail with the true variance \(v\), the same leading behaviour as Bernstein. The range \(b\) only matters in the large-deviation regime.

cards.name: Sub-exponential variables & Bernstein condition
cards.lay: Some variables (squares of Gaussians, products, exponential waiting times) have heavier, exponential tails. They still concentrate, but with a two-regime tail: Gaussian for small deviations, exponential for large ones.
cards.st: \(X\) (mean \(\mu\)) is \(( u,\alpha)\)-sub-exponential if \({\mathbb{E}} e^{\lambda(X-\mu)}\le e^{ u^2\lambda^2/2}\) for \(|\lambda|<1/\alpha\). Then \[ \Pr(|X-\mu|\ge t)\le2\exp\Bigl(-\min\Bigl\{ rac{t^2}{2 u^2}, rac{t}{2\alpha}\Bigr\}\Bigr). \] For independent sub-exponential \(X_i\), \(\sum X_i\) is \((\sqrt{\sum u_i^2},\max\alpha_i)\)-sub-exponential.
ver: \(\psi_1\)-norm characterisation: \({\lVert X\rVert}_{\psi_1}=\inf\{K:{\mathbb{E}} e^{|X|/K}\le2\}\); \({\lVert XY\rVert}_{\psi_1}\le{\lVert X\rVert}_{\psi_2}{\lVert Y\rVert}_{\psi_2}\).
Chi-square: \(\sum_{i=1}^nZ_i^2\) satisfies \(\Pr(|\tfrac1n\sum Z_i^2-1|\ge t)\le2e^{-nt^2/8}\) for \(t\in(0,1)\) (Laurent–Massart give sharp versions).
cards.det: Bernstein's inequality is exactly the concentration of sums of sub-exponential variables. Appears when analysing squared errors (least-squares losses with sub-Gaussian noise), empirical covariance matrices, and products of features with noise.
cards.ex: Least-squares value estimation: the excess loss \((f(x)-y)^2-(f^\star(x)-y)^2\) with sub-Gaussian noise is sub-exponential; Bernstein-type fast rates follow.
cards.use: Fast rates for least squares (FQI, LSTD), covariance estimation, chi-square concentration in Gaussian lower bounds.

qz.q: \(X\) is \((\nu,\alpha)\)-sub-exponential, so \(\Pr(|X-\mu|\ge t)\le2\exp(-\min\{\tfrac{t^2}{2\nu^2},\tfrac{t}{2\alpha}\})\). At which \(t\) does the tail switch from the Gaussian to the exponential regime?
qz.why: \(\tfrac{t^2}{2\nu^2}=\tfrac t{2\alpha}\) iff \(t=\nu^2/\alpha\); beyond it the linear term \(t/(2\alpha)\) is the smaller one and governs the tail.

qz.q: \(X_1,\dots,X_n\) i.i.d. \((\nu,\alpha)\)-sub-exponential, \(L=\log(2/\delta)\). W.p. \(\ge1-\delta\), \(|\bar X_n-\mu|\le\)
qz.why: The sum is \((\sqrt n u,\alpha)\)-sub-exponential, so \( ar X_n\) is \(( u/\sqrt n,\alpha/n)\); requiring both \(nt^2/(2 u^2)\ge L\) and \(nt/(2\alpha)\ge L\) gives \(t\le\max( u\sqrt{2L/n},2\alpha L/n)\). Both terms shrink with \(n\), at different rates (the Bernstein shape); \( u\sqrt{2L}/n\) would beat the CLT, and \(\alpha L/n^2\) or no linear term fails for \(L\gg n\) (e.g. exponential data).

qz.q: \(Z\sim{\mathcal{N}}(0,1)\). Why is \(Z^2\) sub-exponential but not sub-Gaussian?
a: \(Z^2\) has nonzero mean, which sub-Gaussianity forbids
\(Z^2\) is unbounded, and sub-Gaussian variables must be bounded
\({\operatorname{Var}}(Z^2)=2\) exceeds the proxy allowed for sub-Gaussians
qz.why: A sub-Gaussian tail would need \(e^{-ct^2}\); equivalently \({\mathbb{E}} e^{\lambda Z^2}=(1-2\lambda)^{-1/2}\) is finite only for \(\lambda<1/2\). Centring handles the mean, and Gaussians are unbounded yet sub-Gaussian.

cards.name: Matrix Bernstein / matrix Chernoff (Tropp)
cards.lay: Sums of independent random matrices concentrate in operator norm much like scalar sums, with an extra \(\log d\) factor for the dimension. Used to show empirical feature covariances are well-conditioned.
cards.st: Let \(X_k\) be independent symmetric \(d\times d\) random matrices with \({\mathbb{E}} X_k=0\), \({\lVert X_k\rVert}\le L\), and \(\sigma^2={\lVert \sum_k{\mathbb{E}} X_k^2\rVert}\). Then \[ \Pr\Bigl(\Bigl\|\sum_kX_k\Bigr\|\ge t\Bigr)\le2d\exp\Bigl(-\frac{t^2/2}{\sigma^2+Lt/3}\Bigr). \]
ver: Matrix Chernoff (PSD summands \(0\preceq X_k\preceq LI\), \(\mu_{\min}=\lambda_{\min}(\sum{\mathbb{E}} X_k)\)): \(\Pr(\lambda_{\min}(\sum X_k)\le(1-{\varepsilon})\mu_{\min})\le d\bigl(\tfrac{e^{-{\varepsilon}}}{(1-{\varepsilon})^{1-{\varepsilon}}}\bigr)^{\mu_{\min}/L}\).
Rectangular matrices via the Hermitian dilation; matrix Freedman for martingales (Tropp 2011).
Covariance estimation: \({\lVert \widehat\Sigma-\Sigma\rVert}\lesssim{\lVert \Sigma\rVert}\bigl(\sqrt{\tfrac{r\log d}{n}}+\tfrac{r\log d}{n}\bigr)\) with \(r\) the effective rank.
cards.det: Proof via the matrix Laplace transform and Lieb's concavity theorem Trace inequalities & von Neumann's trace inequality. In offline linear RL, matrix concentration + Weyl Weyl's inequality (eigenvalue perturbation) shows \(\widehat\Sigma\succeq\Sigma/2\) once \(n\gtrsim\tfrac{L^2}{\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma)}\log\tfrac d\delta\).
cards.ex: Random features \(\phi_i\) with \({\lVert \phi_i\rVert}^2\le L\): \(\lambda_{\min}(\tfrac1n\sum\phi_i\phi_i^\top)\ge\tfrac12\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma)\) w.h.p. once \(n\ge\tfrac{8L}{\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma)}\log\tfrac d\delta\) (matrix Chernoff).
cards.use: Offline RL with linear features, LSTD/FQI conditioning, experimental design, spectral methods.

qz.q: In matrix Bernstein for \(d\times d\) symmetric summands, \(\Pr({\lVert \sum_kX_k\rVert}\ge t)\le2d\exp(-\tfrac{t^2/2}{\sigma^2+Lt/3})\). How does the dimension enter the high-probability deviation?
a: As a factor \(d\) multiplying the deviation
As a factor \(\sqrt d\) multiplying the deviation
It does not: the deviation is dimension-free
qz.why: Setting the bound to \(\delta\) gives \(t\approx\sqrt{2\sigma^2\log(2d/\delta)}+\tfrac{2L}3\log(2d/\delta)\): the prefactor \(2d\) only adds \(\log d\). That mild \(\log d\) is what makes matrix concentration so useful.

qz.q: In Tropp's matrix Bernstein for independent zero-mean symmetric \(X_k\), the variance parameter \(\sigma^2\) is
qz.why: The operator norm of the summed second moment. The other quantities are upper bounds on it (possibly by a factor up to \(d\)), so using them would give a weaker statement.

qz.q: Offline linear RL: features with \({\lVert \phi_i\rVert}^2\le L\), population covariance \(\Sigma\). What sample size does matrix Chernoff yield (up to constants) to ensure \(\lambda_{\min}(\tfrac1n\sum\phi_i\phi_i^\top)\ge\tfrac12\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma)\) w.h.p.?
qz.why: With \(\mu_{\min}=n\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma)\) and \({\varepsilon}=\tfrac12\), matrix Chernoff gives failure \(\le d\,e^{-c\,n\lambda_{\min}/L}\), so \(n\gtrsim\tfrac{L}{\lambda_{\min}}\log\tfrac d\delta\) (the card uses constant \(8\)). Like scalar multiplicative Chernoff, the dependence on the ratio is linear, not quadratic.

cards.name: Gaussian concentration of Lipschitz functions
cards.lay: Any Lipschitz function of a standard Gaussian vector — no matter how high the dimension — is concentrated around its mean with dimension-free sub-Gaussian tails.
cards.st: (Tsirelson–Ibragimov–Sudakov) If \(X\sim{\mathcal{N}}(0,I_d)\) and \(f\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz w.r.t. \({\lVert \cdot\rVert}_2\): \[ \Pr\bigl(f(X)-{\mathbb{E}} f(X)\ge t\bigr)\le e^{-t^2/(2L^2)}. \]
ver: Norms: \({\lVert X\rVert}_2\) concentrates around \(\sqrt d\) with \(O(1)\) fluctuations.
Log-Sobolev route (Herbst argument); analogous results for strongly log-concave measures.
Talagrand's convex-distance inequality for product measures Talagrand's convex-distance inequality.
cards.det: Important in high-dimensional and Gaussian lower-bound constructions; also gives concentration of the supremum of Gaussian processes around its mean, complementing Dudley Dudley's entropy integral (chaining).
cards.ex: \(\max_iZ_i\) (1-Lipschitz) concentrates within \(O(1)\) of \({\mathbb{E}}\max_iZ_i\approx\sqrt{2\log n}\).
cards.use: Gaussian process bandits, randomised value functions (RLSVI), high-dimensional lower bounds.

qz.q: \(X\sim{\mathcal{N}}(0,I_d)\) with \(d=10^6\). Typical fluctuations of \({\lVert X\rVert}_2\) around its mean (about \(\sqrt d=1000\)) are of order
qz.why: \(x\mapsto{\lVert x\rVert}_2\) is \(1\)-Lipschitz, so \(\Pr(|{\lVert X\rVert}_2-{\mathbb{E}}{\lVert X\rVert}_2|\ge t)\le2e^{-t^2/2}\): dimension-free \(O(1)\) fluctuations, although the mean grows like \(\sqrt d\).

qz.q: \(X\sim{\mathcal{N}}(0,I_d)\) and \(f(X)=\sum_{i=1}^dX_i\). Gaussian concentration gives \(\Pr(f(X)-{\mathbb{E}} f(X)\ge t)\le\)
qz.why: \(f\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz with \(L={\lVert (1,\dots,1)\rVert}_2=\sqrt d\), so the bound is \(e^{-t^2/(2L^2)}=e^{-t^2/(2d)}\), matching \(f(X)\sim{\mathcal{N}}(0,d)\). Dimension-free means “depends only on \(L\)”, not that \(L\) is always \(1\).

qz.q: \(Z_1,\dots,Z_n\) i.i.d. \({\mathcal{N}}(0,1)\) and \(M=\max_iZ_i\). What does Gaussian (Lipschitz) concentration give for \(M\)?
a: \(\Pr(M-{\mathbb{E}} M\ge t)\le e^{-t^2/(2n)}\), as \(M\) uses \(n\) coordinates
\(\Pr(M-{\mathbb{E}} M\ge t)\le e^{-t^2/(4\log n)}\), growing with \({\mathbb{E}} M\)
Gaussian concentration does not apply, as \(M\) is not differentiable
qz.why: \(x\mapsto\max_ix_i\) is \(1\)-Lipschitz in \({\lVert \cdot\rVert}_2\), so \(M\) concentrates within \(O(1)\) of \({\mathbb{E}} M\approx\sqrt{2\log n}\) for every \(n\). Lipschitz continuity suffices; differentiability is not required.

cards.name: Characterisations of convexity
cards.lay: A convex function lies above all of its tangent planes and below its chords. Equivalently, its Hessian is positive semidefinite. Local minima of convex functions are global, which is why convexity makes analysis easy.
cards.st: For differentiable \(f\) on a convex set, the following are equivalent: \[ egin{aligned}& ext{(i) } f( heta x+(1- heta)y)\le heta f(x)+(1- heta)f(y)\ \ orall heta\in[0,1];\ & ext{(ii) } f(y)\ge f(x)+{\langle abla f(x), y-x angle};\ & ext{(iii) } {\langle abla f(x)- abla f(y), x-y angle}\ge0.\end{aligned} \] If \(f\) is twice differentiable these are equivalent to \( abla^2f(x)\succeq0\).
ver: First-order optimality: \(x^\star\) minimises convex \(f\) over convex \(C\) iff \({\langle \nabla f(x^\star), y-x^\star\rangle}\ge0\) for all \(y\in C\).
Subgradients for non-smooth \(f\): \(f(y)\ge f(x)+{\langle g, y-x\rangle}\) for \(g\in\partial f(x)\).
Operations preserving convexity: non-negative sums, pointwise sup (e.g. \(V^\star\) is convex in the reward vector \(r\)), composition with affine maps, partial minimisation.
Quasi-/pseudo-convexity and invexity are weaker notions; the policy-optimisation objective is non-convex but satisfies gradient domination Gradient domination for policy optimisation.
cards.det: The value \(V^\pi(\rho)\) is not concave in policy parameters, but it is linear in the occupancy measure Discounted occupancy measures — so RL is a convex problem (an LP LP formulation of MDPs & its dual) in the right coordinates. Many “hidden convexity” results in policy optimisation exploit this.
cards.ex: \(V^\star(r)=\max_\pi{\langle d^\pi, r\rangle}/(1-\gamma)\) is a max of linear functions of \(r\), hence convex in \(r\) — used in inverse RL and robust reward analyses.
cards.use: Every optimisation argument; recognising hidden convexity (occupancy measures); subgradient methods for constrained MDPs.

qz.q: Fix the dynamics of a finite discounted MDP and a start distribution \(\rho\). View the optimal value \(V^\star(\rho)\) as a function of the reward vector \(r\in{\mathbb{R}}^{SA}\). What is its shape?
a: Neither convex nor concave in general
qz.why: \(V^\star(r)=\max_\pi{\langle d^\pi_\rho, r\rangle}/(1-\gamma)\) is a pointwise max of linear functions of \(r\), hence convex. Each \(V^\pi\) is linear in \(r\), but the maximum over policies is not (it is piecewise linear with kinks where the optimal policy changes).

qz.q: For a finite discounted MDP, let \(d^\pi_\rho\) be the discounted state–action occupancy measure of policy \(\pi\). Which statement is correct?
a: \(V^\pi(\rho)\) is linear in \(d^\pi_\rho\) but in general not concave in \(\pi\)
\(V^\pi(\rho)\) is concave in \(\pi(a\mid s)\) for every finite MDP
\(V^\pi(\rho)\) is linear in \(\pi(a\mid s)\) for every finite MDP
\(V^\pi(\rho)\) is convex in \(d^\pi_\rho\) but linear in \(\pi\)
qz.why: \(V^\pi(\rho)={\langle d^\pi_\rho, r\rangle}/(1-\gamma)\), and the set of occupancies is a polytope, so RL is an LP in occupancy coordinates LP formulation of MDPs & its dual. As a function of \(\pi\) the value is a rational function, linear for a one-state bandit but non-concave in general, which is why policy gradient needs gradient domination Gradient domination for policy optimisation rather than concavity.

qz.q: \(f\) is convex and differentiable, \(C\) is a closed convex set, and \(x^\star\in{\operatorname*{arg\,min}}_{x\in C}f(x)\). Which condition must hold?
a: \(f(y)\le f(x^\star)+{\langle \nabla f(x^\star), y-x^\star\rangle}\) for all \(y\in C\)
qz.why: No feasible direction may decrease \(f\) to first order. \(\nabla f(x^\star)=0\) is only needed in the interior: minimising \(f(x)=x\) on \([1,2]\) gives \(x^\star=1\) with \(f'=1\). The option \(f(y)\le f(x^\star)+{\langle \nabla f(x^\star), y-x^\star\rangle}\) reverses the tangent-plane inequality, which for convex \(f\) goes the other way.

cards.name: \(L\)-smoothness & the descent lemma
cards.lay: If a function's gradient doesn't change too fast (\(L\)-Lipschitz gradient), then it is sandwiched by quadratics, and a gradient step of size \(1/L\) is guaranteed to decrease it by \({\lVert \nabla f\rVert}^2/(2L)\). The starting point of every gradient-method analysis, including policy gradient.
cards.st: If \( abla f\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz then for all \(x,y\): \[ igl|f(y)-f(x)-{\langle abla f(x), y-x angle} igr|\le rac L2{\lVert y-x Vert}^2. \] Hence a gradient step \(x^+=x- frac1L abla f(x)\) satisfies \(f(x^+)\le f(x)- frac{1}{2L}{\lVert abla f(x) Vert}^2\).
ver: Non-convex rate: \(\min_{t<T}{\lVert \nabla f(x_t)\rVert}^2\le\tfrac{2L(f(x_0)-f^\star)}{T}\).
Convex \(+\) smooth: GD with step \(1/L\) gives \(f(x_T)-f^\star\le\tfrac{L{\lVert x_0-x^\star\rVert}^2}{2T}\); Nesterov acceleration gives \(O(L{\lVert x_0-x^\star\rVert}^2/T^2)\).

Co-coercivity (convex \(+\) smooth): \({\langle 
abla f(x)-
abla f(y), x-yangle}\ge	frac1L{\lVert 
abla f(x)-
abla f(y)Vert}^2\).
Smoothness of the RL objective: for softmax policies, \(V^{\pi_\theta}(\rho)\) is \(\tfrac{8}{(1-\gamma)^3}\)-smooth in \(\theta\) (Agarwal et al. 2021; Mei et al. 2020).
cards.det:
Proof: integral form of Taylor Taylor's theorem with remainder plus Cauchy–Schwarz: \(f(y)-f(x)-{\langle abla f(x), y-x angle}=\int_0^1{\langle abla f(x+t(y-x))- abla f(x), y-x angle}{\mathrm{d}} t\le\int_0^1Lt{\lVert y-x Vert}^2{\mathrm{d}} t\).

For policy gradient, smoothness alone gives only convergence to stationary points; global optimality needs gradient domination Gradient domination for policy optimisation.
cards.ex: Softmax PG with exact gradients and step \(\eta=(1-\gamma)^3/8\): by the descent lemma \(V^{(t+1)}\ge V^{(t)}+\tfrac{\eta}{2}{\lVert \nabla V^{(t)}\rVert}^2\), so values increase monotonically; combining with the non-uniform Łojasiewicz inequality gives \(O(1/t)\) rates (Mei et al. 2020).
cards.use: Policy-gradient convergence, actor–critic analyses, gradient-EM, any GD/SGD proof.

qz.q: \(f\) has \(4\)-Lipschitz gradient and \({\lVert \nabla f(x)\rVert}=2\). By the descent lemma, how much does one gradient step \(x^+=x-\frac14\nabla f(x)\) decrease \(f\) at least?
qz.why: \(f(x^+)\le f(x)- frac{1}{2L}{\lVert abla f(x) Vert}^2=f(x)- frac{4}{8}\). \(1={\lVert abla f Vert}^2/L\) is the first-order decrease \(\eta{\lVert abla f Vert}^2\) without subtracting the curvature penalty \( frac{L}{2}\eta^2{\lVert abla f Vert}^2\).

qz.q: For \(L\)-smooth non-convex \(f\), GD with step \(1/L\) gives \(\min_{t<T}{\lVert \nabla f(x_t)\rVert}^2\le\frac{2L(f(x_0)-f^\star)}{T}\). To guarantee a point with \({\lVert \nabla f\rVert}\le{\varepsilon}\), how does the required \(T\) change when \({\varepsilon}\) is halved?
qz.why: The bound controls the squared gradient norm, so \(T\approx2L\Delta/{\varepsilon}^2\); halving \({\varepsilon}\) quadruples \(T\). The factor \(2\) results from reading the bound as a rate on \({\lVert \nabla f\rVert}\) instead of \({\lVert \nabla f\rVert}^2\).

qz.q: For tabular softmax policies, \(V^{\pi_\theta}(\rho)\) is \(\frac{8}{(1-\gamma)^3}\)-smooth in \(\theta\), so exact-gradient ascent increases the value monotonically. Which property, actually established for this setting, upgrades convergence to a stationary point into convergence to the optimum?
a: A PL inequality with a constant independent of \(\theta\)
qz.why: Mei et al. show \({\lVert \nabla_\theta V\rVert}\ge c(\theta)(V^\star-V^{\pi_\theta})\) with \(c(\theta)\propto\min_s\pi_\theta(a^\star(s)|s)\) Gradient domination for policy optimisation. The value is not concave in \(\theta\), and no uniform PL constant exists: near a deterministic suboptimal policy the gradient vanishes while the suboptimality stays positive.

cards.name: Strong convexity, PL & quadratic growth
cards.lay: Strongly convex functions curve upward at least quadratically, so they have a unique minimiser and gradient descent converges linearly. The weaker Polyak–Łojasiewicz (PL) condition — gradient large whenever you are far from optimal in value — is enough for linear rates and holds for some non-convex problems.
cards.st: \(f\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex if \(f(y)\ge f(x)+{\langle \nabla f(x), y-x\rangle}+\tfrac\mu2{\lVert y-x\rVert}^2\). \(f\) satisfies \(\mu\)-PL if \[ \tfrac12{\lVert \nabla f(x)\rVert}^2\ge\mu\bigl(f(x)-f^\star\bigr)\quad\forall x. \] If \(f\) is \(L\)-smooth and \(\mu\)-PL, GD with step \(1/L\) gives \(f(x_t)-f^\star\le(1-\mu/L)^t(f(x_0)-f^\star)\).
ver: Strong convexity \(\Rightarrow\) PL \(\Rightarrow\) quadratic growth \(f(x)-f^\star\ge\tfrac{\mu}{2}\mathrm{dist}(x,X^\star)^2\) (with constants).
Strong convexity w.r.t. a general norm: negative entropy is \(1\)-strongly convex w.r.t. \({\lVert \cdot\rVert}_1\) on the simplex (Pinsker Pinsker's inequality is equivalent to this!).

Strongly convex \(\Rightarrow\) \({\lVert x-x^\starVert}\le	frac1\mu{\lVert 
abla f(x)Vert}\) and \({\langle 
abla f(x)-
abla f(y), x-yangle}\ge\mu{\lVert x-yVert}^2\) (strong monotonicity).
Gradient domination in RL Gradient domination for policy optimisation is a (non-uniform) PL-type inequality.
cards.det:
Linear-rate proof under PL: descent lemma gives \(f(x_{t+1})-f^\star\le f(x_t)-f^\star-\tfrac{1}{2L}{\lVert \nabla f(x_t)\rVert}^2\le(1-\tfrac\mu L)(f(x_t)-f^\star)\).

In EM theory, strong concavity of \(Q(\cdot\mid\theta^\star)\) (Balakrishnan–Wainwright–Yu's \(\lambda\)-strong concavity condition) is exactly what makes the population EM operator a contraction Balakrishnan–Wainwright–Yu: population EM contraction.
cards.ex: Entropy-regularised RL: adding \(\tau\mathcal H(\pi)\) makes the problem strongly concave in the right geometry; regularised NPG converges linearly at rate \((1-\eta\tau)^t\) (Cen et al. 2021).
cards.use: Linear convergence of regularised policy optimisation, EM contraction conditions, strongly convex regularisers in FTRL/OMD, fast rates in online learning (logarithmic regret).

qz.q: \(f\) is \(L\)-smooth and \(\mu\)-PL with \(L/\mu=100\). By the bound \(f(x_t)-f^\star\le(1-\mu/L)^t(f(x_0)-f^\star)\), roughly what is the smallest number of GD steps (step \(1/L\)) for which this bound guarantees that the gap has shrunk by a factor \(10^6\)?
qz.why: \((1-1/100)^t\le e^{-t/100}\le10^{-6}\) needs \(t\ge100\ln10^6\approx1382\). \(140\approx\sqrt{L/\mu}\ln10^6\) is the accelerated rate, which plain GD does not achieve; \(1.4\times10^5\) would correspond to a \((L/\mu)^2\) dependence.

qz.q: Which statement about the Polyak–Łojasiewicz (PL) condition \(\frac12{\lVert \nabla f(x)\rVert}^2\ge\mu(f(x)-f^\star)\) is correct?
a: A smooth PL function need not be convex
A PL function must be convex
A PL function has a unique minimiser
Smooth and PL together imply strong convexity
qz.why: \(f(x)=x^2+3\sin^2x\) is PL but not convex. \(f(x_1,x_2)=x_1^2\) on \({\mathbb{R}}^2\) is smooth and PL (with \(\mu=2\)) yet has a whole line of minimisers and is not strongly convex. PL is all that the linear-rate GD proof uses.

qz.q: Negative entropy \(\psi(p)=\sum_ip_i\log p_i\) is \(1\)-strongly convex on the simplex w.r.t. \({\lVert \cdot\rVert}_1\). Since its Bregman divergence is \({\mathrm{KL}}\), this statement is equivalent to which inequality (for all \(p,q\) in the simplex)?
qz.why: \(\mu\)-strong convexity is \(D_\psi(p,q)\ge\tfrac\mu2{\lVert p-q\rVert}^2\), and \(D_\psi(p,q)={\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q)\): this is Pinsker Pinsker's inequality. The constant \(\tfrac12\) is sharp, so constant \(1\) fails, and a bound linear in \({\lVert p-q\rVert}_1\) fails for nearby \(p,q\) because \({\mathrm{KL}}\) is locally quadratic.

cards.name: Gradient domination for policy optimisation
cards.lay: Even though the RL objective is non-convex in the policy, every stationary point is globally optimal (for direct parameterisation), because the suboptimality is bounded by how much a policy could still improve along the gradient — scaled by a distribution-mismatch factor.
cards.st: (Agarwal, Kakade, Lee, Mahajan 2021) For direct policy parameterisation and any start distribution \(\mu\), \[ V^\star(\rho)-V^\pi(\rho)\le\Bigl\|\frac{d^{\pi^\star}_\rho}{\mu}\Bigr\|_\infty\max_{\bar\pi}\bigl(\bar\pi-\pi\bigr)^\top\nabla_\pi V^\pi(\mu)\cdot\frac{1}{1-\gamma}, \] where \({\lVert d^{\pi^\star}_\rho/\mu\rVert}_\infty\) is the distribution-mismatch coefficient.
ver: Softmax parameterisation (Mei et al. 2020) — non-uniform Łojasiewicz: \({\lVert \nabla_\theta V^{\pi_\theta}(\mu)\rVert}_2\ge\tfrac{\min_s\pi_\theta(a^\star(s)|s)}{\sqrt S\,{\lVert d^{\pi^\star}_\rho/d^{\pi_\theta}_\mu\rVert}_\infty}(V^\star(\rho)-V^{\pi_\theta}(\rho))\).
Linear-quadratic regulators: the LQR cost is gradient dominated in the gain \(K\) (Fazel et al. 2018).
Proof backbone: performance difference lemma Performance difference lemma (Kakade–Langford) + pushing \(\max_a A^\pi(s,a)\) through the mismatch ratio.
cards.det: By the PDL, \(V^\star-V^\pi=\tfrac{1}{1-\gamma}{\mathbb{E}}_{s\sim d^{\pi^\star}_\rho}{\mathbb{E}}_{a\sim\pi^\star}A^\pi(s,a)\le\tfrac{1}{1-\gamma}{\mathbb{E}}_{d^{\pi^\star}_\rho}\max_aA^\pi(s,a)\). Change measure to \(d^\pi_\mu\) using the mismatch coefficient, and recognise \({\mathbb{E}}_{d^\pi_\mu}\max_aA^\pi\) as \((1-\gamma)\max_{\bar\pi}(\bar\pi-\pi)^\top\nabla_\pi V^\pi(\mu)\). Hence a policy with small “projected gradient” is near-optimal.
cards.ex: Projected gradient ascent on the simplex with step \(\eta=(1-\gamma)^3/(2\gamma|{\mathcal{A}}|)\) finds an \({\varepsilon}\)-optimal policy in \(O\bigl(\tfrac{|{\mathcal{S}}||{\mathcal{A}}|}{(1-\gamma)^6{\varepsilon}^2}{\lVert d^{\pi^\star}_\rho/\mu\rVert}^2_\infty\bigr)\) iterations.
cards.use: Global convergence of policy gradient methods, actor–critic theory, LQR policy gradient, understanding why exploration (via \(\mu\)) matters for PG.
cards.ll: Agarwal, Jiang, Kakade & Sun — RL Theory book

qz.q: Gradient domination for direct policy parameterisation bounds \(V^\star(\rho)-V^\pi(\rho)\) using gradients at a start distribution \(\mu\), scaled by \({\lVert d^{\pi^\star}_\rho/\mu\rVert}_\infty\). Suppose \(\mu(s)=0\) at a state \(s\) with \(d^{\pi^\star}_\rho(s)>0\). What follows?
a: The coefficient is infinite and the bound is vacuous
The bound still holds with coefficient \(1\)
The coefficient is \(0\), so stationary points are optimal
The bound improves, since fewer states are visited
qz.why: The mismatch ratio is \(\max_s d^{\pi^\star}_\rho(s)/\mu(s)\), which is \(+\infty\) when \(\mu\) misses a state the optimal policy visits. Then a stationary point can be suboptimal there: PG cannot see states its start distribution never reaches, which is why exploratory \(\mu\) matters.

qz.q: Projected gradient ascent with direct parameterisation needs \(O\bigl(\frac{|{\mathcal{S}}||{\mathcal{A}}|}{(1-\gamma)^6{\varepsilon}^2}{\lVert d^{\pi^\star}_\rho/\mu\rVert}_\infty^2\bigr)\) iterations. If \(1-\gamma\) is halved (all else fixed), the iteration bound is multiplied by:
qz.why: \((1-\gamma)^{-6}\) becomes \(2^6=64\) times larger. The factor \(8\) would correspond to a \((1-\gamma)^{-3}\) dependence, i.e. confusing the iteration count with the smoothness constant of \(V^\pi\).

qz.q: Direct parameterisation, \(\mu\) with full support. A policy \(\pi\) satisfies \(\max_{\bar\pi}(\bar\pi-\pi)^\top\nabla_\pi V^\pi(\mu)=0\) (a first-order stationary point on the product of simplices). What follows?
a: \(\pi\) is locally but possibly not globally optimal
\(\pi\) may be a saddle point of \(V^\pi(\mu)\)
qz.why: With full-support \(\mu\) the mismatch coefficient is finite, so gradient domination gives \(V^\star(\rho)-V^\pi(\rho)\le0\) for every \(\rho\). On a constrained set stationarity does not mean a zero gradient: at a deterministic optimal policy the gradient is generally non-zero but points out of the simplex.

cards.name: Convex conjugate & Fenchel–Young
cards.lay: The conjugate \(f^*\) describes a convex function by its supporting lines (slope \(\mapsto\) intercept). It turns maximisation problems into dual problems and produces variational formulas — e.g. log-sum-exp is the conjugate of negative entropy, KL is the conjugate of the log-MGF.
cards.st: The Fenchel conjugate of \(f\) is \(f^*(y)=\sup_x\{{\langle x, y\rangle}-f(x)\}\). It is always convex, \(f^{**}=f\) for closed convex \(f\) (Fenchel–Moreau), and \[ {\langle x, y\rangle}\le f(x)+f^*(y)\quad\text{(Fenchel--Young)},\quad\text{with equality iff }y\in\partial f(x). \]
ver: Negative entropy on the simplex \(f(p)=\sum p_i\log p_i\) has \(f^*(y)=\log\sum_ie^{y_i}\) Log-sum-exp (soft-max) sandwich.
\(f(x)=\tfrac12{\lVert x\rVert}^2\Rightarrow f^*(y)=\tfrac12{\lVert y\rVert}_*^2\); \(f(x)=\tfrac1p|x|^p\Rightarrow f^*(y)=\tfrac1q|y|^q\) (Young Young's inequality (incl. Peter–Paul)).
Duality of smoothness/strong convexity: \(f\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex w.r.t. \({\lVert \cdot\rVert}\) iff \(f^*\) is \(\tfrac1\mu\)-smooth w.r.t. \({\lVert \cdot\rVert}_*\).
Fenchel duality: \(\inf_x\{f(x)+g(Ax)\}\ge\sup_y\{-f^*(-A^\top y)-g^*(y)\}\), with equality under constraint qualification.

Legendre transform of the log-MGF gives the Chernoff rate function Chernoff bound / Cramér–Chernoff method; Donsker–Varadhan is a conjugate-duality statement Donsker–Varadhan & Gibbs variational principle.
cards.det: Conjugate duality explains: (i) why regularised RL has softmax optimal policies (\(\nabla\)LSE \(=\) softmax); (ii) why FTRL with regulariser \(R\) plays \(\nabla R^*(-\eta\sum\ell)\); (iii) the dual LP for MDPs; (iv) variational formulas for divergences \(f\)-divergences: Hellinger, \(\chi^2\) and their relations used in GAIL/IRL and in off-policy estimation (DualDICE).
cards.ex: Soft Bellman backup: \(\max_{\pi(\cdot|s)}\{{\langle \pi, Q(s,\cdot)\rangle}+\tau\mathcal H(\pi)\}=\tau\log\sum_ae^{Q(s,a)/\tau}\), attained at \(\pi\propto e^{Q/\tau}\).
cards.use: Entropy-regularised RL, FTRL/OMD, Lagrangian duality, variational divergence estimation, DICE-family off-policy estimators.

qz.q: Let \(a>0\) and \(f(x)=\frac a2x^2\) on \({\mathbb{R}}\). What is the convex conjugate \(f^*(y)=\sup_x\{xy-f(x)\}\)?
qz.why: The sup is attained at \(x=y/a\), giving \(y^2/a-y^2/(2a)=y^2/(2a)\). This is the duality “\(a\)-strongly convex \(\iff\) \(f^*\) is \(\tfrac1a\)-smooth”; the answer \(\tfrac{ay^2}{2}\) would make \(f\) self-conjugate for every \(a\), which is true only for \(a=1\).

qz.q: Two actions with \(Q(s,\cdot)=(1,1)\) and temperature \(\tau>0\). What is \(\max_{\pi\in\Delta_2}\{{\langle \pi, Q(s,\cdot)\rangle}+\tau\mathcal H(\pi)\}\), with \(\mathcal H\) the Shannon entropy (natural log)?
qz.why: This equals \(\tau\log\sum_ae^{Q(s,a)/\tau}=\tau\log(2e^{1/\tau})=1+\tau\log2\), attained at the uniform policy. Dropping the entropy bonus gives \(1\); forgetting the \(\tau\) scaling gives \(1+\log2\) (correct only for \(\tau=1\)).

qz.q: What is the convex conjugate of \(f(x)={\lvert x\rvert}\) on \({\mathbb{R}}\)?
qz.why: \(\sup_x\{xy-{\lvert x\rvert}\}\) is \(0\) (at \(x=0\)) when \({\lvert y\rvert}\le1\) and unbounded otherwise: the conjugate of a norm is the indicator of the dual-norm unit ball. \({\lvert y\rvert}\) would be self-conjugacy, which holds for \(\tfrac12x^2\), not for \({\lvert x\rvert}\).

cards.name: Projection theorem & non-expansiveness of projections
cards.lay: Onto a closed convex set, every point has a unique closest point, and projecting two points never increases their distance. This is why projected gradient methods and projected Bellman operators behave well.
cards.st: Let \(C\) be nonempty closed convex in a Hilbert space. Then \(\Pi_C(x)={\operatorname*{arg\,min}}_{y\in C}{\lVert x-y\rVert}\) exists, is unique, and is characterised by \({\langle x-\Pi_C(x), y-\Pi_C(x)\rangle}\le0\) for all \(y\in C\). Moreover \[ {\lVert \Pi_C(x)-\Pi_C(y)\rVert}\le{\lVert x-y\rVert}. \]
ver: Pythagorean inequality: \({\lVert y-\Pi_C(x)\rVert}^2+{\lVert \Pi_C(x)-x\rVert}^2\le{\lVert y-x\rVert}^2\) for \(y\in C\).

Subspaces: \(\Pi\) is linear and self-adjoint; weighted projections \(\Pi_D\) onto span\((\Phi)\) in \({\lVert \cdot\rVert}_D\) are used in TD Projected Bellman equation & TD fixed point (Tsitsiklis–Van Roy).
Bregman projections satisfy a generalised Pythagorean inequality Bregman divergences & the three-point identity.
cards.det: In projected gradient descent the analysis \({\lVert x_{t+1}-x^\star\rVert}^2\le{\lVert x_t-\eta g_t-x^\star\rVert}^2\) uses non-expansiveness with \(x^\star\in C\). For TD with linear function approximation, the projected Bellman operator \(\Pi_DT^\pi\) is a \(\gamma\)-contraction in \({\lVert \cdot\rVert}_D\) because \(\Pi_D\) is non-expansive in \({\lVert \cdot\rVert}_D\) and \(T^\pi\) is a contraction in \({\lVert \cdot\rVert}_D\) when \(D\) is the stationary distribution Projected Bellman equation & TD fixed point (Tsitsiklis–Van Roy).
cards.ex: Projection onto the probability simplex can be computed in \(O(n\log n)\) by sorting; used in projected policy gradient with direct parameterisation.
cards.use: Projected gradient methods, TD with linear function approximation, constrained policy optimisation.

qz.q: Linear TD uses the projected Bellman operator \(\Pi_DT^\pi\), with \(\Pi_D\) the projection onto \(\mathrm{span}(\Phi)\) in \({\lVert \cdot\rVert}_D\) and \(D\) the stationary distribution of \(P^\pi\). Why is \(\Pi_DT^\pi\) a \(\gamma\)-contraction in \({\lVert \cdot\rVert}_D\)?
a: \(\Pi_D\) is non-expansive and \(T^\pi\) is a \(\gamma\)-contraction, both in \({\lVert \cdot\rVert}_D\)
\(T^\pi\) contracts in every weighted \(\ell_2\) norm, whatever \(D\)
qz.why: Orthogonal projections are non-expansive in their own Hilbert norm, and \({\lVert P^\pi V\rVert}_D\le{\lVert V\rVert}_D\) when \(D\) is stationary (Jensen). \(\Pi_D\) is generally not non-expansive in \({\lVert \cdot\rVert}_\infty\) — the root of off-policy divergence — and \(T^\pi\) need not contract in \({\lVert \cdot\rVert}_D\) for non-stationary \(D\).

qz.q: Let \(C=\{(t,1-t):t\in[0,1]\}\subset{\mathbb{R}}^2\) (a segment) and \(x=(2,0)\). What is the Euclidean projection \(\Pi_C(x)\)?
qz.why: Check the variational inequality: \(x-(1,0)=(1,0)\) and \(y-(1,0)=(t-1,1-t)\) give inner product \(t-1\le0\) for all \(y\in C\). \((1.5,-0.5)\) is the projection onto the whole line \(x_1+x_2=1\), which lies outside the segment.

qz.q: Let \(C\subset{\mathbb{R}}^2\) be non-empty and closed. Which additional property of \(C\) guarantees that every point has a unique nearest point in \(C\)?
qz.why: The projection theorem needs convexity. The unit circle is compact and bounded, yet the origin is equidistant from all of its points. The complement of the open unit disc has non-empty interior and the same failure at the origin.

cards.name: Lagrangian duality & Slater's condition
cards.lay: Constrained problems can be turned into unconstrained min–max games by pricing the constraints with multipliers. The dual problem always gives a bound (weak duality) and, for convex problems with a strictly feasible point, the bound is tight (strong duality). This is the foundation of constrained MDPs.
cards.st: For \(\min_xf(x)\) s.t. \(g_i(x)\le0\), define \(L(x,\lambda)=f(x)+\sum_i\lambda_ig_i(x)\) and \(D(\lambda)=\inf_xL(x,\lambda)\). Then \(\sup_{\lambda\ge0}D(\lambda)\le f^\star\) (weak duality). If \(f,g_i\) are convex and some \(x\) has \(g_i(x)<0\) for all \(i\) (Slater), then \[ \max_{\lambda\ge0}D(\lambda)=f^\star. \]
ver: Constrained MDPs: \(\max_\pi V_r^\pi\) s.t. \(V_g^\pi\ge b\) has zero duality gap (Altman 1999; Paternain et al. 2019) because it is an LP in occupancy measures — even though it is non-convex in \(\pi\).
Saddle point characterisation: \((x^\star,\lambda^\star)\) optimal iff it is a saddle point of \(L\).
Bound on the optimal multiplier under Slater: \({\lVert \lambda^\star\rVert}_1\le\tfrac{f(\bar x)-f^\star}{\min_i(-g_i(\bar x))}\) — crucial for primal–dual CMDP regret.
cards.det: Primal–dual algorithms for CMDPs alternate policy updates on \(L(\pi,\lambda)=V_r^\pi+\lambda(V_g^\pi-b)\) with (projected) gradient steps on \(\lambda\). The multiplier bound keeps \(\lambda\) in a known box, which is needed to bound the dual regret.
cards.ex: CMDP with Slater slack \(\xi\) (\(V_g^{\bar\pi}\ge b+\xi\)): \(\lambda^\star\le\tfrac{V_r^\star-V_r^{\bar\pi}}{\xi}\le\tfrac{1}{(1-\gamma)\xi}\).
cards.use: Constrained/safe RL, primal–dual policy optimisation, LP duality for MDPs, entropy/KL-regularised formulations.

qz.q: A CMDP \(\max_\pi V^\pi_r\) s.t. \(V^\pi_g\ge b\) has rewards \(r\in[0,1]\), \(\gamma=0.9\), and a Slater policy \(\bar\pi\) with slack \(V^{\bar\pi}_g\ge b+0.1\). Using the Slater bound \(\lambda^\star\le(V^\star_r-V^{\bar\pi}_r)/\xi\) with slack \(\xi\), what is the smallest upper bound on the optimal multiplier \(\lambda^\star\) that these facts alone guarantee?
qz.why: \(\lambda^\star\le\tfrac{V^\star_r-V^{\bar\pi}_r}{\xi}\le\tfrac{1}{(1-\gamma)\xi}=\tfrac{1}{0.1\cdot0.1}=100\). \(10\) forgets that values range up to \(1/(1-\gamma)\), and \(1000\) is valid but loose; this box for \(\lambda\) is what primal–dual CMDP algorithms project onto.

qz.q: Constrained MDPs have zero duality gap even though \(V^\pi_r\) and \(V^\pi_g\) are non-concave in \(\pi\). Why?
a: In occupancy measures the problem is a linear program
\(V^\pi_r\) is concave in the direct parameters \(\pi(a\mid s)\)
Slater's condition implies strong duality for any problem
The constraint \(V^\pi_g\ge b\) is linear in \(\pi\)
qz.why: Values are linear in \(d^\pi\) and the occupancy set is a polytope, so the CMDP is an LP and Slater (or LP duality) closes the gap. Slater gives strong duality only together with convexity; neither the objective nor the constraint is concave or linear in \(\pi\).

qz.q: For \(\min f(x)\) s.t. \(g_i(x)\le0\) with \(D(\lambda)=\inf_x\{f(x)+\sum_i\lambda_ig_i(x)\}\) and no convexity or Slater assumption, which relation always holds (\(f^\star\) the primal optimum)?
qz.why: Weak duality: for feasible \(x\) and \(\lambda\ge0\), \(D(\lambda)\le f(x)+\sum\lambda_ig_i(x)\le f(x)\). Equality needs convexity plus a constraint qualification; non-convex problems can have a strictly positive gap.

cards.name: Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) conditions
cards.lay: At an optimum of a constrained problem, the gradient of the objective is balanced by a non-negative combination of the active constraint gradients. For convex problems these conditions are also sufficient — they let you guess and verify optimal solutions.
cards.st: For \(\min f(x)\) s.t. \(g_i(x)\le0\), \(h_j(x)=0\) (under a constraint qualification), an optimum \(x^\star\) admits \(\lambda\ge0, u\) with \[ abla f(x^\star)+\sum_i\lambda_i abla g_i(x^\star)+\sum_j u_j abla h_j(x^\star)=0,\quad\lambda_ig_i(x^\star)=0,\quad g_i(x^\star)\le0,\ h_j(x^\star)=0. \]
ver: For convex problems with Slater's condition, KKT is necessary and sufficient.
Simplex constraint example: maximising \({\langle p, q\rangle}+\tau\mathcal H(p)\) over \(p\in\Delta\) gives \(p_i\propto e^{q_i/\tau}\).
Water-filling, maximum-entropy distributions, and the M-step of EM for mixtures (\(\pi_k=\tfrac1n\sum_i\gamma_{ik}\)) are all KKT solutions.
cards.det: Complementary slackness (\(\lambda_ig_i=0\)) is what makes the dual LP of an MDP pick out optimal actions: the dual variables (occupancies) are positive only on actions where the Bellman inequality is tight.
cards.ex: M-step for mixture weights: maximise \(\sum_k n_k\log\pi_k\) s.t. \(\sum\pi_k=1\); KKT gives \(n_k/\pi_k=\nu\), so \(\pi_k=n_k/n\).
cards.use: Deriving closed-form M-steps, regularised policy updates, LP complementary slackness for MDPs, constrained RL.

qz.q: EM for a 3-component mixture: the E-step gives soft counts \(n_k=\sum_i\gamma_{ik}=(3,5,2)\) with \(n=10\). The M-step maximises \(\sum_kn_k\log\pi_k\) s.t. \(\sum_k\pi_k=1\). What does KKT give?
qz.why: Stationarity \(n_k/\pi_k=\nu\) gives \(\pi_k\propto n_k\), and the constraint fixes \(\nu=n\). The softmax answer is the solution for a linear objective with entropy bonus, \(\sum_kn_k\pi_k+\mathcal H(\pi)\), not for the log-likelihood.

qz.q: Minimise \(f(x)=x^2\) subject to \(g(x)=1-x\le0\). What is the KKT multiplier \(\lambda\) at the optimum?
qz.why: The constraint is active at \(x^\star=1\); stationarity \(2x^\star+\lambda\cdot(-1)=0\) gives \(\lambda=2\ge0\). \(\lambda=0\) would be correct only for an inactive constraint (complementary slackness), and multipliers of inequality constraints are never negative.

qz.q: Minimise \(f(x)=x\) subject to \(g(x)=x^2\le0\) on \({\mathbb{R}}\). The only feasible, hence optimal, point is \(x^\star=0\). What about the KKT conditions there?
a: They hold, as KKT is necessary for convex problems
qz.why: Stationarity needs \(1+\lambda\cdot2x^\star=1=0\), impossible. The problem is convex but has no strictly feasible point, so no constraint qualification holds and KKT need not be necessary; convexity alone only makes KKT sufficient.

cards.name: Minimax theorems (von Neumann, Sion)
cards.lay: In a zero-sum game with convex–concave payoff (e.g. mixed strategies), it does not matter who moves first: \(\min\max=\max\min\). Used for games, robust RL, Lagrangian duality and Yao's principle in lower bounds.
cards.st: (Sion) Let \(X\) be compact convex, \(Y\) convex, \(f(x,y)\) convex and lsc in \(x\), concave and usc in \(y\). Then \[ \min_{x\in X}\sup_{y\in Y}f(x,y)=\sup_{y\in Y}\min_{x\in X}f(x,y). \] (von Neumann) For a matrix \(A\): \(\min_{p\in\Delta_m}\max_{q\in\Delta_n}p^\top Aq=\max_q\min_pp^\top Aq\).
ver: Weak inequality \(\sup\min\le\min\sup\) always holds (no assumptions).
Markov games: Shapley's theorem — the minimax value exists and satisfies a contracting Bellman equation Non-expansiveness of \(\max\) / \(\sup\).
Yao's principle: worst-case expected cost of the best randomised algorithm \(=\) best deterministic algorithm against the worst input distribution — basis of lower bounds.
No-regret dynamics: if both players run sublinear-regret algorithms, average play converges to the minimax value at rate \(({\mathrm{Reg}}_1+{\mathrm{Reg}}_2)/T\).
cards.det: Minimax lower bounds in learning theory, \(\inf_{\text{alg}}\sup_{\text{env}}{\mathbb{E}}[\text{loss}]\), are typically lower bounded by switching to a Bayesian prior over environments (sup \(\ge\) average), which is the easy direction of the minimax theorem.
cards.ex: Robust MDP with \((s,a)\)-rectangular uncertainty sets: \(\max_\pi\min_{P\in{\mathcal{P}}}V^\pi_P=\min_P\max_\pi V^\pi_P\), and the robust Bellman operator is a contraction.
cards.use: Markov games, robust RL, adversarial training (GAIL), primal–dual analysis, lower bounds via Yao's principle, no-regret learning in games.

qz.q: Matching pennies: \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\-1&1\end{pmatrix}\), the row player minimises \(A_{ij}\) and the column player maximises. With pure strategies only, what are \(\min_i\max_jA_{ij}\) and \(\max_j\min_iA_{ij}\)?
qz.why: Every row has max \(1\) and every column has min \(-1\), so a gap of \(2\) remains: pure strategies are not a convex set. Mixing restores equality at the value \(0\) (von Neumann). \(-1\) and \(1\) is impossible since \(\max\min\le\min\max\) always.

qz.q: To lower-bound the minimax risk one writes \(\inf_{\text{alg}}\sup_\theta R(\text{alg},\theta)\ge\inf_{\text{alg}}{\mathbb{E}}_{\theta\sim\pi}R(\text{alg},\theta)\) for a prior \(\pi\). What does this step require?
a: Nothing: a supremum dominates any average
qz.why: For each algorithm \(\sup_\theta R\ge{\mathbb{E}}_\pi R\), so the inequality holds for every prior. This is the easy (weak) direction; Sion's theorem is needed only to claim equality with the best Bayes risk, and a least-favourable prior only makes the bound tight.

qz.q: Both players of an \(n\times n\) zero-sum matrix game (payoffs in \([0,1]\)) run Hedge with regret \(\le\sqrt{2T\log n}\). Average play then has duality gap at most \(({\mathrm{Reg}}_1+{\mathrm{Reg}}_2)/T\). How does this bound scale?
qz.why: \(2\sqrt{2T\log n}/T=2\sqrt{2\log n/T}\). \(O(\sqrt{T\log n})\) is the regret itself, before dividing by \(T\); \(O(\log n/T)\) would require logarithmic regret, which plain Hedge does not give.

cards.name: Bregman divergences & the three-point identity
cards.lay: A Bregman divergence measures how far a convex function is above its tangent: it generalises squared Euclidean distance (and KL divergence) and obeys a “law of cosines” that makes mirror descent analyses telescope.
cards.st: For strictly convex differentiable \(\psi\): \(D_\psi(x,y)=\psi(x)-\psi(y)-{\langle abla\psi(y), x-y angle}\ge0\). For all \(x,y,z\): \[ {\langle abla\psi(z)- abla\psi(y), x-z angle}=D_\psi(x,y)-D_\psi(x,z)-D_\psi(z,y)\quad ext{(three-point identity)}. \]
ver: \(\psi=\tfrac12{\lVert \cdot\rVert}_2^2\Rightarrow D_\psi(x,y)=\tfrac12{\lVert x-y\rVert}^2\); \(\psi(p)=\sum p_i\log p_i\) on the simplex \(\Rightarrow D_\psi(p,q)={\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q)\) KL divergence & Gibbs' inequality.
Generalised Pythagoras: for Bregman projection \(z={\operatorname*{arg\,min}}_{u\in C}D_\psi(u,y)\), \(D_\psi(x,y)\ge D_\psi(x,z)+D_\psi(z,y)\) for all \(x\in C\).
Exponential families: \(D_A(\theta',\theta)={\mathrm{KL}}(p_\theta\|p_{\theta'})\) where \(A\) is the log-partition function.
If \(\psi\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex w.r.t. \({\lVert \cdot\rVert}\): \(D_\psi(x,y)\ge\tfrac\mu2{\lVert x-y\rVert}^2\).
cards.det: The three-point identity is the single line that powers mirror descent Online mirror descent (OMD) lemma, NPG/policy mirror descent Natural policy gradient & policy mirror descent convergence, and the mirror-descent view of EM EM as minorise–maximise and as mirror descent. It is proved by simply expanding the three divergences.
cards.ex: KL three-point identity on the simplex: \({\langle \log\tfrac{p_{t+1}}{p_t}, p^\star-p_{t+1}\rangle}={\mathrm{KL}}(p^\star\|p_t)-{\mathrm{KL}}(p^\star\|p_{t+1})-{\mathrm{KL}}(p_{t+1}\|p_t)\) — the core step of Hedge and NPG analyses.
cards.use: Mirror descent / NPG / policy mirror descent, Hedge, EM as mirror descent, Bregman projections in online learning, exponential-family statistics.

qz.q: With \(\psi(p)=\sum_ip_i\log p_i\) on the simplex, what is \(D_\psi(x,y)=\psi(x)-\psi(y)-{\langle \nabla\psi(y), x-y\rangle}\)?
qz.why: Expanding, the linear terms cancel on the simplex and leave \(\sum_ix_i\log(x_i/y_i)={\mathrm{KL}}(x\|y)\). The first argument of \(D_\psi\) becomes the first argument of \({\mathrm{KL}}\); the base point \(y\) (where the tangent is taken) is the reference measure.

qz.q: For an exponential family \(p_\theta(x)\propto\exp({\langle \theta, T(x)\rangle})\) with log-partition \(A\), what is \(D_A(\theta',\theta)=A(\theta')-A(\theta)-{\langle \nabla A(\theta), \theta'-\theta\rangle}\)?
qz.why: \({\mathrm{KL}}(p_\theta\|p_{\theta'})={\mathbb{E}}_\theta[{\langle \theta-\theta', T\rangle}]-A(\theta)+A(\theta')\) and \({\mathbb{E}}_\theta T=\nabla A(\theta)\), which matches \(D_A(\theta',\theta)\). The arguments are swapped relative to the parameters — unlike the negative-entropy case, where they are not.

qz.q: Take \(\psi=\frac12{\lVert \cdot\rVert}_2^2\). Which form does the three-point identity take for all \(x,y,z\)?
qz.why: Write \(x-y=(x-z)+(z-y)\) and expand: \({\lVert x-y\rVert}^2={\lVert x-z\rVert}^2+{\lVert z-y\rVert}^2+2{\langle x-z, z-y\rangle}\) — the law of cosines. This matches \(D_\psi(x,y)-D_\psi(x,z)-D_\psi(z,y)\) with \(\nabla\psi=\mathrm{id}\).

cards.name: Online mirror descent (OMD) lemma
cards.lay: Mirror descent takes gradient steps in a geometry tailored to the constraint set (e.g. multiplicative updates on the simplex). Its regret is (initial divergence)/\(\eta\) + \(\eta\times\)(sum of squared gradient norms in the dual norm). Natural policy gradient is mirror descent per state.
cards.st: Let \(\psi\) be \(1\)-strongly convex w.r.t. \({\lVert \cdot\rVert}\) on \(C\) and \(x_{t+1}={\operatorname*{arg\,min}}_{x\in C}\{\eta{\langle g_t, x\rangle}+D_\psi(x,x_t)\}\). Then for any \(u\in C\): \[ \sum_{t=1}^T{\langle g_t, x_t-u\rangle}\le\frac{D_\psi(u,x_1)}{\eta}+\frac\eta2\sum_{t=1}^T{\lVert g_t\rVert}_*^2. \]
ver: Entropic MD on the simplex \(=\) Hedge: \({\langle g_t, x_t-u\rangle}\) regret \(\le\tfrac{\log n}{\eta}+\tfrac\eta2\sum_t{\lVert g_t\rVert}_\infty^2\) Exponential weights (Hedge) regret bound.
Euclidean MD \(=\) projected OGD Online gradient descent regret (Zinkevich).
Local-norm refinement (for non-negative losses with entropy): \(\le\tfrac{\log n}{\eta}+\eta\sum_t\sum_ix_{t,i}g_{t,i}^2\) — key for EXP3 EXP3 & importance-weighted loss estimators.

Policy mirror descent: \(\pi_{k+1}(\cdot|s)\propto\pi_k(\cdot|s)e^{\eta Q^{\pi_k}(s,\cdot)}\) is OMD in each state with linear losses \(-Q^{\pi_k}(s,\cdot)\) Natural policy gradient & policy mirror descent convergence.
cards.det: Proof. Optimality of \(x_{t+1}\) gives \({\langle \eta g_t+\nabla\psi(x_{t+1})-\nabla\psi(x_t), u-x_{t+1}\rangle}\ge0\). Apply the three-point identity Bregman divergences & the three-point identity, then bound \(\eta{\langle g_t, x_t-x_{t+1}\rangle}-D_\psi(x_{t+1},x_t)\le\tfrac{\eta^2}{2}{\lVert g_t\rVert}_*^2\) by Young Young's inequality (incl. Peter–Paul) and strong convexity. Telescope Telescoping sums.
cards.ex: With \(n\) experts and losses in \([0,1]\): \(\eta=\sqrt{2\log n/T}\) gives regret \(\le\sqrt{2T\log n}\).
cards.use: Natural policy gradient / PMD convergence, adversarial MDPs (O-REPS), Hedge/EXP3, online learning in non-stationary environments, game dynamics.

qz.q: Hedge with tuned \(\eta\) has regret \(\sqrt{2T\log n}\) against \(n\) experts with losses in \([0,1]\). Going from \(n=2^{10}\) to \(n=2^{20}\) experts (same \(T\)) multiplies the bound by:
qz.why: \(\log n\) doubles (from \(10\log2\) to \(20\log2\)), so the bound grows by \(\sqrt2\). A factor \(2^5=\sqrt{2^{10}}\) is what \(\sqrt n\) scaling would give; entropic geometry avoids that.

qz.q: On the simplex \(\Delta_n\) with losses \(g_t\in[0,1]^n\), run Euclidean OMD (\(\psi=\frac12{\lVert \cdot\rVert}_2^2\), i.e. projected OGD) from an arbitrary start \(x_1\in\Delta_n\). Bounding \(D_\psi(u,x_1)\) by its worst case over \(u,x_1\in\Delta_n\), what regret does the OMD lemma give with the best fixed \(\eta\)?
qz.why: Here \(D_\psi(u,x_1)\le\tfrac12\cdot2=1\) (the simplex has \(\ell_2\) diameter \(\sqrt2\); from the uniform start it would be \(\le\tfrac12\), giving \(\sqrt{nT}\)) and \({\lVert g_t\rVert}_2^2\le n\), so \(\tfrac1\eta+\tfrac{\eta nT}{2}\) is minimised at \(\sqrt{2nT}\). \(\sqrt{2T\log n}\) is the entropic (Hedge) bound, which uses \({\lVert g_t\rVert}_\infty\le1\) instead.

qz.q: Policy mirror descent updates \(\pi_{k+1}(\cdot\mid s)\propto\pi_k(\cdot\mid s)\,e^{\eta Q^{\pi_k}(s,\cdot)}\). Which online mirror descent instance is this?
a: Entropic OMD in each state with loss \(-Q^{\pi_k}(s,\cdot)\)
Entropic OMD in each state with loss \(+Q^{\pi_k}(s,\cdot)\)
Euclidean OMD in each state with loss \(-Q^{\pi_k}(s,\cdot)\)
Hedge over deterministic policies with loss \(-V^\pi(\rho)\)
qz.why: Multiplicative updates are the KL-regularised OMD step \({\operatorname*{arg\,min}}_x\{\eta{\langle g, x\rangle}+{\mathrm{KL}}(x\|\pi_k)\}\), giving \(x\propto\pi_ke^{-\eta g}\); matching requires \(g=-Q\) (maximising \(Q\)). A Euclidean step would be additive plus a projection, not multiplicative.

cards.name: Stochastic gradient descent convergence
cards.lay: With unbiased noisy gradients, SGD on convex problems converges at rate \(1/\sqrt T\) (or \(1/T\) under strong convexity). Non-convex smooth problems reach stationary points at rate \(1/\sqrt T\) in gradient norm squared. The template for stochastic policy gradient and TD analyses.
cards.st: Let \(f\) be convex, \({\mathbb{E}}[g_t\mid x_t]\in\partial f(x_t)\), \({\mathbb{E}}{\lVert g_t\rVert}^2\le G^2\), \({\lVert x_1-x^\star\rVert}\le D\). With \(\eta=\tfrac{D}{G\sqrt T}\) and averaged iterate \(\bar x_T\): \[ {\mathbb{E}} f(\bar x_T)-f^\star\le\frac{DG}{\sqrt T}. \]
ver: \(\mu\)-strongly convex with \(\eta_t=\tfrac{1}{\mu t}\): \({\mathbb{E}} f(\bar x_T)-f^\star=O\bigl(\tfrac{G^2\log T}{\mu T}\bigr)\) (or \(O(G^2/(\mu T))\) with suffix/weighted averaging).

\(L\)-smooth non-convex, variance \(\sigma^2\), \(\eta\asymp\min(1/L,1/(\sigma\sqrt T))\): \(\min_t{\mathbb{E}}{\lVert \nabla f(x_t)\rVert}^2=O\bigl(\tfrac{L\Delta}{T}+\tfrac{\sigma\sqrt{L\Delta}}{\sqrt T}\bigr)\), \(\Delta=f(x_1)-f^\star\).
High-probability versions via Azuma/Freedman on the martingale \(\sum_t{\langle \nabla f(x_t)-g_t, x_t-x^\star\rangle}\).
Markovian noise (as in TD/actor–critic): rates degrade by a mixing-time factor Mixing time & geometric ergodicity.
cards.det: Proof: same telescoping argument as OGD Online gradient descent regret (Zinkevich) applied in expectation, followed by Jensen on the average. Equivalent to online-to-batch conversion Online-to-batch conversion of the OGD regret.
cards.ex: Stochastic policy gradient (REINFORCE with batch size \(B\)): gradient variance \(\sigma^2\propto\tfrac{1}{B(1-\gamma)^4}\); combined with smoothness gives \({\widetilde{O}}({\varepsilon}^{-4})\) samples to an \({\varepsilon}\)-stationary point.
cards.use: Stochastic policy gradient sample complexity, TD/Q-learning with linear FA (as SGD-like updates), training critics, EM with stochastic E-steps.

qz.q: Convex SGD with \({\mathbb{E}}{\lVert g_t\rVert}^2\le G^2\), \({\lVert x_1-x^\star\rVert}\le D\), step \(\eta=\frac{D}{G\sqrt T}\). With \(D=1\), \(G=10\), \(T=10^4\), what bound on \({\mathbb{E}} f(\bar x_T)-f^\star\) follows?
qz.why: \(DG/\sqrt T=10/100=0.1\). \(10^{-3}=DG/T\) is the rate one would get with \(1/T\) convergence, which is not available for general convex non-smooth stochastic problems.

qz.q: Compared with general convex \(f\), how does the rate of SGD (step \(\eta_t=\frac{1}{\mu t}\), averaged iterate) change for \(\mu\)-strongly convex \(f\) with bounded stochastic gradients?
a: It stays \(O(1/\sqrt T)\); only the constant improves
qz.why: Strong convexity gives \(O\bigl(\tfrac{G^2\log T}{\mu T}\bigr)\) (or \(O(1/T)\) with suffix averaging). Linear rates \(e^{-cT}\) are what deterministic GD gets under smoothness and strong convexity; gradient noise prevents them for SGD with bounded-variance gradients.

qz.q: \(L\)-smooth non-convex \(f\), stochastic gradients with variance \(\sigma^2>0\): \(\min_t{\mathbb{E}}{\lVert \nabla f(x_t)\rVert}^2=O\bigl(\frac{L\Delta}{T}+\frac{\sigma\sqrt{L\Delta}}{\sqrt T}\bigr)\). For small \({\varepsilon}\), how many iterations ensure \(\min_t{\mathbb{E}}{\lVert \nabla f(x_t)\rVert}^2\le{\varepsilon}^2\)?
qz.why: For small \({\varepsilon}\) the noise term dominates: \(\sigma\sqrt{L\Delta/T}\le{\varepsilon}^2\) needs \(T\gtrsim\sigma^2L\Delta/{\varepsilon}^4\), the source of the \({\widetilde{O}}({\varepsilon}^{-4})\) REINFORCE sample complexity. \({\varepsilon}^{-2}\) is the noiseless (\(\sigma=0\)) rate from the first term.

cards.name: KL divergence & Gibbs' inequality
cards.lay: The KL divergence \({\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)\) is the expected log-likelihood ratio: how surprised you are, on average, if you believe \(Q\) but data come from \(P\). It is always non-negative and zero only when \(P=Q\) — but it is not symmetric and not a metric.
cards.st: For \(P\ll Q\): \({\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)={\mathbb{E}}_P\Bigl[\log\frac{{\mathrm{d}} P}{{\mathrm{d}} Q}\Bigr]=\sum_xP(x)\log\frac{P(x)}{Q(x)}\) (and \(+\infty\) otherwise). Gibbs' inequality: \[ {\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)\ge0,\quad\text{with equality iff }P=Q. \]
ver: Cross-entropy decomposition: \({\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)=H(P,Q)-H(P)\); minimising cross-entropy \(=\) maximum likelihood.
Gaussians and Bernoullis have closed forms KL for Bernoulli & Gaussian distributions.
Convexity: \((P,Q)\mapsto{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)\) is jointly convex.
Chain rule Chain rule for KL & trajectory divergence decomposition; data processing Data-processing inequality; Pinsker Pinsker's inequality.

Reverse vs. forward KL: \({\mathrm{KL}}(q\|p)\) (mode-seeking, used in variational inference / the ELBO ELBO decomposition (free-energy view of EM)) vs. \({\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q)\) (mass-covering, used in MLE).
cards.det:
Proof of Gibbs. By \(\log x\le x-1\) Logarithm bounds: \(-{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)=\sum_xP(x)\log\tfrac{Q(x)}{P(x)}\le\sum_xP(x)(\tfrac{Q(x)}{P(x)}-1)\le0\). Alternatively by Jensen Jensen's inequality with concave \(\log\).

KL is the Bregman divergence of negative entropy Bregman divergences & the three-point identity, the rate function of large deviations Chernoff bound / Cramér–Chernoff method, and the quantity that appears in both bandit lower bounds Lai–Robbins asymptotic lower bound and EM ELBO decomposition (free-energy view of EM).
cards.ex: For policies: \({\mathrm{KL}}(\pi'(\cdot|s)\|\pi(\cdot|s))\) is the trust-region measure in TRPO and the regulariser in policy mirror descent; the KL between two trajectory distributions under the same dynamics is \({\mathbb{E}}\sum_t{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi'(\cdot|s_t)\|\pi(\cdot|s_t))\) (chain rule).
cards.use: Lower bounds, trust regions (TRPO/PPO), KL-regularised RL, EM/variational inference, KL-UCB, PAC-Bayes, maximum likelihood.

qz.q: Let \(P\) be uniform on \(\{0,1\}\) and \(Q=\delta_0\) (all mass on \(0\)). Which statement about the two KL divergences is correct?
a: Both equal \(\log2\), since the supports overlap at \(0\)
Both are \(+\infty\), since the two supports differ
qz.why: \(Q\ll P\), so \({\mathrm{KL}}(Q\|P)=1\cdot\log\frac{1}{1/2}=\log2\); but \(P\) puts mass \(\tfrac12\) on \(1\) where \(Q\) has none, so \(P\not\ll Q\) and \({\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)=+\infty\). KL is finite only when the first argument is absolutely continuous w.r.t. the second.

qz.q: A bimodal density \(p\) is approximated by a single Gaussian \(q\) chosen to minimise the reverse KL \({\mathrm{KL}}(q\|p)\) (as in variational inference). What does the fit typically look like?
a: It locks onto one mode, since \(q\) pays for mass where \(p\) is small
It spreads over both modes, since \(q\) pays wherever \(p>0\) but \(q\approx0\)
It is identical to the MLE fit, since the KL minimiser ignores argument order
It matches the mean and variance of \(p\) exactly (moment matching)
qz.why: \({\mathrm{KL}}(q\|p)={\mathbb{E}}_q\log\frac qp\) blows up where \(q>0\) and \(p\approx0\), so \(q\) avoids the gap between modes: mode-seeking. Mass-covering and moment matching describe the forward KL \({\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q)\), which is the MLE objective.

qz.q: On a finite set, let \(\hat P_n\) be the empirical distribution of samples \(x_1,\dots,x_n\) and \(\{Q_\theta\}\) a model family. Minimising \({\mathrm{KL}}(\hat P_n\|Q_\theta)\) over \(\theta\) is equivalent to:
a: minimising \({\mathrm{KL}}(Q_\theta\|\hat P_n)\), by symmetry of KL
qz.why: \({\mathrm{KL}}(\hat P_n\|Q_\theta)=H(\hat P_n,Q_\theta)-H(\hat P_n)\) and \(H(\hat P_n)\) does not depend on \(\theta\), so minimising KL = minimising cross-entropy \(-\frac1n\sum_i\log Q_\theta(x_i)\) = maximum likelihood. KL is not symmetric, so the reverse KL is a different problem.

cards.name: Total variation distance
cards.lay: Total variation is the largest possible difference in the probability that two distributions assign to the same event. It controls how much any bounded quantity's expectation can change between them — the bridge from “models are close” to “values are close”.
cards.st: \({\mathrm{TV}}(P,Q)=\sup_A|P(A)-Q(A)|=\tfrac12{\lVert P-Q\rVert}_1\), and for bounded \(f\): \[ \bigl|{\mathbb{E}}_Pf-{\mathbb{E}}_Qf\bigr|\le2{\lVert f\rVert}_\infty{\mathrm{TV}}(P,Q),\qquad{\mathrm{TV}}(P,Q)=\sup_{{\lVert f\rVert}_\infty\le1/2}\bigl({\mathbb{E}}_Pf-{\mathbb{E}}_Qf\bigr). \]
ver: Span refinement: \(|{\mathbb{E}}_Pf-{\mathbb{E}}_Qf|\le{\operatorname{sp}}(f)\,{\mathrm{TV}}(P,Q)\).
Coupling characterisation: \({\mathrm{TV}}(P,Q)=\min\{\Pr(X\ne Y):X\sim P,Y\sim Q\}\) Coupling inequality.
Testing: the minimum sum of type-I and type-II errors for distinguishing \(P\) and \(Q\) is \(1-{\mathrm{TV}}(P,Q)\) (Le Cam Le Cam's two-point method).
Bounds by other divergences: Pinsker Pinsker's inequality, Bretagnolle–Huber Bretagnolle–Huber inequality, Hellinger \(f\)-divergences: Hellinger, \(\chi^2\) and their relations.
Trajectory TV: \({\mathrm{TV}}(P^{\pi}_\tau,P^{\pi'}_\tau)\le\sum_{h}{\mathbb{E}}_{s_h\sim\pi}{\mathrm{TV}}(\pi_h(\cdot|s_h),\pi'_h(\cdot|s_h))\) (sub-additivity via coupling/telescoping).
cards.det: Value differences under two distributions: since returns lie in \([0,\tfrac{1}{1-\gamma}]\), \(|{\mathbb{E}}_Pf-{\mathbb{E}}_Qf|\le\tfrac{1}{1-\gamma}{\mathrm{TV}}(P,Q)\). This is the step that turns distribution shift into value error in behaviour cloning (\(H^2{\varepsilon}\) compounding errors), conservative policy iteration, and the simulation lemma Simulation lemma (model error \(\to\) value error).
cards.ex: Behaviour cloning: if the learned policy disagrees with the expert with probability \({\varepsilon}\) per step, the trajectory TV is \(\le H{\varepsilon}\), so \(|V^{\hat\pi}-V^{\pi_E}|\le H\cdot H{\varepsilon}=H^2{\varepsilon}\) (finite horizon, rewards in \([0,1]\)).
cards.use: Simulation lemma, behaviour cloning and imitation, distribution shift, coupling arguments for mixing, testing lower bounds.

qz.q: Let \({\mathrm{TV}}(P,Q)=0.1\). Over all measurable \(f\) with values in \([0,B]\), what is the largest possible value of \(|{\mathbb{E}}_Pf-{\mathbb{E}}_Qf|\)?
qz.why: The span bound gives \(|{\mathbb{E}}_Pf-{\mathbb{E}}_Qf|\le{\operatorname{sp}}(f){\mathrm{TV}}=0.1B\), attained by \(f=B{\mathbf{1}}_A\) with \(A\) the event achieving \(\sup_A|P(A)-Q(A)|\). The bound \(2{\lVert f\rVert}_\infty{\mathrm{TV}}=0.2B\) is valid but loose because it ignores that \(f\ge0\).

qz.q: A test must decide between \(P\) and \(Q\) from one observation, with \({\mathrm{TV}}(P,Q)=0.3\). What is the minimum achievable sum of type-I and type-II error probabilities?
qz.why: By Le Cam, \(\inf_\psi\{P(\psi=1)+Q(\psi=0)\}=1-{\mathrm{TV}}(P,Q)=0.7\), attained by the likelihood-ratio test. \(0.35\) is the minimum average of the two errors, not their sum; \(0.3\) confuses the error with \({\mathrm{TV}}\) itself.

qz.q: Behaviour cloning, horizon \(H\), rewards in \([0,1]\): the learner disagrees with the expert with probability \({\varepsilon}\) per step, giving \(|V^{\hat\pi}-V^{\pi_E}|\le H^2{\varepsilon}\). Where does the second factor \(H\) come from (the first being trajectory \({\mathrm{TV}}\le H{\varepsilon}\))?
a: the return ranges over \([0,H]\), so value gap \(\le H\cdot{\mathrm{TV}}\)
a union bound over the \(H\) actions the expert takes per episode
Pinsker's inequality, applied separately at each of the \(H\) steps
the mixing time of the dynamics, which is at most \(H\) steps
qz.why: Sub-additivity of TV along the trajectory (coupling) gives \({\mathrm{TV}}\le H{\varepsilon}\); then \(|{\mathbb{E}}_Pf-{\mathbb{E}}_Qf|\le{\operatorname{sp}}(f){\mathrm{TV}}\) with \(f\) the return, whose span is \(H\). Together: \(H\cdot H{\varepsilon}\).

cards.name: Chain rule for KL & trajectory divergence decomposition
cards.plain: Chain rule for KL & trajectory divergence decomposition
cards.lay: The KL between two joint distributions splits into the KL of the first variable plus the expected KL of the next variable given the first, and so on. For trajectories with shared dynamics, only the policy terms survive; for shared policies, only the dynamics terms survive.
cards.st: For joint distributions on \((X,Y)\): \[ {\mathrm{KL}}(P_{XY}\|Q_{XY})={\mathrm{KL}}(P_X\|Q_X)+{\mathbb{E}}_{x\sim P_X}\bigl[{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{Y|X=x}\|Q_{Y|X=x})\bigr]. \] For trajectories of length \(H\) generated by \((\pi,P)\) and \((\pi',P')\) from the same initial distribution: \[ {\mathrm{KL}}(\mathbb P_{\pi,P}\|\mathbb P_{\pi',P'})={\mathbb{E}}_{\pi,P}\sum_{h}\Bigl[{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi(\cdot|s_h)\|\pi'(\cdot|s_h))+{\mathrm{KL}}(P(\cdot|s_h,a_h)\|P'(\cdot|s_h,a_h))\Bigr]. \]
ver: Bandit divergence decomposition: \({\mathrm{KL}}(\mathbb P_ u\|\mathbb P_{ u'})=\sum_a{\mathbb{E}}_ u[N_a(T)]{\mathrm{KL}}( u_a\| u'_a)\) Divergence decomposition for bandits.
Independent product: \({\mathrm{KL}}(P^{\otimes n}\|Q^{\otimes n})=n{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)\).
Chain rule for mutual information and entropy Entropy, mutual information & their chain rules.
Same structure for \(\chi^2\) fails (it is not additive), but \(1+\chi^2\) is multiplicative for products; Hellinger affinity is multiplicative.
cards.det: This is why KL is the natural divergence for sequential lower bounds: adaptivity of the algorithm is absorbed into the expectation \({\mathbb{E}}_{\pi,P}\), and only local (per-step) divergences need computing. It is also the basis of TRPO's surrogate: when dynamics are shared, \({\mathrm{KL}}\) between trajectory distributions is a sum of per-state policy KLs.
cards.ex: Two MDPs differing only at one \((s,a)\) pair by \({\mathrm{KL}}(P(\cdot|s,a)\|P'(\cdot|s,a))={\varepsilon}^2\): any algorithm's trajectory distributions differ by \({\mathbb{E}}[N(s,a)]{\varepsilon}^2\) in KL, so to tell them apart it must visit \((s,a)\) about \(1/{\varepsilon}^2\) times.
cards.use: Lower bounds for bandits and MDPs, TRPO/PPO theory, KL-regularised RL, likelihood decomposition in EM for HMMs.

qz.q: Two policies \(\pi,\pi'\) run in the same MDP (same dynamics \(P\) and initial distribution) for \(H\) steps. \({\mathrm{KL}}(\mathbb P_{\pi,P}\|\mathbb P_{\pi',P})\) equals:
qz.why: Chain rule: the dynamics terms vanish because \(P=P'\), and the expectation is under the first argument's law, \(\mathbb P_{\pi,P}\). The max over states is only an upper bound, not an identity.

qz.q: For a single sample, \(\chi^2(P\|Q)=c\). For \(n\) i.i.d. samples, \(\chi^2(P^{\otimes n}\|Q^{\otimes n})\) equals:
qz.why: \(1+\chi^2={\mathbb{E}}_Q[({\mathrm{d}} P/{\mathrm{d}} Q)^2]\) factorises over independent coordinates, so it is multiplicative: \(1+\chi^2(P^{\otimes n}\|Q^{\otimes n})=(1+c)^n\). Additivity \(n\,D\) holds for KL, not for \(\chi^2\).

qz.q: Two MDPs differ only at one pair \((s,a)\), with \({\mathrm{KL}}(P(\cdot|s,a)\|P'(\cdot|s,a))={\varepsilon}^2\). Telling them apart needs trajectory KL of order \(1\). If \({\varepsilon}\) is halved, the expected number of visits to \((s,a)\) needed:
a: is unchanged, since an adaptive algorithm can choose where to go
qz.why: The chain rule gives trajectory KL \(={\mathbb{E}}[N(s,a)]{\varepsilon}^2\), with the algorithm's adaptivity absorbed into \({\mathbb{E}}[N(s,a)]\); so one needs \({\mathbb{E}}[N(s,a)]\gtrsim1/{\varepsilon}^2\), which grows by \(4\) when \({\varepsilon}\) halves.

cards.name: Data-processing inequality
cards.lay: Processing data cannot make two distributions more distinguishable. Whatever you compute from samples (a statistic, a decision, a policy's actions), the divergence between the two worlds can only shrink.
cards.st: For any Markov kernel (channel) \(K\) and any \(f\)-divergence \(D_f\) (KL, TV, \(\chi^2\), Hellinger, ...): \[ D_f(PK\,\|\,QK)\le D_f(P\|Q). \] For mutual information: if \(X\to Y\to Z\) is a Markov chain then \(I(X;Z)\le I(X;Y)\).
ver: Deterministic processing: \({\mathrm{KL}}(P\circ g^{-1}\|Q\circ g^{-1})\le{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)\).
Event version (used in lower bounds): for any event \(A\), \(\mathrm{kl}(P(A),Q(A))\le{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)\) (binary KL on the left).
Strong data-processing: contracting kernels shrink divergences by a factor \(<1\) (Dobrushin coefficient for TV) Mixing time & geometric ergodicity.
cards.det: The event version is the key step in the modern proof of the Lai–Robbins lower bound Lai–Robbins asymptotic lower bound (Garivier, Ménard & Stoltz): \(\sum_a{\mathbb{E}}_ u[N_a]{\mathrm{KL}}( u_a\| u'_a)\ge\mathrm{kl}(\Pr_ u(E),\Pr_{ u'}(E))\) for any event \(E\).
cards.ex: Two transition kernels \(P,P'\) followed by the same policy for one step: \({\mathrm{TV}}(\mu P,\mu P')\le{\mathrm{TV}}(\mu,\mu)+\max_s{\mathrm{TV}}(P(s),P'(s))\), and pushing two state distributions through the same \(P\) cannot increase their TV.
cards.use: Lower bounds (bandits, MDPs, Fano), stability of state distributions under shared dynamics, privacy, mixing arguments.

qz.q: All you know is \({\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)\le0.1\). Which conclusion follows?
a: Some statistic \(g\) may give \({\mathrm{KL}}(P\circ g^{-1}\|Q\circ g^{-1})=0.2\)
qz.why: Event DPI: \(\mathrm{kl}(P(A),Q(A))\le0.1\), but \(\mathrm{kl}(0.9,0.1)=0.8\log9\approx1.76\). Differences \(|P(A)-Q(A)|\) up to \(\sqrt{0.05}\approx0.22\) are allowed by Pinsker (and e.g. \(0.15\) is achievable), processing cannot raise KL, and KL is not symmetric.

qz.q: In which situation can the divergence between the two resulting distributions increase, so that the data-processing inequality gives no guarantee?
a: \(P=Q\) pushed through two different kernels \(K\ne K'\)
\(P,Q\) pushed through the same randomised policy
a deterministic statistic computed from samples of \(P\) and of \(Q\)
\(P,Q\) pushed \(k\) times through the same transition kernel
qz.why: DPI needs the same channel for both: \(D_f(PK\|QK)\le D_f(P\|Q)\). With different kernels even identical inputs (\(D_f=0\)) can give different outputs. Random or deterministic, one-step or iterated, a shared kernel can only contract.

qz.q: A parameter \(\theta\) generates data \(D\), and an algorithm outputs a (possibly randomised) policy \(\pi(D)\) using only \(D\). Which statement is correct?
a: \(I(\theta;\pi(D))\le I(\theta;D)\) only if the algorithm is deterministic
qz.why: \(\theta\to D\to\pi(D)\) is a Markov chain whenever the algorithm's randomness is independent of \(\theta\) given \(D\), so DPI applies to randomised processing too. Equality holds only for sufficient statistics, not for every deterministic map.

cards.name: Pinsker's inequality
cards.lay: If two distributions have small KL divergence, they are also close in total variation: TV is at most \(\sqrt{{\mathrm{KL}}/2}\). Lets you convert KL constraints (from trust regions, likelihood bounds or regularisation) into bounds on expected values.
cards.st: For any \(P,Q\): \[ {\mathrm{TV}}(P,Q)\le\sqrt{\tfrac12{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)}. \]
ver: \(\ell_1\) form: \({\lVert P-Q\rVert}_1\le\sqrt{2{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)}\).
Binary (refined) form: \(\mathrm{kl}(p,q)\ge2(p-q)^2\) KL for Bernoulli & Gaussian distributions.
Strong convexity of negative entropy w.r.t. \({\lVert \cdot\rVert}_1\) on the simplex is equivalent to Pinsker Strong convexity, PL & quadratic growth.
When \({\mathrm{KL}}\) is large (\(>2\)), Pinsker is vacuous; use Bretagnolle–Huber Bretagnolle–Huber inequality instead.

Reverse Pinsker (finite support): \({\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)\le\tfrac{{\lVert P-Q\rVert}_1^2}{\min_xQ(x)}\) (more precisely bounded by \(\chi^2\) \(f\)-divergences: Hellinger, \(\chi^2\) and their relations).
cards.det:
Proof idea. By data processing Data-processing inequality reduce to two-point distributions (via the event \(A\) achieving TV), then verify \(\mathrm{kl}(p,q)\ge2(p-q)^2\) by calculus.

In policy optimisation, Pinsker converts a KL trust region \({\mathrm{KL}}(\pi'\|\pi)\le\delta\) into \({\mathrm{TV}}\le\sqrt{\delta/2}\), which plugs into the performance difference lemma Performance difference lemma (Kakade–Langford) to bound the surrogate error (\(\propto\gamma{\varepsilon}\sqrt{\delta}/(1-\gamma)^2\) in TRPO's improvement bound).
cards.ex: Lower bounds: if \({\mathrm{KL}}(\mathbb P_1\|\mathbb P_2)\le\tfrac18\) then \({\mathrm{TV}}\le\tfrac14\), so any test errs with probability \(\ge\tfrac38\) under one of the two hypotheses.
cards.use: TRPO/PPO improvement bounds, lower bounds, converting KL model error to value error, mirror descent analysis on the simplex.

qz.q: A policy update satisfies the KL trust region \({\mathrm{KL}}(\pi'(\cdot|s)\|\pi(\cdot|s))\le0.02\). What bound does Pinsker give on \({\mathrm{TV}}(\pi'(\cdot|s),\pi(\cdot|s))\)?
qz.why: \({\mathrm{TV}}\le\sqrt{{\mathrm{KL}}/2}=\sqrt{0.01}=0.1\). The value \(0.2=\sqrt{2{\mathrm{KL}}}\) is the bound on \({\lVert \pi'-\pi\rVert}_1=2{\mathrm{TV}}\), a factor \(2\) off for TV.

qz.q: Suppose \({\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)=3\). Which statement is correct?
a: Pinsker is vacuous here but Bretagnolle–Huber still gives \({\mathrm{TV}}<1\)
Bretagnolle–Huber is vacuous here but Pinsker still gives \({\mathrm{TV}}<1\)
Both only give the trivial bound \({\mathrm{TV}}\le1\)
qz.why: Pinsker: \(\sqrt{3/2}\approx1.22>1\), vacuous. BH: \({\mathrm{TV}}\le\sqrt{1-e^{-3}}\approx0.97<1\), still informative; BH never exceeds \(1\).

qz.q: Which statement about bounding KL by total variation (the reverse of Pinsker) is correct?
a: No bound \({\mathrm{KL}}\le g({\mathrm{TV}})\) holds without assumptions on \(Q\)
qz.why: Take \(P=\mathrm{Ber}({\varepsilon})\), \(Q=\delta_0\): \({\mathrm{TV}}={\varepsilon}\) but \({\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)=\infty\). Reverse Pinsker needs a lower bound on \(\min_xQ(x)\): \({\mathrm{KL}}\le{\lVert P-Q\rVert}_1^2/\min_xQ(x)\).

cards.name: KL for Bernoulli & Gaussian distributions
cards.lay: Closed forms you will use constantly in bandit theory: KL between two Gaussians with the same variance is the squared mean gap over \(2\sigma^2\); between Bernoullis it is the binary \(\mathrm{kl}\), bounded below by \(2(p-q)^2\) and above by \(\chi^2\).
cards.st: \[ {\mathrm{KL}}\bigl({\mathcal{N}}(\mu_1,\sigma^2)\,\|\,{\mathcal{N}}(\mu_2,\sigma^2)\bigr)=\frac{(\mu_1-\mu_2)^2}{2\sigma^2},\qquad\mathrm{kl}(p,q)=p\log\frac pq+(1-p)\log\frac{1-p}{1-q}, \] \[ 2(p-q)^2\le\mathrm{kl}(p,q)\le\frac{(p-q)^2}{q(1-q)}. \]
ver: Multivariate Gaussians: \({\mathrm{KL}}({\mathcal{N}}(\mu_1,\Sigma_1)\|{\mathcal{N}}(\mu_2,\Sigma_2))=\tfrac12\bigl[{\operatorname{tr}}(\Sigma_2^{-1}\Sigma_1)+(\mu_2-\mu_1)^\top\Sigma_2^{-1}(\mu_2-\mu_1)-d+\log\tfrac{\det\Sigma_2}{\det\Sigma_1}\bigr]\).

Near \(\tfrac12\): \(\mathrm{kl}(\tfrac12+{\varepsilon},\tfrac12)\approx2{\varepsilon}^2\) and \(\mathrm{kl}(\tfrac12+{\varepsilon},\tfrac12-{\varepsilon})\le\tfrac{8{\varepsilon}^2}{1-4{\varepsilon}^2}\) — the standard lower-bound construction.
Exponential families: \({\mathrm{KL}}(p_{\theta}\|p_{\theta'})=D_A(\theta',\theta)\), the Bregman divergence of the log-partition Bregman divergences & the three-point identity.
Small-mean regime: \(\mathrm{kl}(p,q)\ge\tfrac{(p-q)^2}{2\max(p,q)}\), much stronger than \(2(p-q)^2\) when \(p,q\) are small.
cards.det: The upper bound \(\mathrm{kl}(p,q)\le\chi^2=\tfrac{(p-q)^2}{q(1-q)}\) follows from \({\mathrm{KL}}\le\log(1+\chi^2)\le\chi^2\) \(f\)-divergences: Hellinger, \(\chi^2\) and their relations. These closed forms turn the abstract lower bounds (Lai–Robbins, minimax) into explicit \(\tfrac{\log T}{\Delta}\) and \(\sqrt{KT}\) rates.
cards.ex: Two Bernoulli arms with means \(\tfrac12\) and \(\tfrac12+\Delta\): \(\mathrm{kl}\approx2\Delta^2\), so Lai–Robbins gives \({\mathbb{E}} N_{\text{sub}}(T)\gtrsim\tfrac{\log T}{2\Delta^2}\) and regret \(\gtrsim\tfrac{\log T}{2\Delta}\).
cards.use: Every bandit lower bound, KL-UCB indices, Gaussian MDP constructions, Thompson sampling posteriors.

qz.q: What is \({\mathrm{KL}}\bigl({\mathcal{N}}(0,\sigma^2)\,\|\,{\mathcal{N}}(1,\sigma^2)\bigr)\) with \(\sigma=2\)?
qz.why: \(\frac{(\mu_1-\mu_2)^2}{2\sigma^2}=\frac{1}{2\cdot4}=\frac18\). \(1/4=1/\sigma^2\) forgets the \(2\) (or uses \(2\sigma\) for \(2\sigma^2\)); \(1/2=1/\sigma\) and \(1/16=1/\sigma^4\) get the power of \(\sigma\) wrong.

qz.q: Bernoulli means \(p=2q\) with \(q\to0\) (rare rewards); the true \(\mathrm{kl}(2q,q)\approx(2\log2-1)q\approx0.39q\). Which lower bound has the right order?
a: \(\frac{(p-q)^2}{q(1-q)}\approx q\), used as a lower bound
\(2(p-q)^2\), since Pinsker is tight for Bernoullis
qz.why: The small-mean bound gives order \(q\), matching \(\mathrm{kl}\). Pinsker's \(2(p-q)^2=2q^2\) (and anything of order \(q^2\)) is off by a factor \(1/q\); Pinsker is tight only near \(p=q=\tfrac12\). \(\frac{(p-q)^2}{q(1-q)}\) is the \(\chi^2\) upper bound, not a lower bound.

qz.q: Two Bernoulli arms with means \(\tfrac12\) and \(\tfrac12+\Delta\). Lai–Robbins gives \({\mathbb{E}} N_{\text{sub}}(T)\gtrsim\frac{\log T}{\mathrm{kl}}\) with \(\mathrm{kl}\approx2\Delta^2\). If \(\Delta\) is halved, the regret lower bound:
a: halves, as each bad pull costs \(\Delta/2\)
qz.why: Regret \(=\Delta\,{\mathbb{E}} N_{\text{sub}}\gtrsim\Delta\cdot\frac{\log T}{2\Delta^2}=\frac{\log T}{2\Delta}\), which doubles. The pull count does quadruple, but each pull costs half as much.

cards.name: Bretagnolle–Huber inequality
cards.lay: A version of “small KL \(\Rightarrow\) hard to distinguish” that stays informative even when the KL is large: the sum of the probabilities of an event under \(P\) and of its complement under \(Q\) is at least \(\tfrac12e^{-{\mathrm{KL}}}\). The go-to tool for minimax bandit lower bounds.
cards.st: For any distributions \(P,Q\) and any event \(A\): \[ P(A)+Q(A^c)\ge\frac12\exp\bigl(-{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)\bigr). \] Equivalently \({\mathrm{TV}}(P,Q)\le\sqrt{1-e^{-{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)}}\le1-\tfrac12e^{-{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)}\).
ver: Bandit minimax lower bound: choosing two environments differing in one arm by \(\Delta\) with \({\mathrm{KL}}\approx{\mathbb{E}}[N_i]\Delta^2\) yields \({\mathrm{Reg}}_T\ge c\sqrt{KT}\) Minimax \(\Omega(\sqrt{KT})\) lower bound.
Compare with Pinsker: \({\mathrm{TV}}\le\sqrt{{\mathrm{KL}}/2}\) (better for small KL); BH never exceeds 1.
cards.det: Proof idea. \(P(A)+Q(A^c)\ge\int\min(p,q)\) and \(\bigl(\int\sqrt{pq}\bigr)^2\le\int\min(p,q)\int\max(p,q)\le2\int\min(p,q)\); finally \(\int\sqrt{pq}\ge e^{-{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)/2}\) by Jensen Jensen's inequality.
cards.ex: Lattimore & Szepesvári, Thm. 15.2: for \(K\)-armed Gaussian bandits and any policy, \(\max_\nu{\mathrm{Reg}}_T(\nu)\ge\tfrac{1}{27}\sqrt{(K-1)T}\) — proved with BH and the divergence decomposition.
cards.use: Minimax lower bounds for bandits and RL, non-stationary lower bounds, best-arm identification lower bounds.

qz.q: Let \({\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)=2\). What lower bound does Bretagnolle–Huber give on \(P(A)+Q(A^c)\), for any event \(A\)?
qz.why: BH: \(P(A)+Q(A^c)\ge\tfrac12e^{-{\mathrm{KL}}}=\tfrac12e^{-2}\). The exponent is the KL itself, not \({\mathrm{KL}}/2\) or \(\sqrt{\mathrm{KL}}\); by contrast Pinsker here gives only the trivial \(1-{\mathrm{TV}}\ge0\).

qz.q: Minimax lower bound for \(K\)-armed bandits: environment \( u'\) raises the mean of an arm \(i\) with \({\mathbb{E}}_ u[N_i(T)]\le T/(K-1)\) by \(2\Delta\), so \({\mathrm{KL}}(\mathbb P_ u\|\mathbb P_{ u'})\approx{\mathbb{E}}_ u[N_i]\Delta^2\). Why choose \(\Delta\asymp\sqrt{K/T}\)?
a: It keeps \({\mathbb{E}}_\nu[N_i]\Delta^2=O(1)\), so \(e^{-{\mathrm{KL}}}\) stays bounded below
It makes \(T\Delta^2=O(1)\), so that no arm at all can be identified
It makes the KL grow like \(\log T\), as in the Lai–Robbins argument
It makes \(\Delta\) exceed the Hoeffding width of the least-pulled arm
qz.why: With \({\mathbb{E}}[N_i]\le T/(K-1)\) and \(\Delta^2\asymp K/T\), the KL is \(O(1)\), so BH keeps the error probability constant and regret \(\gtrsim T\Delta\asymp\sqrt{KT}\). Using \(T\Delta^2=O(1)\) ignores the \(K\)-fold split of pulls and loses the \(\sqrt K\).

qz.q: Let \({\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)=0.01\). Compare the TV bounds from Pinsker, \(\sqrt{{\mathrm{KL}}/2}\), and Bretagnolle–Huber, \(\sqrt{1-e^{-{\mathrm{KL}}}}\):
a: They coincide to first order as \({\mathrm{KL}}\to0\)
BH is tighter, because it never exceeds \(1\)
qz.why: For small KL, \(\sqrt{1-e^{-{\mathrm{KL}}}}\approx\sqrt{{\mathrm{KL}}}\), which is \(\sqrt2\) times Pinsker's \(\sqrt{{\mathrm{KL}}/2}\). BH wins only for large KL, where Pinsker exceeds \(1\).

cards.name: \(f\)-divergences: Hellinger, \(\chi^2\) and their relations
cards.plain: f-divergences: Hellinger, χ^2 and their relations
cards.lay: KL and TV are members of a family \(D_f(P\|Q)={\mathbb{E}}_Q f({\mathrm{d}} P/{\mathrm{d}} Q)\). Hellinger distance is the friendly one for products of distributions, \(\chi^2\) controls importance-sampling variance. Knowing the ordering lets you move between them.
cards.st: For convex \(f\) with \(f(1)=0\): \(D_f(P\|Q)={\mathbb{E}}_Q\bigl[f\bigl(\tfrac{{\mathrm{d}} P}{{\mathrm{d}} Q}\bigr)\bigr]\). With \(H^2(P,Q)=\tfrac12\int(\sqrt{{\mathrm{d}} P}-\sqrt{{\mathrm{d}} Q})^2\) and \(\chi^2(P\|Q)={\mathbb{E}}_Q[(\tfrac{{\mathrm{d}} P}{{\mathrm{d}} Q})^2]-1\): \[ H^2\le{\mathrm{TV}}\le\sqrt2\,H,\qquad{\mathrm{TV}}\le\sqrt{\tfrac12{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)}, \] \[ 2H^2\le{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)\le\log\bigl(1+\chi^2(P\|Q)\bigr)\le\chi^2(P\|Q). \]
ver: Generators: KL \(f=t\log t\); TV \(f=\tfrac12|t-1|\); \(\chi^2\) \(f=(t-1)^2\); squared Hellinger \(f=\tfrac12(\sqrt t-1)^2\).
Hellinger tensorises: \(1-H^2(P^{\otimes n},Q^{\otimes n})=(1-H^2(P,Q))^n\).
Variational (dual) form: \(D_f(P\|Q)=\sup_g\{{\mathbb{E}}_Pg-{\mathbb{E}}_Qf^*(g)\}\) — basis of \(f\)-GAN, GAIL and DICE estimators Convex conjugate & Fenchel–Young.

\(\chi^2\) and importance sampling: \({\operatorname{Var}}_Q(\tfrac{{\mathrm{d}} P}{{\mathrm{d}} Q})=\chi^2(P\|Q)\); Chapman–Robbins/Hammersley lower bound \({\operatorname{Var}}(\hat\theta)\ge\sup\tfrac{({\mathbb{E}}_P\hat\theta-{\mathbb{E}}_Q\hat\theta)^2}{\chi^2(P\|Q)}\).

Squared Hellinger is the right loss for MLE: \({\mathbb{E}} H^2(\hat P,P)\lesssim\tfrac{\log|{\mathcal{P}}|}{n}\) for MLE over a finite class — used in model-based RL with general function approximation.
cards.det: Data processing Data-processing inequality holds for every \(f\)-divergence. The Hellinger–TV sandwich \(H^2\le{\mathrm{TV}}\le\sqrt2H\) (with the normalisation above, \({\mathrm{TV}}\le H\sqrt{2-H^2}\)) together with tensorisation is how one proves that \(n\asymp1/H^2(P,Q)\) samples are necessary and sufficient to test \(P\) vs. \(Q\).
cards.ex: Off-policy evaluation with importance weights: the variance of the IS estimator of \({\mathbb{E}}_P[f]\) with \(|f|\le1\) is at most \(1+\chi^2(P\|Q)\) — so \(\chi^2\), not KL, governs OPE sample complexity.
cards.use: Choosing the right divergence for OPE (\(\chi^2\)), MLE-based model learning (Hellinger), testing lower bounds, imitation learning and GAIL variational objectives.

qz.q: Off-policy evaluation with importance weights \(w={\mathrm{d}} P/{\mathrm{d}} Q\) (target \(P\), behaviour \(Q\)). Which divergence equals the variance of \(w\) under \(Q\)?
qz.why: \({\operatorname{Var}}_Q(w)={\mathbb{E}}_Q[w^2]-({\mathbb{E}}_Qw)^2={\mathbb{E}}_Q[w^2]-1=\chi^2(P\|Q)\). KL can be moderate while \(\chi^2\) is huge, so KL does not control IS variance.

qz.q: Using \(2H^2\le{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)\le\log(1+\chi^2(P\|Q))\), which combination of values is possible?
qz.why: \(\log(1+10^6)\approx13.8\ge1\), consistent (a rare point with a large likelihood ratio does this). The others violate the chain: \(\log11\approx2.4<5\), \(\log1.5\approx0.41<1\), and \(2H^2=0.8>0.5\).

qz.q: With \(H^2(P,Q)=0.01\) for one sample, the Hellinger affinity of \(n\) i.i.d. samples is \(1-H^2(P^{\otimes n},Q^{\otimes n})=0.99^n\). For which order of \(n\) does it drop to about \(1/e\), i.e. testing becomes possible?
qz.why: \(0.99^n\approx e^{-0.01n}\), which is \(1/e\) at \(n=100=1/H^2\). This is the \(n\asymp1/H^2(P,Q)\) testing rate from tensorisation; \(10=1/H\) and \(10^4=1/H^4\) have the wrong power.
