cards.name: Donsker–Varadhan & Gibbs variational principle
cards.lay: The log of an exponential moment is the best trade-off between “expected value of \(f\)” and “KL distance from the base distribution”. It explains why softmax/Boltzmann policies are optimal for KL-regularised objectives and is the engine of PAC-Bayes bounds.
cards.st: For a base measure \(Q\) and measurable \(f\) with \({\mathbb{E}}_Qe^f<\infty\): \[ \log{\mathbb{E}}_Q\bigl[e^{f}\bigr]=\sup_{P\ll Q}\bigl\{{\mathbb{E}}_P[f]-{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)\bigr\}, \] with the supremum attained by the Gibbs measure \({\mathrm{d}} P^\star\propto e^f{\mathrm{d}} Q\). Equivalently \({\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)=\sup_f\{{\mathbb{E}}_Pf-\log{\mathbb{E}}_Qe^f\}\).
ver: Change-of-measure inequality: \({\mathbb{E}}_Pf\le{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)+\log{\mathbb{E}}_Qe^f\) for every \(P\) — combined with Markov this gives PAC-Bayes PAC-Bayes bounds.
KL-regularised RL: \(\max_\pi\{{\mathbb{E}}_\pi Q(s,\cdot)-\tau{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi\|\pi_0)\}=\tau\log{\mathbb{E}}_{a\sim\pi_0}e^{Q(s,a)/\tau}\), attained by \(\pi\propto\pi_0e^{Q/\tau}\).
Finite uniform \(Q\): log-sum-exp \(=\max_p\{{\langle p, f\rangle}+H(p)\}-\log n\) Log-sum-exp (soft-max) sandwich.
Transportation lemma: \(f\) is \(\sigma\)-sub-Gaussian under \(Q\) iff \(|{\mathbb{E}}_Pf-{\mathbb{E}}_Qf|\le\sqrt{2\sigma^2{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)}\) for all \(P\).
cards.det: Proof. For any \(P\): \({\mathbb{E}}_Pf-{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)=\log{\mathbb{E}}_Qe^f-{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|P^\star)\le\log{\mathbb{E}}_Qe^f\), with equality at \(P=P^\star\). The ELBO ELBO decomposition (free-energy view of EM) is exactly this identity with \(f=\log p(x,z)-\log q_0(z)\): \(\log p(x)=\max_q\mathrm{ELBO}(q)\), attained at the posterior.
cards.ex: Policy mirror descent update \(\pi_{k+1}(\cdot|s)\propto\pi_k(\cdot|s)e^{\eta Q^{\pi_k}(s,\cdot)}\) is the Gibbs maximiser of \(\eta{\mathbb{E}}_\pi Q-{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi\|\pi_k)\).
cards.use: KL-/entropy-regularised RL, PAC-Bayes, ELBO and EM (E-step as Gibbs posterior), transportation-cost concentration, MINE-type estimators.

qz.q: Two actions, reference \(\pi_0\) uniform, \(Q(s,\cdot)=(0,1)\), temperature \(\tau=1\). What is \(\max_\pi\{{\mathbb{E}}_{a\sim\pi}Q(s,a)-{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi\|\pi_0)\}\) and its maximiser?
qz.why: Gibbs variational principle: the value is \(\log{\mathbb{E}}_{\pi_0}e^{Q}=\log\frac{1+e}{2}\), attained by \(\pi\propto\pi_0e^{Q}\). \(\log(1+e)\) drops the base measure \(\pi_0\); \(\frac{e}{1+e}\) is only \({\mathbb{E}}_\pi Q\), ignoring the KL penalty.

qz.q: KL-regularised objective \(\max_\pi\{{\mathbb{E}}_\pi Q(s,\cdot)-\tau{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi\|\pi_0)\}\) with a non-uniform, full-support reference \(\pi_0\). As \(\tau\to\infty\), the optimal policy and value tend to:
qz.why: \(\pi\propto\pi_0e^{Q/\tau}\to\pi_0\) and \(\tau\log{\mathbb{E}}_{\pi_0}e^{Q/\tau}\to{\mathbb{E}}_{\pi_0}Q\). The greedy limit is \(\tau\to0\); the uniform policy appears only if \(\pi_0\) is uniform.

qz.q: Let \(f(X)\in[a,b]\) under \(Q\), so \(f\) is \(\tfrac{b-a}{2}\)-sub-Gaussian under \(Q\). What does the transportation lemma give for every \(P\)?
qz.why: \(\sqrt{2\sigma^2{\mathrm{KL}}}\) with \(\sigma=\frac{b-a}2\) gives \((b-a)\sqrt{{\mathrm{KL}}/2}\) — exactly span \(\times\) Pinsker. Halving it is false (Bernoulli \(\tfrac12\) vs. \(\tfrac12+\eta\): gap \(\eta\), \({\mathrm{KL}}\approx2\eta^2\)), and the dependence on KL is a square root, not linear, for sub-Gaussian \(f\).

cards.name: Le Cam's two-point method
cards.lay: To show a problem is hard, find two instances that are far apart (so a good algorithm must distinguish them) but statistically close (so it can't). The minimax error is then at least the separation times the overlap.
cards.st: Let \(\theta_0,\theta_1\) be parameters with loss satisfying \(\ell(\hat\theta,\theta_0)+\ell(\hat\theta,\theta_1)\ge2\Delta\) for every \(\hat\theta\). Then for any estimator based on data from \(P_{\theta}\): \[ \max_{j\in\{0,1\}}{\mathbb{E}}_{\theta_j}\ell(\hat\theta,\theta_j)\ge\frac\Delta2\bigl(1-{\mathrm{TV}}(P_{\theta_0},P_{\theta_1})\bigr)\ge\frac\Delta4\exp\bigl(-{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{\theta_0}\|P_{\theta_1})\bigr). \]
ver: Testing form: \(\inf_\psi\{P_0(\psi=1)+P_1(\psi=0)\}=1-{\mathrm{TV}}(P_0,P_1)\) (Neyman–Pearson / Le Cam).
Mixture version (Le Cam's convex hull method): compare \(P_0\) with a mixture \(\bar P=\tfrac1M\sum_jP_j\) — gives \(\sqrt{d}\)-type lower bounds.
Many hypotheses: Fano Fano's inequality & Fano's method, Assouad Assouad's lemma.
cards.det: Typical RL usage: two MDPs that differ by \({\varepsilon}\) in one transition probability out of a state reached with probability \(p\); values differ by \(\approx{\varepsilon}/(1-\gamma)\) while \({\mathrm{KL}}\approx np{\varepsilon}^2\) after \(n\) episodes, giving \(n\gtrsim\tfrac{1}{p{\varepsilon}^2}\).
cards.ex: Estimating a coin's bias: \(P_0=\mathrm{Ber}(\tfrac12)^{\otimes n}\), \(P_1=\mathrm{Ber}(\tfrac12+{\varepsilon})^{\otimes n}\); \({\mathrm{KL}}=n\,\mathrm{kl}(\tfrac12,\tfrac12+{\varepsilon})\approx2n{\varepsilon}^2\), so error \(\gtrsim{\varepsilon}\) unless \(n\gtrsim1/{\varepsilon}^2\).
cards.use: Sample-complexity lower bounds (generative model, PAC-RL), non-stationary lower bounds, estimation lower bounds for EM-type problems.

qz.q: Estimating a coin's bias: \(\mathrm{Ber}(\tfrac12)^{\otimes n}\) vs. \(\mathrm{Ber}(\tfrac12+{\varepsilon})^{\otimes n}\) have \({\mathrm{KL}}\approx2n{\varepsilon}^2\). To estimate the bias to accuracy \({\varepsilon}=0.01\), Le Cam's method shows \(n\) must be of order:
qz.why: The error stays \(\gtrsim{\varepsilon}\) unless \({\mathrm{KL}}=2n{\varepsilon}^2\gtrsim1\), i.e. \(n\gtrsim1/{\varepsilon}^2=10^4\). \(10^2\) corresponds to the wrong rate \(1/{\varepsilon}\).

qz.q: Same coin problem with loss \(|\hat\theta-\theta|\): two hypotheses \({\varepsilon}\) apart give separation \(\Delta={\varepsilon}/2\) and \({\mathrm{KL}}\approx2n{\varepsilon}^2\). What is the best choice of \({\varepsilon}\) and the resulting lower bound?
a: \({\varepsilon}\) as large as possible, risk \(\gtrsim\) constant
qz.why: The bound is \(\frac{\Delta}{4}e^{-{\mathrm{KL}}}\asymp{\varepsilon}\,e^{-2n{\varepsilon}^2}\), maximised at \({\varepsilon}\asymp1/\sqrt n\) where it is \(\asymp1/\sqrt n\). Large \({\varepsilon}\) kills the factor \(e^{-{\mathrm{KL}}}\); small \({\varepsilon}\) kills the separation.

qz.q: Two MDPs differ by \({\varepsilon}\) in one transition out of a state reached with probability \(p\) per episode, so \({\mathrm{KL}}\approx np{\varepsilon}^2\) after \(n\) episodes. Compared with \(p=1\), if \(p=0.01\) the number of episodes needed to distinguish them:
qz.why: Distinguishing needs \(np{\varepsilon}^2\gtrsim1\), i.e. \(n\gtrsim\frac{1}{p{\varepsilon}^2}\): linear in \(1/p\). Only the expected number of visits \(np\) matters.

cards.name: Entropy, mutual information & their chain rules
cards.plain: Entropy, mutual information & their chain rules
cards.lay: Entropy measures uncertainty; mutual information measures how much observing one variable reduces uncertainty about another. They quantify “information gain”, the key quantity in information-directed sampling and Bayesian regret bounds.
cards.st: \(H(X)=-\sum_xp(x)\log p(x)\le\log|{\mathcal{X}}|\), \(I(X;Y)={\mathrm{KL}}(P_{XY}\|P_X\otimes P_Y)=H(X)-H(X\mid Y)\ge0\). Chain rules: \[ H(X_1,\dots,X_n)=\sum_iH(X_i\mid X_{<i}),\qquad I(X;Y_1,\dots,Y_n)=\sum_iI(X;Y_i\mid Y_{<i}). \]
ver: Conditioning reduces entropy: \(H(X\mid Y)\le H(X)\).
Total information gain is bounded: \(\sum_tI_t(\theta;O_t)\le H(\theta)\le\log|\Theta|\) (Bayesian regret via information ratio).
Gaussian information gain: \(I(\theta;y_{1:T})=\tfrac12\log\det(I+\sigma^{-2}K_T)\) — the \(\gamma_T\) in GP-UCB, a log-det potential as in Elliptical potential lemma.
cards.det: Russo & Van Roy's information-ratio analysis: if \(\Gamma_t=\tfrac{({\mathbb{E}}_t[\Delta_t])^2}{I_t(A^\star;(A_t,Y_t))}\le\bar\Gamma\), then Bayesian regret \(\le\sqrt{\bar\Gamma\,H(A^\star)\,T}\) — via Cauchy–Schwarz and the chain rule for MI Information-ratio analysis (Russo–Van Roy).
cards.ex: \(K\)-armed bandits with Thompson sampling: \(\bar\Gamma\le K/2\), \(H(A^\star)\le\log K\), giving Bayesian regret \(\le\sqrt{\tfrac12KT\log K}\).
cards.use: Information-directed sampling, Bayesian regret of Thompson sampling/PSRL, Fano lower bounds, GP-UCB information gain.

qz.q: \(\theta\) is uniform over \(1024\) hypotheses; observations \(O_1,\dots,O_T\) arrive sequentially. Measured in bits, what is the smallest upper bound on \(\sum_{t=1}^TI(\theta;O_t\mid O_{<t})\) valid for every \(T\) and every observation model?
qz.why: By the chain rule the sum equals \(I(\theta;O_{1:T})\le H(\theta)=\log_21024=10\), attained if \(O_1=\theta\). This finite budget of total information is what bounds Bayesian regret via the information ratio.

qz.q: Which statement about conditional entropy is correct?
a: \(H(X\mid Y)\le H(X)\), though \(H(X\mid Y=y)>H(X)\) is possible
\(H(X\mid Y)\le H(X)\) only when \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent
\(I(X;Y)<0\) is possible when \(Y\) is misleading about \(X\)
qz.why: Conditioning reduces entropy only on average: \(H(X)-H(X\mid Y)=I(X;Y)\ge0\). A rare \(y\) can make \(X\) more uncertain (e.g. \(X\) almost surely \(0\), but uniform given \(Y=1\)). Independence gives equality, not the inequality's condition.

qz.q: \(\theta\sim{\mathcal{N}}(0,1)\) and \(y_t=\theta+{\varepsilon}_t\) for \(t=1,\dots,T\) with i.i.d. \({\varepsilon}_t\sim{\mathcal{N}}(0,1)\). What is \(I(\theta;y_{1:T})\)?
qz.why: The posterior variance is \(1/(1+T)\), so \(I=\tfrac12\log\frac{1}{1/(1+T)}\); equivalently \(\tfrac12\log\det(I+J)\) with \(J\) the all-ones matrix. Repeated observations of the same \(\theta\) have diminishing information gain, so it is not \(T\) times the first one.

cards.name: Fano's inequality & Fano's method
cards.lay: If you must identify one of \(M\) hypotheses but the data carry little information about which one is true, you will often be wrong. The error probability is at least \(1-\tfrac{I+\log2}{\log M}\). Gives lower bounds with \(\log M\sim d\) factors (dimension dependence).
cards.st: Let \(V\) be uniform on \(\{1,\dots,M\}\), data \(X\sim P_V\), and \(\hat V=\hat V(X)\). Then \[ \Pr(\hat V\ne V)\ge1-\frac{I(V;X)+\log2}{\log M},\qquad I(V;X)\le\frac1M\sum_j{\mathrm{KL}}(P_j\|\bar P)\le\max_{j,k}{\mathrm{KL}}(P_j\|P_k). \]
ver: Fano's method: with a \(2\delta\)-packing \(\{\theta_j\}\) (loss \(\ge\delta\) when wrong), \(\inf_{\hat\theta}\max_j{\mathbb{E}}\ell(\hat\theta,\theta_j)\ge\delta\bigl(1-\tfrac{I+\log2}{\log M}\bigr)\).
Gilbert–Varshamov: there exist \(M\ge2^{d/8}\) points of \(\{0,1\}^d\) with pairwise Hamming distance \(\ge d/8\) — the standard packing.
Generalised/continuum Fano (Duchi–Wainwright) for non-uniform priors.
cards.det: Proof: entropy chain rule plus data processing Data-processing inequality: \(H(V|\hat V)\le\log2+\Pr(\hat V\ne V)\log M\) and \(H(V|\hat V)\ge H(V)-I(V;X)\).
cards.ex: Linear bandits lower bound \(\Omega(d\sqrt T)\): hypotheses \(\theta\in\{\pm{\varepsilon}\}^d\) (or a packing), each coordinate must be learned — Fano/Assouad give the \(d\) factor.
cards.use: Dimension-dependent lower bounds (linear bandits, linear MDPs), PAC lower bounds with \(\log|{\mathcal{S}}|\) or \(S\) factors, estimation lower bounds.

qz.q: \(V\) is uniform over \(M=1024\) hypotheses and \(I(V;X)=4\) bits. What is Fano's lower bound on \(\Pr(\hat V\ne V)\) (with \(\log2=1\) bit)?
qz.why: \(1-\frac{I+\log2}{\log M}=1-\frac{4+1}{10}=0.5\). Dropping the \(\log2\) gives \(0.6\), which is not implied.

qz.q: Fano with a Gilbert–Varshamov packing of \(M\ge2^{d/8}\) hypotheses, all pairwise \({\mathrm{KL}}(P_j\|P_k)\le\beta\). To keep \(\Pr(\hat V\ne V)\ge\tfrac12\), what is the largest order of \(\beta\) allowed (for large \(d\))?
a: of order \(1\), as in Le Cam
qz.why: Need \(\frac{\beta+\log2}{\log M}\le\frac12\) with \(\log M\ge\frac d8\log2\), i.e. \(\beta\lesssim\frac{d}{16}\log2\). Allowing pairwise KL of order \(d\) (vs. \(O(1)\) for two points) is where Fano's dimension factor comes from.

qz.q: Why is \(\frac1M\sum_j{\mathrm{KL}}(P_j\|\bar P)\le\max_{j,k}{\mathrm{KL}}(P_j\|P_k)\), where \(\bar P=\frac1M\sum_kP_k\)?
a: \(\bar P\) is one of the \(P_k\), so each term is a pairwise KL
Pinsker bounds each \({\mathrm{KL}}(P_j\|\bar P)\) by a pairwise TV
data processing applied to the estimator \(\hat V\)
qz.why: KL is jointly convex, in particular convex in its second argument; averaging over \(k\) and then over \(j\) is bounded by the maximum. \(\bar P\) is a mixture, not one of the \(P_k\).

cards.name: Assouad's lemma
cards.lay: For problems with \(d\) “independent” binary sub-problems (a hypercube of instances), the overall error is at least \(d\) times the error on one coordinate. The workhorse for \(\Omega(\sqrt{SA\ldots})\) and \(\Omega(d\sqrt T)\) lower bounds in RL.
cards.st: Let \(\{P_v:v\in\{-1,1\}^d\}\) and a loss that decomposes as \(\ell(\hat\theta,\theta_v)\ge\alpha\sum_{j=1}^d{\mathbf{1}}\{\hat v_j\ne v_j\}\). Then \[ \max_v{\mathbb{E}}_v\ell(\hat\theta,\theta_v)\ge\frac{\alpha d}{2}\min_{v\sim v'}\bigl(1-{\mathrm{TV}}(P_v,P_{v'})\bigr), \] where \(v\sim v'\) means they differ in exactly one coordinate.
ver: KL form: replace \(1-{\mathrm{TV}}\) by \(\tfrac12e^{-{\mathrm{KL}}}\) (Bretagnolle–Huber Bretagnolle–Huber inequality) or \(1-\sqrt{{\mathrm{KL}}/2}\) (Pinsker).
Typical outcome: \(\Omega(\sqrt{H^2SAT})\)-type regret lower bounds for episodic MDPs and \(\Omega(d\sqrt T)\) for linear bandits.
cards.det: Assouad reduces a \(d\)-dimensional estimation problem to \(d\) two-point problems (Le Cam Le Cam's two-point method) and sums. It needs the loss to be (lower bounded by) a Hamming-type separable loss; regret in MDPs can often be lower bounded this way by building one “hard bandit” per state.
cards.ex: Hard MDP family: \(S\) independent bandit problems each with \(A\) arms, one slightly better arm per state chosen by \(v\); Assouad gives regret \(\Omega(\sqrt{SAT})\) (times horizon factors).
cards.use: Minimax lower bounds for tabular and linear RL, linear bandits, density estimation.

qz.q: Assouad setting: loss \(\ge\alpha\sum_{j=1}^d{\mathbf{1}}\{\hat v_j\ne v_j\}\) and \({\mathrm{TV}}(P_v,P_{v'})\le\tfrac12\) for all neighbours \(v\sim v'\). The lemma gives \(\max_v{\mathbb{E}}_v\ell\ge\):
qz.why: \(\frac{\alpha d}{2}\min_{v\sim v'}(1-{\mathrm{TV}})\ge\frac{\alpha d}2\cdot\frac12\). The factor \(d\) comes from summing \(d\) two-point problems; one coordinate alone gives only \(\alpha/4\).

qz.q: Which hypothesis is specific to Assouad's lemma (as stated on the card)?
a: the loss is at least a sum of per-coordinate errors
every pair \(P_v,P_{v'}\) is close in TV, not just neighbours
the observations are independent across the \(d\) coordinates
qz.why: Assouad needs a Hamming-type separable loss and closeness only between neighbours (differing in one coordinate). Packings belong to Fano, and no independence across coordinates is required.

qz.q: Hard MDP family: \(S\) states, each an independent \(A\)-armed bandit receiving about \(T/S\) of the \(T\) rounds; a \(K\)-armed bandit over \(n\) rounds has minimax regret \(\asymp\sqrt{Kn}\). The total lower bound is of order:
qz.why: Summing over states: \(S\cdot\sqrt{A\,T/S}=\sqrt{SAT}\). \(S\sqrt{AT}\) forgets that the \(T\) rounds are split among the \(S\) states.

cards.name: Martingales & the martingale convergence theorem
cards.lay: A martingale is a “fair game”: its expected next value, given everything so far, is its current value. Martingale differences behave like independent zero-mean noise for concentration purposes. Bounded-in-\(L^1\) martingales converge almost surely.
cards.st: \((M_t)\) adapted to \(({\mathcal{F}}_t)\) is a martingale if \({\mathbb{E}}|M_t|<\infty\) and \({\mathbb{E}}[M_{t+1}\mid{\mathcal{F}}_t]=M_t\) (supermartingale: \(\le\); submartingale: \(\ge\)). (Doob's convergence theorem) If \(\sup_t{\mathbb{E}}|M_t|<\infty\) (e.g. \(M_t\ge0\) supermartingale), then \(M_t\to M_\infty\) almost surely, with \(M_\infty\) finite a.s.
ver: Martingale difference sequence (MDS): \({\mathbb{E}}[D_t\mid{\mathcal{F}}_{t-1}]=0\). Orthogonality: \({\mathbb{E}}[(\sum_tD_t)^2]=\sum_t{\mathbb{E}} D_t^2\).
Doob martingale: \(M_k={\mathbb{E}}[f(X)\mid{\mathcal{F}}_k]\) for any integrable \(f(X)\) (used in McDiarmid McDiarmid's bounded-differences inequality).
\(L^2\)-bounded martingales converge in \(L^2\); uniformly integrable martingales converge in \(L^1\).
Almost-supermartingale version: Robbins–Siegmund Robbins–Siegmund theorem (almost-supermartingales).
cards.det: Recognising martingales is half of every online analysis. Standard RL MDS: \(\xi_t=r_t+\gamma V(s_{t+1})-(T^\pi V)(s_t)\) for a fixed (or predictable) \(V\); the “realised minus expected” terms in regret decompositions; importance-weighted estimators \(\hat\ell_t-\ell_t\) in EXP3.
cards.ex: Likelihood ratio \(L_t=\prod_{s\le t}\tfrac{q(X_s)}{p(X_s)}\) under \(X\sim p\) is a non-negative martingale with mean 1; by convergence and Ville Ville's inequality & method of mixtures (time-uniform bounds), \(\Pr_p(\sup_tL_t\ge1/\delta)\le\delta\) — the sequential probability ratio test.
cards.use: All concentration for adaptive data, almost-sure convergence of SA algorithms, sequential testing, regret analysis.

qz.q: Let \((M_t)\) be a martingale with respect to \(({\mathcal{F}}_t)\). Which extra condition, on its own, guarantees that \(M_t\) converges almost surely to a finite limit?
qz.why: A non-negative martingale has \({\mathbb{E}}|M_t|={\mathbb{E}} M_0\), so it is \(L^1\)-bounded and Doob's theorem applies. The simple symmetric random walk satisfies each of the other three conditions and does not converge.

qz.q: \((D_t)_{t=1}^n\) is a martingale difference sequence (not independent) with \({\mathbb{E}}[D_t^2]=\sigma^2\) for every \(t\). Let \(S_n=\sum_{t=1}^nD_t\). What is \({\mathbb{E}}[S_n^2]\)?
qz.why: Cross terms vanish: for \(s<t\), \({\mathbb{E}}[D_sD_t]={\mathbb{E}}[D_s{\mathbb{E}}[D_t\mid{\mathcal{F}}_{t-1}]]=0\) by the tower rule. Orthogonality of martingale differences is enough; independence is not needed.

qz.q: \(X_1,X_2,\dots\) are i.i.d. from \(p\), \(q\ne p\) is another density, and \(L_t=\prod_{s\le t}q(X_s)/p(X_s)\), \(L_0=1\). Which statement is true?
qz.why: \(L_t\) is a non-negative mean-1 martingale under \(p\), so Ville's inequality Ville's inequality & method of mixtures (time-uniform bounds) gives \(\Pr_p(\sup_tL_t\ge1/\delta)\le\delta\). In fact \(L_t\to0\) a.s. (since \({\mathbb{E}}_p\log L_t=-t\,{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q)<0\)); mean 1 does not force the limit to be 1.

cards.name: Existence & uniqueness of stationary distributions
cards.lay: A Markov chain that can get from any state to any other (irreducible) on a finite state space has exactly one stationary distribution — a distribution that one step of the chain leaves unchanged — and it gives the long-run fraction of time spent in each state.
cards.st: A finite irreducible chain with transition matrix \(P\) has a unique stationary distribution \(\mu\) (\(\mu^\top P=\mu^\top\), \(\mu>0\)), and \(\mu(s)=1/{\mathbb{E}}_s[\tau_s^+]\) where \(\tau_s^+\) is the return time to \(s\). If it is also aperiodic, \(P^t(x,\cdot)\to\mu\) for every \(x\).
ver: Reversible chains: detailed balance \(\mu(x)P(x,y)=\mu(y)P(y,x)\) implies stationarity.
Unichain MDPs: under every stationary policy the chain has a single recurrent class \(\Rightarrow\) the average reward \(\rho^\pi\) is state-independent.
General state spaces: Harris recurrence / Doeblin conditions Doeblin / minorisation condition & uniform ergodicity.
Perron–Frobenius gives the linear-algebraic proof Perron–Frobenius theorem.
cards.det: The stationary distribution \(d^\pi\) of the chain induced by \(\pi\) is the natural weighting for on-policy TD learning Projected Bellman equation & TD fixed point (Tsitsiklis–Van Roy) and the weighting in the average-reward objective \(\rho^\pi={\langle d^\pi, r^\pi\rangle}\).
cards.ex: Random walk on a connected undirected graph: \(\mu(v)=\deg(v)/(2|E|)\) (detailed balance).
cards.use: Average-reward RL, on-policy TD convergence, policy evaluation from a single trajectory, MCMC.

qz.q: Simple random walk on a star graph: one centre joined to \(3\) leaves (no other edges). Starting from a leaf, what is the expected time to return to that leaf?
qz.why: \(\mu(v)=\deg(v)/(2|E|)\) gives \(\mu(\text{leaf})=1/6\), and \({\mathbb{E}}_s\tau_s^+=1/\mu(s)=6\). The value \(4\) would come from the uniform distribution, which is not stationary here.

qz.q: A finite Markov chain is irreducible but periodic (e.g. two states that alternate deterministically). Which statement holds?
a: A unique stationary \(\mu\) exists, but \(P^t(x,\cdot)\) need not converge
A stationary distribution exists but is not unique
qz.why: Irreducibility on a finite space alone gives existence and uniqueness; aperiodicity is needed only for \(P^t(x,\cdot)\to\mu\). The alternating chain has \(\mu=(\tfrac12,\tfrac12)\) but \(P^t(x,\cdot)\) oscillates forever.

qz.q: For a finite chain with transition matrix \(P\) and distribution \(\mu\), how does detailed balance \(\mu(x)P(x,y)=\mu(y)P(y,x)\) relate to stationarity \(\mu^\top P=\mu^\top\)?
qz.why: Summing detailed balance over \(x\) gives \(\sum_x\mu(x)P(x,y)=\mu(y)\). The deterministic 3-cycle has uniform stationary \(\mu\) but \(\mu(1)P(1,2)=\tfrac13\ne0=\mu(2)P(2,1)\), so it is not reversible.

cards.name: Robbins–Monro stochastic approximation
cards.lay: To find a root of \(g(\theta)=0\) when you only observe noisy values, take steps \(\theta_{t+1}=\theta_t+\alpha_t(g(\theta_t)+\text{noise})\) with step sizes that sum to infinity (to get anywhere) but whose squares sum to something finite (to average out noise). TD and Q-learning are exactly such schemes.
cards.st: Consider \(\theta_{t+1}=\theta_t+\alpha_t\bigl(g(\theta_t)+\xi_{t+1}\bigr)\) with \({\mathbb{E}}[\xi_{t+1}\mid{\mathcal{F}}_t]=0\), \({\mathbb{E}}[{\lVert \xi_{t+1}\rVert}^2\mid{\mathcal{F}}_t]\le C(1+{\lVert \theta_t\rVert}^2)\), and step sizes \[ \sum_t\alpha_t=\infty,\qquad\sum_t\alpha_t^2<\infty. \] If \(g\) has a unique root \(\theta^\star\) with \({\langle \theta-\theta^\star, g(\theta)\rangle}<0\) for \(\theta\ne\theta^\star\) (and growth conditions), then \(\theta_t\to\theta^\star\) almost surely.
ver: Q-learning (Watkins & Dayan; Tsitsiklis 1994; Jaakkola et al. 1994): asynchronous SA for a sup-norm contraction \(T^\star\); converges a.s. if every \((s,a)\) is updated infinitely often with Robbins–Monro steps.
Contraction-based SA (Tsitsiklis 1994): if the expected update is a \({\lVert \cdot\rVert}_\infty\) (weighted max-norm) pseudo-contraction, asynchronous SA converges.
Typical step sizes: \(\alpha_t=\tfrac{1}{t^\omega}\) with \(\omega\in(\tfrac12,1]\); \(\alpha_t=\tfrac{H+1}{H+t}\) in episodic Q-learning (Jin et al. 2018).
Constant step size: converges to a neighbourhood of size \(O(\sqrt\alpha)\) (stationary distribution of iterates).
Polyak–Ruppert averaging achieves the optimal asymptotic covariance with slower steps.
cards.det: Proof sketch (Lyapunov): with \(L(\theta)={\lVert \theta-\theta^\star\rVert}^2\), \({\mathbb{E}}[L(\theta_{t+1})\mid{\mathcal{F}}_t]\le L(\theta_t)(1+C\alpha_t^2)+2\alpha_t{\langle \theta_t-\theta^\star, g(\theta_t)\rangle}+C\alpha_t^2\), then Robbins–Siegmund Robbins–Siegmund theorem (almost-supermartingales). The ODE method ODE method (Borkar–Meyn) & two-timescale SA handles general (non-gradient, non-monotone) cases.
cards.ex: Tabular TD(0): \(V_{t+1}(s_t)=V_t(s_t)+\alpha_t\bigl(r_t+\gamma V_t(s_{t+1})-V_t(s_t)\bigr)\) is SA for the root of \(T^\pi V-V=0\).
cards.use: Convergence of TD, Q-learning, SARSA, actor–critic (two-timescale), EM with stochastic E-steps (SAEM), SGD.

qz.q: Which step-size schedule satisfies the Robbins–Monro conditions \(\sum_t\alpha_t=\infty\), \(\sum_t\alpha_t^2<\infty\)?
qz.why: \(t^{-\omega}\) works iff \(\omega\in(\tfrac12,1]\). With \(\omega=0.4\) the squares are not summable (noise never averages out); with \(\omega=1.2\) the steps sum to a finite amount (the iterate may stop short of \(\theta^\star\)).

qz.q: Run the Robbins–Monro recursion (same assumptions on \(g\) and noise) with a small constant step size \(\alpha\), and noise whose conditional variance does not vanish near \(\theta^\star\). What does the theory give?
a: Iterates settle in a neighbourhood of size \(O(\sqrt\alpha)\) of \(\theta^\star\)
Almost-sure convergence to \(\theta^\star\) if \(\alpha\) is small enough
Iterates settle in a neighbourhood of size \(O(\alpha^2)\) of \(\theta^\star\)
qz.why: With constant \(\alpha\) the noise injected per step, \(\alpha^2\sigma^2\), balances the contraction \(\alpha\), giving stationary squared error \(O(\alpha)\), i.e. distance \(O(\sqrt\alpha)\). Exact a.s. convergence needs \(\sum\alpha_t^2<\infty\).

qz.q: Asynchronous tabular Q-learning with Robbins–Monro step sizes for each \((s,a)\). What further condition is needed for a.s. convergence to \(Q^\star\)?
a: The behaviour policy is greedy in the current \(Q\)
qz.why: Q-learning is asynchronous SA for the sup-norm contraction \(T^\star\); each coordinate must keep receiving updates. It is off-policy, so the behaviour policy only needs to explore; a purely greedy behaviour can stop visiting some pairs.

cards.name: Optional stopping theorem
cards.lay: You can't beat a fair game by choosing when to stop, as long as you don't wait too long: at a (well-behaved) stopping time, a martingale still has its starting mean.
cards.st: If \((M_t)\) is a martingale and \(\tau\) a stopping time, then \({\mathbb{E}} M_\tau={\mathbb{E}} M_0\) provided any of: (i) \(\tau\) is bounded; (ii) \({\mathbb{E}}\tau<\infty\) and increments are bounded, \(|M_{t+1}-M_t|\le c\); (iii) \((M_{t\wedge\tau})\) is uniformly integrable (e.g. bounded).
ver: Supermartingales: \({\mathbb{E}} M_\tau\le{\mathbb{E}} M_0\) — proves Ville's inequality Ville's inequality & method of mixtures (time-uniform bounds) and Doob's maximal inequality Doob's maximal inequalities.
Wald's identities as corollaries Wald's identity.
Gambler's ruin probabilities and expected hitting times via suitable martingales.
cards.det: In RL, episodes ending at random times (SSPs, terminal states) and algorithms with data-dependent stopping (best-arm identification) are handled by optional stopping. The integrability conditions matter: the simple random walk stopped at \(+1\) has \({\mathbb{E}} M_\tau=1\ne0\) because \({\mathbb{E}}\tau=\infty\).
cards.ex: Simple symmetric random walk started at \(0\), stopped on hitting \(-a\) or \(b\): \(\Pr(\text{hit } b)=\tfrac{a}{a+b}\), and using \(M_t^2-t\), \({\mathbb{E}}\tau=ab\).
cards.use: Sequential testing, best-arm identification, stochastic shortest path, expected hitting times, deriving maximal inequalities.

qz.q: \(M_t\) is a simple symmetric random walk from \(M_0=0\), \(\tau=\min\{t:M_t=1\}\). Then \(\tau<\infty\) a.s. and \(M_\tau=1\), so \({\mathbb{E}} M_\tau\ne{\mathbb{E}} M_0\). Why does optional stopping not apply?
a: \({\mathbb{E}}\tau=\infty\), so the bounded-increment condition is not enough
\(\tau\) is not a stopping time for the walk's filtration
The increments of the walk are unbounded
The walk is only a supermartingale, not a martingale
qz.why: \(\tau\) is a stopping time and increments are bounded by 1, but condition (ii) also needs \({\mathbb{E}}\tau<\infty\), which fails here; \(\tau\) is unbounded and \((M_{t\wedge\tau})\) is not uniformly integrable either.

qz.q: A simple symmetric random walk starts at \(0\) and stops at the first time \(\tau\) it hits \(-2\) or \(3\). What are \(\Pr(\text{hit }3\text{ first})\) and \({\mathbb{E}}\tau\)?
qz.why: Optional stopping for \(M_t\): \(0=3p-2(1-p)\), so \(p=a/(a+b)=2/5\). Optional stopping for \(M_t^2-t\): \({\mathbb{E}}\tau={\mathbb{E}} M_\tau^2=9\cdot\tfrac25+4\cdot\tfrac35=6=ab\).

qz.q: A gambler plays a fair game (martingale wealth, bets of size \(1\)) and uses the rule: stop as soon as you are \(1\) ahead, or after \(1000\) rounds, whichever comes first. What is the expected profit?
a: Strictly positive, since you stop when ahead
Strictly negative, since you may stop while behind
qz.why: \(\tau\le1000\) is a bounded stopping time, so condition (i) gives \({\mathbb{E}} M_\tau={\mathbb{E}} M_0\). The frequent \(+1\) wins are exactly offset by rare large losses at round 1000.

cards.name: Coupling inequality
cards.lay: To show two distributions are close, build them on the same probability space so that the random variables are usually equal. The TV distance is at most the probability they differ. Coupling two chains until they meet bounds mixing times.
cards.st: For any coupling \((X,Y)\) with \(X\sim P\), \(Y\sim Q\): \({\mathrm{TV}}(P,Q)\le\Pr(X\ne Y)\), and an optimal (maximal) coupling attains equality. For Markov chains \((X_t,Y_t)\) coupled to move together after meeting time \(\tau\): \[ {\mathrm{TV}}\bigl(P^t(x,\cdot),P^t(y,\cdot)\bigr)\le\Pr_{x,y}(\tau>t). \]
ver: Trajectories: if two policies agree with probability \(\ge1-{\varepsilon}\) at each step (coupled), trajectories agree for \(H\) steps with probability \(\ge1-H{\varepsilon}\) (union bound) — behaviour cloning compounding error.
Path coupling (Bubley–Dyer) for contraction in a metric; Wasserstein contraction.
cards.det: Proof: \(P(A)-Q(A)=\Pr(X\in A)-\Pr(Y\in A)\le\Pr(X\in A,Y\notin A)\le\Pr(X\ne Y)\).
cards.ex: Lazy random walk on the hypercube \(\{0,1\}^n\): couple by updating the same coordinate with the same bit; coupon collector gives \(t_{\mathrm{mix}}\le n\log n+O(n)\).
cards.use: Mixing time bounds, imitation learning error compounding, comparing policies or models trajectory-wise, Markov-chain concentration.

qz.q: You construct one coupling \((X,Y)\) of distributions \(P\) and \(Q\) (not known to be optimal) and find \(\Pr(X\ne Y)=0.3\). What can you conclude?
qz.why: Every coupling gives an upper bound \({\mathrm{TV}}(P,Q)\le\Pr(X\ne Y)\); equality needs a maximal coupling. With \({\mathrm{TV}}=\sup_A|P(A)-Q(A)|\) there is no extra factor \(\tfrac12\).

qz.q: An imitation policy agrees with the expert with probability \(\ge1-{\varepsilon}\) at every step (given the same state), \({\varepsilon}=0.01\). With horizon \(H=50\), what bound does the trajectory coupling give on the TV distance between the two trajectory distributions?
qz.why: Coupling the two rollouts step by step and a union bound give \(\Pr(\text{trajectories differ})\le H{\varepsilon}=0.5\), hence TV \(\le0.5\). Errors compound linearly in \(H\), not like \(\sqrt H{\varepsilon}\approx0.07\) or \({\varepsilon}\).

qz.q: For the lazy random walk on the hypercube \(\{0,1\}^n\), the coupling “update the same random coordinate with the same random bit” yields a mixing-time upper bound of what order?
qz.why: The two copies agree once every coordinate has been chosen at least once: a coupon-collector time, about \(n\log n\). The state space has \(2^n\) points, but mixing is far faster than visiting them all.

cards.name: Mixing time & geometric ergodicity
cards.lay: The mixing time is how long a chain must run before its state distribution is close to stationary, from any start. Once you know it, dependent Markov data behave roughly like \(n/t_{\mathrm{mix}}\) independent samples.
cards.st: \(d(t)=\max_x{\mathrm{TV}}(P^t(x,\cdot),\mu)\), \(t_{\mathrm{mix}}({\varepsilon})=\min\{t:d(t)\le{\varepsilon}\}\), \(t_{\mathrm{mix}}=t_{\mathrm{mix}}(\tfrac14)\). Then \(d\) is non-increasing, \(d(\ell t_{\mathrm{mix}})\le2^{-\ell}\), so \[ t_{\mathrm{mix}}({\varepsilon})\le\lceil\log_2(1/{\varepsilon})\rceil\,t_{\mathrm{mix}}. \] For reversible chains with spectral gap \(\gamma_\star=1-\lambda_2\): \((\tfrac{1}{\gamma_\star}-1)\log2\le t_{\mathrm{mix}}\le\tfrac{1}{\gamma_\star}\log\tfrac{4}{\mu_{\min}}\).
ver: Dobrushin contraction coefficient \(\delta(P)=\max_{x,y}{\mathrm{TV}}(P(x,\cdot),P(y,\cdot))\): \({\mathrm{TV}}( u P, u'P)\le\delta(P){\mathrm{TV}}( u, u')\) and \({\operatorname{sp}}(PV)\le\delta(P){\operatorname{sp}}(V)\) Induced operator norms (\(\ell_\infty\) norm of stochastic matrices).
Uniform ergodicity (Doeblin): \({\mathrm{TV}}(P^t(x,\cdot),\mu)\le C\rho^t\) Doeblin / minorisation condition & uniform ergodicity.
Average-reward MDPs: bias span and diameter relate to mixing; \({\operatorname{sp}}(h^\pi)\le O(t_{\mathrm{mix}})\) for rewards in \([0,1]\).
cards.det:
Submultiplicativity: \(\bar d(s+t)\le\bar d(s)\bar d(t)\) where \(\bar d(t)=\max_{x,y}{\mathrm{TV}}(P^t(x,\cdot),P^t(y,\cdot))\le2d(t)\). This gives the \(\log_2(1/{\varepsilon})\) amplification.

Sample-complexity results for TD/Q-learning from a single trajectory typically scale with \(t_{\mathrm{mix}}\) (or \(1/\mu_{\min}\)), because consecutive samples are dependent.
cards.ex: Two-state chain with switching probabilities \(p,q\): \(\lambda_2=1-p-q\), so \(d(t)\le|1-p-q|^t\) and \(t_{\mathrm{mix}}\approx\tfrac{1}{p+q}\).
cards.use: Single-trajectory TD/Q-learning analyses, average-reward RL, Markovian-noise SGD for actor–critic, choosing burn-in and thinning.

qz.q: A chain has \(t_{\mathrm{mix}}=t_{\mathrm{mix}}(\tfrac14)=100\). Using \(d(\ell\,t_{\mathrm{mix}})\le2^{-\ell}\), what is the smallest number of steps \(t\) for which this bound guarantees \(d(t)\le1/1024\)?
qz.why: \(2^{-\ell}\le2^{-10}\) needs \(\ell=10\), so \(t=10\,t_{\mathrm{mix}}=1000\). The cost of higher accuracy is logarithmic in \(1/{\varepsilon}\), not linear (\(102400\)) or square-root (\(3200\)).

qz.q: Two-state chain: from state 1 switch with probability \(p=0.1\), from state 2 switch with probability \(q=0.3\). What is the spectral gap \(\gamma_\star=1-\lambda_2\)?
qz.why: The eigenvalues are \(1\) and \(\lambda_2=1-p-q=0.6\), so \(\gamma_\star=p+q=0.4\) and \(t_{\mathrm{mix}}\approx1/(p+q)=2.5\). The value \(0.6\) is \(\lambda_2\) itself, not the gap.

qz.q: A reversible chain on \(10^6\) states has uniform stationary distribution and spectral gap \(\gamma_\star=0.01\). What do the spectral bounds \((\tfrac1{\gamma_\star}-1)\log2\le t_{\mathrm{mix}}\le\tfrac1{\gamma_\star}\log\tfrac4{\mu_{\min}}\) imply?
qz.why: Lower: \(99\log2\approx69\); upper: \(100\log(4\cdot10^6)\approx100\cdot15.2=1520\). The relaxation time \(1/\gamma_\star=100\) is not itself an upper bound; the \(\log(1/\mu_{\min})\) factor can matter.

cards.name: Ergodic theorem for Markov chains
cards.lay: Time averages along a single long trajectory converge to averages under the stationary distribution. Justifies estimating long-run quantities (average reward, stationary feature covariances) from one run.
cards.st: For an irreducible positive-recurrent Markov chain with stationary distribution \(\mu\) and any \(f\) with \({\mathbb{E}}_\mu|f|<\infty\), from any initial state: \[ \frac1n\sum_{t=0}^{n-1}f(X_t)\xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}}{\mathbb{E}}_\mu f. \]
ver: Average reward: \(\rho^\pi=\lim_{T\to\infty}\tfrac1T{\mathbb{E}}\sum_{t<T}r(s_t,a_t)={\langle d^\pi, r^\pi\rangle}\) for unichain \(\pi\).

Markov chain CLT: \(\sqrt n(\bar f_n-{\mathbb{E}}_\mu f)\Rightarrow{\mathcal{N}}(0,\sigma^2_f)\) with \(\sigma^2_f={\operatorname{Var}}_\mu f+2\sum_{k\ge1}{\operatorname{Cov}}_\mu(f(X_0),f(X_k))\), expressible via the Poisson equation Poisson equation, bias & Laurent expansion (average reward).
Birkhoff's pointwise ergodic theorem for general stationary ergodic processes.
cards.det: The ergodic theorem is qualitative; quantitative versions come from mixing Mixing time & geometric ergodicity or Markov-chain Hoeffding/Bernstein Concentration for Markov chains (Paulin; Lezaud). The CLT variance \(\sigma_f^2\) can be much larger than \({\operatorname{Var}}_\mu f\) (by a factor \(\approx t_{\mathrm{rel}}\)).
cards.ex: Estimating the average reward of a fixed policy from one trajectory: the running mean of rewards converges to \(\rho^\pi\), with fluctuations of order \(\sqrt{t_{\mathrm{mix}}/n}\).
cards.use: Average-reward evaluation, on-policy TD fixed points, asymptotic variance of Monte Carlo along trajectories.

qz.q: Two states alternate deterministically (\(1\to2\to1\to\cdots\)); \(f\) is the indicator of state 1. What happens to \(\tfrac1n\sum_{t<n}f(X_t)\)?
a: It converges to \(\tfrac12\) from either start
It does not converge: the chain is periodic
It converges in expectation only, not a.s.
qz.why: The ergodic theorem needs irreducibility and positive recurrence, not aperiodicity. Periodicity stops \(P^t(x,\cdot)\) from converging, but time averages still converge to \({\mathbb{E}}_\mu f=\tfrac12\).

qz.q: Stationary two-state chain that switches state with probability \(0.01\) from either state, so \({\operatorname{Cov}}_\mu(f(X_0),f(X_k))=\tfrac14(0.98)^k\) for \(f=\) indicator of state 1. What is the CLT variance \(\sigma_f^2={\operatorname{Var}}_\mu f+2\sum_{k\ge1}{\operatorname{Cov}}_\mu(f(X_0),f(X_k))\)?
qz.why: \(\sum_{k\ge1}0.98^k=49\), so \(\sigma_f^2=\tfrac14+2\cdot\tfrac{49}{4}=\tfrac{99}{4}\), about \(99\) times the i.i.d. value \(\tfrac14\): dependence inflates the variance by roughly \(t_{\mathrm{rel}}\). Forgetting the factor 2 gives \(25/2\).

qz.q: The running mean of rewards along one trajectory estimates \(\rho^\pi\) with fluctuations of order \(\sqrt{t_{\mathrm{mix}}/n}\). If \(t_{\mathrm{mix}}\) grows by a factor \(4\), by what factor must \(n\) grow to keep the same accuracy?
a: \(1\): the ergodic theorem holds from any start
qz.why: Keeping \(t_{\mathrm{mix}}/n\) constant requires \(n\propto t_{\mathrm{mix}}\). The ergodic theorem is only asymptotic and says nothing about how large \(n\) must be.

cards.name: Poisson equation, bias & Laurent expansion (average reward)
cards.plain: Poisson equation, bias & Laurent expansion (average reward)
cards.lay: In average-reward problems the “value” of a state is its bias: the extra total reward you collect starting there compared to the average. It solves a Poisson equation. The discounted value is approximately (average reward)/\((1-\gamma)\) + bias.
cards.st: For a unichain policy with gain \(\rho^\pi\), the bias \(h^\pi\) solves the Poisson (average-reward Bellman) equation \[ h^\pi+\rho^\pi{\mathbf{1}}=r^\pi+P^\pi h^\pi,\qquad{\langle d^\pi, h^\pi\rangle}=0, \] and the discounted value satisfies \(V_\gamma^\pi=\frac{\rho^\pi}{1-\gamma}{\mathbf{1}}+h^\pi+o(1)\) as \(\gamma\to1\) (Laurent expansion).
ver: Bias as a series (aperiodic case): \(h^\pi=\sum_{t\ge0}(P^{\pi})^t(r^\pi-\rho^\pi{\mathbf{1}})\).
Optimality equation: \(h^\star(s)+\rho^\star=\max_a\{r(s,a)+P(\cdot|s,a)^\top h^\star\}\).
Diameter bound (communicating MDPs): \({\operatorname{sp}}(h^\star)\le D\) where \(D=\max_{s\ne s'}\min_\pi{\mathbb{E}}[\text{time } s\to s']\) (Bartlett & Tewari 2009).
Discounted-to-average reduction: \(|(1-\gamma)V_\gamma^\star(s)-\rho^\star|\le(1-\gamma){\operatorname{sp}}(h^\star)\).
cards.det: Regret bounds for average-reward RL scale with \({\operatorname{sp}}(h^\star)\) or \(D\) (UCRL2: \({\widetilde{O}}(DS\sqrt{AT})\)), because \(h^\star\) plays the role that \(\tfrac{1}{1-\gamma}\) plays in discounted problems. Many average-reward algorithms are analysed by running discounted ones with \(\gamma=1-1/\sqrt T\) and using the reduction above.
cards.ex: Two-state chain alternating deterministically with rewards \(1\) and \(0\): \(\rho=\tfrac12\), \(h=(\tfrac14,-\tfrac14)\) (periodic, defined as a Cesàro limit).
cards.use: Average-reward regret (UCRL2, bias-span-based algorithms), discounted-to-average reductions, Markov chain CLT variance, policy gradient in average reward.

qz.q: Two states alternate deterministically, reward \(1\) in state \(a\) and \(0\) in state \(b\); gain \(\rho=\tfrac12\), bias \(h=(\tfrac14,-\tfrac14)\). For \(\gamma=0.99\), the discounted value \(V_\gamma(a)\) is closest to
qz.why: Laurent: \(V_\gamma\approx\rho/(1-\gamma)+h(a)=50+0.25\); exactly, \(V_\gamma(a)=1/(1-\gamma^2)\approx50.25\). The bias is the state-dependent correction to the \(\rho/(1-\gamma)\) term.

qz.q: For a unichain policy, \(h\) solves \(h+\rho{\mathbf{1}}=r^\pi+P^\pi h\). Which other vectors also solve this equation (with the same \(\rho\))?
qz.why: Since \(P^\pi{\mathbf{1}}={\mathbf{1}}\), adding a constant leaves both sides balanced, and for unichain policies these are the only solutions. The normalisation \({\langle d^\pi, h\rangle}=0\) picks one of them.

qz.q: In a communicating MDP, \({\operatorname{sp}}(h^\star)\le D=10\). You want \(|(1-\gamma)V_\gamma^\star(s)-\rho^\star|\le0.01\) from the bound \((1-\gamma){\operatorname{sp}}(h^\star)\). What is the largest \(1-\gamma\) this bound allows?
qz.why: \((1-\gamma)\cdot10\le0.01\) gives \(1-\gamma\le10^{-3}\). The effective horizon \(1/(1-\gamma)\) must be about \({\operatorname{sp}}(h^\star)/{\varepsilon}\).

cards.name: Robbins–Siegmund theorem (almost-supermartingales)
cards.lay: If a non-negative quantity decreases in expectation up to small summable perturbations, it converges almost surely, and the total “decrease” is finite. The universal tool for almost-sure convergence of stochastic iterative algorithms.
cards.st: Let \(V_t,a_t,b_t,c_t\ge0\) be adapted with \[ {\mathbb{E}}[V_{t+1}\mid{\mathcal{F}}_t]\le(1+a_t)V_t+b_t-c_t,\qquad\sum_ta_t<\infty,\ \sum_tb_t<\infty\text{ a.s.} \] Then \(V_t\) converges almost surely to a finite limit and \(\sum_tc_t<\infty\) almost surely.
ver: Supermartingale convergence theorem: the case \(a_t=b_t=c_t=0\) Martingales & the martingale convergence theorem.
Deterministic analogue: if \(v_{t+1}\le(1+a_t)v_t+b_t\) with summable \(a_t,b_t\ge0\) then \(v_t\) converges.
cards.det: Typical use: \(V_t={\lVert \theta_t-\theta^\star\rVert}^2\), \(c_t=2\alpha_t{\langle \theta_t-\theta^\star, -g(\theta_t)\rangle}\). Then \(\sum_t\alpha_t{\langle \theta_t-\theta^\star, -g(\theta_t)\rangle}<\infty\) together with \(\sum\alpha_t=\infty\) forces the inner product to vanish along a subsequence; convergence of \(V_t\) finishes the argument.
cards.ex: SGD on a strongly convex \(f\) with \(\sum\alpha_t=\infty\), \(\sum\alpha_t^2<\infty\), bounded gradient variance converges a.s. to \(x^\star\).
cards.use: Almost-sure convergence of SGD, Q-learning, TD, stochastic EM; Lyapunov-based convergence proofs.

qz.q: With \(\alpha_t=1/t\), which choice of \((a_t,b_t)\) in \({\mathbb{E}}[V_{t+1}\mid{\mathcal{F}}_t]\le(1+a_t)V_t+b_t-c_t\) satisfies the Robbins–Siegmund hypotheses?
qz.why: The theorem needs \(\sum a_t<\infty\) and \(\sum b_t<\infty\); \(\sum1/t^2<\infty\) but \(\sum1/t=\infty\) and \(\sum t^{-1/2}=\infty\). This is why the noise must enter at order \(\alpha_t^2\).

qz.q: Suppose \(V_t,a_t,b_t,c_t\ge0\) satisfy the Robbins–Siegmund hypotheses. What does the theorem itself conclude?
a: \(V_t\) converges a.s. to a finite limit and \(\sum_tc_t<\infty\) a.s.
qz.why: The limit of \(V_t\) can be any finite random variable (e.g. \(a_t=b_t=c_t=0\), \(V_t\) constant). Showing the limit is \(0\) needs an extra argument using the summability of \(c_t\).

qz.q: SGD on a strongly convex \(f\): Robbins–Siegmund gives \(V_t={\lVert x_t-x^\star\rVert}^2\to V_\infty\) a.s. and \(\sum_t\alpha_tV_t<\infty\) a.s. If \(\sum_t\alpha_t=\infty\), what follows?
a: \(V_\infty>0\) is possible, since the noise never vanishes
Nothing about \(V_\infty\); only \({\mathbb{E}} V_t\) is controlled
qz.why: If \(V_\infty>0\) then \(V_t\ge V_\infty/2\) eventually and \(\sum\alpha_tV_t=\infty\), a contradiction. This is exactly where \(\sum\alpha_t=\infty\) enters.

cards.name: Concentration for Markov chains (Paulin; Lezaud)
cards.lay: Hoeffding and Bernstein inequalities still hold for sums along a Markov chain, but the effective sample size is reduced by the mixing time (or spectral gap): \(n\) dependent samples count as about \(n/t_{\mathrm{mix}}\) independent ones.
cards.st: (Paulin 2015) For a stationary, uniformly ergodic chain with mixing time \(t_{\mathrm{mix}}\) and \(f:{\mathcal{X}}\to[a,b]\): \[ \Pr\Bigl(\Bigl|\frac1n\sum_{t=1}^nf(X_t)-{\mathbb{E}}_\mu f\Bigr|\ge{\varepsilon}\Bigr)\le2\exp\Bigl(-\frac{2n{\varepsilon}^2}{9\,t_{\mathrm{mix}}(b-a)^2}\Bigr). \]
ver: Spectral-gap Bernstein (Lezaud 1998; Paulin 2015) for reversible chains: variance replaced by asymptotic variance, rate \(\propto\gamma_{\mathrm{ps}}n{\varepsilon}^2/\sigma^2\).
Non-stationary start: multiply the bound by \({\lVert {\mathrm{d}}\nu/{\mathrm{d}}\mu\rVert}_{2,\mu}\) or discard a burn-in of \(t_{\mathrm{mix}}\log(1/\delta)\) steps.
Blocking technique: split the trajectory into blocks of length \(\approx t_{\mathrm{mix}}\log(1/{\varepsilon})\) and couple to independent blocks.
cards.det: Proof via Marton couplings: the chain satisfies a bounded-differences property with an effective constant scaled by \(t_{\mathrm{mix}}\), then a McDiarmid-type McDiarmid's bounded-differences inequality argument.
cards.ex: Single-trajectory evaluation of \({\mathbb{E}}_\mu[r]\): \(n\approx\tfrac{9t_{\mathrm{mix}}\log(2/\delta)}{2{\varepsilon}^2}\) samples suffice (rewards in \([0,1]\)).
cards.use: Finite-sample TD/Q-learning along trajectories, actor–critic with Markovian sampling, average-reward estimation.

qz.q: Stationary, uniformly ergodic chain with \(t_{\mathrm{mix}}=10\), rewards in \([0,1]\). Using the Paulin bound \(2\exp(-2n{\varepsilon}^2/(9t_{\mathrm{mix}}))\), how many samples give \({\varepsilon}=0.1\) at \(\delta=0.05\)? (\(\log40\approx3.69\))
qz.why: \(n=9t_{\mathrm{mix}}\log(2/\delta)/(2{\varepsilon}^2)=9\cdot10\cdot3.69/0.02\approx16{,}600\). The i.i.d. Hoeffding answer is \(185\); Markov dependence costs a factor \(9t_{\mathrm{mix}}=90\) here.

qz.q: The Paulin bound assumes a stationary start. Your trajectory starts at a fixed state \(x\). Which fix does the card give?
a: Discard a burn-in of about \(t_{\mathrm{mix}}\log(1/\delta)\) steps
None: the bound holds unchanged from any start
Discard a burn-in of about \(n/t_{\mathrm{mix}}\) steps
qz.why: After a burn-in of order \(t_{\mathrm{mix}}\log(1/\delta)\) the chain is close to stationary; alternatively multiply the bound by \({\lVert {\mathrm{d}}\nu/{\mathrm{d}}\mu\rVert}_{2,\mu}\). The burn-in length depends on mixing and \(\delta\), not on \(n\).

qz.q: For a stationary uniformly ergodic chain and \(f\) with values in \([0,1]\), with probability \(1-\delta\) the deviation \(|\tfrac1n\sum_tf(X_t)-{\mathbb{E}}_\mu f|\) is of order
qz.why: Inverting the exponent \(2n{\varepsilon}^2/(9t_{\mathrm{mix}})\) gives \({\varepsilon}\asymp\sqrt{t_{\mathrm{mix}}\log(1/\delta)/n}\): effective sample size \(n/t_{\mathrm{mix}}\). Mixing enters under the square root, not linearly or only logarithmically.

cards.name: ODE method (Borkar–Meyn) & two-timescale SA
cards.lay: With small step sizes, a noisy iterative algorithm tracks the solution of an ordinary differential equation obtained by averaging out the noise. If that ODE is globally stable, the algorithm converges. Two-timescale versions treat the fast iterate as already converged when analysing the slow one.
cards.st: (Borkar & Meyn 2000) For \(\theta_{t+1}=\theta_t+\alpha_t(h(\theta_t)+M_{t+1})\) with Robbins–Monro steps, Lipschitz \(h\), MDS noise with \({\mathbb{E}}[{\lVert M_{t+1}\rVert}^2|{\mathcal{F}}_t]\le C(1+{\lVert \theta_t\rVert}^2)\): if the scaled ODE \(\dot x=h_\infty(x)\), \(h_\infty(x)=\lim_{c\to\infty}h(cx)/c\), has the origin as globally asymptotically stable equilibrium, then \(\sup_t{\lVert \theta_t\rVert}<\infty\) a.s.; if moreover \(\dot x=h(x)\) has a globally asymptotically stable equilibrium \(x^\star\), then \(\theta_t\to x^\star\) a.s.
ver: Two-timescale (Borkar 1997): fast \(w\) with steps \(\beta_t\), slow \(\theta\) with \(\alpha_t\), \(\alpha_t/\beta_t\to0\); \(w_t\) tracks \(w^\star(\theta_t)\) and \(\theta_t\) tracks \(\dot\theta=h(\theta,w^\star(\theta))\) — actor–critic and GTD analyses.
Linear SA \(h(\theta)=A\theta+b\): converges iff \(A\) is Hurwitz (all eigenvalues have negative real part) Gershgorin circle theorem.
Finite-time versions: \({\mathbb{E}}{\lVert \theta_t-\theta^\star\rVert}^2=O(\alpha_t\cdot t_{\mathrm{mix}})\) for linear SA with Markovian noise (Srikant & Ying 2019).
cards.det: The interpolated iterates form an asymptotic pseudo-trajectory of the ODE: over any finite time window, Grönwall Grönwall's inequality (continuous & discrete) plus a martingale bound on accumulated noise shows the iterate stays close to the ODE solution. Stability of the ODE then transfers to the algorithm.
cards.ex: TD(0) with linear features: \(h(\theta)=\Phi^\top D(\gamma P\Phi-\Phi)\theta+\Phi^\top Dr\) with \(D={\operatorname{diag}}(\mu)\); \(A=\Phi^\top D(\gamma P-I)\Phi\) is negative definite on-policy, so TD converges (Tsitsiklis & Van Roy 1997).
cards.use: Convergence of TD with linear FA, actor–critic, GTD/TDC, Q-learning with function approximation (and why it can diverge off-policy).

qz.q: Linear SA \(\theta_{t+1}=\theta_t+\alpha_t(A\theta_t+b+M_{t+1})\) with Robbins–Monro steps and MDS noise. For which \(A\) does it converge?
qz.why: Convergence holds iff \(A\) is Hurwitz. The triangular matrix has eigenvalues \(-1,-2\) (Hurwitz, though \(A+A^\top\) is indefinite). The matrix with rows \((-1,4),(1,-1)\) has eigenvalues \(-1\pm2=1,-3\); the rotation has eigenvalues \(\pm i\) (real part 0); \({\operatorname{diag}}(-3,1)\) has eigenvalue \(1\).

qz.q: Actor–critic: the critic \(w\) uses steps \(\beta_t\), the actor \(\theta\) uses steps \(\alpha_t\). Which schedule fits the two-timescale theorem (critic fast, actor slow)?
qz.why: Need \(\alpha_t/\beta_t=t^{-0.3}\to0\) with both schedules Robbins–Monro. Swapping makes the actor faster; equal steps give no separation; \(t^{-0.4}\) is not square-summable and is larger than \(\beta_t\).

qz.q: Linear TD(0) has mean dynamics \(h(\theta)=A\theta+b\) with \(A=\Phi^\top D(\gamma P-I)\Phi\), \(D={\operatorname{diag}}(\mu)\) the sampling distribution. Why can it diverge off-policy?
a: If \(\mu\) is not stationary for \(P\), \(A\) need not be Hurwitz
Off-policy, \(T^\pi\) is no longer a sup-norm contraction
Off-policy noise is not an MDS, so the ODE method fails
Off-policy, step sizes cannot satisfy Robbins–Monro
qz.why: On-policy (\(\mu=\) stationary distribution of \(P\)) \(A\) is negative definite; with another \(D\) it can have eigenvalues with positive real part, so the ODE is unstable. \(T^\pi\) is a \(\gamma\)-contraction regardless of how data are sampled.

cards.name: Recursion lemmas for SA rates (Chung's lemma)
cards.plain: Recursion lemmas for SA rates (Chung's lemma)
cards.lay: Many convergence-rate proofs boil down to a scalar recursion: error shrinks by a factor \((1-c\alpha_t)\) each step but gains noise \(\alpha_t^2\sigma^2\). These lemmas solve such recursions and show the resulting \(1/t\) rates.
cards.st: (Chung 1954) If \(u_{t+1}\le\bigl(1-\tfrac{c}{t}\bigr)u_t+\tfrac{d}{t^{2}}\) for \(t\ge t_0\) with \(c>1\), \(d>0\), then \[ u_t\le\frac{d}{c-1}\cdot\frac1t+o\Bigl(\frac1t\Bigr). \] General form: \(u_{t+1}\le(1-a_t)u_t+b_t\) with \(a_t\in[0,1]\) gives \(u_T\le u_{t_0}\prod_{t=t_0}^{T-1}(1-a_t)+\sum_{t=t_0}^{T-1}b_t\prod_{s=t+1}^{T-1}(1-a_s)\).
ver: If \(c<1\) the rate degrades to \(t^{-c}\) — the classical pitfall of \(\alpha_t=1/t\) with too small strong-convexity constant (and of Q-learning with \(1/t\) steps: \(\Omega(t^{-(1-\gamma)})\) rates).
Constant steps: \(u_{t+1}\le(1-a)u_t+b\Rightarrow u_t\le(1-a)^tu_0+b/a\) Geometric series & discounted sums.
cards.det: Proof by induction using \(\prod_{s=t+1}^T(1-c/s)\approx(t/T)^c\) (from \(\log(1-x)\le-x\) Logarithm bounds). This explains why the effective strong-convexity constant times the step-size constant must exceed 1 for optimal \(1/t\) rates — and why rescaled step sizes \(\alpha_t=\tfrac{1}{(1-\gamma)t}\) fix Q-learning's slow convergence.
cards.ex: SGD on a \(\mu\)-strongly convex function with \(\alpha_t=\tfrac{2}{\mu t}\) and gradient variance \(\sigma^2\): \({\mathbb{E}}{\lVert x_t-x^\star\rVert}^2\le\tfrac{4\sigma^2}{\mu^2t}+o(1/t)\).
cards.use: Finite-time rates for TD/Q-learning/SGD, step-size design, analysing Polyak averaging.

qz.q: \(u_{t+1}\le(1-\tfrac{3}{t})u_t+\tfrac{4}{t^2}\) for \(t\ge t_0\). Chung's lemma gives \(u_t\le\tfrac{K}{t}+o(\tfrac1t)\) with \(K=\)
qz.why: \(K=d/(c-1)=4/(3-1)=2\). The tempting \(d/c=4/3\) ignores that the \(1/t\) target itself shrinks each step, which costs one unit of \(c\).

qz.q: Q-learning with \(\alpha_t=1/t\) has effective contraction constant \(c\approx1-\gamma\) in the recursion \(u_{t+1}\le(1-\tfrac ct)u_t+\tfrac d{t^2}\). For \(\gamma=0.9\), the rate is
qz.why: When \(c<1\) the rate degrades to \(t^{-c}=t^{-(1-\gamma)}\). Rescaled steps \(\alpha_t=\tfrac{1}{(1-\gamma)t}\) make \(c\approx1\) or larger and restore the \(1/t\) rate.

qz.q: Constant step size \(\alpha\): \(u_{t+1}\le(1-c\alpha)u_t+\sigma^2\alpha^2\) with \(c\alpha\in(0,1)\). What is the limiting bound as \(t\to\infty\)?
qz.why: \(u_t\le(1-a)^tu_0+b/a\) with \(a=c\alpha\), \(b=\sigma^2\alpha^2\) gives the floor \(b/a=\alpha\sigma^2/c\). It is proportional to \(\alpha\); reaching \(0\) needs decaying steps.

cards.name: Finite-class uniform convergence (Occam bound)
cards.lay: For a finite set of hypotheses, empirical averages are simultaneously close to their means for all hypotheses, at a price of only \(\log|{\mathcal{F}}|\) inside the square root. The simplest way to handle function approximation in theory.
cards.st: Let \({\mathcal{F}}\) be finite, \(f(z)\in[0,1]\), and \(Z_1,\dots,Z_n\) i.i.d. With probability \(\ge1-\delta\), simultaneously for all \(f\in{\mathcal{F}}\): \[ \Bigl|\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nf(Z_i)-{\mathbb{E}} f(Z)\Bigr|\le\sqrt{\frac{\log(2|{\mathcal{F}}|/\delta)}{2n}}. \]
ver: Realisable / ERM fast rate: if some \(f^\star\) has zero loss, ERM has excess risk \(\le\tfrac{\log(|{\mathcal{F}}|/\delta)}{n}\).

Least-squares (Bernstein) fast rate: for squared loss with realisability, ERM satisfies \({\mathbb{E}}(\hat f-f^\star)^2\lesssim\tfrac{\log(|{\mathcal{F}}|/\delta)}{n}\) — used in FQI and model-based RL analyses.
MLE over a finite model class: \({\mathbb{E}}[H^2(\hat P,P^\star)]\lesssim\tfrac{\log(|{\mathcal{P}}|/\delta)}{n}\) \(f\)-divergences: Hellinger, \(\chi^2\) and their relations.

Infinite classes: replace \(\log|{\mathcal{F}}|\) by \(\log\) covering number Covering & packing numbers (volumetric bound), VC dimension VC dimension & Sauer–Shelah lemma, or Rademacher complexity Symmetrisation & Rademacher complexity bounds.
cards.det: Hoeffding Hoeffding's inequality for each \(f\), union bound Union bound (Boole's inequality) over \({\mathcal{F}}\). Many RL papers state results for finite classes \({\mathcal{F}}\) (\(Q\)-functions, models) and extend to infinite classes via covering numbers, so understanding this case is enough to read them.
cards.ex: Fitted Q-iteration with a finite class \({\mathcal{F}}\) under completeness: per-iteration regression error \(\lesssim\tfrac{\log(|{\mathcal{F}}|K/\delta)}{n}\) in squared \(L^2(\mu)\), and the final suboptimality is \(\lesssim\tfrac{\sqrt{C}}{(1-\gamma)^2}\sqrt{\tfrac{\log(|{\mathcal{F}}|/\delta)}{n}}\) with concentrability \(C\) Concentrability coefficients & error propagation.
cards.use: FQI/offline RL with general function approximation, model selection, PAC bounds for policy classes, MLE-based model learning.

qz.q: Finite class \({\mathcal{F}}\) of \([0,1]\)-valued functions, uniform deviation \(\sqrt{\log(2|{\mathcal{F}}|/\delta)/(2n)}\). With \(\delta\) and the target accuracy fixed and \(|{\mathcal{F}}|\) large, if \(|{\mathcal{F}}|\) is squared, the required \(n\):
qz.why: \(n\propto\log(2|{\mathcal{F}}|/\delta)\) and \(\log|{\mathcal{F}}|^2=2\log|{\mathcal{F}}|\), so \(n\) roughly doubles. The price of a larger class is only logarithmic, which is the whole point of the Occam bound.

qz.q: ERM over a finite class \({\mathcal{F}}\) with \([0,1]\) losses. To reach excess risk \({\varepsilon}\) with probability \(1-\delta\), the sample size scales as:
a: \(\frac{\log(|{\mathcal{F}}|/\delta)}{{\varepsilon}^2}\) in both cases; realisability only improves constants
qz.why: Realisable ERM has excess risk \(\le\log(|{\mathcal{F}}|/\delta)/n\) (fast rate), while the uniform Hoeffding bound gives \(\sqrt{\log(|{\mathcal{F}}|/\delta)/n}\). In both, the class enters only through \(\log|{\mathcal{F}}|\).

qz.q: In fitted Q-iteration the regression target uses \(\widehat V\) computed from earlier data in the same sample. Why must concentration hold uniformly over the class of possible \(\widehat V\), rather than just for the realised one?
a: \(\widehat V\) depends on the data, so a fixed-function bound does not apply
Hoeffding's inequality requires the function to be Lipschitz
uniformity improves the rate from \(1/\sqrt n\) to \(1/n\)
the realised \(\widehat V\) need not be bounded by \(\tfrac{1}{1-\gamma}\)
qz.why: Hoeffding applies to a function fixed before the data are drawn. A data-dependent function can be selected precisely where the sample is atypical; a union bound over the class (or a cover) handles every possible choice at a \(\log|{\mathcal{F}}|\) price.

cards.name: Covering & packing numbers (volumetric bound)
cards.lay: A cover is a finite set of “representative” points such that every element of a (possibly infinite) class is within \({\varepsilon}\) of one of them. Union bounding over the cover, then paying \({\varepsilon}\) for the approximation, handles infinite classes. For a ball in \({\mathbb{R}}^d\), about \((3/{\varepsilon})^d\) points suffice.
cards.st: \(N({\varepsilon},T,d)\) is the smallest number of \({\varepsilon}\)-balls covering \(T\); \(M({\varepsilon},T,d)\) is the largest \({\varepsilon}\)-separated subset. They satisfy \(M(2{\varepsilon})\le N({\varepsilon})\le M({\varepsilon})\), and for the unit ball \(B\) of any norm on \({\mathbb{R}}^d\): \[ \Bigl(\frac1{\varepsilon}\Bigr)^d\le N({\varepsilon},B,{\lVert \cdot\rVert})\le\Bigl(1+\frac2{\varepsilon}\Bigr)^d\le\Bigl(\frac3{\varepsilon}\Bigr)^d\quad({\varepsilon}\le1). \]
ver: Linear function classes: \(\{\phi^\top\theta:{\lVert \theta\rVert}_2\le W\}\) with \({\lVert \phi\rVert}\le1\) has sup-norm \({\varepsilon}\)-cover of size \((1+2W/{\varepsilon})^d\).

Value-function classes in linear MDPs (Jin et al. 2020): \(V(\cdot)=\min\{\max_a\phi^\top w+\beta{\lVert \phi\rVert}_{\Lambda^{-1}},H\}\) has \(\log N_{\varepsilon}\le d\log(1+4W/{\varepsilon})+d^2\log(1+8d^{1/2}\beta^2/(\lambda{\varepsilon}^2))\).

\({\varepsilon}\)-net argument for operator norms: \({\lVert A\rVert}\le\tfrac{1}{1-{\varepsilon}}\max_{x\in{\mathcal{N}}_{\varepsilon}}{\lVert Ax\rVert}\) for an \({\varepsilon}\)-net \({\mathcal{N}}_{\varepsilon}\) of the sphere.
Lipschitz parameterisation: if \(\theta\mapsto f_\theta\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz into sup-norm, \(N({\varepsilon},{\mathcal{F}})\le N({\varepsilon}/L,\Theta)\).
cards.det:
Volumetric proof: an \({\varepsilon}\)-separated set gives disjoint balls of radius \({\varepsilon}/2\), all inside \((1+{\varepsilon}/2)B\); compare volumes.

The covering trick is essential in optimistic RL with function approximation: the value function \(\widehat V_{h+1}\) used in a regression target depends on all previous data, so concentration must hold uniformly over the class of possible value functions. One covers that class, applies the self-normalised bound Self-normalised bound for vector martingales (Abbasi-Yadkori et al.) to each element and union bounds — producing the extra \(\sqrt d\) factor in LSVI-UCB's \({\widetilde{O}}(\sqrt{d^3H^3T})\) regret.
cards.ex: Uniform Hoeffding over \(\{\phi^\top\theta:{\lVert \theta\rVert}\le1\}\), \(|\phi^\top\theta|\le1\): with an \({\varepsilon}=1/\sqrt n\) cover, \(\sup_\theta|\hat{\mathbb{E}}_n-{\mathbb{E}}|\lesssim\sqrt{\tfrac{d\log(3\sqrt n)+\log(1/\delta)}{n}}+\tfrac{2}{\sqrt n}\).
cards.use: Uniform concentration over value-function classes (LSVI-UCB, FQI), operator-norm bounds, metric entropy in Dudley's integral, \({\varepsilon}\)-net lower-bound constructions.

qz.q: For the unit ball \(B\) of a norm on \({\mathbb{R}}^d\), how does \(\log N({\varepsilon},B,{\lVert \cdot\rVert})\) grow, for \({\varepsilon}\le1\)?
qz.why: \(d\log(1/{\varepsilon})\le\log N\le d\log(3/{\varepsilon})\). The number \(N\) itself is exponential in \(d\), but its logarithm, which is what enters union bounds, is linear.

qz.q: \(\Theta\) is the unit Euclidean ball in \({\mathbb{R}}^d\) and \(\theta\mapsto f_\theta\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz into sup-norm. Which bound on \(N({\varepsilon},{\mathcal{F}},{\lVert \cdot\rVert}_\infty)\) follows?
qz.why: An \({\varepsilon}/L\)-cover of \(\Theta\) maps to an \({\varepsilon}\)-cover of \({\mathcal{F}}\), so \(N({\varepsilon},{\mathcal{F}})\le N({\varepsilon}/L,\Theta)\le(1+2L/{\varepsilon})^d\). The Lipschitz constant rescales the radius, not the count; \(f_\theta(x)=L{\langle \theta, x\rangle}\) needs about \((L/{\varepsilon})^d\) functions, which the other options undercount.

qz.q: You have found \(500\) points in \(T\) that are pairwise more than \(0.1\) apart (a \(0.1\)-separated set). Which conclusion about covering numbers (closed balls) is guaranteed?
qz.why: \(M(0.1)\ge500\) and \(M(2{\varepsilon})\le N({\varepsilon})\) with \({\varepsilon}=0.05\) give \(N(0.05)\ge500\): two points more than \(0.1\) apart cannot share a ball of radius \(0.05\) (its diameter is \(\le0.1\)). At radius \(0.1\) one ball may contain two such points, so \(N(0.1)\) can be smaller.

cards.name: Symmetrisation & Rademacher complexity bounds
cards.lay: How well can a function class fit pure noise? That is its Rademacher complexity, and it controls the worst-case gap between empirical and true averages over the class. Symmetrisation (comparing the sample to an independent “ghost” sample) is the trick that makes it work.
cards.st: Empirical Rademacher complexity: \(\widehat{\mathfrak R}_n({\mathcal{F}})={\mathbb{E}}_\sigma\sup_{f\in{\mathcal{F}}}\frac1n\sum_i\sigma_if(Z_i)\) with i.i.d. signs \(\sigma_i\). Symmetrisation: \({\mathbb{E}}\sup_f({\mathbb{E}} f-\hat{\mathbb{E}}_nf)\le2\mathfrak R_n({\mathcal{F}})\). For \(f\in[0,1]\), with probability \(\ge1-\delta\), for all \(f\in{\mathcal{F}}\): \[ {\mathbb{E}} f\le\hat{\mathbb{E}}_nf+2\mathfrak R_n({\mathcal{F}})+\sqrt{\frac{\log(1/\delta)}{2n}}. \]
ver: Data-dependent version: replace \(\mathfrak R_n\) by \(\widehat{\mathfrak R}_n\) at cost \(3\sqrt{\log(2/\delta)/(2n)}\).
Linear class \(\{x\mapsto{\langle w, x\rangle}:{\lVert w\rVert}_2\le W\}\), \({\lVert x\rVert}_2\le X\): \(\widehat{\mathfrak R}_n\le\tfrac{WX}{\sqrt n}\).
Finite class: \(\widehat{\mathfrak R}_n\le\max_f{\lVert f\rVert}_{L^2(\hat P_n)}\sqrt{2\log|{\mathcal{F}}|/n}\) (Massart Massart's finite class lemma).
Lipschitz losses: contraction lemma Ledoux–Talagrand contraction lemma; chaining: Dudley Dudley's entropy integral (chaining).
Local Rademacher complexities give fast \(1/n\) rates under variance conditions.
cards.det: Proof structure: McDiarmid McDiarmid's bounded-differences inequality concentrates the supremum around its mean; symmetrisation introduces a ghost sample and random signs, bounding the mean by \(2\mathfrak R_n\).
cards.ex: Policy classes for contextual bandits / offline policy learning: the regret of the empirical-IPS maximiser over \(\Pi\) is \(\lesssim\tfrac{1}{p_{\min}}\bigl(\mathfrak R_n(\Pi)+\sqrt{\log(1/\delta)/n}\bigr)\).
cards.use: Generalisation of value/policy classes, offline policy learning, neural-network function approximation bounds, Bellman-error minimisation guarantees.

qz.q: Linear class \(\{x\mapsto{\langle w, x\rangle}:{\lVert w\rVert}_2\le W\}\) with \({\lVert x\rVert}_2\le X\), so \(\widehat{\mathfrak R}_n\le WX/\sqrt n\). If \(W\) is doubled, by what factor must \(n\) grow to keep this bound fixed?
qz.why: \(WX/\sqrt n\) is unchanged iff \(\sqrt n\) doubles, i.e. \(n\) grows by \(4\). The bound is dimension-free: it depends on norms, not on the ambient dimension.

qz.q: \({\mathcal{F}}\) contains every function from the domain to \(\{0,1\}\), and \(Z_1,\dots,Z_n\) are distinct. What is \(\widehat{\mathfrak R}_n({\mathcal{F}})\)?
a: \(1/2\), so the bound is vacuous for every \(n\)
\(1/\sqrt n\), as for a single function
qz.why: The supremum picks \(f(Z_i)={\mathbf{1}}\{\sigma_i=1\}\), giving \(\frac1n\#\{i:\sigma_i=1\}\) with mean \(\tfrac12\); then \(2\mathfrak R_n=1\) and the bound says nothing for \([0,1]\) losses. \({\mathbb{E}}\sigma_i=0\) does not help because the sup is taken before averaging.

qz.q: What is gained by using the empirical \(\widehat{\mathfrak R}_n({\mathcal{F}})\) in place of \(\mathfrak R_n({\mathcal{F}})={\mathbb{E}}\widehat{\mathfrak R}_n({\mathcal{F}})\) in the generalisation bound?
a: it is computable from the sample, at a larger deviation term
it removes the factor \(2\) coming from symmetrisation
it gives a \(1/n\) rate without any variance condition
it makes the bound valid for dependent \(Z_i\)
qz.why: \(\widehat{\mathfrak R}_n\) needs only the observed points and random signs, not the unknown distribution; replacing \(\mathfrak R_n\) costs \(3\sqrt{\log(2/\delta)/(2n)}\) instead of \(\sqrt{\log(1/\delta)/(2n)}\). The factor \(2\), the \(1/\sqrt n\) rate and the i.i.d. assumption all stay.

cards.name: Massart's finite class lemma
cards.lay: The Rademacher complexity of a finite set of vectors is at most its largest Euclidean norm times \(\sqrt{2\log N}/n\). The finite-class workhorse inside chaining and VC arguments.
cards.st: For a finite set \(A\subset{\mathbb{R}}^n\) with \(\max_{a\in A}{\lVert a\rVert}_2\le r\): \[ {\mathbb{E}}_\sigma\Bigl[\max_{a\in A}\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\sigma_ia_i\Bigr]\le\frac{r\sqrt{2\log|A|}}{n}. \]
ver: Equivalent to the sub-Gaussian maximal inequality Maximal inequality for sub-Gaussian maxima since \(\sum_i\sigma_ia_i\) is \({\lVert a\rVert}_2\)-sub-Gaussian.
Combined with Sauer–Shelah VC dimension & Sauer–Shelah lemma: \(\mathfrak R_n\le\sqrt{\tfrac{2d\log(en/d)}{n}}\) for \(\{0,1\}\)-valued classes of VC dimension \(d\).
cards.det: Proof: exactly the log-sum-exp argument Log-sum-exp (soft-max) sandwich for sub-Gaussian maxima.
cards.ex: Restricted to \(n\) sample points, a class with \(N\) distinct behaviours (projections) has \(\widehat{\mathfrak R}_n\le\sqrt{2\log N/n}\) for \([0,1]\)-valued functions (since \(r\le\sqrt n\)).
cards.use: VC bounds, chaining, finite policy classes, Rademacher bounds for discretised classes.

qz.q: Restricted to \(n\) sample points, a \(\{0,1\}\)-valued class has at most \(N=n^d\) distinct behaviours. What does Massart's lemma give for \(\widehat{\mathfrak R}_n\)?
qz.why: With \(r\le\sqrt n\): \(\frac{\sqrt n\sqrt{2\log n^d}}{n}=\sqrt{2d\log n/n}\). Removing the \(\log n\) to get \(\sqrt{d/n}\) needs chaining Dudley's entropy integral (chaining), not Massart alone.

qz.q: Functions take values in \([0,B]\) and have \(N\) distinct behaviours on \(n\) points. Massart's lemma gives \(\widehat{\mathfrak R}_n\le\):
qz.why: Each behaviour vector has \({\lVert a\rVert}_2\le B\sqrt n\), so \(r\sqrt{2\log N}/n=B\sqrt{2\log N/n}\). Rademacher complexity is positively homogeneous: scaling the class by \(B\) scales it by \(B\).

qz.q: Which assumption does Massart's finite class lemma need on the set \(A\subset{\mathbb{R}}^n\)?
a: only that \(A\) is finite with \(\max_{a\in A}{\lVert a\rVert}_2\le r\)
that the sums \(\sum_i\sigma_ia_i\) are independent across \(a\in A\)
that \(A\) is symmetric, i.e. closed under \(a\mapsto-a\)
qz.why: Each \(\sum_i\sigma_ia_i\) is \({\lVert a\rVert}_2\)-sub-Gaussian, and the sub-Gaussian maximal inequality needs no independence between the \(|A|\) variables — that is why only \(\sqrt{\log|A|}\) appears.

cards.name: VC dimension & Sauer–Shelah lemma
cards.lay: The VC dimension is the largest number of points a class of binary functions can label in all possible ways. Sauer–Shelah shows a class with finite VC dimension \(d\) can only produce polynomially many (\(\approx n^d\)) labellings of \(n\) points, so it behaves like a finite class with \(\log|{\mathcal{F}}|\approx d\log n\).
cards.st: If \(\mathrm{VC}({\mathcal{F}})=d\), then the number of distinct labellings (growth function) of any \(n\) points satisfies \[ \Pi_{\mathcal{F}}(n)\le\sum_{i=0}^d\binom ni\le\Bigl(\frac{en}{d}\Bigr)^d\quad(n\ge d). \] Consequently, with probability \(\ge1-\delta\), \(\sup_{f\in{\mathcal{F}}}|\hat{\mathbb{E}}_nf-{\mathbb{E}} f|\le C\sqrt{\frac{d+\log(1/\delta)}{n}}\) for a universal \(C\).
ver: Half-spaces in \({\mathbb{R}}^d\): VC dimension \(d+1\); axis-aligned rectangles: \(2d\).
Real-valued classes: pseudo-dimension and fat-shattering dimension play the same role.
Natarajan / graph dimension for multi-class (policy classes with \(|{\mathcal{A}}|>2\)): \(\log\Pi\lesssim d_N\log(n|{\mathcal{A}}|)\).
cards.det: Sauer–Shelah by induction on \(n\); the \((en/d)^d\) step uses Binomial coefficient & Stirling bounds. The \(\sqrt{d/n}\) (rather than \(\sqrt{d\log n/n}\)) rate needs chaining Dudley's entropy integral (chaining).
cards.ex: Contextual bandits with a policy class \(\Pi\) of Natarajan dimension \(d\): EXP4-type algorithms achieve regret \({\widetilde{O}}(\sqrt{T|{\mathcal{A}}|d\log|{\mathcal{A}}|})\), replacing \(\log|\Pi|\) by \(d\log(T|{\mathcal{A}}|)\).
cards.use: Policy-class complexity in contextual bandits, classification-based RL, half-space policy classes, PAC lower bounds.

qz.q: A class has VC dimension \(d=3\). What is the Sauer–Shelah bound \(\sum_{i=0}^d\binom ni\) on the number of labellings of \(n=10\) points?
qz.why: \(1+10+45+120=176\), far below \(2^{10}=1024\). \(120=\binom{10}{3}\) is only the last term; \(n^d=1000\) is not the binomial sum.

qz.q: Which statement about VC dimension is correct?
a: A one-parameter class can have infinite VC dimension
The VC dimension equals the number of real parameters
Half-spaces with offset in \({\mathbb{R}}^d\) have VC dimension \(d\)
A class with finite VC dimension must be a finite class
qz.why: \(\{x\mapsto{\mathbf{1}}\{\sin(\omega x)>0\}:\omega\in{\mathbb{R}}\}\) has one parameter but infinite VC dimension. Half-spaces with offset have VC dimension \(d+1\), and infinite classes (e.g. half-spaces) can have finite VC dimension.

qz.q: Plugging the Sauer–Shelah bound \(\Pi_{\mathcal{F}}(n)\le(en/d)^d\) into Massart's lemma gives which rate for \(\widehat{\mathfrak R}_n\), and what removes the extra logarithm?
a: \(\sqrt{d/n}\) directly, so chaining is never needed
\(\sqrt{d\log(n/d)/n}\); a union bound over \(\delta\) removes the \(\log\)
qz.why: Massart gives \(\sqrt{2\log\Pi(n)/n}\asymp\sqrt{d\log(n/d)/n}\), a single-scale bound. Chaining over scales yields the sharp \(\sqrt{d/n}\); McDiarmid only concentrates the supremum around its mean.

cards.name: Ledoux–Talagrand contraction lemma
cards.lay: Composing every function in a class with the same Lipschitz function can only shrink Rademacher complexity (up to the Lipschitz constant). So bounds for a class of predictors transfer to bounds for their losses.
cards.st: If \(\phi_i:{\mathbb{R}}\to{\mathbb{R}}\) are \(L\)-Lipschitz with \(\phi_i(0)=0\), then for any \(T\subset{\mathbb{R}}^n\): \[ {\mathbb{E}}_\sigma\sup_{t\in T}\sum_i\sigma_i\phi_i(t_i)\le L\,{\mathbb{E}}_\sigma\sup_{t\in T}\sum_i\sigma_it_i. \] Hence \(\mathfrak R_n(\ell\circ{\mathcal{F}})\le L\,\mathfrak R_n({\mathcal{F}})\) for \(L\)-Lipschitz losses.
ver: Vector-valued contraction (Maurer 2016): for \(L\)-Lipschitz \(\phi_i:{\mathbb{R}}^K\to{\mathbb{R}}\) w.r.t. \({\lVert \cdot\rVert}_2\), \({\mathbb{E}}\sup\sum_i\sigma_i\phi_i(t_i)\le\sqrt2L\,{\mathbb{E}}\sup\sum_{i,k}\sigma_{ik}t_{ik}\) — useful for multi-action Q-functions and \(\max_a\).
cards.det: Squared loss on bounded predictions \([0,B]\) is \(2B\)-Lipschitz, so \(\mathfrak R_n(\text{sq.\ loss}\circ{\mathcal{F}})\le2B\,\mathfrak R_n({\mathcal{F}})\). The Bellman backup involves \(\max_a\), which is \(1\)-Lipschitz in \({\lVert \cdot\rVert}_\infty\) Non-expansiveness of \(\max\) / \(\sup\) but needs the vector contraction for Rademacher arguments.
cards.ex: Empirical Bellman error \(\tfrac1n\sum(f(s,a)-r-\gamma\max_{a'}g(s',a'))^2\) over \(f,g\in{\mathcal{F}}\): its complexity is bounded by a constant times \(\mathfrak R_n({\mathcal{F}})\) (plus \(|{\mathcal{A}}|\)-dependent factors via vector contraction).
cards.use: Loss-class complexity in FQI/BRM, classification-based policy iteration, neural-network RL generalisation.

qz.q: Predictions and labels lie in \([0,B]\). For the squared loss \((t-y)^2\), contraction gives \(\mathfrak R_n(\text{loss}\circ{\mathcal{F}})\le c\,\mathfrak R_n({\mathcal{F}})\) with \(c\) equal to:
qz.why: On \([0,B]\), \(|\partial_t(t-y)^2|=2|t-y|\le2B\), so the loss is \(2B\)-Lipschitz in \(t\). \(B^2\) is the loss's range, not its Lipschitz constant.

qz.q: The loss \(\phi_i(t)=|t-y_i|\) with \(y_i\ne0\) violates the condition \(\phi_i(0)=0\). What is the right fix?
a: none: contraction fails, so use Dudley's integral instead
restrict to classes with \(f(Z_i)=0\) at every sample point
qz.why: \({\mathbb{E}}_\sigma\sup_t\sum_i\sigma_i(\phi_i(t_i)-c_i)={\mathbb{E}}_\sigma\sup_t\sum_i\sigma_i\phi_i(t_i)-{\mathbb{E}}\sum_i\sigma_ic_i\) and the last term is \(0\). So the shifted losses are \(1\)-Lipschitz with \(\phi_i(0)=0\) and the same complexity.

qz.q: To bound the Rademacher complexity of the Bellman target \(\max_{a'}g(s',a')\), \(g\in{\mathcal{F}}\), in terms of the class of action-value vectors, which tool fits?
a: scalar contraction, since \(\max\) is 1-Lipschitz in each coordinate
Massart's lemma, since the action set \({\mathcal{A}}\) is finite
qz.why: Scalar Ledoux–Talagrand needs \(\phi_i:{\mathbb{R}}\to{\mathbb{R}}\) applied to one number per sample; \(\max_{a'}\) takes a vector. Maurer's vector contraction handles it at a \(\sqrt2\) cost: \(|\max x-\max y|\le{\lVert x-y\rVert}_\infty\le{\lVert x-y\rVert}_2\).

cards.name: Dudley's entropy integral (chaining)
cards.lay: Instead of one union bound at a single scale, chain together covers at many scales. The supremum of a sub-Gaussian process is bounded by an integral of the square root of log-covering numbers, which removes spurious log factors.
cards.st: For a process \((X_t)_{t\in T}\) with sub-Gaussian increments w.r.t. a metric \(d\) (\(X_s-X_t\) is \(d(s,t)\)-sub-Gaussian): \[ {\mathbb{E}}\sup_{t\in T}X_t\le C\int_0^{\mathrm{diam}(T)}\sqrt{\log N({\varepsilon},T,d)}\,{\mathrm{d}}{\varepsilon}. \] For Rademacher complexity: \(\widehat{\mathfrak R}_n({\mathcal{F}})\le\inf_{\alpha>0}\Bigl(4\alpha+\frac{12}{\sqrt n}\int_\alpha^{1}\sqrt{\log N({\varepsilon},{\mathcal{F}},L^2(\hat P_n))}\,{\mathrm{d}}{\varepsilon}\Bigr)\).
ver: Generic chaining (Talagrand's \(\gamma_2\) functional) is tight up to constants for Gaussian processes (majorising measure theorem).
For parametric classes with \(N({\varepsilon})\le(C/{\varepsilon})^d\): \({\mathbb{E}}\sup\lesssim\sqrt{d/n}\), no \(\log n\).
cards.det: Chaining writes \(X_t=X_{t_0}+\sum_k(X_{\pi_{k+1}(t)}-X_{\pi_k(t)})\) where \(\pi_k(t)\) is the nearest point in a \(2^{-k}\)-cover; each link has few possibilities and small increments, so maximal inequalities Maximal inequality for sub-Gaussian maxima at each scale sum to the integral.
cards.ex: Neural-network or nonparametric value-function classes with \(\log N({\varepsilon})\asymp{\varepsilon}^{-p}\): Dudley gives Rademacher complexity \(n^{-1/2}\) for \(p<2\) and \(n^{-1/p}\) for \(p>2\).
cards.use: Sharp rates for function-approximation RL, nonparametric FQI, sub-Gaussian process suprema.

qz.q: A value-function class has metric entropy \(\log N({\varepsilon})\asymp{\varepsilon}^{-3}\). What rate does Dudley's integral (with the optimal truncation \(\alpha\)) give for its Rademacher complexity?
qz.why: For \(p>2\), \(\alpha+\frac1{\sqrt n}\int_\alpha^1{\varepsilon}^{-p/2}{\mathrm{d}}{\varepsilon}\asymp\alpha+n^{-1/2}\alpha^{1-p/2}\), balanced at \(\alpha\asymp n^{-1/p}\); here \(n^{-1/3}\). The parametric \(n^{-1/2}\) holds only when \(p<2\).

qz.q: Why does the Rademacher form of Dudley's bound integrate from \(\alpha>0\) and add a \(4\alpha\) term, instead of integrating from \(0\)?
a: for rich classes \(\int_0\sqrt{\log N}\) diverges, so chaining stops at scale \(\alpha\)
covering numbers are undefined at scales below \(1/n\)
the \(4\alpha\) term corrects the bias of the empirical measure \(\hat P_n\)
the Rademacher process is identically zero below scale \(\alpha\)
qz.why: If \(\log N({\varepsilon})\asymp{\varepsilon}^{-p}\) with \(p\ge2\), \(\sqrt{\log N}\) is not integrable at \(0\). Stopping the chain at \(\alpha\) and bounding the remaining fine-scale error crudely by \(\asymp\alpha\) fixes this.

qz.q: Which statement about Dudley's entropy integral is correct?
a: It can be loose; Talagrand's \(\gamma_2\) is tight for Gaussian processes
It is tight up to constants for every Gaussian process
It requires bounded \(X_t\), not just sub-Gaussian increments
It applies only when the index set \(T\) is finite
qz.why: Dudley is an upper bound that can lose a logarithmic factor; generic chaining's \(\gamma_2(T,d)\) matches \({\mathbb{E}}\sup X_t\) up to constants for Gaussian processes (majorising measures). Dudley needs only sub-Gaussian increments and covers infinite \(T\).

cards.name: PAC-Bayes bounds
cards.lay: A generalisation bound for randomised predictors: if you output a distribution \(\rho\) over hypotheses, its true risk is close to its empirical risk plus a penalty \({\mathrm{KL}}(\rho\|\pi)\) to a prior \(\pi\) chosen before seeing data.
cards.st: (McAllester / Maurer) For losses in \([0,1]\), any prior \(\pi\) and \(\delta\in(0,1)\), with probability \(\ge1-\delta\), simultaneously for all posteriors \(\rho\): \[ {\mathbb{E}}_{h\sim\rho}L(h)\le{\mathbb{E}}_{h\sim\rho}\widehat L_n(h)+\sqrt{\frac{{\mathrm{KL}}(\rho\|\pi)+\log\frac{2\sqrt n}{\delta}}{2n}}. \]
ver: Catoni / Seeger forms with \(\mathrm{kl}(\widehat L_\rho\|L_\rho)\le\tfrac{{\mathrm{KL}}(\rho\|\pi)+\log(2\sqrt n/\delta)}{n}\).
Optimal posterior is the Gibbs posterior \(\rho\propto\pi e^{-\lambda\widehat L_n}\) (Donsker–Varadhan Donsker–Varadhan & Gibbs variational principle).
Finite class with uniform prior and point-mass posterior recovers the Occam bound Finite-class uniform convergence (Occam bound).
cards.det: Proof: change of measure Donsker–Varadhan & Gibbs variational principle \({\mathbb{E}}_\rho[\lambda\Delta(h)]\le{\mathrm{KL}}(\rho\|\pi)+\log{\mathbb{E}}_\pi e^{\lambda\Delta(h)}\) with \(\Delta=L-\widehat L_n\); bound the last term by Markov on its expectation (using Hoeffding's lemma per \(h\)).
cards.ex: PAC-Bayesian analyses of posterior sampling and of KL-regularised policy optimisation, where the policy is literally a distribution over actions or parameters.
cards.use: Generalisation of stochastic policies, Thompson-sampling-style analyses, KL-regularised RL, deep RL generalisation bounds.

qz.q: In the PAC-Bayes bound over a finite class \({\mathcal{F}}\), take the uniform prior \(\pi\) and a point-mass posterior \(\rho=\delta_h\). Then \({\mathrm{KL}}(\rho\|\pi)\) equals:
qz.why: \({\mathrm{KL}}(\delta_h\|\pi)=\log\frac{1}{1/|{\mathcal{F}}|}=\log|{\mathcal{F}}|\), so PAC-Bayes recovers the Occam bound Finite-class uniform convergence (Occam bound) (up to the \(\log\sqrt n\) term). KL is never negative.

qz.q: Which choice invalidates the PAC-Bayes guarantee?
a: choosing the prior \(\pi\) after looking at the training sample
choosing the posterior \(\rho\) after looking at the training sample
taking \(\rho\) to be the Gibbs posterior \(\rho\propto\pi e^{-\lambda\widehat L_n}\)
taking \(\rho=\pi\), so that the KL term vanishes
qz.why: The bound holds simultaneously for all posteriors, so \(\rho\) may depend on data arbitrarily; the prior must be fixed before seeing the sample, since the proof applies Markov's inequality to \({\mathbb{E}}_\pi e^{\lambda\Delta(h)}\).

qz.q: Prior \(\pi={\mathcal{N}}(0,\sigma^2I_d)\) and posterior \(\rho={\mathcal{N}}(w,\sigma^2I_d)\) on the parameters of a network. What is the KL term in the PAC-Bayes bound?
