qz.why: With equal covariances the trace, \(-d\) and log-det terms cancel, leaving \(\tfrac12(w-0)^\top(\sigma^2I)^{-1}(w-0)\) KL for Bernoulli & Gaussian distributions. The bound depends on \({\lVert w\rVert}_2\), not on the parameter count \(d\).

cards.name: Eluder dimension
cards.field: RL / bandit theory with function approximation
cards.lay: A complexity measure for sequential decision-making: the longest sequence of actions such that each one's value cannot be predicted from the previous ones (by functions in the class that agree so far). It bounds how often optimistic algorithms can be surprised.
cards.st: (Russo & Van Roy 2013) An action \(x\) is \({\varepsilon}\)-dependent on \(x_1,\dots,x_n\) w.r.t. \({\mathcal{F}}\) if every \(f,f'\in{\mathcal{F}}\) with \(\sqrt{\sum_i(f(x_i)-f'(x_i))^2}\le{\varepsilon}\) also satisfy \(|f(x)-f'(x)|\le{\varepsilon}\). The eluder dimension \(\dim_E({\mathcal{F}},{\varepsilon})\) is the length of the longest sequence in which each element is \({\varepsilon}'\)-independent of its predecessors for some \({\varepsilon}'\ge{\varepsilon}\). Then optimistic algorithms satisfy \[ {\mathrm{Reg}}_T={\widetilde{O}}\Bigl(\sqrt{\dim_E({\mathcal{F}},T^{-1})\,\log N({\mathcal{F}},T^{-1})\,T}\Bigr). \]
ver: Linear class in \({\mathbb{R}}^d\): \(\dim_E=O(d\log(1/{\varepsilon}))\); generalised linear: \(O(d\tfrac{\bar\kappa^2}{\underline\kappa^2}\log(1/{\varepsilon}))\).
RL extensions: Bellman–eluder dimension (Jin, Liu, Miryoosefi 2021), Bellman rank (Jiang et al. 2017), decision–estimation coefficient (Foster et al. 2021).
Sum-of-widths lemma: \(\sum_t\min(1,w_t(x_t))\le O(\dim_E\log T)+\ldots\) — the general-class analogue of the elliptical potential lemma Elliptical potential lemma.
cards.det: The key lemma bounds the number of times the confidence width at the chosen action exceeds \({\varepsilon}\) by \(O\bigl(\tfrac{\beta}{{\varepsilon}^2}\dim_E({\mathcal{F}},{\varepsilon})\bigr)\), then sums over a dyadic range of \({\varepsilon}\). It is the function-class generalisation of the pigeonhole/potential arguments Pigeonhole / count-summation lemma (tabular RL).
cards.ex: For linear bandits it recovers \({\widetilde{O}}(d\sqrt T)\) regret, matching OFUL.
cards.use: Optimism with general function approximation (GOLF, OLIVE-family), contextual bandits with regression oracles, complexity measures for RL.

qz.q: For a linear class in \({\mathbb{R}}^d\), \(\dim_E({\mathcal{F}},{\varepsilon})=O(d\log(1/{\varepsilon}))\) and \(\log N({\mathcal{F}},{\varepsilon})=O(d\log(1/{\varepsilon}))\). Plugging into \({\mathrm{Reg}}_T={\widetilde{O}}(\sqrt{\dim_E\log N\,T})\) at \({\varepsilon}=1/T\) gives:
qz.why: \(\sqrt{d\log T\cdot d\log T\cdot T}=d\sqrt T\log T\), matching OFUL. One factor \(\sqrt d\) comes from the eluder dimension, the other from the covering number.

qz.q: What does it mean that an action \(x\) is \({\varepsilon}\)-independent of \(x_1,\dots,x_n\) with respect to \({\mathcal{F}}\)?
a: some \(f,f'\in{\mathcal{F}}\) nearly agree on \(x_{1:n}\) yet differ by \(>{\varepsilon}\) at \(x\)
the feature vector of \(x\) is linearly independent of those of \(x_{1:n}\)
every pair \(f\ne f'\) in \({\mathcal{F}}\) differs by more than \({\varepsilon}\) at \(x\)
qz.why: Independence means the past does not pin down the value at \(x\): there exist \(f,f'\) with \(\sqrt{\sum_i(f(x_i)-f'(x_i))^2}\le{\varepsilon}\) but \(|f(x)-f'(x)|>{\varepsilon}\). Linear independence is not the definition, and new actions can be fully predictable.

qz.q: In the eluder-dimension regret analysis, what does the key lemma bound by \(O\bigl(\tfrac{\beta}{{\varepsilon}^2}\dim_E({\mathcal{F}},{\varepsilon})\bigr)\)?
a: the number of rounds the confidence width at the played action exceeds \({\varepsilon}\)
the number of distinct actions the optimistic algorithm ever plays
the covering number of \({\mathcal{F}}\) at scale \({\varepsilon}\), which sets \(\beta\)
the probability that the true function leaves the confidence set
qz.why: Each large-width round needs an action that is \({\varepsilon}\)-independent of many previous ones, which the eluder dimension limits. Summing over dyadic \({\varepsilon}\) gives the sum-of-widths bound, the analogue of the elliptical potential lemma Elliptical potential lemma.

cards.name: Bellman equations & contraction of Bellman operators
cards.plain: Bellman equations & contraction of Bellman operators
cards.lay: The value of a state equals the immediate reward plus the discounted value of where you go next. The Bellman operators that encode this are \(\gamma\)-contractions in sup-norm, so their fixed points (the value functions) exist, are unique, and can be found by iteration.
cards.st: For a discounted MDP define \((T^\pi V)(s)=r^\pi(s)+\gamma\sum_{s'}P^\pi(s'|s)V(s')\) and \((T^\star V)(s)=\max_a\{r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'}P(s'|s,a)V(s')\}\). Both satisfy \[ {\lVert TV-TU\rVert}_\infty\le\gamma{\lVert V-U\rVert}_\infty, \] \(V^\pi\) is the unique fixed point of \(T^\pi\), \(V^\star\) the unique fixed point of \(T^\star\), and any policy greedy w.r.t. \(V^\star\) is optimal.
ver: Monotonicity: \(V\le U\Rightarrow TV\le TU\); constant shift: \(T(V+c{\mathbf{1}})=TV+\gamma c{\mathbf{1}}\).
Q-function forms: \((T^\star Q)(s,a)=r(s,a)+\gamma{\mathbb{E}}_{s'}\max_{a'}Q(s',a')\).
Finite horizon: backward induction \(V_h=T_hV_{h+1}\), \(V_{H+1}=0\) — no contraction needed.
Regularised: soft Bellman operator with log-sum-exp is also a \(\gamma\)-contraction Log-sum-exp (soft-max) sandwich.
Average reward: \(T\) is non-expansive in span seminorm and contractive under ergodicity Poisson equation, bias & Laurent expansion (average reward).
cards.det: Contraction of \(T^\pi\) is Induced operator norms (\(\ell_\infty\) norm of stochastic matrices); contraction of \(T^\star\) adds non-expansiveness of \(\max\) Non-expansiveness of \(\max\) / \(\sup\). Existence/uniqueness then comes from Banach Banach fixed-point theorem (contraction mapping). Optimality of greedy policies follows from monotonicity: if \(\pi\) is greedy w.r.t. \(V^\star\) then \(T^\pi V^\star=T^\star V^\star=V^\star\), so \(V^\pi=V^\star\).
cards.ex: Two-state chain, one action, rewards \((1,0)\), \(\gamma=0.9\), deterministic swap: \(V=(I-\gamma P)^{-1}r=\tfrac{1}{1-0.81}(1,0.9)\approx(5.26,4.74)\).
cards.use: Everything: VI/PI, Q-learning, TD, error propagation, existence of optimal stationary policies.

qz.q: Each \(T^\pi\) is a \(\gamma\)-contraction in \({\lVert \cdot\rVert}_\infty\) because \(P^\pi\) is a stochastic matrix. Which additional fact is used to show that the Bellman optimality operator \((T^\star V)(s)=\max_a\{r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'}P(s'|s,a)V(s')\}\) is also a \(\gamma\)-contraction?
a: \(\max_a\) is a linear operator on functions of \(a\)
qz.why: The max is non-expansive in sup-norm Non-expansiveness of \(\max\) / \(\sup\), so the per-action contraction survives the maximisation. The max is convex but not linear; symmetry or sign of rewards plays no role.

qz.q: Discounted MDP with \(\gamma<1\). Value iteration \(V_{k+1}=T^\star V_k\) is started at \(V_0=V^\star+c{\mathbf{1}}\) for a constant \(c\) (\({\mathbf{1}}\) is the all-ones vector). What is \(V_k-V^\star\)?
qz.why: By the constant-shift property \(T^\star(V+c{\mathbf{1}})=T^\star V+\gamma c{\mathbf{1}}\) and \(T^\star V^\star=V^\star\), each step multiplies the offset by \(\gamma\). The shift is not preserved (that would contradict contraction).

qz.q: Two states, one action, rewards \(r=(1,0)\), \(\gamma=0.5\), deterministic swap transitions (\(1\to2\), \(2\to1\)). What is \(V=(V(1),V(2))\)?
qz.why: Solve \(V(1)=1+\tfrac12V(2)\), \(V(2)=\tfrac12V(1)\): \(V(1)=1+\tfrac14V(1)\), so \(V(1)=4/3\), \(V(2)=2/3\). \((1,1/2)\) is only the first two terms of the series; \((2,0)\) treats state 1 as absorbing.

cards.name: Discounted occupancy measures
cards.lay: A policy's discounted occupancy measure records how often (with discounting) it visits each state–action pair. Values become linear functions of it: \(V^\pi=\tfrac{1}{1-\gamma}\langle d^\pi,r\rangle\). Turning nonlinear policy questions into linear ones over occupancies is a powerful trick.
cards.st: For initial distribution \(\rho\): \[ d^\pi_\rho(s,a)=(1-\gamma)\sum_{t\ge0}\gamma^t\Pr^\pi_\rho(s_t=s,a_t=a),\qquad V^\pi(\rho)=\frac{1}{1-\gamma}{\mathbb{E}}_{(s,a)\sim d^\pi_\rho}[r(s,a)]. \] \(d^\pi_\rho\) is a probability distribution satisfying the flow constraints \(\sum_ad(s,a)=(1-\gamma)\rho(s)+\gamma\sum_{s',a'}P(s|s',a')d(s',a')\).
ver: Matrix form: \(d^\pi_\rho=(1-\gamma)\rho^\top(I-\gamma P^\pi)^{-1}\) (state occupancy) Neumann series & the resolvent \((I-\gamma P)^{-1}\).
Lower bound: \(d^\pi_\rho(s)\ge(1-\gamma)\rho(s)\) — the reason exploratory start distributions \(\mu\) help policy gradient Gradient domination for policy optimisation.
Bijection: every \(d\) satisfying the flow constraints is the occupancy of the stationary policy \(\pi(a|s)=d(s,a)/\sum_bd(s,b)\) — basis of the LP formulation LP formulation of MDPs & its dual.
Finite horizon: per-step occupancies \(d_h^\pi(s,a)=\Pr^\pi(s_h=s,a_h=a)\).
cards.det: Swapping expectation and discounted sum (Fubini Fubini–Tonelli theorem (swapping sums/integrals)) gives the value identity. Occupancy measures convert policy optimisation into a linear program over a convex polytope, explain why constrained MDPs have zero duality gap Lagrangian duality & Slater's condition, and underlie distribution-correction (DICE) methods for off-policy evaluation.
cards.ex: Policy-gradient theorem in occupancy form: \(\nabla V^{\pi_\theta}(\rho)=\tfrac{1}{1-\gamma}{\mathbb{E}}_{(s,a)\sim d^{\pi_\theta}_\rho}[Q^{\pi_\theta}(s,a)\nabla\log\pi_\theta(a|s)]\) Policy gradient theorem.
cards.use: LP methods, constrained MDPs, PDL, policy gradient, distribution mismatch, offline RL coverage, imitation learning via occupancy matching.
cards.ll: Agarwal, Jiang, Kakade & Sun — RL Theory book

qz.q: Let \(d^\pi_\rho(s)=(1-\gamma)\sum_{t\ge0}\gamma^t\Pr^\pi_\rho(s_t=s)\) be the normalised discounted state occupancy from initial distribution \(\rho\). Which inequality holds for every policy \(\pi\) and state \(s\)?
qz.why: The \(t=0\) term alone contributes \((1-\gamma)\rho(s)\) and the others are non-negative. \(d\ge\rho\) fails because the policy may leave \(s\) forever; \(\rho/(1-\gamma)\) cannot be a lower bound of a probability distribution.

qz.q: Rewards are in \(\{0,1\}\) and \(\gamma=0.9\). The normalised occupancy \(d^\pi_\rho\) (a probability distribution over \((s,a)\)) puts total mass \(0.3\) on pairs with reward \(1\). What is \(V^\pi(\rho)\)?
qz.why: \(V^\pi(\rho)=\tfrac{1}{1-\gamma}{\mathbb{E}}_{(s,a)\sim d^\pi_\rho}[r]=0.3/0.1=3\). Answering \(0.3\) forgets that \(d\) is normalised by the factor \((1-\gamma)\).

qz.q: A non-negative \(d(s,a)\) satisfies the flow constraints \(\sum_ad(s,a)=(1-\gamma)\rho(s)+\gamma\sum_{s',a'}P(s|s',a')d(s',a')\). Which stationary policy has \(d\) as its occupancy measure (at states with \(\sum_bd(s,b)>0\))?
qz.why: Conditioning the occupancy on the state recovers the policy; this bijection underlies the LP formulation LP formulation of MDPs & its dual. \(d(s,a)\) itself is a joint distribution, not a conditional, and dividing by \(\rho(s)\) ignores later visits.

cards.name: Performance difference lemma (Kakade–Langford)
cards.lay: The value gap between two policies equals the expected advantage of one policy's actions, measured under the other policy's state visitation. It is the most important identity in policy optimisation theory.
cards.st: For any policies \(\pi,\pi'\) and initial distribution \(\rho\): \[ V^{\pi'}(\rho)-V^{\pi}(\rho)=\frac{1}{1-\gamma}{\mathbb{E}}_{s\sim d^{\pi'}_\rho}{\mathbb{E}}_{a\sim\pi'(\cdot|s)}\bigl[A^{\pi}(s,a)\bigr], \] where \(A^\pi(s,a)=Q^\pi(s,a)-V^\pi(s)\).
ver: Finite horizon: \(V_1^{\pi'}(s_1)-V_1^\pi(s_1)={\mathbb{E}}_{\pi'}\sum_{h=1}^H\bigl[Q_h^\pi(s_h,a_h)-V_h^\pi(s_h)\bigr]\).

With arbitrary \(V\) in place of \(V^\pi\) (“value-difference”): \(V^{\pi'}(\rho)-V(\rho)=\tfrac{1}{1-\gamma}{\mathbb{E}}_{d^{\pi'}_\rho}[(T^{\pi'}V-V)(s)]\) Value-difference (Bellman-error telescoping) decomposition.
Inner-product form: \(V^{\pi'}-V^{\pi}=\tfrac{1}{1-\gamma}{\mathbb{E}}_{s\sim d^{\pi'}}{\langle \pi'(\cdot|s)-\pi(\cdot|s), Q^\pi(s,\cdot)\rangle}\).

Approximate (surrogate) form with \(d^\pi\) in place of \(d^{\pi'}\): error \(\le\tfrac{2\gamma\epsilon}{(1-\gamma)^2}\max_s{\mathrm{TV}}(\pi'(\cdot|s),\pi(\cdot|s))\) — TRPO/CPI Conservative policy iteration & TRPO improvement bound.
cards.det:
Proof. Along a trajectory of \(\pi'\), telescope Telescoping sums: \(V^{\pi'}(s_0)-V^\pi(s_0)={\mathbb{E}}_{\pi'}\sum_t\gamma^t\bigl[r(s_t,a_t)+\gamma V^\pi(s_{t+1})-V^\pi(s_t)\bigr]={\mathbb{E}}_{\pi'}\sum_t\gamma^tA^\pi(s_t,a_t)\), using \({\mathbb{E}}[r+\gamma V^\pi(s')\mid s,a]=Q^\pi(s,a)\). Convert the discounted sum to \(d^{\pi'}\) Discounted occupancy measures.

Consequences: policy improvement Policy improvement theorem & policy iteration, gradient domination Gradient domination for policy optimisation, NPG/PMD convergence Natural policy gradient & policy mirror descent convergence, CPI/TRPO bounds Conservative policy iteration & TRPO improvement bound, regret of policy-optimisation algorithms in adversarial MDPs.
cards.ex: If \(\pi'\) is greedy w.r.t. \(Q^\pi\) then \({\mathbb{E}}_{a\sim\pi'}A^\pi(s,a)=\max_aA^\pi(s,a)\ge0\) in every state, so \(V^{\pi'}\ge V^\pi\): policy improvement in one line.
cards.use: Policy gradient global convergence, NPG/PPO/TRPO theory, policy iteration, imitation learning (DAgger analysis), regret decomposition for policy-optimisation methods.
cards.ll: Agarwal, Jiang, Kakade & Sun — RL Theory book

qz.q: Which identity is the performance difference lemma? (\(d^\pi_\rho\) is the normalised discounted occupancy, \(A^\pi=Q^\pi-V^\pi\).)
qz.why: States come from the new policy \(\pi'\), advantages are those of the old policy \(\pi\). Using \(d^\pi\) gives only the TRPO surrogate Conservative policy iteration & TRPO improvement bound; \({\mathbb{E}}_{a\sim\pi'}A^{\pi'}=0\) makes that version vanish; averaging \(A^{\pi'}\) under \(\pi\) gives the gap with the wrong sign.

qz.q: Suppose \({\mathbb{E}}_{a\sim\pi'(\cdot|s)}A^\pi(s,a)\ge{\varepsilon}>0\) in every state \(s\). What is the strongest lower bound on \(V^{\pi'}(\rho)-V^\pi(\rho)\) that the PDL guarantees?
qz.why: \(d^{\pi'}_\rho\) is a probability distribution, so the expectation is \(\ge{\varepsilon}\), and the PDL multiplies by \(\tfrac{1}{1-\gamma}\) (\(\ge{\varepsilon}\) and \(\ge(1-\gamma){\varepsilon}\) also hold but are weaker). There is no second horizon factor: no value function is being multiplied by a model error.

qz.q: Why can one not simply maximise the right-hand side of the PDL, \(\tfrac{1}{1-\gamma}{\mathbb{E}}_{s\sim d^{\pi'}_\rho,a\sim\pi'}A^\pi(s,a)\), over \(\pi'\) using data from \(\pi\)?
a: The state distribution \(d^{\pi'}_\rho\) depends on the unknown \(\pi'\)
The PDL only holds for deterministic \(\pi\) and \(\pi'\)
The PDL only holds when \(\pi'\) is close to \(\pi\) in TV
qz.why: The PDL is exact for all policy pairs, and \(A^\pi\) is fixed once \(\pi\) is; the difficulty is that states are drawn from the new policy's occupancy. Replacing it by \(d^\pi\) gives the surrogate whose error TRPO controls Conservative policy iteration & TRPO improvement bound.

cards.name: Simulation lemma (model error \(\to\) value error)
cards.lay: If your learned model's transitions and rewards are close to the truth, then every policy's value in the model is close to its true value — with an amplification of \(1/(1-\gamma)^2\) (or \(H^2\)) because errors compound over time.
cards.st: For models \(M=(P,r)\) and \(\widehat M=(\widehat P,\hat r)\) and any policy \(\pi\): \[ V^\pi_{\widehat M}-V^\pi_M=(I-\gamma\widehat P^\pi)^{-1}\bigl[(\hat r^\pi-r^\pi)+\gamma(\widehat P^\pi-P^\pi)V^\pi_M\bigr]. \] Hence, with rewards in \([0,1]\): \({\lVert V^\pi_{\widehat M}-V^\pi_M\rVert}_\infty\le\frac{{\lVert \hat r-r\rVert}_\infty}{1-\gamma}+\frac{\gamma\max_{s,a}{\lVert \widehat P(\cdot|s,a)-P(\cdot|s,a)\rVert}_1}{(1-\gamma)^2}\).
ver: Finite horizon: \(V_1^{\pi,\widehat M}-V_1^{\pi,M}={\mathbb{E}}_{\pi,\widehat M}\sum_h\bigl[(\hat r_h-r_h)+(\widehat P_h-P_h)V^{\pi,M}_{h+1}\bigr](s_h,a_h)\), giving \(\le H{\varepsilon}_r+H^2{\varepsilon}_P\).

Expectation under the true model instead (swap roles): \(V^\pi_{\widehat M}-V^\pi_M=\tfrac{1}{1-\gamma}{\mathbb{E}}_{(s,a)\sim d^\pi_M}\bigl[(\hat r-r)+\gamma(\widehat P-P)V^\pi_{\widehat M}\bigr](s,a)\) — needed when model error is only controlled on-distribution.

Fixed-vector refinement: \(|(\widehat P-P)V^\star|\lesssim\sqrt{{\operatorname{Var}}_P(V^\star)\log/n}\) avoids the \(\sqrt S\) of the \(\ell_1\) bound \(\ell_1\) deviation of the empirical distribution (Weissman et al.).
Optimal-value version: \(|V^\star_{\widehat M}-V^\star_M|\le\max_\pi|V^\pi_{\widehat M}-V^\pi_M|\) Non-expansiveness of \(\max\) / \(\sup\).
cards.det:
Derivation: subtract the two Bellman equations \(V_{\widehat M}=\hat r+\gamma\widehat PV_{\widehat M}\), \(V_M=r+\gamma PV_M\) and rearrange: \((I-\gamma\widehat P)(V_{\widehat M}-V_M)=(\hat r-r)+\gamma(\widehat P-P)V_M\). Invert with the Neumann bound Neumann series & the resolvent \((I-\gamma P)^{-1}\) and use Hölder Hölder's inequality.

For non-stationary environments, the same lemma bounds how much a policy's value changes when the environment drifts: replace \(\widehat M\) by \(M_{t+1}\) and \(M\) by \(M_t\); the drift budget enters through \(\sum_t{\lVert P_{t+1}-P_t\rVert}\) Drift-to-value lemma (sensitivity of values to environment change).
cards.ex: Generative-model planning: with \(n\) samples per \((s,a)\), \({\lVert \widehat P-P\rVert}_1\lesssim\sqrt{S/n}\), so the plug-in optimal policy is \({\varepsilon}\)-optimal once \(n\gtrsim\tfrac{S}{(1-\gamma)^4{\varepsilon}^2}\) (naive); refined arguments give the optimal \(\tfrac{1}{(1-\gamma)^3{\varepsilon}^2}\).
cards.use: Model-based RL (R-max, UCRL2, PSRL), sim-to-real gap bounds, robust RL, non-stationary RL drift-to-value bounds, offline model-based RL.
cards.ll: Agarwal, Jiang, Kakade & Sun — RL Theory book

qz.q: In the simulation lemma \({\lVert V^\pi_{\widehat M}-V^\pi_M\rVert}_\infty\le\frac{{\varepsilon}_r}{1-\gamma}+\frac{\gamma{\varepsilon}_P}{(1-\gamma)^2}\) (rewards in \([0,1]\), \({\varepsilon}_P\) a max \(\ell_1\) transition error), where does the second factor \(1/(1-\gamma)\) on the transition term come from?
a: The \(\ell_1\) error is multiplied by \({\lVert V^\pi_M\rVert}_\infty\le1/(1-\gamma)\)
The transition error enters the value quadratically
Pinsker's inequality squares the transition error
Each transition error is counted at two consecutive steps
qz.why: One factor is the Neumann series \((I-\gamma\widehat P^\pi)^{-1}\) accumulating per-step errors; the other is Hölder, \(|(\widehat P-P)V|\le{\lVert \widehat P-P\rVert}_1{\lVert V\rVert}_\infty\) with \({\lVert V\rVert}_\infty\le\tfrac1{1-\gamma}\). The error enters linearly, not quadratically.

qz.q: Episodic MDP with horizon \(H=10\), rewards in \([0,1]\), per-step reward error \({\varepsilon}_r=0.01\) and per-step \(\ell_1\) transition error \({\varepsilon}_P=0.01\). What does the finite-horizon simulation lemma bound \(H{\varepsilon}_r+H^2{\varepsilon}_P\) give for the value error?
qz.why: \(10\cdot0.01+100\cdot0.01=0.1+1=1.1\). Treating both terms as linear in \(H\) gives \(0.2\); the transition term is dominant because each error is multiplied by a value of size up to \(H\).

qz.q: Model error is only controlled on the true model's occupancy \(d^\pi_M\). In the identity \(V^\pi_{\widehat M}-V^\pi_M=\tfrac{1}{1-\gamma}{\mathbb{E}}_{(s,a)\sim d^\pi_M}\bigl[(\hat r-r)+\gamma(\widehat P-P)W\bigr](s,a)\), which value function is \(W\)?
qz.why: Subtracting Bellman equations as \((I-\gamma P^\pi)(V_{\widehat M}-V_M)=(\hat r-r)+\gamma(\widehat P-P)V_{\widehat M}\) puts the true \(P\) in the inverse (hence \(d^\pi_M\)) and the model's value inside. Putting \(V^\pi_M\) inside requires the inverse with \(\widehat P\), i.e. expectation under \(\widehat M\).

cards.name: Value-difference (Bellman-error telescoping) decomposition
cards.lay: The gap between an arbitrary value estimate and a policy's true value equals the sum of Bellman errors of the estimate along that policy's trajectories. Optimism-based regret proofs are this identity plus concentration.
cards.st: For any \(V\) (or \(Q\)) and policy \(\pi\): \[ V(\rho)-V^\pi(\rho)=\frac{1}{1-\gamma}{\mathbb{E}}_{s\sim d^\pi_\rho}\bigl[(V-T^\pi V)(s)\bigr]. \] Finite horizon with estimates \(\{Q_h\}\) and \(\pi_h\) greedy w.r.t. \(Q_h\): \(V_1(s_1)-V_1^{\pi}(s_1)={\mathbb{E}}_\pi\sum_{h=1}^H\bigl[Q_h-r_h-P_hV_{h+1}\bigr](s_h,a_h)\).
ver: Optimism \(\Rightarrow\) regret bound: if \(V_1\ge V_1^\star\) (optimism) then \(V^\star_1-V^{\pi}_1\le V_1-V^\pi_1={\mathbb{E}}_\pi\sum_h(\text{Bellman error})_h\), and the Bellman error is bounded by twice the bonus Optimism principle (regret \(\le\) sum of confidence widths).
Sample-path version: replacing expectations by realised transitions adds martingale differences handled by Azuma Azuma–Hoeffding inequality (martingales).
Generalised to function approximation: average Bellman error under the policy's distribution — the starting point of Bellman rank/Bellman–eluder analyses Eluder dimension.
cards.det: Proof: \(V-V^\pi=V-T^\pi V+T^\pi V-T^\pi V^\pi=(V-T^\pi V)+\gamma P^\pi(V-V^\pi)\); solve the linear equation with the Neumann series Neumann series & the resolvent \((I-\gamma P)^{-1}\) and use the occupancy identity Discounted occupancy measures.
cards.ex: UCBVI: with bonuses \(b_h\) ensuring optimism, the per-episode regret is \(\le{\mathbb{E}}_{\pi_k}\sum_h\bigl[2b_h+(\widehat P_h-P_h)(V_{h+1}-V^\star_{h+1})\bigr]\), and summing bonuses over episodes with the pigeonhole lemma Pigeonhole / count-summation lemma (tabular RL) gives \({\widetilde{O}}(\sqrt{H^3SAT})\).
cards.use: Regret analyses of optimistic algorithms (UCBVI, LSVI-UCB, GOLF), offline RL pessimism analyses, Bellman-error-based complexity measures.
cards.ll: Agarwal, Jiang, Kakade & Sun — RL Theory book

qz.q: In optimistic regret proofs one has \(V^\star_1-V^{\pi}_1\le V_1-V^{\pi}_1={\mathbb{E}}_\pi\sum_h(\text{Bellman error})_h\) for the algorithm's estimate \(V_1\) and its greedy policy \(\pi\). What exactly does optimism \(V_1\ge V_1^\star\) contribute?
a: It replaces the unknown \(V^\star_1\) by the computable \(V_1\)
It makes every Bellman error equal to zero
It makes \(\pi\) greedy with respect to \(Q^\star\)
It removes the need for concentration bounds
qz.why: Optimism only gives the first inequality; the value-difference identity then rewrites \(V_1-V_1^\pi\) along \(\pi\)'s own trajectories. Bellman errors are bounded by twice the bonus, which itself needs concentration Optimism principle (regret \(\le\) sum of confidence widths).

qz.q: A function \(V\) satisfies \((V-T^\pi V)(s)={\varepsilon}\) for every state \(s\). What is \(V(\rho)-V^\pi(\rho)\)?
qz.why: By the identity \(V(\rho)-V^\pi(\rho)=\tfrac{1}{1-\gamma}{\mathbb{E}}_{d^\pi_\rho}[V-T^\pi V]\), a constant residual \({\varepsilon}\) gives \({\varepsilon}/(1-\gamma)\) (check: \(V=V^\pi+\tfrac{{\varepsilon}}{1-\gamma}{\mathbf{1}}\) has residual \({\varepsilon}\)).

qz.q: In the sample-path version of the finite-horizon decomposition, terms \(\xi_h^k=(P_hV^k_{h+1})(s^k_h,a^k_h)-V^k_{h+1}(s^k_{h+1})\) appear, where \(V^k\) is computed from data of episodes \(1,\dots,k-1\). Which tool bounds \(\sum_{k,h}\xi^k_h\), and why?
a: Azuma–Hoeffding: they form a bounded martingale difference sequence
Hoeffding: they are i.i.d. across episodes
Pinsker's inequality: they are KL divergences
qz.why: Given the past and \((s_h,a_h)\), \(s_{h+1}\sim P_h\) so \(\xi\) has conditional mean zero, but \(V^k\) depends on earlier data, so the terms are not independent Azuma–Hoeffding inequality (martingales). They take both signs, so Markov does not apply.

cards.name: Policy improvement theorem & policy iteration
cards.lay: Acting greedily with respect to your current policy's \(Q\)-function never makes things worse, and strictly improves unless you are already optimal. Policy iteration therefore converges, in finitely many steps for finite MDPs, at least as fast as value iteration.
cards.st: If \(\pi'(s)\in{\operatorname*{arg\,max}}_aQ^\pi(s,a)\) for all \(s\), then \(V^{\pi'}\ge V^\pi\) pointwise, with equality iff \(\pi\) is optimal. Policy iteration \(\pi_{k+1}=\mathrm{greedy}(Q^{\pi_k})\) satisfies \[ {\lVert V^\star-V^{\pi_k}\rVert}_\infty\le\gamma^k{\lVert V^\star-V^{\pi_0}\rVert}_\infty \] and terminates in at most \(O\bigl(\tfrac{SA}{1-\gamma}\log\tfrac{1}{1-\gamma}\bigr)\) iterations (Ye 2011; Scherrer 2013).
ver: Approximate PI (Bertsekas & Tsitsiklis): with evaluation error \({\varepsilon}\) and greedy error \(\delta\), \(\limsup_k{\lVert V^\star-V^{\pi_k}\rVert}_\infty\le\tfrac{\delta+2\gamma{\varepsilon}}{(1-\gamma)^2}\).
Modified PI / optimistic PI interpolate between VI and PI.
Conservative policy iteration (mixtures \(\pi_{k+1}=(1-\alpha)\pi_k+\alpha\pi'\)) for robust approximate improvement Conservative policy iteration & TRPO improvement bound.
cards.det: Proof via PDL Performance difference lemma (Kakade–Langford) (advantages of the greedy policy are non-negative everywhere), or via monotonicity: \(T^{\pi'}V^\pi=T^\star V^\pi\ge T^\pi V^\pi=V^\pi\), iterate \(T^{\pi'}\) and use monotonicity to get \(V^{\pi'}\ge V^\pi\). The \(\gamma^k\) rate follows from \(V^{\pi_{k+1}}\ge T^\star V^{\pi_k}\).
cards.ex: In approximate PI with neural network critics, the \((1-\gamma)^{-2}\) amplification of evaluation error explains instability when \(\gamma\to1\).
cards.use: Convergence of PI and actor–critic schemes, approximate DP error bounds, strongly polynomial results.

qz.q: Policy iteration \(\pi_{k+1}=\mathrm{greedy}(Q^{\pi_k})\) satisfies \({\lVert V^\star-V^{\pi_k}\rVert}_\infty\le\gamma^k{\lVert V^\star-V^{\pi_0}\rVert}_\infty\). Which inequality is the key step for this geometric rate?
qz.why: From \(V^\star\ge V^{\pi_{k+1}}\ge T^\star V^{\pi_k}\): \(0\le V^\star-V^{\pi_{k+1}}\le T^\star V^\star-T^\star V^{\pi_k}\), which contracts by \(\gamma\). Monotone improvement alone gives no rate; the reverse inequality fails (PI is at least as good as VI), and \(V^{\pi_{k+1}}\) is the fixed point of \(T^{\pi_{k+1}}\), not of \(T^{\pi_k}\).

qz.q: Approximate policy iteration with policy-evaluation error \({\varepsilon}=0.01\) (sup-norm), exact greedy step (\(\delta=0\)) and \(\gamma=0.9\). What is the bound \(\limsup_k{\lVert V^\star-V^{\pi_k}\rVert}_\infty\le\frac{\delta+2\gamma{\varepsilon}}{(1-\gamma)^2}\)?
qz.why: \(2\cdot0.9\cdot0.01/0.01=1.8\). The value \(0.18\) uses one horizon factor, as in the one-shot greedy-loss lemma Greedy-policy loss bound (Singh–Yee; Williams–Baird); approximate PI pays \((1-\gamma)^{-2}\) because errors propagate across iterations.

qz.q: Running exact policy iteration on a finite MDP, at some iteration the greedy policy does not change: \(\pi_{k+1}=\pi_k\). What follows?
a: \(V^{\pi_k}\) is a fixed point of \(T^{\pi_k}\) but maybe not of \(T^\star\)
\(\pi_k\) is optimal only if \(\rho\) has full support
qz.why: If \(\pi_k\) is greedy w.r.t. \(Q^{\pi_k}\) then \(T^\star V^{\pi_k}=T^{\pi_k}V^{\pi_k}=V^{\pi_k}\), so \(V^{\pi_k}\) is the unique fixed point \(V^\star\) of \(T^\star\) Bellman equations & contraction of Bellman operators. Optimality holds state-wise, independent of \(\rho\).

cards.name: Value iteration convergence & stopping rules
cards.lay: Repeatedly applying the Bellman optimality operator converges geometrically to \(V^\star\), and you can tell from two consecutive iterates how close you are. The greedy policy of a near-optimal value is near-optimal.
cards.st: \(V_{k+1}=T^\star V_k\) satisfies \({\lVert V_k-V^\star\rVert}_\infty\le\gamma^k{\lVert V_0-V^\star\rVert}_\infty\) and \({\lVert V_k-V^\star\rVert}_\infty\le\frac{\gamma}{1-\gamma}{\lVert V_k-V_{k-1}\rVert}_\infty\). If \({\lVert V_k-V_{k-1}\rVert}_\infty<{\varepsilon}\frac{1-\gamma}{2\gamma}\), the greedy policy w.r.t. \(V_k\) is \({\varepsilon}\)-optimal.
ver: Iterations needed for \({\varepsilon}\)-accuracy from \(V_0=0\): \(k\ge\tfrac{1}{1-\gamma}\log\tfrac{1}{{\varepsilon}(1-\gamma)}\).

Approximate VI: \({\lVert V_{k+1}-T^\star V_k\rVert}\le{\varepsilon}\Rightarrow\limsup{\lVert V_k-V^\star\rVert}\le\tfrac{{\varepsilon}}{1-\gamma}\) Geometric series & discounted sums, and greedy loss \(\le\tfrac{2\gamma{\varepsilon}}{(1-\gamma)^2}\) Greedy-policy loss bound (Singh–Yee; Williams–Baird).
Weighted \(L^p\) error propagation (Munos 2005/2007) with concentrability Concentrability coefficients & error propagation.
cards.det: All three statements are corollaries of the contraction property Banach fixed-point theorem (contraction mapping) and the greedy-policy loss lemma Greedy-policy loss bound (Singh–Yee; Williams–Baird).
cards.ex: With \(\gamma=0.99\), to get \({\varepsilon}=0.01\) accuracy (rewards in \([0,1]\)) you need \(k\approx100\log(10^4)\approx920\) iterations.
cards.use: Planning, fitted value iteration analyses, stopping criteria, sample complexity with generative models.

qz.q: Value iteration with \(\gamma=0.9\) gives \({\lVert V_k-V_{k-1}\rVert}_\infty=0.01\). What bound on \({\lVert V_k-V^\star\rVert}_\infty\) does the stopping rule give?
qz.why: \({\lVert V_k-V^\star\rVert}_\infty\le\tfrac{\gamma}{1-\gamma}{\lVert V_k-V_{k-1}\rVert}_\infty=9\cdot0.01\). The successive difference understates the error: the remaining steps form a geometric series Geometric series & discounted sums; \(0.009=\gamma\cdot0.01\) is only the next step's size and \(0.001\) inverts the factor.

qz.q: Value iteration from \(V_0=0\), rewards in \([0,1]\). Which number of iterations \(k\) suffices for \({\lVert V_k-V^\star\rVert}_\infty\le{\varepsilon}\), for every MDP and every \(\gamma\in(0,1)\), \({\varepsilon}>0\)?
qz.why: Need \(\gamma^k/(1-\gamma)\le{\varepsilon}\); since \(\gamma^k\le e^{-(1-\gamma)k}\) this holds for the stated \(k\), and a reward-\(1\) self-loop (error exactly \(\gamma^k/(1-\gamma)\)) shows the others can fail. Dropping the \(\tfrac1{1-\gamma}\) prefactor ignores that \(\log(1/\gamma)\approx1-\gamma\) is small; dropping \(\log\tfrac1{1-\gamma}\) ignores that the initial error can be \(\tfrac1{1-\gamma}\).

qz.q: Approximate VI with \({\lVert V_{k+1}-T^\star V_k\rVert}_\infty\le{\varepsilon}\) at every step. Combining the accumulated value error with the greedy-loss lemma, what asymptotic bound results for the suboptimality \({\lVert V^\star-V^{\pi_k}\rVert}_\infty\) of the policy greedy w.r.t. \(V_k\)?
qz.why: Errors accumulate to \(\limsup{\lVert V_k-V^\star\rVert}\le\tfrac{{\varepsilon}}{1-\gamma}\), and the greedy-loss lemma Greedy-policy loss bound (Singh–Yee; Williams–Baird) multiplies by \(\tfrac{2\gamma}{1-\gamma}\). \(\tfrac{{\varepsilon}}{1-\gamma}\) bounds the value error, not the policy loss; there is no third horizon factor.

cards.name: Greedy-policy loss bound (Singh–Yee; Williams–Baird)
cards.lay: If your value estimate is within \({\varepsilon}\) of optimal everywhere, the policy that acts greedily on it loses at most \(2\gamma{\varepsilon}/(1-\gamma)\) in value. Also: a small Bellman residual implies a small value error.
cards.st: If \({\lVert Q-Q^\star\rVert}_\infty\le{\varepsilon}\) and \(\pi\) is greedy w.r.t. \(Q\), then \[ {\lVert V^\star-V^\pi\rVert}_\infty\le\frac{2{\varepsilon}}{1-\gamma}. \] If \({\lVert V-V^\star\rVert}_\infty\le{\varepsilon}\) and \(\pi\) is greedy w.r.t. \(V\) (one-step lookahead), then \({\lVert V^\star-V^\pi\rVert}_\infty\le\frac{2\gamma{\varepsilon}}{1-\gamma}\). Bellman residual: \({\lVert V-V^\pi\rVert}_\infty\le\frac{{\lVert V-T^\pi V\rVert}_\infty}{1-\gamma}\).
ver: Finite horizon: if \({\lVert Q_h-Q_h^\star\rVert}_\infty\le{\varepsilon}\) for all \(h\), greedy loss \(\le2H{\varepsilon}\).
cards.det: Proof: \(V^\star-V^\pi=T^\star V^\star-T^\pi V^\pi=(T^\star V^\star-T^\pi V)+(T^\pi V-T^\pi V^\pi)\), and \(T^\pi V=T^\star V\) since \(\pi\) is greedy; \({\lVert T^\star V^\star-T^\star V\rVert}\le\gamma{\varepsilon}\) so \({\lVert V^\star-V^\pi\rVert}\le\gamma{\varepsilon}+\gamma({\varepsilon}+{\lVert V^\star-V^\pi\rVert})\). Rearranging gives \(\tfrac{2\gamma{\varepsilon}}{1-\gamma}\).
cards.ex: Q-learning output with \({\lVert \widehat Q-Q^\star\rVert}_\infty\le0.01\) and \(\gamma=0.9\): the greedy policy is \(0.2\)-optimal.
cards.use: Converting \(Q\)-estimation guarantees into policy guarantees (Q-learning, FQI, model-based planning).

qz.q: Q-learning returns \(\widehat Q\) with \({\lVert \widehat Q-Q^\star\rVert}_\infty\le0.01\), \(\gamma=0.9\). What is the guaranteed bound on \({\lVert V^\star-V^\pi\rVert}_\infty\) for the greedy policy \(\pi\) of \(\widehat Q\)?
qz.why: The \(Q\)-version is \(\tfrac{2{\varepsilon}}{1-\gamma}=0.02/0.1\). The value \(0.18\) is the \(V\)-version \(\tfrac{2\gamma{\varepsilon}}{1-\gamma}\), which applies to one-step lookahead on a \(V\)-estimate, not to a \(Q\)-estimate. The bound is tight (a \(2{\varepsilon}\)-worse self-loop action can be chosen forever), so smaller values are not guaranteed.

qz.q: Why does the greedy-loss bound for \({\lVert V-V^\star\rVert}_\infty\le{\varepsilon}\) (greedy by one-step lookahead with the true \(r,P\)) carry an extra factor \(\gamma\) compared with the bound \(\tfrac{2{\varepsilon}}{1-\gamma}\) for \({\lVert Q-Q^\star\rVert}_\infty\le{\varepsilon}\)?
a: The lookahead uses exact \(r\) and \(P\), so \(V\)'s error enters only via \(\gamma PV\)
The \(V\)-bound is stated in a weaker norm than the \(Q\)-bound
\(V\) has fewer entries than \(Q\), so a union bound is smaller
For \(Q\), the greedy policy is evaluated with an extra \(\gamma\) removed
qz.why: With \(Q=r+\gamma PV\), an \({\varepsilon}\)-accurate \(V\) yields a \(\gamma{\varepsilon}\)-accurate \(Q\), and the \(Q\)-bound then gives \(\tfrac{2\gamma{\varepsilon}}{1-\gamma}\). Both bounds are in sup-norm and involve no union bound.

qz.q: A critic \(V\) for policy \(\pi\) has Bellman residual \({\lVert V-T^\pi V\rVert}_\infty=0.05\), and \(\gamma=0.95\). What bound on \({\lVert V-V^\pi\rVert}_\infty\) follows?
qz.why: \({\lVert V-V^\pi\rVert}\le{\lVert V-T^\pi V\rVert}+\gamma{\lVert V-V^\pi\rVert}\), so \({\lVert V-V^\pi\rVert}\le\tfrac{0.05}{0.05}=1\). A small residual does not mean a small value error: it is amplified by the horizon \(\tfrac1{1-\gamma}=20\). The bound is tight: \(V=V^\pi+{\mathbf{1}}\) has residual exactly \(0.05\).

cards.name: Policy gradient theorem
cards.lay: The gradient of a policy's value equals the expected \(Q\)-value times the gradient of the log-probability of the action, averaged over states the policy visits. Remarkably, you never need to differentiate the state distribution — so it can be estimated from rollouts without a model.
cards.st: (Sutton et al. 2000) For a differentiable policy \(\pi_\theta\): \[ \nabla_\theta V^{\pi_\theta}(\rho)=\frac{1}{1-\gamma}{\mathbb{E}}_{s\sim d^{\pi_\theta}_\rho}{\mathbb{E}}_{a\sim\pi_\theta(\cdot|s)}\bigl[Q^{\pi_\theta}(s,a)\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(a|s)\bigr]. \]
ver: Advantage form: \(Q^{\pi}\) may be replaced by \(A^\pi\) or \(Q^\pi-b(s)\) for any state baseline.

Trajectory (REINFORCE) form: \(\nabla V={\mathbb{E}}_\tau\bigl[\sum_t\gamma^t\nabla\log\pi_\theta(a_t|s_t)\sum_{t'\ge t}\gamma^{t'-t}r_{t'}\bigr]\) Log-derivative (score-function) trick & differentiating under the integral.

Deterministic policy gradient (Silver et al. 2014): \(
abla V=	frac{1}{1-\gamma}{\mathbb{E}}_{s\sim d^\mu} igl[
abla_	heta\mu_	heta(s)
abla_aQ^\mu(s,a)|_{a=\mu_	heta(s)} igr]\).

Softmax tabular: \(\tfrac{\partial V^{\pi_\theta}(\rho)}{\partial\theta_{s,a}}=\tfrac{1}{1-\gamma}d^{\pi_\theta}_\rho(s)\pi_\theta(a|s)A^{\pi_\theta}(s,a)\) Softmax policy gradient: smoothness & convergence.
Average-reward version with stationary distribution \(d^\pi\) and differential \(Q\).
cards.det: Proof. Differentiate the Bellman equation \(V^\pi(s)=\sum_a\pi(a|s)Q^\pi(s,a)\): \( abla V(s)=\sum_a abla\pi(a|s)Q(s,a)+\gamma\sum_a\pi(a|s)\sum_{s'}P(s'|s,a) abla V(s')\). Unroll the recursion (Neumann series Neumann series & the resolvent \((I-\gamma P)^{-1}\)): \( abla V( ho)=\sum_t\gamma^t{\mathbb{E}}_{s_t}\sum_a abla\pi(a|s_t)Q(s_t,a)\) and use \( abla\pi=\pi abla\log\pi\) Log-derivative (score-function) trick & differentiating under the integral.
cards.ex: Gaussian policy \(\pi_\theta(a|s)={\mathcal{N}}(\theta^\top\phi(s),\sigma^2)\): \(\nabla\log\pi=\tfrac{(a-\theta^\top\phi(s))\phi(s)}{\sigma^2}\), so the PG estimator is \(\tfrac{1}{\sigma^2}{\mathbb{E}}[(a-\theta^\top\phi)\phi\,\hat Q]\).
cards.use: REINFORCE, actor–critic, PPO/TRPO derivations, convergence analyses of PG methods, meta-gradients.

qz.q: In the policy gradient theorem, \(Q^{\pi_\theta}(s,a)\) is replaced by \(Q^{\pi_\theta}(s,a)-b\). For which baselines \(b\) is the gradient unchanged in general?
a: Any \(b=b(s)\) depending only on the state
qz.why: \({\mathbb{E}}_{a\sim\pi(\cdot|s)} abla\log\pi(a|s)=\sum_a abla\pi(a|s)= abla1=0\), so any state-dependent term drops out. An action-dependent \(b\) generally biases the gradient; \(V^\pi\) is just one (popular) choice.

qz.q: What property of the policy gradient theorem \(\nabla_\theta V^{\pi_\theta}(\rho)=\tfrac{1}{1-\gamma}{\mathbb{E}}_{s\sim d^{\pi_\theta}_\rho,a\sim\pi_\theta}[Q^{\pi_\theta}\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta]\) makes it estimable from rollouts without a model?
a: No \(\nabla_\theta d^{\pi_\theta}_\rho\) term appears, although \(d^{\pi_\theta}_\rho\) depends on \(\theta\)
\(d^{\pi_\theta}_\rho\) does not depend on \(\theta\), so its gradient is zero
\(Q^{\pi_\theta}\) does not depend on \(\theta\), so only \(\pi_\theta\) is differentiated
It needs \(\nabla_\theta d^{\pi_\theta}_\rho\), which rollouts estimate directly
qz.why: Unrolling the differentiated Bellman equation absorbs the effect on the state distribution into the occupancy weights Discounted occupancy measures; the state distribution does depend on \(\theta\), its derivative simply never appears.

qz.q: Tabular softmax policy, \(\gamma=0.9\). At a state with \(d^{\pi_\theta}_\rho(s)=0.5\), action \(a\) has \(\pi_\theta(a|s)=0.2\) and \(A^{\pi_\theta}(s,a)=1\). What is \(\partial V^{\pi_\theta}(\rho)/\partial\theta_{s,a}\)?
qz.why: \(\tfrac{1}{1-\gamma}d(s)\pi(a|s)A(s,a)=10\cdot0.5\cdot0.2\cdot1=1\). Forgetting the factor \(\pi(a|s)\) gives \(5\); this factor is why softmax PG is slow when the optimal action has small probability Softmax policy gradient: smoothness & convergence.

cards.name: Softmax policy gradient: smoothness & convergence
cards.lay: For tabular softmax policies, the value is a smooth function of the logits, gradient ascent never decreases value, and it converges to the optimum at rate \(O(1/t)\) — but with constants that can be exponentially bad in the worst case.
cards.st: (Mei, Xiao, Szepesvári, Schuurmans 2020) With \(\pi_\theta(a|s)\propto e^{\theta_{s,a}}\), \(V^{\pi_\theta}(\mu)\) is \(\tfrac{8}{(1-\gamma)^3}\)-smooth, and gradient ascent with \(\eta=\tfrac{(1-\gamma)^3}{8}\) satisfies \[ V^\star(\rho)-V^{\pi_{\theta_t}}(\rho)\le\frac{16S}{c^2(1-\gamma)^6t}\Bigl\|\frac{d^{\pi^\star}_\mu}{\mu}\Bigr\|_\infty^2\Bigl\|\frac1\mu\Bigr\|_\infty, \] where \(c=\inf_t\min_s\pi_{\theta_t}(a^\star(s)|s)>0\).
ver: Entropy-regularised softmax PG converges linearly (Mei et al. 2020; Cen et al. 2021 for NPG).
Lower bound: softmax PG can take \(\Omega(\exp(S))\) iterations on chain MDPs (Li et al. 2021), so the constant \(c\) can be exponentially small.
Escort / log-barrier regularised parameterisations change the constants (Agarwal et al. 2021).
cards.det: Ingredients: descent lemma \(L\)-smoothness & the descent lemma for monotone improvement, a non-uniform Łojasiewicz inequality Gradient domination for policy optimisation lower-bounding \({\lVert \nabla V\rVert}\) by suboptimality times \(\pi(a^\star|s)\), and a proof that \(\pi_\theta(a^\star|s)\) stays bounded away from 0.
cards.ex: Two-armed bandit with softmax PG: if the initial probability of the optimal arm is tiny, progress is very slow at first (gradient \(\propto\pi(a^\star)\)), illustrating the \(1/c^2\) dependence.
cards.use: Understanding vanilla PG, motivating natural gradients and entropy regularisation.

qz.q: In the softmax PG rate \(V^\star(\rho)-V^{\pi_{\theta_t}}(\rho)\le\frac{16S}{c^2(1-\gamma)^6t}{\lVert d^{\pi^\star}_\mu/\mu\rVert}_\infty^2{\lVert 1/\mu\rVert}_\infty\), what is \(c\) and how does it enter?
a: the smoothness constant of \(V^{\pi_\theta}\), entering as \(1/c^2\)
qz.why: The gradient w.r.t. \(\theta_{s,a^\star}\) is proportional to \(\pi(a^\star|s)\), so the Łojasiewicz inequality Gradient domination for policy optimisation degrades with the probability of the optimal action. \(c\) can be exponentially small, which explains the \(\Omega(\exp(S))\) lower bound.

qz.q: Tabular softmax PG uses smoothness \(\tfrac{8}{(1-\gamma)^3}\) and step size \(\eta=1/L\). For \(\gamma=0.5\), what is \(\eta\)?
qz.why: \(L=8/(0.5)^3=64\), so \(\eta=(1-\gamma)^3/8=1/64\). The step size shrinks cubically in the effective horizon, part of why vanilla PG is slow.

qz.q: Compare the softmax PG rate with the tabular NPG rate \(\frac{\log|{\mathcal{A}}|}{\eta T}+\frac{1}{(1-\gamma)^2T}\) Natural policy gradient & policy mirror descent convergence. Which quantity appears in the softmax PG bound but not in the NPG bound?
a: The rate \(1/T\) in the number of iterations
A power of the effective horizon \(1/(1-\gamma)\)
The term \(\log|{\mathcal{A}}|\) from the action set
qz.why: Both bounds are \(O(1/T)\) and both depend on \(1/(1-\gamma)\); \(\log|{\mathcal{A}}|\) appears in NPG only. NPG is free of \(S\), the mismatch coefficient and \(\min\pi(a^\star|s)\).

cards.name: Natural policy gradient & policy mirror descent convergence
cards.plain: Natural policy gradient & policy mirror descent convergence
cards.lay: Natural policy gradient preconditions by the Fisher information; for softmax policies it becomes a multiplicative-weights update on each state's action distribution. Treating each state as an online-learning problem and gluing with the PDL gives dimension-free \(O(1/T)\) convergence.
cards.st: (Agarwal et al. 2021) For tabular softmax NPG, equivalently \(\pi_{t+1}(a|s)\propto\pi_t(a|s)\exp\bigl(\tfrac{\eta}{1-\gamma}A^{\pi_t}(s,a)\bigr)\), starting from uniform \(\pi_0\): \[ V^\star(\rho)-V^{\pi_T}(\rho)\le\frac{\log|{\mathcal{A}}|}{\eta T}+\frac{1}{(1-\gamma)^2T}. \] With \(\eta\ge(1-\gamma)^2\log|{\mathcal{A}}|\) this is \(\le\frac{2}{(1-\gamma)^2T}\).
ver: Policy mirror descent with increasing step sizes converges linearly: \(V^\star-V^{\pi_k}\le\gamma^k\cdot O(\cdot)\) (Xiao 2022; Lan 2022).
Entropy-regularised NPG: linear convergence at rate \((1-\eta\tau)^t\) (Cen et al. 2021).

Inexact \(Q\) estimates: error \({\varepsilon}_{\mathrm{stat}}\) adds \(\tfrac{2{\varepsilon}_{\mathrm{stat}}}{1-\gamma}\)-type terms; with function approximation, compatible function approximation Compatible function approximation and transfer error appear.

abla\log\pi
abla\log\pi^	op]\).
cards.det: Proof: per state, NPG is Hedge/OMD Online mirror descent (OMD) lemma with “gains” \(A^{\pi_t}(s,\cdot)\); its regret against \(\pi^\star(\cdot|s)\) is \(\le\tfrac{\log|{\mathcal{A}}|}{\eta}+\ldots\). The PDL Performance difference lemma (Kakade–Langford) weighted by \(d^{\pi^\star}_\rho\) turns the sum of per-state regrets into \(\sum_t(V^\star-V^{\pi_t})\); monotone improvement of NPG makes the last iterate as good as the average.
cards.ex: Dimension-free: unlike vanilla softmax PG, the NPG bound has no \(S\), no mismatch coefficient and no \(\min\pi(a^\star|s)\).
cards.use: NPG/TRPO/PPO theory, policy optimisation in adversarial and non-stationary MDPs (OMD per state), actor–critic with linear critics.
cards.ll: Agarwal, Jiang, Kakade & Sun — RL Theory book

qz.q: Tabular softmax NPG with \(\eta=(1-\gamma)^2\log|{\mathcal{A}}|\) satisfies \(V^\star(\rho)-V^{\pi_T}(\rho)\le\frac{2}{(1-\gamma)^2T}\). For \(\gamma=0.9\) and \(T=1000\) iterations, what is the bound?
qz.why: \(2/(0.01\cdot1000)=0.2\). Using one horizon factor gives \(0.02\). The bound has no dependence on \(S\), \(|{\mathcal{A}}|\) (beyond the step size) or on \(\rho\).

qz.q: Tabular softmax NPG is equivalent to which per-state update of \(\pi_{t+1}(a|s)\), up to normalisation over \(a\)?
qz.why: The Fisher preconditioner cancels the \(d(s)\pi(a|s)\) factors of the vanilla softmax gradient Softmax policy gradient: smoothness & convergence, leaving a multiplicative-weights (Hedge) step with gains \(A^{\pi_t}\) in each state Compatible function approximation.

qz.q: The NPG proof bounds the sum \(\sum_{t<T}(V^\star(\rho)-V^{\pi_t}(\rho))\) via per-state Hedge regret and the PDL. What turns this into a bound for the last iterate \(\pi_T\)?
a: \(V^\pi(\rho)\) is concave in \(\pi\), so Jensen applies
The KL regulariser is strongly convex in \(\pi\)
\(\pi_T\) is defined as a uniform mixture of \(\pi_0,\dots,\pi_{T-1}\)
qz.why: With monotone values, \(V^\star-V^{\pi_T}\le\tfrac1T\sum_t(V^\star-V^{\pi_t})\). \(V^\pi\) is not concave in \(\pi\) in general, and the bound is for the actual last iterate, not a mixture.

cards.name: LP formulation of MDPs & its dual
cards.plain: LP formulation of MDPs & its dual
cards.lay: Finding an optimal value function is a linear program (smallest \(V\) satisfying all Bellman inequalities), and its dual is a linear program over occupancy measures (maximise expected reward subject to flow constraints). Duality ties values and occupancies together.
cards.st: Primal: \(\min_V\ (1-\gamma){\langle \rho, V\rangle}\) s.t. \(V(s)\ge r(s,a)+\gamma P(\cdot|s,a)^\top V\) for all \((s,a)\). Dual: \[ \max_{d\ge0}\ \sum_{s,a}d(s,a)r(s,a)\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\sum_ad(s,a)=(1-\gamma)\rho(s)+\gamma\sum_{s',a'}P(s|s',a')d(s',a')\ \ \forall s. \] Optimal primal \(=V^\star\) (where \(\rho>0\)), optimal dual \(=d^{\pi^\star}_\rho\), and both have value \((1-\gamma)V^\star(\rho)\).
ver: Lagrangian (saddle-point) form: \(\min_V\max_{d\ge0}\ (1-\gamma){\langle \rho, V\rangle}+\sum_{s,a}d(s,a)\bigl[r+\gamma PV-V\bigr](s,a)\) — basis of primal–dual RL algorithms and DICE methods.
Constrained MDPs: add \(\sum d\,g\ge b\) to the dual LP; zero duality gap Lagrangian duality & Slater's condition.
Average reward LP: maximise \({\langle d, r\rangle}\) over stationary occupancies.
cards.det: Complementary slackness Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) conditions: \(d^\star(s,a)>0\) only where \(V^\star(s)=r(s,a)+\gamma P(\cdot|s,a)^\top V^\star\), i.e. on optimal actions. The LP view gives strongly polynomial algorithms (Ye 2011) and is the foundation of saddle-point methods for sample-efficient planning.
cards.ex: Adversarial MDPs with known dynamics (O-REPS): run online mirror descent with negative-entropy regulariser directly over the occupancy polytope; regret \({\widetilde{O}}(H\sqrt{T\log(SA)})\).
cards.use: CMDPs, adversarial MDPs, DICE off-policy estimation, primal–dual sample complexity, inverse RL.

qz.q: In the MDP linear program, complementary slackness links the optimal dual (occupancy) \(d^\star\) to \(V^\star\). Which statement follows?
a: \(d^\star(s,a)>0\) only if \(a\) attains the max in the Bellman equation at \(s\)
\(d^\star(s,a)>0\) for every action that is optimal at \(s\)
qz.why: A positive dual variable forces its primal constraint \(V^\star(s)\ge r(s,a)+\gamma P(\cdot|s,a)^\top V^\star\) to be tight Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) conditions, i.e. \(a\) is optimal. The converse fails: \(d^\star\) may put zero mass on some optimal actions, and immediate reward alone does not decide optimality.

qz.q: The primal LP is \(\min_V(1-\gamma){\langle \rho, V\rangle}\) subject to \(V(s)\ge r(s,a)+\gamma P(\cdot|s,a)^\top V\) for all \((s,a)\). If \(\gamma=0.9\) and \(V^\star(\rho)=5\), what is the optimal value of the dual LP \(\max_d\sum_{s,a}d(s,a)r(s,a)\)?
qz.why: Strong duality: both optima equal \((1-\gamma)V^\star(\rho)=0.5\). The dual objective is the expected reward under the normalised occupancy, i.e. \((1-\gamma)\) times the value Discounted occupancy measures.

qz.q: Let \(V\) be any feasible point of the primal LP, i.e. \(V\ge T^\star V\) componentwise. What must hold?
qz.why: By monotonicity, \(V\ge T^\star V\ge(T^\star)^2V\ge\dots\to V^\star\) Bellman equations & contraction of Bellman operators. Feasible points can be arbitrarily large, so neither closeness nor equality is implied; the objective picks out the smallest one.

cards.name: Concentrability coefficients & error propagation
cards.lay: Errors made under one distribution (the data's) must be transferred to the distributions the evaluated or learned policies actually visit. Concentrability coefficients bound this density ratio; offline and approximate RL bounds scale with them.
cards.st: Single-policy concentrability: \(C^{\pi}=\Bigl\|\frac{d^{\pi}_\rho}{\mu}\Bigr\|_\infty\). (Munos 2007; Munos & Szepesvári 2008) For approximate VI with \({\lVert V_{k+1}-T^\star V_k\rVert}_{2,\mu}\le{\varepsilon}\): \[ \limsup_{k\to\infty}{\lVert V^\star-V^{\pi_k}\rVert}_{1,\rho}\le\frac{2\gamma}{(1-\gamma)^2}\sqrt{C_{\rho,\mu}}\;{\varepsilon}, \] where \(C_{\rho,\mu}\) is a (discounted, all-policy) concentrability coefficient.
ver: Pessimistic offline RL needs only single-policy concentrability \(C^{\pi^\star}\) (Rashidinejad et al. 2021; Xie et al. 2021).
Linear-feature analogue: relative condition number \(\sup_v\tfrac{v^\top\Sigma_{\pi}v}{v^\top\Sigma_\mu v}\) Rayleigh quotient & Courant–Fischer min–max.
Distribution mismatch in policy gradient: \({\lVert d^{\pi^\star}_\rho/\mu\rVert}_\infty\) Gradient domination for policy optimisation.

Change of measure for \(L^1\): \({\mathbb{E}}_{d^\pi}|f|\le C^\pi{\mathbb{E}}_\mu|f|\); for \(L^2\): \({\mathbb{E}}_{d^\pi}|f|\le\sqrt{C^\pi{\mathbb{E}}_\mu f^2}\) (Cauchy–Schwarz Cauchy–Schwarz inequality).
cards.det: Mechanism: the error \(V^\star-V^{\pi_K}\) is a sum over past iterations of products of transition matrices applied to per-iteration errors \({\varepsilon}_k\). Bounding \(\rho^\top(P^{\pi_1}\cdots P^{\pi_m})|{\varepsilon}_k|\) in terms of \({\lVert {\varepsilon}_k\rVert}_\mu\) requires the density ratio of the pushed-forward distribution w.r.t. \(\mu\) — that is the concentrability coefficient.
cards.ex: If the data distribution \(\mu\) is uniform over \(S\) states, \(C^\pi\le S\) for every \(\pi\); if \(\mu\) never visits a state \(\pi^\star\) reaches, \(C^{\pi^\star}=\infty\) and no offline guarantee is possible.
cards.use: Offline RL, FQI/FVI bounds, pessimism, policy gradient exploration conditions, off-policy evaluation.

qz.q: Offline data distribution \(\mu\) is uniform over \(S=100\) states. What is the largest value the single-policy concentrability \(C^\pi={\lVert d^\pi_\rho/\mu\rVert}_\infty\) can take, over all MDPs on these states, initial distributions \(\rho\) and policies \(\pi\)?
qz.why: \(d^\pi_\rho(s)\le1\) and \(\mu(s)=1/S\), so \(C^\pi\le S\), attained when \(d^\pi_\rho\) concentrates on one state (e.g. \(\rho\) a point mass on an absorbing state). Uniform data does not give \(C^\pi=1\): that requires \(d^\pi_\rho=\mu\).

qz.q: An offline method guarantees \({\mathbb{E}}_\mu f^2\le{\varepsilon}^2\) for an error function \(f\). Using \(C^\pi={\lVert d^\pi_\rho/\mu\rVert}_\infty\), what bound on \({\mathbb{E}}_{d^\pi_\rho}|f|\) follows?
qz.why: Cauchy–Schwarz Cauchy–Schwarz inequality: \({\mathbb{E}}_{d^\pi}|f|\le\sqrt{{\mathbb{E}}_{d^\pi}f^2}\le\sqrt{C^\pi{\mathbb{E}}_\mu f^2}\). It is tight (\(f={\varepsilon}\sqrt{C^\pi}\) on a set of \(\mu\)-mass \(1/C^\pi\) carrying all of \(d^\pi_\rho\)), so \({\varepsilon}\) alone is not guaranteed. \(C^\pi{\varepsilon}\) also holds but is weaker: it is the \(L^1\) change of measure.

qz.q: To learn a policy competitive with \(\pi^\star\) from offline data \(\mu\), which coverage condition suffices for pessimistic offline RL (per the card), in contrast to classical fitted-VI analyses?
a: \(\mu\) must be uniform over all state–action pairs
No coverage condition: pessimism replaces it
qz.why: Pessimism needs only single-policy concentrability \(C^{\pi^\star}\); fitted VI analyses use all-policy coefficients. Without any coverage of states that \(\pi^\star\) reaches, no offline guarantee is possible.

cards.name: Projected Bellman equation & TD fixed point (Tsitsiklis–Van Roy)
cards.plain: Projected Bellman equation & TD fixed point (Tsitsiklis–Van Roy)
cards.lay: With linear function approximation, TD learning does not find the best approximation of \(V^\pi\); it finds the fixed point of the projected Bellman operator. On-policy, that operator is a contraction and the fixed point is within a \(1/\sqrt{1-\gamma^2}\) factor of the best approximation.
cards.st: Let \(\mu\) be the stationary distribution of \(P^\pi\), \(D={\operatorname{diag}}(\mu)\), \(\Pi\) the \({\lVert \cdot\rVert}_D\)-projection onto \(\{\Phi\theta\}\). Then \(\Pi T^\pi\) is a \(\gamma\)-contraction in \({\lVert \cdot\rVert}_D\), TD(0) converges to its fixed point \(\Phi\theta_{\mathrm{TD}}\), and \[ {\lVert \Phi\theta_{\mathrm{TD}}-V^\pi\rVert}_D\le\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-\gamma^2}}\min_\theta{\lVert \Phi\theta-V^\pi\rVert}_D. \]
ver: Key lemma: \({\lVert P^\pi V\rVert}_D\le{\lVert V\rVert}_D\) when \(D\) is stationary (Jensen Jensen's inequality).
TD(\(\lambda\)): factor \(\tfrac{1-\lambda\gamma}{1-\gamma}\) (Tsitsiklis & Van Roy 1997); as \(\lambda\to1\) it recovers the best approximation.
Off-policy: \(\Pi_DT^\pi\) need not be a contraction — Baird's counterexample; motivates GTD/TDC and emphatic TD.

Finite-time: \({\mathbb{E}}{\lVert \theta_T-\theta_{\mathrm{TD}}\rVert}^2={\widetilde{O}}\bigl(\tfrac{t_{\mathrm{mix}}}{(1-\gamma)^2\omega^2T}\bigr)\) with \(\omega=\lambda_{\min}(\Phi^\top D\Phi)\) (Bhandari, Russo, Singal 2018).
cards.det: Contraction: \({\lVert \Pi T^\pi V-\Pi T^\pi U\rVert}_D\le{\lVert T^\pi V-T^\pi U\rVert}_D=\gamma{\lVert P^\pi(V-U)\rVert}_D\le\gamma{\lVert V-U\rVert}_D\), using non-expansiveness of the projection Projection theorem & non-expansiveness of projections and stationarity. The approximation bound follows from Pythagoras: \({\lVert V^\pi-\Phi\theta_{\mathrm{TD}}\rVert}^2={\lVert V^\pi-\Pi V^\pi\rVert}^2+{\lVert \Pi V^\pi-\Pi T^\pi\Phi\theta_{\mathrm{TD}}\rVert}^2\le{\lVert V^\pi-\Pi V^\pi\rVert}^2+\gamma^2{\lVert V^\pi-\Phi\theta_{\mathrm{TD}}\rVert}^2\).
cards.ex: With \(\gamma=0.99\) the factor \(1/\sqrt{1-\gamma^2}\approx7.1\): TD's fixed point can be up to \(7\times\) worse than the best linear fit in \({\lVert \cdot\rVert}_D\).
cards.use: Linear TD/LSTD analysis, actor–critic critics, understanding the deadly triad, finite-sample TD bounds.

qz.q: On-policy linear TD(0) with \(\gamma=0.99\) satisfies \({\lVert \Phi\theta_{\mathrm{TD}}-V^\pi\rVert}_D\le\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-\gamma^2}}\min_\theta{\lVert \Phi\theta-V^\pi\rVert}_D\). What is the amplification factor (approximately)?
qz.why: \(1-0.99^2=0.0199\) and \(1/\sqrt{0.0199}\approx7.09\). The factor \(50\approx1/(1-\gamma^2)\) forgets the square root from the Pythagorean argument.

qz.q: Which hypothesis is used to show that the projected Bellman operator \(\Pi T^\pi\) is a \(\gamma\)-contraction in \({\lVert \cdot\rVert}_D\), \(D={\operatorname{diag}}(\mu)\)?
a: The feature matrix \(\Phi\) has orthonormal columns
\(V^\pi\) lies in the span of the features
qz.why: Stationarity gives \({\lVert P^\pi V\rVert}_D\le{\lVert V\rVert}_D\) via Jensen Jensen's inequality; projection is non-expansive in the same norm. Off-policy weighting breaks this (Baird's counterexample).

qz.q: With linear features and on-policy sampling, what does TD(0) converge to?
a: The fixed point of \(\Pi T^\pi\), in general not \(\Pi V^\pi\)
The minimiser of the mean squared Bellman error
\(V^\pi\) whenever the features are linearly independent
qz.why: TD solves the projected Bellman equation \(\Phi\theta=\Pi T^\pi\Phi\theta\); its solution can be worse than \(\Pi V^\pi\) by up to the factor \(1/\sqrt{1-\gamma^2}\). Only TD(\(\lambda\to1\)) recovers \(\Pi V^\pi\).

cards.name: Conservative policy iteration & TRPO improvement bound
cards.plain: Conservative policy iteration & TRPO improvement bound
cards.lay: If the new policy is close to the old one (in TV or KL), you can predict its performance using the old policy's state distribution, with an error quadratic in the distance. Optimising this surrogate guarantees monotone improvement.
cards.st: (Kakade & Langford 2002; Schulman et al. 2015) Let \(L_\pi(\pi')=V^\pi(\rho)+\tfrac{1}{1-\gamma}{\mathbb{E}}_{s\sim d^\pi_\rho}{\mathbb{E}}_{a\sim\pi'}A^\pi(s,a)\), \(\epsilon=\max_{s,a}|A^\pi(s,a)|\), \(\alpha=\max_s{\mathrm{TV}}(\pi(\cdot|s),\pi'(\cdot|s))\). Then \[ V^{\pi'}(\rho)\ge L_\pi(\pi')-\frac{4\gamma\epsilon\,\alpha^2}{(1-\gamma)^2}. \]
ver: KL version (via Pinsker Pinsker's inequality): \(\alpha^2\le\tfrac12\max_s{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi(\cdot|s)\|\pi'(\cdot|s))\).

CPI with mixture \(\pi'=(1-\alpha)\pi+\alpha\pi_{\mathrm{greedy}}\): improvement \(\ge\tfrac{\alpha}{1-\gamma}\mathbb A-\tfrac{2\alpha^2\gamma\epsilon}{(1-\gamma)^2}\) where \(\mathbb A\) is the average advantage.
cards.det: Proof: PDL Performance difference lemma (Kakade–Langford) gives the exact gap with \(d^{\pi'}\); the surrogate uses \(d^\pi\). The two state distributions differ in TV by at most \(\tfrac{\gamma\alpha}{1-\gamma}\)-ish (coupling the policies Coupling inequality), and the expected advantage of \(\pi'\) under \(\pi\) is itself \(O(\alpha\epsilon)\) since \({\mathbb{E}}_{a\sim\pi}A^\pi=0\); multiplying gives the \(\alpha^2\) term.
cards.ex: Monotone improvement: maximise \(L_\pi(\pi')-C\max_s{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi\|\pi')\) with \(C=\tfrac{2\gamma\epsilon}{(1-\gamma)^2}\); the result is never worse than \(\pi\) (TRPO's theoretical motivation).
cards.use: Trust-region methods, PPO clipping motivation, safe policy improvement, CPI analysis.

qz.q: TRPO/CPI bound: \(V^{\pi'}(\rho)\ge L_\pi(\pi')-\frac{4\gamma\epsilon\alpha^2}{(1-\gamma)^2}\) with \(\alpha=\max_s{\mathrm{TV}}(\pi(\cdot|s),\pi'(\cdot|s))\) and \(L_\pi\) the surrogate using \(d^\pi_\rho\). As \(\alpha\to0\) with everything else fixed, the guaranteed surrogate error is of which order?
qz.why: The surrogate is accurate to first order in the policy change, so maximising it gives a genuine improvement for small steps. A linear error would swamp the \(O(\alpha)\) gain \(\tfrac{1}{1-\gamma}{\mathbb{E}} A^\pi\).

qz.q: Using Pinsker (\({\mathrm{TV}}^2\le\tfrac12{\mathrm{KL}}\)) on the bound \(V^{\pi'}(\rho)\ge L_\pi(\pi')-\frac{4\gamma\epsilon\alpha^2}{(1-\gamma)^2}\), one gets \(V^{\pi'}(\rho)\ge L_\pi(\pi')-C\max_s{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi(\cdot|s)\|\pi'(\cdot|s))\). What constant \(C\) does this substitution give?
qz.why: \(\alpha^2\le\tfrac12\max_s{\mathrm{KL}}\) Pinsker's inequality turns \(4\alpha^2\) into \(2\max{\mathrm{KL}}\); the TRPO paper's \(4\) comes from the looser \({\mathrm{TV}}^2\le{\mathrm{KL}}\). The horizon factor stays squared: one from the PDL, one from the shift in state distributions.

qz.q: The TRPO error is quadratic in \(\alpha\): one factor comes from the change in state distribution (\({\mathrm{TV}}(d^{\pi'},d^\pi)\lesssim\tfrac{\gamma\alpha}{1-\gamma}\)). Which fact supplies the other factor of \(\alpha\)?
a: \(A^\pi(s,a)\ge0\) for all actions, so it is \(O(\alpha)\)
Applying the PDL a second time with roles swapped
qz.why: \({\mathbb{E}}_{a\sim\pi'}A^\pi=\sum_a(\pi'-\pi)(a|s)A^\pi(s,a)\), bounded by \({\lVert \pi'-\pi\rVert}_1\epsilon=2\alpha\epsilon\). Pinsker only converts TV to KL afterwards, and advantages have mean zero under \(\pi\), so they are not all non-negative.

cards.name: Compatible function approximation
cards.lay: If the critic's features are exactly the policy's score function \(\nabla\log\pi_\theta\), then plugging the best linear critic into the policy gradient gives the exact gradient. Also shows the NPG direction is the least-squares fit of advantages on score features.
cards.st: (Sutton et al. 2000; Kakade 2001) Let \(w^\star={\operatorname*{arg\,min}}_w{\mathbb{E}}_{s\sim d^\pi,a\sim\pi} igl(w^ op abla_ heta\log\pi_ heta(a|s)-A^\pi(s,a) igr)^2\). Then \[ abla_ heta V^{\pi_ heta}= rac{1}{1-\gamma}F( heta)w^\star,\qquad ext{so}\qquad F( heta)^\dagger abla_ heta V^{\pi_ heta}= rac{w^\star}{1-\gamma}, \] where \(F( heta)={\mathbb{E}}_{d^\pi,\pi}[ abla\log\pi abla\log\pi^ op]\). The natural gradient is the advantage regression coefficient.
ver: Log-linear policies \(\pi\propto e^{\theta^\top\phi(s,a)}\): score features are centred features \(\phi-{\mathbb{E}}_\pi\phi\); NPG \(=\) regressing \(Q\) onto \(\phi\) (Q-NPG).

With approximation error \({\varepsilon}_{\mathrm{approx}}\), NPG converges up to \(\tfrac{\sqrt{|{\mathcal{A}}|\kappa\,{\varepsilon}_{\mathrm{approx}}}}{(1-\gamma)^{3/2}}\)-type terms (Agarwal et al. 2021).
cards.det: Proof: the first-order optimality condition of the regression is \({\mathbb{E}}[ abla\log\pi( abla\log\pi^ op w^\star-A^\pi)]=0\), i.e. \(Fw^\star={\mathbb{E}}[ abla\log\pi\,A^\pi]=(1-\gamma) abla V\) by the PG theorem Policy gradient theorem.
cards.ex: Tabular softmax: score features are \(e_{s,a}-\pi(\cdot|s)\); the regression recovers \(w^\star_{s,a}=A^\pi(s,a)\), so NPG is \(\theta\leftarrow\theta+\tfrac{\eta}{1-\gamma}A^\pi\) — the multiplicative weights update of Natural policy gradient & policy mirror descent convergence.
cards.use: Natural actor–critic, NPG with function approximation, understanding critic bias in actor–critic.
cards.ll: Agarwal, Jiang, Kakade & Sun — RL Theory book

qz.q: Let \(w^\star\) minimise \({\mathbb{E}}_{d^\pi,\pi}(w^ op abla_ heta\log\pi_ heta-A^\pi)^2\) and \(F={\mathbb{E}}_{d^\pi,\pi}[ abla\log\pi abla\log\pi^ op]\). Which expression is the natural gradient \(F^\dagger abla_ heta V^{\pi_ heta}\) (per the card)?
qz.why: The normal equations give \(Fw^\star={\mathbb{E}}[ abla\log\pi\,A^\pi]=(1-\gamma) abla V\) by the PG theorem Policy gradient theorem, so \( abla V=Fw^\star/(1-\gamma)\) and preconditioning by \(F^\dagger\) leaves \(w^\star/(1-\gamma)\). \(Fw^\star/(1-\gamma)\) is the vanilla gradient.

qz.q: Plugging the best linear critic \(\hat A(s,a)=w^\top\phi(s,a)\) into the policy gradient gives the exact gradient under which condition?
a: The critic is trained by TD(0) on on-policy data
The critic features include the state value \(V^\pi(s)\)
qz.why: With score features the least-squares residual is orthogonal to \(\nabla\log\pi\), which is exactly the direction the PG theorem integrates against, so the approximation error has no effect on the gradient.

qz.q: In the compatible regression, why can the target \(A^\pi\) be replaced by \(Q^\pi\) without changing the right-hand side \({\mathbb{E}}_{d^\pi,\pi}[\nabla\log\pi\cdot\text{target}]\) of the normal equations?
a: \(V^\pi(s)=0\) in every state at a stationary point
The Fisher matrix \(F\) is invertible, which cancels \(V^\pi\)
qz.why: \(Q^\pi=A^\pi+V^\pi(s)\) and the state-only term is killed by the zero-mean score, the same fact that makes state baselines unbiased Policy gradient theorem. \(Q^\pi\) and \(A^\pi\) differ unless \(V^\pi=0\).

cards.name: Regret decomposition (bandits)
cards.lay: Total regret equals, for each suboptimal arm, how much worse it is times how often you pull it. So bounding regret reduces to bounding the number of pulls of each bad arm.
cards.st: For a stochastic \(K\)-armed bandit with gaps \(\Delta_a=\mu^\star-\mu_a\) and pull counts \(N_a(T)\): \[ {\mathrm{Reg}}_T=T\mu^\star-{\mathbb{E}}\sum_{t=1}^TX_t=\sum_{a}\Delta_a\,{\mathbb{E}}[N_a(T)]. \]
ver: Gap-dependent to gap-independent: split arms at threshold \(\Delta\): \({\mathrm{Reg}}_T\le T\Delta+\sum_{a:\Delta_a>\Delta}\Delta_a{\mathbb{E}} N_a(T)\); with \({\mathbb{E}} N_a\lesssim\tfrac{\log T}{\Delta_a^2}\) this gives \(O(\sqrt{KT\log T})\).

MDP analogue: \({\mathrm{Reg}}_K=\sum_{k}\bigl(V^\star_1(s_1^k)-V^{\pi_k}_1(s_1^k)\bigr)=\sum_k{\mathbb{E}}_{\pi_k}\sum_h\mathrm{gap}_h(s_h,a_h)\) via the PDL Performance difference lemma (Kakade–Langford) — gap-dependent RL bounds.
Pseudo-regret vs. realised regret: they differ by a martingale Azuma–Hoeffding inequality (martingales).
cards.det: Proof: \({\mathbb{E}}\sum_tX_t=\sum_a\mu_a{\mathbb{E}} N_a(T)\) by the tower property Tower property & law of total expectation (Wald-like Wald's identity), and \(\sum_a{\mathbb{E}} N_a(T)=T\).
cards.ex: UCB1 has \({\mathbb{E}} N_a(T)\le\tfrac{8\log T}{\Delta_a^2}+1+\tfrac{\pi^2}{3}\), so \({\mathrm{Reg}}_T\le\sum_{a:\Delta_a>0}\bigl(\tfrac{8\log T}{\Delta_a}+(1+\tfrac{\pi^2}{3})\Delta_a\bigr)\).
cards.use: All stochastic bandit regret analyses, gap-dependent RL regret.

qz.q: A stochastic 3-armed bandit has means \(\mu=(0.9,\,0.8,\,0.5)\). After \(T\) rounds an algorithm has \({\mathbb{E}} N_2(T)=100\) and \({\mathbb{E}} N_3(T)=20\). What is the pseudo-regret \({\mathrm{Reg}}_T=T\mu^\star-{\mathbb{E}}\sum_tX_t\)?
qz.why: \({\mathrm{Reg}}_T=\sum_a\Delta_a{\mathbb{E}} N_a(T)=0.1\cdot100+0.4\cdot20=18\). Swapping which count goes with which gap gives \(42\); summing raw counts ignores the gaps.

qz.q: A \(K\)-armed algorithm satisfies \({\mathbb{E}} N_a(T)\le C\log T/\Delta_a^2\) for every suboptimal arm. Splitting arms at a threshold \(\Delta\) gives \({\mathrm{Reg}}_T\le T\Delta+KC\log T/\Delta\). Balancing the two terms gives which choice and worst-case rate?
qz.why: Setting \(T\Delta=KC\log T/\Delta\) gives \(\Delta^2\asymp K\log T/T\) and both terms equal \(\sqrt{KCT\log T}\). Dropping \(K\) from the threshold still leaves the second term of order \(K\sqrt{T\log T}\), so a \(K\)-free rate is wrong.

qz.q: The identity \({\mathrm{Reg}}_T=\sum_a\Delta_a{\mathbb{E}}[N_a(T)]\) is proved by \({\mathbb{E}}\sum_tX_t=\sum_a\mu_a{\mathbb{E}} N_a(T)\). In which situation does this identity (with fixed gaps \(\Delta_a\)) stop being available?
a: Arm means drift over time, \(\mu_{a,t}\) depends on \(t\)
The policy randomises its choice of \(A_t\)
\(N_a(T)\) depends on the rewards observed so far
Rewards are unbounded but have finite means
qz.why: The tower property only needs \({\mathbb{E}}[X_t\mid A_t,\text{past}]=\mu_{A_t}\) with a fixed \(\mu_a\) per arm; adaptivity and randomisation of the policy are exactly what it handles. With time-varying means there is no fixed gap per arm.

cards.name: Optimism principle (regret \(\le\) sum of confidence widths)
cards.plain: Optimism principle (regret ≤ sum of confidence widths)
cards.lay: If your index is an upper bound on the true value of every action (optimism), then the regret of picking the largest index is at most the width of the confidence interval of the action you picked. Exploration happens automatically: uncertain actions look good until tried.
cards.st: Suppose on a good event, for all \(t\) and \(a\): \(\mu_a\le U_t(a)\) and \(U_t(a)-\mu_a\le2w_t(a)\). If \(A_t={\operatorname*{arg\,max}}_aU_t(a)\), then \[ \mu^\star-\mu_{A_t}\le U_t(A_t)-\mu_{A_t}\le2w_t(A_t),\qquad{\mathrm{Reg}}_T\le2\sum_{t=1}^Tw_t(A_t)+T\Pr(\text{bad event}). \]
ver: Linear bandits: \(w_t(x)=\beta_t{\lVert x\rVert}_{V_{t-1}^{-1}}\), summed with the elliptical potential lemma Elliptical potential lemma \(\Rightarrow{\widetilde{O}}(d\sqrt T)\).

Tabular RL: optimistic \(Q\)-values plus value-difference decomposition Value-difference (Bellman-error telescoping) decomposition \(\Rightarrow\) regret \(\le\sum_{k,h}\)(bonus) \(+\) martingale terms; bonuses summed with the pigeonhole lemma Pigeonhole / count-summation lemma (tabular RL).
Posterior sampling: optimism holds in expectation (Bayesian regret) rather than deterministically.
Pessimism (offline RL) is the mirror image: lower confidence bounds; suboptimality \(\le2{\mathbb{E}}_{\pi^\star}\sum(\text{widths})\).
cards.det: The proof is one line, and all the work is in (i) constructing valid confidence sets (concentration + union bounds) and (ii) showing widths at played actions sum to \(o(T)\) (potential or pigeonhole arguments).
cards.ex: \(K\)-armed UCB with Hoeffding widths \(w_t(a)=\sqrt{\tfrac{2\log(1/\delta)}{N_a}}\): \(\sum_tw_t(A_t)=\sum_a\sum_{n=1}^{N_a(T)}\sqrt{\tfrac{2\log(1/\delta)}{n}}\le\sum_a2\sqrt{2N_a\log(1/\delta)}\le2\sqrt{2KT\log(1/\delta)}\).
cards.use: UCB, OFUL, UCRL2, UCBVI, LSVI-UCB, GOLF; offline pessimism (mirror argument).

qz.q: On the good event, \(\mu_a\le U_t(a)\) and \(U_t(a)-\mu_a\le2w_t(a)\) for all \(t,a\), and \(A_t={\operatorname*{arg\,max}}_aU_t(a)\). In the chain \(\mu^\star-\mu_{A_t}\le U_t(A_t)-\mu_{A_t}\le2w_t(A_t)\), where is optimism \(\mu_a\le U_t(a)\) used?
a: To guarantee every arm is pulled at least once
qz.why: Optimism is applied to the optimal arm only, and the argmax step transfers it to \(A_t\). The width bound is a separate assumption, and the bad-event probability comes from concentration plus a union bound.

qz.q: For \(K\)-armed UCB the widths sum to \(\sum_tw_t(A_t)\le\sum_{a=1}^K2\sqrt{2N_a\log(1/\delta)}\) with \(\sum_aN_a=T\). What is the maximum of the right-hand side over all allocations \((N_a)\)?
qz.why: By Cauchy–Schwarz \(\sum_a\sqrt{N_a}\le\sqrt{K\sum_aN_a}=\sqrt{KT}\), with equality at \(N_a=T/K\). \(2\sqrt{2T\log(1/\delta)}\) is the value when one arm takes all pulls, which is the minimum, not the maximum.

qz.q: In offline RL with pessimism (act greedily w.r.t. lower confidence bounds), the suboptimality is bounded by \(2{\mathbb{E}}_{\pi^\star}\sum(\text{widths})\). What coverage condition on the data does this require?
a: Good coverage of the states/actions that \(\pi^\star\) visits
Good coverage of every policy's reachable states/actions
Good coverage of the learned policy's states/actions only
No coverage, since pessimism removes the need for it
qz.why: The widths are evaluated along \(\pi^\star\), so only \(\pi^\star\)'s occupancy must be well covered (single-policy concentrability). Uniform coverage of all policies is what greedy, non-pessimistic methods need.

cards.name: Pigeonhole / count-summation lemma (tabular RL)
cards.lay: Summing \(1/\sqrt{\text{visit count}}\) over all visits is at most about \(\sqrt{(\#\text{cells})\times(\#\text{visits})}\). This converts per-step bonuses into \(\sqrt{SAT}\)-type regret.
cards.st: Let \((x_t)_{t\le T}\) take values in a finite set of size \(N\) and \(n_t(x)=\sum_{s<t}{\mathbf{1}}\{x_s=x\}\). Then \[ \sum_{t=1}^T\frac{1}{\sqrt{\max(1,n_t(x_t))}}\le N+2\sqrt{NT},\qquad\sum_{t=1}^T\frac{1}{\max(1,n_t(x_t))}\le N(2+\log T). \]
ver: Tabular RL: with \(x_t=(s_h^k,a_h^k,h)\), \(N=SAH\), \(T=KH\): \(\sum_{k,h}\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\le SAH+2\sqrt{SAH\cdot KH}\).
Weighted counts / doubling epochs (UCRL2): \(\sum_k\tfrac{\nu_k(s,a)}{\sqrt{\max(1,N_k(s,a))}}\le(\sqrt2+1)\sqrt{N(s,a)}\).
Generalisations: elliptical potential (linear) Elliptical potential lemma, eluder dimension (general classes) Eluder dimension.
cards.det: Proof: group the sum by value of \(x\): \(\sum_x\sum_{n=0}^{N_T(x)-1}\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{\max(1,n)}}\le\sum_x\bigl(1+2\sqrt{N_T(x)}\bigr)\) by Sums of \(1/\sqrt{t}\), harmonic sums & integral comparison, then Cauchy–Schwarz Cauchy–Schwarz inequality: \(\sum_x\sqrt{N_T(x)}\le\sqrt{N\sum_xN_T(x)}=\sqrt{NT}\).
cards.ex: Q-learning with UCB-Hoeffding bonuses \(b_n=c\sqrt{H^3\iota/n}\): with \(N=SAH\) cells and \(KH\) visits, \(\sum_{k,h}b_{n_h^k}\le c\sqrt{H^3\iota}\bigl(SAH+2\sqrt{SAH\cdot KH}\bigr)={\widetilde{O}}(\sqrt{H^4SAT})\) for \(T=KH\).
cards.use: Summing exploration bonuses in all tabular RL regret/PAC analyses.
cards.ll: Agarwal, Jiang, Kakade & Sun — RL Theory book

qz.q: Episodic tabular RL with \(S\) states, \(A\) actions, horizon \(H\), \(K\) episodes, \(T=KH\). Step \((k,h)\) gets bonus \(c\sqrt{H^2\iota/n}\) with \(n\) the visit count of \((s_h^k,a_h^k,h)\). For large \(K\), the bound the pigeonhole lemma gives on the sum of all bonuses is of order
qz.why: With \(N=SAH\) cells and \(KH=T\) visits, \(\sum1/\sqrt n\lesssim\sqrt{SAH\cdot T}\); multiplying by \(\sqrt{H^2}\) gives \(\sqrt{H^3SAT}\). Forgetting that \(h\) is part of the cell gives the \(\sqrt{H^2SAT}\) trap; dropping the bonus scale \(\sqrt{H^2}\) gives \(\sqrt{HSAT}\); the number of visits is \(T=KH\), not \(K\).

qz.q: For fixed \(N\ge3\) cells and \(T\gg N\) visits, which visit pattern makes \(\sum_{t=1}^T1/\sqrt{\max(1,n_t(x_t))}\) (approximately) largest?
a: Every cell is visited about \(T/N\) times
All \(T\) visits fall in a single cell
Visits alternate between just two cells
Half the visits go to one cell, the rest are spread out
qz.why: Grouping by cell, the sum is \(\sum_x\sum_{n<N_T(x)}1/\sqrt{\max(1,n)}\approx\sum_x2\sqrt{N_T(x)}\), which depends only on the final counts (not on the order) and is maximised by equal counts, the Cauchy–Schwarz equality case.

qz.q: In a tabular analysis (cells \((s,a,h)\), \(N=SAH\), \(T=KH\)), a lower-order term \(cH^2S\iota/n\) is paid at every step, with \(n\) the visit count. The bound that the \(1/n\) part of the pigeonhole lemma gives on the total is of order
qz.why: \(\sum1/\max(1,n)\le N(2+\log T)={\widetilde{O}}(SAH)\), so the term totals \({\widetilde{O}}(H^2S\cdot SAH)\). The \(\sqrt{NT}\) bound is for \(1/\sqrt n\) summands, not \(1/n\); \({\widetilde{O}}(SAH)\) forgets the per-step factor \(H^2S\), and \({\widetilde{O}}(H^2S)\) forgets the number of cells.

cards.name: Elliptical potential lemma
cards.lay: In linear bandits, the uncertainty of the chosen action (measured in the inverse design matrix) can only be large a limited number of times: the sum of squared uncertainties is at most \(O(d\log T)\). Each time you learn something, the “volume” of remaining uncertainty shrinks.
cards.st: Let \(V_0=\lambda I\), \(V_t=V_{t-1}+x_tx_t^\top\) with \({\lVert x_t\rVert}_2\le L\). Then \[ \sum_{t=1}^T\min\bigl(1,{\lVert x_t\rVert}^2_{V_{t-1}^{-1}}\bigr)\le2\log\frac{\det V_T}{\det V_0}\le2d\log\Bigl(1+\frac{TL^2}{d\lambda}\Bigr). \] Consequently \(\sum_{t=1}^T\min(1,{\lVert x_t\rVert}_{V_{t-1}^{-1}})\le\sqrt{2dT\log(1+TL^2/(d\lambda))}\).
ver: If \(\lambda\ge\max(1,L^2)\) the \(\min(1,\cdot)\) can be dropped.
Batched / rarely-switching versions: number of times \(\det V_t\) doubles is \(O(d\log T)\) Loewner order facts.
Kernelised: replace \(d\log T\) by information gain \(\gamma_T\) Entropy, mutual information & their chain rules; general classes: eluder dimension Eluder dimension.
Weighted (for non-stationary / heteroscedastic noise): \(V_t=\lambda I+\sum w_sx_sx_s^\top\), same bound with weighted features.
cards.det: Proof: \(\det V_t=\det V_{t-1}(1+{\lVert x_t\rVert}^2_{V_{t-1}^{-1}})\) (matrix determinant lemma Matrix determinant lemma); telescoping gives \(\sum_t\log(1+{\lVert x_t\rVert}^2_{V_{t-1}^{-1}})=\log\tfrac{\det V_T}{\det V_0}\). Use \(\min(1,u)\le2\log(1+u)\) Logarithm bounds, and AM–GM on eigenvalues for \(\det V_T\le(\lambda+TL^2/d)^d\) Spectral theorem for symmetric matrices. The second claim is Cauchy–Schwarz Cauchy–Schwarz inequality.
cards.ex: OFUL regret: \({\mathrm{Reg}}_T\le2\beta_T\sum_t\min(1,{\lVert x_t\rVert}_{V_{t-1}^{-1}})\le2\beta_T\sqrt{2dT\log(1+T/(d\lambda))}={\widetilde{O}}(d\sqrt T)\) with \(\beta_T={\widetilde{O}}(\sqrt d)\) from Self-normalised bound for vector martingales (Abbasi-Yadkori et al.).
cards.use: Linear/generalised linear/kernel bandits, linear MDPs (LSVI-UCB), low-switching algorithms, non-stationary linear bandits.

qz.q: Elliptical potential: \(V_0=\lambda I\), \(V_t=V_{t-1}+x_tx_t^\top\), \({\lVert x_t\rVert}_2\le L\). The lemma bounds \(\sum_t\min(1,{\lVert x_t\rVert}^2_{V_{t-1}^{-1}})\). Which condition lets you drop the \(\min(1,\cdot)\)?
a: The \(x_t\) are i.i.d. rather than adaptive
qz.why: \({\lVert x\rVert}^2_{V_{t-1}^{-1}}\le{\lVert x\rVert}_2^2/\lambda_{\min}(V_{t-1})\le L^2/\lambda\le1\) when \(\lambda\ge L^2\), so the min is inactive. The lemma is deterministic, so i.i.d. sampling does nothing for the size of each term.

qz.q: OFUL's regret is \(2\beta_T\sum_t\min(1,{\lVert x_t\rVert}_{V_{t-1}^{-1}})\), and the elliptical potential bounds the sum by \({\widetilde{O}}(\sqrt{dT})\). The final rate is \({\widetilde{O}}(d\sqrt T)\). Where does the second \(\sqrt d\) come from?
a: The radius \(\beta_T={\widetilde{O}}(\sqrt d)\) of the self-normalised confidence set
The bound \(\det V_T\le(\lambda+TL^2/d)^d\) in the potential
A union bound over the \(K\) actions in each round
Cauchy–Schwarz over the \(T\) rounds of the widths
qz.why: The potential lemma (including the determinant bound and Cauchy–Schwarz) produces the \(\sqrt{dT\log T}\) factor; the confidence radius from Self-normalised bound for vector martingales (Abbasi-Yadkori et al.) contributes another \(\sqrt{d\log T}\). No union bound over actions is used, which is why OFUL works with infinite action sets.

qz.q: Take \(d=1\), \(\lambda=1\) and \(x_t=1\) for every \(t\), so \(V_t=1+t\). What is \({\lVert x_t\rVert}^2_{V_{t-1}^{-1}}\), and how does \(\sum_{t\le T}\) of it grow?
a: \(1/\sqrt t\); the sum grows like \(\sqrt T\)
qz.why: \(V_{t-1}=1+(t-1)=t\), so the term is \(1/t\) and the sum is the harmonic number \(\approx\log T\), matching the lemma's \(2\log(1+T)\). Note \(1/(t-1)\) would be infinite at \(t=1\): the \(\lambda I\) term prevents that.

cards.name: Exponential weights (Hedge) regret bound
cards.lay: Keep a weight for each expert, multiply it by \(e^{-\eta\cdot\text{loss}}\) after each round, and play proportionally to the weights. Against any sequence of bounded losses, you lose at most \(\sqrt{(T/2)\log N}\) compared to the best expert in hindsight.
cards.st: With losses \(\ell_t\in[0,1]^N\) and \(p_t(i)\propto\exp(-\eta\sum_{s<t}\ell_s(i))\): \[ \sum_{t=1}^T{\langle p_t, \ell_t\rangle}-\min_i\sum_{t=1}^T\ell_t(i)\le\frac{\log N}{\eta}+\frac{\eta T}{8}, \] so \(\eta=\sqrt{8\log N/T}\) gives regret \(\le\sqrt{\tfrac{T}{2}\log N}\).
ver: Second-order (local norm) bound: regret \(\le\tfrac{\log N}{\eta}+\eta\sum_t\sum_ip_t(i)\ell_t(i)^2\) for \(\eta\ell\ge-1\) — needed for EXP3 EXP3 & importance-weighted loss estimators.
Anytime: \(\eta_t=\sqrt{\log N/t}\) gives \(O(\sqrt{T\log N})\) without knowing \(T\).

Infinite/continuous experts with prior \(\pi\): regret \(\le\tfrac{{\mathrm{KL}}(\rho\|\pi)}{\eta}+\tfrac{\eta T}{8}\) against any \(\rho\) (PAC-Bayes flavour) Donsker–Varadhan & Gibbs variational principle.
It is OMD/FTRL with negative entropy Online mirror descent (OMD) lemma, Follow-the-regularised-leader (FTRL) regret bound.
cards.det: Potential proof: \(\Phi_t=\tfrac1\eta\log\sum_ie^{-\eta L_t(i)}\). Hoeffding's lemma Hoeffding's lemma gives \(\Phi_{t+1}-\Phi_t\le-{\langle p_t, \ell_t\rangle}+\tfrac{\eta}{8}\); telescope Telescoping sums from \(\Phi_0=\tfrac{\log N}{\eta}\), and use \(\Phi_T\ge-\min_iL_T(i)\) (log-sum-exp sandwich Log-sum-exp (soft-max) sandwich). Rearranging gives the bound.
cards.ex: Per-state Hedge on \(Q\)-values is NPG/policy mirror descent Natural policy gradient & policy mirror descent convergence; in adversarial MDPs with full information, running Hedge in each state with \(Q^{\pi_t}\) losses yields \({\widetilde{O}}(\tfrac{\sqrt{T\log|{\mathcal{A}}|}}{(1-\gamma)^2})\)-type regret.
cards.use: Experts, NPG/PMD, adversarial MDPs, boosting, game solving (no-regret dynamics), EXP3/EXP4.

qz.q: Hedge with losses in \([0,1]^N\) satisfies \({\mathrm{Reg}}_T\le\frac{\log N}{\eta}+\frac{\eta T}{8}\). With the tuned \(\eta=\sqrt{8\log N/T}\) the bound equals
qz.why: Both terms equal \(\sqrt{T\log N/8}\), so their sum is \(2\sqrt{T\log N/8}=\sqrt{T\log N/2}\). \(\sqrt{T\log N/8}\) is just one of the two terms.

qz.q: EXP3 feeds Hedge the estimates \(\hat\ell_t(i)=\ell_t(i){\mathbf{1}}\{A_t=i\}/p_t(i)\). Why can it not use the bound \(\frac{\log N}{\eta}+\frac{\eta T}{8}\) directly?
a: \(\hat\ell_t(i)\) can be as large as \(1/p_t(i)\), so it is not in \([0,1]\)
Hedge needs a full loss vector, which \(\hat\ell_t\) is not
