qz.q: Gradient EM with \(Q(\cdot|\theta^\star)\) \(\lambda\)-strongly concave and \(\mu\)-smooth, \(\lambda=1\), \(\mu=3\), gradient stability \(\gamma=0.2\), step \(\alpha=2/(\mu+\lambda)\). What is the contraction factor?
qz.why: \(1-2(\lambda-\gamma)/(\mu+\lambda)=1-1.6/4=0.6\). Plain gradient descent gives \(1-2\lambda/(\mu+\lambda)=0.5\); the gradient-stability term \(\gamma\) makes it slower. \(\gamma/\lambda=0.2\) is the exact-EM factor.

qz.q: In gradient EM, \(Q(\cdot\mid\theta_t)\) is \(\mu\)-smooth. For which steps \(\alpha\) is \(\theta_{t+1}=\theta_t+\alpha\nabla_1Q(\theta_t|\theta_t)\) guaranteed to be a GEM step (so likelihood does not decrease)?
qz.why: By smoothness, \(Q(\theta_{t+1}|\theta_t)-Q(\theta_t|\theta_t)\ge\alpha(1-\alpha\mu/2){\lVert g\rVert}^2\ge0\) for \(\alpha\le2/\mu\), and GEM monotonicity Monotonicity of EM (and GEM) follows. Large steps can overshoot and decrease \(Q\).

qz.q: Suppose \(Q(\cdot|\theta^\star)\) is perfectly conditioned (\(\mu=\lambda\)) with gradient stability \(\gamma<\lambda\). Compare the contraction factors of gradient EM (\(\alpha=2/(\mu+\lambda)\)) and exact EM (BWY, \(\gamma/\lambda\)).
qz.why: With \(\mu=\lambda\): \(1-2(\lambda-\gamma)/(2\lambda)=\gamma/\lambda\). Gradient EM pays extra only through ill-conditioning (\(\mu>\lambda\)).

cards.name: EM as minorise–maximise and as mirror descent
cards.plain: EM as minorise–maximise and as mirror descent
cards.lay: EM is a special case of MM (minorise–maximise): it maximises a surrogate that touches the objective at the current point and lies below it everywhere. For exponential-family models, EM is exactly mirror descent with the KL/Bregman geometry, which yields non-asymptotic rates without strong concavity.
cards.st: (MM) \(g( heta| heta_t)=Q( heta| heta_t)+H(p_{ heta_t}(\cdot|x))\le\log p_ heta(x)\) with equality at \( heta_t\). (Kunstner, Kumar & Schmidt 2021) If the complete-data model is an exponential family with log-partition \(A\), then EM is mirror descent on \(-\log p_ heta(x)\) with mirror map \(A\) and unit step: \[ abla A( heta_{t+1})= abla A( heta_t)+ abla_ heta\log p_{ heta_t}(x), \] and \(-\log p_ heta(x)\) is \(1\)-smooth relative to \(A\), giving \(O(1/T)\) convergence of a KL-based stationarity measure.
ver: Relative smoothness/strong convexity framework (Bauschke, Bolte & Teboulle 2017; Lu, Freund & Nesterov 2018).
Linear convergence if additionally relatively strongly convex near the optimum.

Connection to RL: policy mirror descent/NPG Natural policy gradient & policy mirror descent convergence and EM-style RL (MPO, REPS) share the same KL-proximal structure Donsker–Varadhan & Gibbs variational principle.
cards.det: In the mean-parameter coordinates \(\nabla A(\theta)\), the M-step sets the expected sufficient statistics to their posterior averages, which is a mirror step. The three-point identity for the Bregman divergence of \(A\) Bregman divergences & the three-point identity then gives the standard mirror-descent descent inequality.
cards.ex: Gaussian mixtures with known covariances: EM's update of mixture weights is exactly entropic mirror descent on the simplex (multiplicative update), like Hedge Exponential weights (Hedge) regret bound.
cards.use: Non-asymptotic EM rates without local strong concavity; unifying EM with policy mirror descent and KL-regularised RL; designing EM-like updates in RL.

qz.q: An MM scheme maximises a surrogate \(g(\theta|\theta_t)\). Suppose \(g(\theta|\theta_t)\le\log p_\theta(x)\) for all \(\theta\), but \(g(\theta_t|\theta_t)<\log p_{\theta_t}(x)\) (not tight). What breaks?
a: Nothing: the lower bound alone gives monotonicity
The surrogate may have no maximiser
The surrogate becomes an upper bound
qz.why: The chain \(\log p_{\theta_{t+1}}\ge g(\theta_{t+1}|\theta_t)\ge g(\theta_t|\theta_t)=\log p_{\theta_t}\) needs tightness in the last step. Without it, the new point only beats \(g(\theta_t|\theta_t)\), which is below the current likelihood.

qz.q: For a complete-data exponential family with log-partition \(A\), Kunstner et al. write EM as mirror descent on \(-\log p_\theta(x)\). With which mirror map and step size?
a: Mirror map \(A\), step size \(1/\mu\) from smoothness
qz.why: \( abla A( heta_{t+1})= abla A( heta_t)+ abla\log p_{ heta_t}(x)\): unit step in mean-parameter space. \(-\log p_ heta(x)\) is \(1\)-smooth relative to \(A\), which is why the step is exactly \(1\).

qz.q: What does the mirror-descent analysis of EM (relative smoothness w.r.t. \(A\)) give that the BWY contraction analysis does not?
a: An \(O(1/T)\) rate for a KL stationarity measure, no strong concavity
Linear convergence to \(\theta^\star\) from any initialisation
Convergence to the global maximum of the likelihood
An \(O(1/\sqrt T)\) rate that needs local strong concavity
qz.why: Relative smoothness alone yields a non-asymptotic \(O(1/T)\) rate on a KL-based stationarity measure, without a basin of strong concavity. Linear rates need relative strong convexity in addition; global optimality is not claimed.

cards.name: Paley–Zygmund inequality (anti-concentration)
cards.lay: The reverse of Markov: a non-negative variable with a decent mean and not-too-large second moment exceeds a fraction of its mean with constant probability. Used to show that “good” events happen often enough (e.g. optimism with constant probability).
cards.st: For \(Z\ge0\) with finite variance and \(\theta\in[0,1]\): \[ \Pr\bigl(Z>\theta\,{\mathbb{E}} Z\bigr)\ge(1-\theta)^2\frac{({\mathbb{E}} Z)^2}{{\mathbb{E}} Z^2}. \]
ver: Second-moment method (\(\theta=0\)): \(\Pr(Z>0)\ge\tfrac{({\mathbb{E}} Z)^2}{{\mathbb{E}} Z^2}\).
Cantelli-improved form: \(\Pr(Z>\theta{\mathbb{E}} Z)\ge\tfrac{(1-\theta)^2({\mathbb{E}} Z)^2}{{\operatorname{Var}} Z+(1-\theta)^2({\mathbb{E}} Z)^2}\).
cards.det: Proof: \({\mathbb{E}} Z\le\theta{\mathbb{E}} Z+{\mathbb{E}}[Z{\mathbf{1}}\{Z>\theta{\mathbb{E}} Z\}]\le\theta{\mathbb{E}} Z+\sqrt{{\mathbb{E}} Z^2\Pr(Z>\theta{\mathbb{E}} Z)}\) by Cauchy–Schwarz Cauchy–Schwarz inequality.
cards.ex: Randomised exploration (RLSVI-type): showing that a randomly perturbed value estimate is optimistic with constant probability can use Paley–Zygmund on the perturbation's projection.
cards.use: Anti-concentration in randomised exploration, lower bounds, random-graph connectivity.

qz.q: \(Z\ge0\) with \({\mathbb{E}} Z=1\) and \({\mathbb{E}} Z^2=3\). What lower bound does Paley–Zygmund give for \(\Pr(Z>\tfrac12)\)?
qz.why: \((1-\theta)^2({\mathbb{E}} Z)^2/{\mathbb{E}} Z^2=\tfrac14\cdot\tfrac13=\tfrac1{12}\) with \(\theta=\tfrac12\). \(\tfrac16\) forgets to square \(1-\theta\); \(\tfrac13\) is the \(\theta=0\) (second-moment method) bound for \(\Pr(Z>0)\).

qz.q: \(Z\ge0\) with \({\mathbb{E}} Z=1\). Which extra assumption guarantees \(\Pr(Z>\tfrac12)\ge c\) for a constant \(c>0\) independent of the distribution?
qz.why: With \({\mathbb{E}} Z^2\le4\), Paley–Zygmund gives \(\Pr(Z>\tfrac12)\ge\tfrac14\cdot\tfrac14=\tfrac1{16}\). Otherwise mass can escape: \(Z=n\) w.p. \(1/n\) (else \(0\), or a smoothed version) has mean \(1\), huge variance and \(\Pr(Z>\tfrac12)\approx1/n\); \({\mathbb{E}}\sqrt Z\le1\) holds automatically by Jensen.

qz.q: Paley–Zygmund lower-bounds \(\Pr(Z>\theta{\mathbb{E}} Z)\) only for \(\theta\in[0,1]\). Why can no such bound hold for \(\theta>1\)?
a: For \(\theta>1\) the right-hand side is negative
For \(\theta>1\) Markov gives a stronger lower bound
For \(\theta>1\) the event has probability one
qz.why: A constant variable satisfies every moment condition yet never exceeds its mean, so no positive lower bound is possible above the mean. The right-hand side \((1-\theta)^2(\cdot)\) is never negative, and Markov only gives upper bounds.

cards.name: Efron–Stein inequality
cards.lay: The variance of any function of independent inputs is at most the sum over coordinates of how much the function changes when that coordinate is resampled. A variance analogue of McDiarmid that needs no boundedness.
cards.st: For independent \(X_1,\dots,X_n\), an independent copy \(X'_i\) of each, and \(Z=f(X_1,\dots,X_n)\), \(Z^{(i)}=f(X_1,..,X'_i,..,X_n)\): \[ {\operatorname{Var}}(Z)\le\frac12\sum_{i=1}^n{\mathbb{E}}\bigl[(Z-Z^{(i)})^2\bigr]. \]
ver: Bounded differences \(|Z-Z^{(i)}|\le c_i\): \({\operatorname{Var}} Z\le\tfrac12\sum c_i^2\).
Self-bounding functions get Bernstein-like concentration (Boucheron–Lugosi–Massart).
cards.det: Proof via the martingale (Doob) decomposition of \(Z-{\mathbb{E}} Z\) and Jensen on each increment.
cards.ex: Variance of the maximum of \(n\) i.i.d. variables or of the value of a randomly perturbed planning problem is controlled by the effect of resampling one input.
cards.use: Variance bounds for complex estimators, stability of learned policies to single-sample changes.

qz.q: \(Z=\tfrac1n\sum_{i=1}^nX_i\) with independent \(X_i\in[0,1]\). What variance bound does the bounded-differences form of Efron–Stein, \({\operatorname{Var}} Z\le\tfrac12\sum_ic_i^2\), give?
qz.why: Resampling one coordinate moves \(Z\) by at most \(c_i=1/n\), so \(\tfrac12\cdot n\cdot n^{-2}=\tfrac1{2n}\). The sharper \(\tfrac1{4n}\) comes from Popoviciu applied to each \(X_i\), not from the bounded-differences form.

qz.q: \(Z=f(X_1,\dots,X_n)\) with independent \(X_i\). Compared with McDiarmid's inequality, what does Efron–Stein provide?
a: A variance bound; its general form needs no bounded differences
A variance bound, but only for identically distributed \(X_i\)
Sub-Gaussian tails under the same bounded differences
qz.why: Efron–Stein bounds \({\operatorname{Var}} Z\) by \(\tfrac12\sum_i{\mathbb{E}}(Z-Z^{(i)})^2\), which can be finite even without a.s. bounded differences; tails then come only via Chebyshev. It still needs independence (not identical distribution); exponential tails are McDiarmid's job McDiarmid's bounded-differences inequality.

qz.q: Let \(Z=\sum_{i=1}^nX_i\) with independent, square-integrable \(X_i\). What does the right-hand side \(\tfrac12\sum_i{\mathbb{E}}[(Z-Z^{(i)})^2]\) of Efron–Stein equal?
qz.why: \(Z-Z^{(i)}=X_i-X_i'\) with \(X_i'\) an independent copy, so \({\mathbb{E}}(X_i-X_i')^2=2{\operatorname{Var}} X_i\) and the \(\tfrac12\) cancels the \(2\): Efron–Stein is an equality for sums. The factor \(\tfrac12\) is exactly what makes it tight here.

cards.name: Hanson–Wright inequality
cards.lay: Quadratic forms \(X^\top AX\) of a vector with independent sub-Gaussian entries concentrate around their mean, with a sub-Gaussian regime governed by the Frobenius norm and a sub-exponential regime governed by the operator norm.
cards.st: For \(X\in{\mathbb{R}}^n\) with independent mean-zero \(K\)-sub-Gaussian coordinates and fixed \(A\): \[ \Pr\bigl(|X^\top AX-{\mathbb{E}} X^\top AX|>t\bigr)\le2\exp\Bigl(-c\min\Bigl\{\frac{t^2}{K^4{\lVert A\rVert}_F^2},\frac{t}{K^2{\lVert A\rVert}_2}\Bigr\}\Bigr). \]
ver: Norm concentration: \(\bigl|{\lVert BX\rVert}_2-{\lVert B\rVert}_F\bigr|\) is \(O(K^2{\lVert B\rVert}_2)\)-sub-Gaussian.
cards.det: Decouple diagonal and off-diagonal parts; off-diagonal via decoupling and Gaussian comparison; diagonal via Bernstein for sub-exponential variables Sub-exponential variables & Bernstein condition.
cards.ex: Concentration of \({\lVert \hat\theta-\theta\rVert}_\Sigma^2\) for least squares with sub-Gaussian noise, a quadratic form in the noise vector.
cards.use: Least-squares error concentration, random features, high-dimensional linear RL analyses.

qz.q: \(X\in{\mathbb{R}}^n\) has independent mean-zero \(K\)-sub-Gaussian coordinates and \(A\) is fixed. For small deviations \(t\), which term governs the Hanson–Wright tail of \(X^\top AX-{\mathbb{E}} X^\top AX\)?
qz.why: For small \(t\) the quadratic term in the \(\min\) is the smaller one, giving a sub-Gaussian tail with scale \(K^2{\lVert A\rVert}_F\). The operator norm enters only the large-\(t\), sub-exponential regime \(t/(K^2{\lVert A\rVert}_2)\).

qz.q: \(X\sim{\mathcal{N}}(0,I_n)\). Applying Hanson–Wright with \(A=I_n\), what is the typical size of \(\bigl|{\lVert X\rVert}_2^2-n\bigr|\)?
qz.why: \({\lVert I_n\rVert}_F=\sqrt n\) and \({\lVert I_n\rVert}_2=1\), so fluctuations are of order \(\sqrt n\) (indeed \({\operatorname{Var}}{\lVert X\rVert}^2=2n\)). \(\Theta(1)\) is the scale of \({\lVert X\rVert}_2-\sqrt n\), not of the squared norm.

qz.q: \(X\sim{\mathcal{N}}(0,I_n)\). By the norm-concentration version (with \(B=I_n\)), on what scale does \({\lVert X\rVert}_2-\sqrt n\) fluctuate as \(n\) grows?
qz.why: \(\bigl|{\lVert BX\rVert}_2-{\lVert B\rVert}_F\bigr|\) is sub-Gaussian with parameter \(O({\lVert B\rVert}_2)=O(1)\): the norm sits in a constant-width shell around \(\sqrt n\). Since \({\lVert X\rVert}^2-n\approx2\sqrt n({\lVert X\rVert}-\sqrt n)\), this matches the \(\sqrt n\) fluctuations of \({\lVert X\rVert}^2\).

cards.name: Talagrand's convex-distance inequality
cards.lay: In a product space, the probability of being far (in a special “convex distance”) from a set of probability at least \(\tfrac12\) is exponentially small. Gives dimension-free concentration of convex Lipschitz functions of bounded independent variables.
cards.st: For a product probability \(P\) on \(\Omega^n\) and measurable \(A\): \[ P(A)\,\Pr\bigl(d_T(X,A)\ge t\bigr)\le e^{-t^2/4}, \] where \(d_T\) is Talagrand's convex distance. Consequence: for convex \(1\)-Lipschitz \(f:[0,1]^n\to{\mathbb{R}}\), \(\Pr(|f(X)-\mathrm{Med}f(X)|\ge t)\le4e^{-t^2/4}\).
ver: Talagrand's inequality for suprema of empirical processes (Bousquet's form): Bernstein-type concentration of \(\sup_f\sum_i(f(X_i)-{\mathbb{E}} f)\) with variance \(\sigma^2\).
cards.det: Bousquet's version underlies local Rademacher complexity and fast-rate analyses for regression-based RL (e.g. sharp FQI rates).
cards.ex: Largest eigenvalue of a random matrix with bounded independent entries concentrates around its median with \(O(1)\) fluctuations.
cards.use: Fast rates via localisation, random matrix concentration, combinatorial optimisation.

qz.q: \(f:[0,1]^n\to{\mathbb{R}}\) is convex and \(1\)-Lipschitz (Euclidean), and \(X\) has independent coordinates. On what scale does \(f(X)\) fluctuate around its median?
qz.why: Talagrand gives \(\Pr(|f(X)-\mathrm{Med}f|\ge t)\le4e^{-t^2/4}\): dimension-free. McDiarmid with \(c_i=1\) only gives \(e^{-2t^2/n}\), i.e. scale \(\sqrt n\) — valid but loose here.

qz.q: For \(1\)-Lipschitz \(f:[0,1]^n\to{\mathbb{R}}\) and arbitrary independent \(X_i\in[0,1]\) (e.g. Bernoulli), which hypothesis of the dimension-free consequence cannot be dropped?
a: Continuity of the law of each \(X_i\)
qz.why: The convex-distance inequality holds for any product measure, so identical or continuous laws are not needed and Lipschitz suffices without smoothness. Without convexity it fails: on \(\{0,1\}^n\) the Euclidean distance to \(\{\sum_ix_i\le n/2\}\) is \(1\)-Lipschitz but fluctuates like \(n^{1/4}\).

qz.q: In a product space, \(A\) has \(P(A)=\tfrac12\). What does \(P(A)\Pr(d_T(X,A)\ge t)\le e^{-t^2/4}\) give at \(t=4\)?
qz.why: \(e^{-16/4}=e^{-4}\), then divide by \(P(A)=\tfrac12\). Multiplying by \(P(A)\) instead of dividing gives the wrong \(\tfrac12e^{-4}\).

cards.name: Slepian / Sudakov–Fernique comparison & Sudakov minoration
cards.lay: Compare two Gaussian processes: if one has larger increments, its expected supremum is larger. Combined with Sudakov's minoration, this gives lower bounds on expected maxima — matching Dudley's upper bound up to logs.
cards.st: (Sudakov–Fernique) For centred Gaussian processes \(X,Y\) on \(T\) with \({\mathbb{E}}(X_s-X_t)^2\le{\mathbb{E}}(Y_s-Y_t)^2\) for all \(s,t\): \({\mathbb{E}}\sup_tX_t\le{\mathbb{E}}\sup_tY_t\). (Sudakov minoration) For all \({\varepsilon}>0\): \[ {\mathbb{E}}\sup_{t\in T}X_t\ge c\,{\varepsilon}\sqrt{\log N({\varepsilon},T,d_X)},\quad d_X(s,t)=\sqrt{{\mathbb{E}}(X_s-X_t)^2}. \]
ver: Slepian's lemma (equal variances, ordered covariances) compares probabilities of suprema.
Gordon's min–max comparison (behind Gaussian width bounds).
cards.det: Proof by Gaussian interpolation and Stein's lemma Stein's lemma (Gaussian integration by parts).
cards.ex: Lower bound \({\mathbb{E}}\max_{i\le n}Z_i\ge c\sqrt{\log n}\) for i.i.d. Gaussians follows from Sudakov with \({\varepsilon}=\sqrt2\).
cards.use: Lower bounds on suprema, Gaussian bandit lower bounds, compressed sensing-style arguments.

qz.q: \(X,Y\) are centred Gaussian processes on \(T\) with \({\mathbb{E}}(X_s-X_t)^2\le{\mathbb{E}}(Y_s-Y_t)^2\) for all \(s,t\) (variances not assumed equal). What follows from Sudakov–Fernique?
qz.why: Larger increments mean a larger expected supremum. Only expectations compare: with \(T\) a single point, \(X_t\sim{\mathcal{N}}(0,100)\) and \(Y_t\sim{\mathcal{N}}(0,1)\) satisfy the hypothesis but \(X\) has heavier tails and larger variance; tail comparison needs Slepian's equal-variance setting.

qz.q: \(X_1,\dots,X_n\) are jointly Gaussian with \({\mathbb{E}} X_i=0\), \({\operatorname{Var}} X_i=1\) and all correlations \(\ge0\); \(Z_1,\dots,Z_n\) are i.i.d. \({\mathcal{N}}(0,1)\). How do \({\mathbb{E}}\max_iX_i\) and \({\mathbb{E}}\max_iZ_i\) compare?
a: They are equal, since the marginals agree
qz.why: \({\mathbb{E}}(X_i-X_j)^2=2-2\rho_{ij}\le2={\mathbb{E}}(Z_i-Z_j)^2\), so Sudakov–Fernique gives \(\le\). Intuitively, positive correlation makes the coordinates move together, so the maximum gains less.

qz.q: \(X_t=\langle g,t\rangle\) for \(g\sim{\mathcal{N}}(0,I_d)\) and \(t\in T\subset{\mathbb{R}}^d\). Which metric \(d_X\) enters Sudakov's minoration for this process?
qz.why: \(d_X(s,t)=\sqrt{{\mathbb{E}}\langle g,s-t\rangle^2}={\lVert s-t\rVert}_2\), so Sudakov bounds the Gaussian width of \(T\) below by \(c{\varepsilon}\sqrt{\log N({\varepsilon},T,{\lVert \cdot\rVert}_2)}\). The canonical metric is a standard deviation, not a variance.

cards.name: Stein's lemma (Gaussian integration by parts)
cards.lay: For a Gaussian \(Z\), \({\mathbb{E}}[Zg(Z)]={\mathbb{E}}[g'(Z)]\). Lets you move derivatives onto test functions, compute gradients of Gaussian expectations, and characterise normality.
cards.st: If \(Z\sim{\mathcal{N}}(0,\sigma^2)\) and \(g\) is absolutely continuous with \({\mathbb{E}}|g'(Z)|<\infty\): \[ {\mathbb{E}}[Zg(Z)]=\sigma^2{\mathbb{E}}[g'(Z)]. \] Multivariate: for \(X\sim{\mathcal{N}}(\mu,\Sigma)\), \({\mathbb{E}}[(X-\mu)g(X)]=\Sigma\,{\mathbb{E}}[\nabla g(X)]\).
ver: Gaussian smoothing gradients: \(\nabla_\mu{\mathbb{E}}_{{\mathcal{N}}(\mu,\sigma^2I)}f(X)=\tfrac{1}{\sigma^2}{\mathbb{E}}[(X-\mu)f(X)]\) — the evolution-strategies / zeroth-order gradient estimator.
Second order (Price's theorem): \(\nabla^2_\mu{\mathbb{E}} f={\mathbb{E}}\nabla^2f\).
cards.det: Proof: integration by parts using \(\phi'(z)=-z\phi(z)/\sigma^2\). It is the Gaussian special case of the log-derivative trick Log-derivative (score-function) trick & differentiating under the integral.
cards.ex: Evolution strategies for policy search: \(\nabla_\theta{\mathbb{E}}_{{\varepsilon}}[J(\theta+\sigma{\varepsilon})]=\tfrac1\sigma{\mathbb{E}}[{\varepsilon} J(\theta+\sigma{\varepsilon})]\).
cards.use: Zeroth-order policy optimisation (ES, random search for LQR), Gaussian comparison proofs, SURE.

qz.q: \(Z\sim{\mathcal{N}}(0,\sigma^2)\). Applying Stein's lemma \({\mathbb{E}}[Zg(Z)]=\sigma^2{\mathbb{E}}[g'(Z)]\) with \(g(z)=z^3\), what is \({\mathbb{E}} Z^4\)?
qz.why: \({\mathbb{E}} Z^4=\sigma^2{\mathbb{E}}[3Z^2]=3\sigma^4\). \(\sigma^4\) would be \(({\mathbb{E}} Z^2)^2\), which ignores the Gaussian's kurtosis.

qz.q: Evolution strategies: \({\varepsilon}\sim{\mathcal{N}}(0,I)\) and \(J_\sigma(\theta)={\mathbb{E}}[J(\theta+\sigma{\varepsilon})]\). Which is an unbiased estimator of \(\nabla_\theta J_\sigma(\theta)\) from one sample?
qz.why: With \(X=\theta+\sigma{\varepsilon}\), the smoothing gradient is \(\tfrac1{\sigma^2}{\mathbb{E}}[(X-\theta)J(X)]=\tfrac1{\sigma^2}{\mathbb{E}}[\sigma{\varepsilon} J]=\tfrac1\sigma{\mathbb{E}}[{\varepsilon} J]\). The \(1/\sigma^2\) version applies to \(X-\theta\), not to the standardised \({\varepsilon}\).

qz.q: \(Z\) is Rademacher (\(\pm1\) w.p. \(\tfrac12\)): mean \(0\), variance \(1\). With \(g(z)=z^3\), what are \({\mathbb{E}}[Zg(Z)]\) and \({\mathbb{E}}[g'(Z)]\)?
a: \(1\) and \(3\): the identity fails, as it characterises \({\mathcal{N}}(0,1)\)
\(3\) and \(3\): it holds for every mean-\(0\), variance-\(1\) law
\(1\) and \(1\): it holds for every symmetric law
\(3\) and \(1\): only the multivariate form can fail
qz.why: \({\mathbb{E}} Z^4=1\) but \({\mathbb{E}}[3Z^2]=3\). Matching the first two moments guarantees the identity only for linear \(g\); holding for all \(g\) forces \(Z\sim{\mathcal{N}}(0,1)\) (Stein's characterisation).

cards.name: Kantorovich–Rubinstein duality (Wasserstein-1)
cards.lay: The Wasserstein-1 distance (cheapest cost of moving one distribution's mass onto another) equals the largest difference in expectations over all 1-Lipschitz functions. Lipschitz value functions therefore change by at most \(L\cdot W_1\) when the next-state distribution moves.
cards.st: For probability measures \(P,Q\) with finite first moments on a metric space: \[ W_1(P,Q)=\inf_{\pi\in\Pi(P,Q)}{\mathbb{E}}_{(X,Y)\sim\pi}d(X,Y)=\sup_{{\lVert f\rVert}_{\mathrm{Lip}}\le1}\bigl({\mathbb{E}}_Pf-{\mathbb{E}}_Qf\bigr). \]
ver: Lipschitz MDPs: if \(W_1(P(\cdot|s,a),P(\cdot|s',a'))\le L_P d((s,a),(s',a'))\) and rewards are \(L_r\)-Lipschitz, \(Q^\star\) is \(\tfrac{L_r}{1-\gamma L_P}\)-Lipschitz when \(\gamma L_P<1\).
On \({\mathbb{R}}\): \(W_1(P,Q)=\int|F_P-F_Q|\) (CDF difference) Dvoretzky–Kiefer–Wolfowitz inequality. TV is \(W_1\) under the discrete metric.
Bisimulation metrics are fixed points of a \(W_1\)-based operator.
cards.det: Simulation-lemma analogue in continuous spaces: \(|(P-\widehat P)V|\le{\lVert V\rVert}_{\mathrm{Lip}}W_1(P,\widehat P)\), replacing Hölder/TV when \(V\) is Lipschitz but the distributions are mutually singular (e.g. deterministic dynamics).
cards.ex: Deterministic dynamics \(s'=f(s,a)\) vs. learned \(\hat f\): \(W_1(\delta_{f(s,a)},\delta_{\hat f(s,a)})={\lVert f-\hat f\rVert}\), finite even though TV \(=1\).
cards.use: Model-based RL in continuous spaces, Lipschitz MDP theory, bisimulation metrics, distributional RL (Wasserstein contraction of the distributional Bellman operator).

qz.q: True dynamics \(s'=f(s,a)\) and learned \(s'=\hat f(s,a)\) are deterministic with \({\lVert f(s,a)-\hat f(s,a)\rVert}=0.01\). What are the total variation and \(W_1\) distances between the two next-state distributions?
qz.why: Distinct point masses are mutually singular, so \({\mathrm{TV}}=1\) however close they are, while \(W_1(\delta_x,\delta_y)={\lVert x-y\rVert}\). Hence for Lipschitz \(V\) the simulation-lemma error \({\lVert V\rVert}_{\mathrm{Lip}}W_1\) is small even though a TV-based bound is vacuous.

qz.q: Lipschitz MDP with \(L_r=1\), \(L_P=1.5\) (in \(W_1\)) and \(\gamma=0.5\). What Lipschitz constant does the card's result give for \(Q^\star\)?
qz.why: \(L_r/(1-\gamma L_P)=1/(1-0.75)=4\), valid since \(\gamma L_P=0.75<1\). \(2=L_r/(1-\gamma)\) ignores how much the dynamics stretch distances.

qz.q: On \({\mathbb{R}}\), what is \(W_1\bigl(\mathrm{Unif}[0,1],\mathrm{Unif}[0,2]\bigr)\)?
qz.why: Coupling \(X\mapsto2X\) costs \({\mathbb{E}}|X|=\tfrac12\), and the \(1\)-Lipschitz test \(f(x)=x\) gives \({\mathbb{E}}_Qf-{\mathbb{E}}_Pf=1-\tfrac12=\tfrac12\), so by duality both bounds meet. Equivalently \(\int|F_P-F_Q|=\tfrac14+\tfrac14\).

cards.name: Johnson–Lindenstrauss lemma
cards.lay: Any \(n\) points in high dimension can be mapped to \(O(\log n/{\varepsilon}^2)\) dimensions by a random linear map while preserving all pairwise distances up to \(1\pm{\varepsilon}\). Justifies random projections of features.
cards.st: For \(0<{\varepsilon}<1\) and \(n\) points in \({\mathbb{R}}^D\), if \(m\ge C{\varepsilon}^{-2}\log n\), a random Gaussian matrix \(G\in{\mathbb{R}}^{m\times D}\) scaled by \(1/\sqrt m\) satisfies, with high probability, for all pairs: \[ (1-{\varepsilon}){\lVert x_i-x_j\rVert}^2\le{\lVert Gx_i/\sqrt m-Gx_j/\sqrt m\rVert}^2\le(1+{\varepsilon}){\lVert x_i-x_j\rVert}^2. \]
ver: Sparse / fast JL transforms; subspace embeddings preserving all vectors of a \(d\)-dimensional subspace with \(m=O(d/{\varepsilon}^2)\).
cards.det: For a fixed vector, \({\lVert Gx\rVert}^2/{\lVert x\rVert}^2\) is a scaled \(\chi^2_m\) variable concentrating at rate \(e^{-cm{\varepsilon}^2}\) Sub-exponential variables & Bernstein condition; union bound over \(\binom n2\) pairs Union bound (Boole's inequality).
cards.ex: Compressing \(D=10^6\) sparse state features to \(m\approx10^3\) dimensions for linear value approximation while keeping inner products within \(\pm0.1\).
cards.use: Random-projection features in linear RL, sketching for large-scale LSTD, dimension reduction arguments.

qz.q: Johnson–Lindenstrauss needs \(m\ge C{\varepsilon}^{-2}\log n\). If you halve \({\varepsilon}\) and square the number of points (\(n\to n^2\)), by what factor does the required \(m\) grow?
qz.why: Halving \({\varepsilon}\) multiplies \({\varepsilon}^{-2}\) by \(4\); \(\log(n^2)=2\log n\) doubles the rest, so \(4\cdot2=8\). \(16\) would treat \(\log n\) as if it scaled like \(n\).

qz.q: How does the JL target dimension \(m\) depend on the ambient dimension \(D\) of the \(n\) points?
qz.why: For each fixed difference vector, \({\lVert Gx\rVert}^2/{\lVert x\rVert}^2\) is a scaled \(\chi^2_m\) variable whatever \(D\) is, and the union bound is over the \(\binom n2\) pairs only Union bound (Boole's inequality). So \(m=O({\varepsilon}^{-2}\log n)\) regardless of \(D\).

qz.q: You want a random linear map that preserves the norms of all vectors in a fixed \(d\)-dimensional subspace of \({\mathbb{R}}^D\) up to \(1\pm{\varepsilon}\). Which target dimension suffices?
qz.why: A net argument over the unit sphere of the subspace (size \(e^{O(d)}\)) plus JL gives \(m=O(d/{\varepsilon}^2)\). With \(m<d\) some subspace vector is mapped to \(0\), so \(\log d\) is impossible; \(m=d\) gives a square Gaussian matrix whose singular values are not all within \(1\pm{\varepsilon}\).

cards.name: Brouwer & Kakutani fixed-point theorems
cards.lay: A continuous map from a compact convex set to itself always has a fixed point (Brouwer); set-valued versions (Kakutani) give existence of Nash equilibria. Unlike Banach, no contraction is needed — but there is no algorithm or rate either.
cards.st: (Brouwer) Every continuous \(f:K\to K\) on a nonempty compact convex \(K\subset{\mathbb{R}}^d\) has a fixed point. (Kakutani) Every upper hemicontinuous correspondence \(F:K\rightrightarrows K\) with nonempty convex closed values has \(x\in F(x)\).
ver: Nash's theorem: every finite game has a mixed-strategy equilibrium (via Kakutani on best responses).
Stationary Markov perfect equilibria exist in discounted stochastic games with finite states/actions (Fink 1964).
Schauder: infinite-dimensional (compact convex subsets of Banach spaces).
cards.det: Existence only: computing Brouwer/Nash fixed points is PPAD-hard in general, in contrast to the efficiently computable Banach fixed points Banach fixed-point theorem (contraction mapping).
cards.ex: General-sum Markov games: existence of stationary Nash equilibria is a Kakutani argument, even though learning them is computationally hard.
cards.use: Existence of equilibria in multi-agent RL, mean-field games, existence of solutions to non-contractive equations.

qz.q: \(f:K\to K\) is continuous on a nonempty compact convex \(K\subset{\mathbb{R}}^d\), but not a contraction. What is guaranteed?
a: A fixed point exists; it may not be unique
A fixed point exists, and \(x_{k+1}=f(x_k)\) converges to it
Nothing: without contraction there may be no fixed point
qz.why: Brouwer gives existence only; e.g. the identity has every point fixed, and \(x\mapsto1-x\) on \([0,1]\) has a fixed point that iteration never reaches from \(x_0\neq\tfrac12\). Uniqueness and convergence of iteration are what Banach's contraction adds Banach fixed-point theorem (contraction mapping).

qz.q: Which continuous self-map has no fixed point, showing that a hypothesis of Brouwer's theorem is essential?
a: Rotation by \(\pi/2\) of the unit circle \(S^1\)
Rotation by \(\pi/2\) of the closed unit disc
qz.why: The circle is compact but not convex, and a rotation moves every point. The disc rotation fixes the centre, \(x^2\) fixes \(0\) and \(1\), and \(1-x\) fixes \(\tfrac12\).

qz.q: Finite discounted general-sum Markov games. Which statement is correct?
a: Stationary Nash equilibria exist, but finding one is PPAD-hard in general
A pure stationary Nash equilibrium always exists
Value iteration on the joint Bellman operator converges to a Nash equilibrium
Nash equilibria may fail to exist in stationary strategies
qz.why: Existence is a Kakutani fixed-point argument (Fink 1964), but already two-player normal-form games make computing Nash PPAD-hard. Matching pennies has no pure equilibrium, and there is no contraction to iterate in the general-sum case.

cards.name: Doeblin / minorisation condition & uniform ergodicity
cards.lay: If, from every state, the chain lands in a common distribution with probability at least \(\alpha\) after \(m\) steps, then it forgets its start geometrically fast: the distance to stationarity shrinks by \((1-\alpha)\) every \(m\) steps. Works on general (continuous) state spaces.
cards.st: If \(P^m(x,\cdot)\ge\alpha\,\nu(\cdot)\) for all \(x\) (some probability \(\nu\), \(\alpha>0\)), then \(P\) has a unique stationary \(\mu\) and for all \(x\), \(t\): \[ {\mathrm{TV}}\bigl(P^t(x,\cdot),\mu\bigr)\le(1-\alpha)^{\lfloor t/m\rfloor}. \]
ver: Dobrushin coefficient form: \(\delta(P^m)\le1-\alpha\) Mixing time & geometric ergodicity.
Drift + local minorisation (Harris' theorem; Meyn–Tweedie) for geometric ergodicity on non-compact spaces.
cards.det: Coupling proof Coupling inequality: every \(m\) steps, both copies can jump to a common draw from \(\nu\) with probability \(\alpha\); once coupled they stay together.
cards.ex: Any MDP with a “reset” action taken with probability \(\ge\alpha\) (or discounted MDPs viewed as chains restarting with probability \(1-\gamma\)) satisfies Doeblin with \(m=1\).
cards.use: Ergodicity assumptions in average-reward and continuous-state RL, mixing-time bounds, convergence of policy evaluation from trajectories.

qz.q: A chain satisfies \(P^{10}(x,\cdot)\ge\tfrac12\nu(\cdot)\) for all \(x\). What is the smallest \(t\) for which the Doeblin bound guarantees \({\mathrm{TV}}(P^t(x,\cdot),\mu)\le2^{-10}\)?
qz.why: The bound is \((1-\alpha)^{\lfloor t/m\rfloor}=2^{-\lfloor t/10\rfloor}\), which is \(\le2^{-10}\) once \(\lfloor t/10\rfloor\ge10\). \(t=10\) forgets that contraction happens only once every \(m=10\) steps.

qz.q: A chain on a general space moves by \(P_\gamma(x,\cdot)=\gamma P(x,\cdot)+(1-\gamma)\rho(\cdot)\) for a fixed distribution \(\rho\). What does Doeblin give, with no assumption on \(P\)?
qz.why: \(P_\gamma(x,\cdot)\ge(1-\gamma)\rho(\cdot)\) for every \(x\), a one-step minorisation with \(\nu=\rho\), so \({\mathrm{TV}}(P_\gamma^t(x,\cdot),\mu)\le\gamma^t\). The restart alone makes the chain uniformly ergodic, whatever \(P\) is.

qz.q: The chain on \(\{1,2\}\) with \(P(1,2)=P(2,1)=1\) has the uniform stationary distribution. Why does no Doeblin condition hold for it?
a: \(P^m(1,\cdot)\), \(P^m(2,\cdot)\) are disjoint point masses for all \(m\)
Minorisation fails at \(m=1\) but holds at \(m=2\)
Doeblin conditions require a continuous state space
qz.why: \(P^m\) is either the swap or the identity, so the rows never share mass and no \(\alpha\nu\) fits under both; correspondingly \(P^t(1,\cdot)\) never converges. A stationary distribution exists (uniform), and \(P^2=I\) has disjoint rows too.

cards.name: Davis–Kahan \(\sin\Theta\) theorem
cards.lay: Eigenvectors are stable under perturbation as long as the corresponding eigenvalue is well separated from the rest: the rotation angle is at most (perturbation size)/(eigengap).
cards.st: Let \(A\) and \(\widehat A=A+E\) be symmetric, \(u\) and \(\hat u\) unit eigenvectors for the \(i\)-th eigenvalue, and \(\delta=\min_{j\ne i}|\lambda_i(A)-\lambda_j(A)|\). Then \[ \sin\angle(u,\hat u)\le\frac{2{\lVert E\rVert}_2}{\delta}. \]
ver: Subspace version: \({\lVert \sin\Theta(U,\widehat U)\rVert}_F\le\tfrac{2\sqrt k{\lVert E\rVert}_2}{\delta}\) (Yu, Wang & Samworth 2015 variant).
Wedin's theorem for singular subspaces of non-symmetric matrices.
cards.det: Combine with matrix concentration Matrix Bernstein / matrix Chernoff (Tropp) to show empirical eigenvectors (features, spectral embeddings) converge at rate \({\lVert E\rVert}/\delta\).
cards.ex: Spectral learning of latent-state models (HMMs, POMDPs, latent MDPs): recovering the latent subspace from empirical moment matrices — an alternative to EM with global guarantees.
cards.use: Spectral methods for latent-variable RL, representation learning (proto-value functions, Laplacian features), PCA-based feature analyses.

qz.q: Symmetric \(A\), perturbation \(E\) with \({\lVert E\rVert}_2=0.05\), eigengap \(\delta=0.5\) around the \(i\)-th eigenvalue. What bound does Davis–Kahan (as stated, with the factor \(2\)) give on \(\sin\angle(u,\hat u)\)?
qz.why: \(2{\lVert E\rVert}_2/\delta=2\cdot0.05/0.5=0.2\). \(0.1\) drops the factor \(2\) of this version; \(0.025\) multiplies by the gap instead of dividing.

qz.q: \(A={\operatorname{diag}}(1,1,0)\) and \(E\) is a tiny symmetric perturbation. What can be said about a top unit eigenvector \(\hat u\) of \(A+E\)?
a: Its direction within \(\mathrm{span}(e_1,e_2)\) is arbitrary; it only stays close to that plane
Its angle to \(e_1\) is at most \(2{\lVert E\rVert}_2\), as the gap to \(0\) is \(1\)
It equals \(e_1\) up to \(O({\lVert E\rVert}_2^2)\), since \(E\) is tiny
It can point anywhere in \({\mathbb{R}}^3\), as the gap is zero
qz.why: The top eigenvalue is repeated, so the gap for an individual eigenvector is \(0\) and a tiny \(E\) can select any direction in the eigenspace. The subspace version applies with gap \(1\) to the 2-dimensional space, so \(\hat u\) stays close to that plane, not anywhere in \({\mathbb{R}}^3\).

qz.q: An empirical covariance satisfies \({\lVert \widehat\Sigma-\Sigma\rVert}_2\lesssim\sqrt{d/n}\), and the target eigenvalue of \(\Sigma\) has gap \(\delta\). How fast does the angle to the true eigenvector shrink?
qz.why: Davis–Kahan is linear in \({\lVert E\rVert}_2/\delta\), so it inherits the \(\sqrt{d/n}\) rate of matrix concentration Matrix Bernstein / matrix Chernoff (Tropp). A smaller gap hurts (divides), but only to the first power.
